pearls: Women are at high risk for urinary tract infections due to a shorter urethra that is close to the anus and vaginal introitus, which allows enteric pathogens to colonize the vagina and ascend to the bladder.
Suprapubic tenderness in female. Patient need not have fever.
E. coli most common cause. HY for USMLE you know fimbriae and pilus proteins facilitate E. coli’s attachment to urothelium.

topics.title: Acute pyelonephritis
topics.summary: Both upper (eg, pyelonephritis) and lower (eg, cystitis) urinary tract infections (UTIs) can show microscopic hemat…
pearls: Both upper (eg, pyelonephritis) and lower (eg, cystitis) urinary tract infections (UTIs) can show microscopic hematuria, pyuria, and bacteriuria on urinalysis with microscopy.

Acute pyelonephritis typically presents with a fever, chills, myalgias, and systemic symptoms such as nausea and vomiting, most commonly in a female patient following symptoms of a lower urinary tract infection.
Infection of the kidney. “Pyelo” means kidney.

topics.title: Chronic pyelonephritis
topics.summary: Pyelonephritis results from retrograde flow of bacteria in the bladder into the ureter, where they can then ascend …
pearls: Pyelonephritis results from retrograde flow of bacteria in the bladder into the ureter, where they can then ascend unimpeded to the kidney.
Due to recurrent acute pyelonephritis.
Almost always pediatric, where they give a 4-year-old who has a small, shrunken kidney with tubular atrophy and blunting and scarring of the renal calyces.

topics.title: Acute kidney injury
topics.summary: This patient developed reduced renal function (ie, elevated creatinine) following hospitalization for acute pyelone…
pearls: This patient developed reduced renal function (ie, elevated creatinine) following hospitalization for acute pyelonephritis.
Compensatory mechanisms for hypovolemia include activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and increased antidiuretic hormone release.

topics.title: Acute interstitial nephritis
topics.summary: Fever, maculopapular rash, and acute renal failure occurring 1-3 weeks after beginning a new medication (eg, antibi…
pearls: Fever, maculopapular rash, and acute renal failure occurring 1-3 weeks after beginning a new medication (eg, antibiotics, proton pump inhibitors) is highly suggestive of acute interstitial nephritis.

Acute interstitial nephritis is a common cause of renal dysfunction; up to 75% of cases are due to medications including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, antibiotics, diuretics, and proton pump inhibitors
Exceedingly HY renal condition often confused with ATN.

topics.title: Chronic interstitial nephritis
topics.summary: Analgesic nephropathy is a form of chronic kidney disease caused by prolonged, heavy intake of nonsteroidal anti-in…
pearls: Analgesic nephropathy is a form of chronic kidney disease caused by prolonged, heavy intake of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and/or acetaminophen.
Grossly, the kidneys appear shrunken with irregular contours and distortion of the caliceal architecture.

topics.summary: Renal papillary necrosis classically presents with gross hematuria, acute flank pain, and passage of tissue fragmen…
pearls: Renal papillary necrosis classically presents with gross hematuria, acute flank pain, and passage of tissue fragments (clots) in urine.

Renal papillae = parts of kidney where the collecting ducts meet the ureters.

pearls: During the recovery stage, glomerular filtration rate improves prior to restoration of renal tubular resorptive capacity, so transient polyuria and electrolyte wasting (eg, hypokalemia) can occur.
Loss of epithelial cell polarity is an early change that occurs in renal tubular cells in response to ischemia (ie, acute tubular necrosis).
Sloughing of PCT tubular epithelial cells due to chemical or ischemic insult.

topics.title: Rhabdomyolysis
topics.summary: Rhabdomyolysis is characterized by the release of intracellular muscle contents (eg, myoglobin, electrolytes) due t…
pearls: Rhabdomyolysis is characterized by the release of intracellular muscle contents (eg, myoglobin, electrolytes) due to myocyte injury; it is common with crush injuries, seizures, or drug use (eg, statins).
Rhabdomyolysis usually presents with myalgia, proximal muscle weakness, and dark urine (myoglobinuria) in the setting of trauma, sepsis, or overexertion.
Myoglobin is nephrotoxic. Big risk factors are alcoholism, falls, intense training (e.g., marathon), McCardle syndrome, statins/fibrates.

pearls: This patient has advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD). CKD can cause hyperphosphatemia due to the impaired ability of the kidneys to excrete phosphorus (particularly when GFR is <20 mL/min/1.73 m2).
Chronic kidney disease and a gradual decline in kidney function can lead to uremia. Uremia can present with nonspecific symptoms including nausea, vomiting, and pruritus.

topics.title: Vascular calcification

Vascular calcifications occur more commonly in patients with chronic kidney disease due to electrolyte abnormalities (eg, hyperphosphatemia, hypercalcemia) and chronic inflammation (secondary to atherosclerosis and/or uremia).

topics.title: Renal osteodystrophy

pearls: This patient's presentation is consistent with metabolic bone disease due to chronic kidney disease (CKD).

topics.title: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)

pearls: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), like many autosomal dominant diseases , manifests later in life (eg, age 40-50).

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease; chromosome 16.

topics.title: Renovascular disease
topics.summary: Fibromuscular dysplasia is characterized by abnormal tissue growth within arterial walls, resulting in stenotic and…
pearls: Fibromuscular dysplasia is characterized by abnormal tissue growth within arterial walls, resulting in stenotic and tortuous arteries that can cause tissue ischemia and are prone to aneurysm formation.
Fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal artery is the most common cause of renal artery stenosis in younger and middle-aged women.

topics.title: Renal infarction

pearls: This patient with flank pain, hematuria, and a wedge-shaped kidney lesion on CT scan likely has a renal infarction, which results from interruption of the normal blood supply to the kidney.

This patient with flank pain, low-grade fever, and hematuria has a renal infarction. Renal infarctions are most commonly caused by cardioembolic disease (ie, originating from the left atrium or ventricle).

topics.title: Renal cell carcinoma
topics.summary: The most common renal malignancy is clear cell carcinoma, which arises from renal proximal tubular cells. Rounded o…
pearls: The most common renal malignancy is clear cell carcinoma, which arises from renal proximal tubular cells. Rounded or polygonal cells with abundant clear cytoplasm are seen on light microscopy.
Risk factors include smoking, toxin exposure, and certain hereditary disorders (eg, von Hippel-Lindau syndrome).
Aka “clear cell carcinoma”; this is most common variant of RCC.

pearls: This patient has intermittent, painless hematuria. His positive urine cytology and negative imaging of the upper urinary tract suggest a urothelial (transitional cell) cancer in the bladder.

NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis → ↓ dilation of afferent arterioles → ↓ renal blood flow.
NSAIDs don’t actively constrict the afferent arterioles. This is incorrect wording. They just merely ↓ vasodilation / ↓ diameter of the afferent arterioles.

topics.title: Pre-, intra-, and post-renal azotemias
topics.summary: BUN/Cr = Blood urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio.
pearls: BUN/Cr = Blood urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio.
FENa = fractional excretion of sodium (i.e., amount of sodium in the urine).
There’s no “normal” range you should be looking for here for either of these.

topics.title: Other renal conditions associated with ischemia
topics.summary: Diffuse cortical necrosis is a term thrown around sometimes and causes confusion for students. I don’t think I’ve e…
pearls: Diffuse cortical necrosis is a term thrown around sometimes and causes confusion for students. I don’t think I’ve ever seen USMLE assess this. I’ve only seen it show up rarely as an incorrect answer choice.
DCN is simply considered an extension of ischemic ATN, where DCN can occur in severe cases of ischemia (e.g., obstetric hemorrhages).
You can be aware it exists, but don’t worry about it for USMLE.

topics.title: Renovascular hypertension
topics.summary: Narrowing of one or both renal arteries due to atherosclerosis that causes renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RA…
pearls: Narrowing of one or both renal arteries due to atherosclerosis that causes renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and ↑ BP.
Q will be patient over the age of 50 with cardiovascular disease risk factors, such as diabetes, HTN, and/or smoking.
Patients who have pre-existing HTN causing atherosclerosis leading to RAS will often have 10-20 years of background HTN that then becomes accelerated over a few-month to 2-year period.

topics.title: Vasculitides affecting the kidney
topics.summary: Vasculitides is a fancy word that is pleural for vasculitis.
pearls: Vasculitides is a fancy word that is pleural for vasculitis.
Formerly known as Wegener granulomatosis.
Answer on USMLE for adult with triad of 1) hematuria, 2) hemoptysis, and 3) “head-itis” – i.e., any problem with the head, such as nasal septal perforation, mastoiditis, sinusitis, otitis.

topics.title: Urolithiasis
topics.summary: Urolithiasis is broad, umbrella term that refers to both nephrolithiasis and ureterolithiasis.
pearls: Urolithiasis is broad, umbrella term that refers to both nephrolithiasis and ureterolithiasis.
Diagnosed with non-contrast CT of abdomen and pelvis.
KUB (X-ray of kidney, ureters, bladder) can be done but isn’t as sensitive (although below I show an X-ray).

topics.title: Cystic kidneys
topics.summary: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease; chromosome 6.
pearls: Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease; chromosome 6.
The answer on USMLE for cystic kidneys in pediatrics.
Can be associated with hepatic fibrosis.

topics.title: anatomic abnormalities
topics.summary: Bit of a weird one, but not me being fancy. It’s on NBME.
pearls: Bit of a weird one, but not me being fancy. It’s on NBME.
“Failure of canalization of proximal ureter” will be the answer if they tell you the renal collecting duct system is dilated, but the ureters are not dilated.
Sounds obvious, but I see students get this wrong a lot.

topics.title: Bladder incontinences
topics.summary: The answer for loss of urine with ↑ intra-abdominal pressure from laughing, sneezing, coughing.
pearls: The answer for loss of urine with ↑ intra-abdominal pressure from laughing, sneezing, coughing.
Stereotypical risk factor is grand multiparity (i.e., Hx of many childbirths) leading to weakened pelvic floor muscles.
I’d say only ~50% of Qs will mention Hx of pregnancy. The other ~50% are idiopathic.

topics.title: Urinary retention diagnoses
topics.summary: Lack of coordination between bladder sphincters and detrusor muscle.
pearls: Lack of coordination between bladder sphincters and detrusor muscle.
HY cause is spinal cord injury, which can cause either inability to void or urinary incontinence.

MS is another theoretical cause, which is where “overflow incontinence” as a result of MS has been asked by students, but once again, I’ve only ever seen urge incontinence for MS on NBME exams. Qbank ¹ NBMEs.

topics.title: Genitourinary injuries
topics.summary: Always presents with blood at the urethral meatus.
pearls: Always presents with blood at the urethral meatus.

3 ways this presents on USMLE: 1) Blood at urethral meatus + saddle injury (dude falls on balance beam). 2) Blood at urethral meatus + pelvic fracture/instability. 3) Blood at urethral meatus + “prostate not palpable.”
Next best step is retrograde urethrogram.

topics.title: Urothelial malignancies
topics.summary: The answer for painless flank mass in a kid age 2-4 years.
pearls: The answer for painless flank mass in a kid age 2-4 years.
Does not present in newborns. If they give you a 12-hour-old male, for instance, with a midline mass, that is posterior urethral valves causing a full
bladder (let alone the fact they say “midline,” not flank). I’ve seen tons of students select Wilms for this, and I’m like, is the kidney in your midline?

topics.title: SIADH vs DI vs PP
topics.summary: Syndrome of Inappropriate Anti-Diuretic Hormone secretion → means too much ADH (vasopressin secretion).
pearls: Syndrome of Inappropriate Anti-Diuretic Hormone secretion → means too much ADH (vasopressin secretion).
ADH is produced by supraoptic nucleus of hypothalamus → stored in posterior pituitary.
ADH ↑ free water reabsorption by the medullary collecting duct (MCD) of the kidney by causing aquaporin insertion.

topics.title: Obscure miscellaneous conditions
topics.summary: Disease that presents as though patient is on loop diuretic.
pearls: Disease that presents as though patient is on loop diuretic.
For whatever magical reason, is associated with juxtaglomerular cell hyperplasia.
Disease that presents as though patient is on thiazide diuretic.

pearls: Q asks about what would be increased in third trimester of pregnancy; answer = “hepatic protein production”; in contrast, CO2 is decreased (a mild respiratory alkalosis can be seen in pregnancy); pulmonary residual capacity is…

topics.title: Early embryonic development
topics.summary: Patient`s menstrual period is 1 week late, intercourse with her boyfriend 20 days ago. In the third week of embryog…
pearls: Patient`s menstrual period is 1 week late, intercourse with her boyfriend 20 days ago. In the third week of embryogenesis, gastrulation has occurred, The neural plate is present, but the neural tube is not yet complete.
By convention, gestational age is calculated from the first day of the last menstrual period, which was 7 weeks ago in this patient.

topics.title: Embryologic derivatives
topics.summary: Craniopharyngiomas are tumors arising from Rathke's pouch remnants in the anterior pituitary. They characteristical…
pearls: Craniopharyngiomas are tumors arising from Rathke's pouch remnants in the anterior pituitary. They characteristically have three components: solid, cystic, and calcified.
Pituitary adenoma is a benign tumor arising from the anterior pituitary and the most common cause of sellar masses (headache, bitemporal hemianopia, hypogonadism) in adults.

topics.title: Teratogenic
topics.summary: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers are teratogens. Both decrease angiotensin II activity, leading …
pearls: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers are teratogens. Both decrease angiotensin II activity, leading to abnormal fetal renal development, oligohydramnios, and potential neonatal Potter sequence (ie, pulmonary…
Valproate is a teratogenic medication that decreases maternal folate levels and increases the risk of fetal neural tube defects (eg, meningocele, myelomeningocele).

topics.title: Deformation
topics.summary: This newborn has talipes equinovarus (clubfoot), a congenital anomaly in which one or both feet are rigidly flexed …
pearls: This newborn has talipes equinovarus (clubfoot), a congenital anomaly in which one or both feet are rigidly flexed downward and inward.
Congenital torticollis is typically noted by 2 to 4 weeks of age, after which the child prefers to hold the head tilted to one side.

topics.title: Disruption
topics.summary: Disruption defines an error in organ morphogenesis that arises from the breakdown of an organ or body region that w…
pearls: Disruption defines an error in organ morphogenesis that arises from the breakdown of an organ or body region that was developmental^ normal. Destruction of formed tissue" → Disruption.

topics.title: Fetal alcohol syndrome
topics.summary: This child's behavioral difficulties (distractibility, hyperactivity, hitting), growth retardation, poor coordinati…
pearls: This child's behavioral difficulties (distractibility, hyperactivity, hitting), growth retardation, poor coordination, and facial anomalies are suggestive of fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS).
Alcohol is a known teratogen that causes fetal alcohol syndrome when used during pregnancy.

topics.title: Neonatal abstinence syndrome
topics.summary: Neonatal abstinence syndrome due to maternal opioid use causes neurologic, gastrointestinal, and autonomic symptoms…
pearls: Neonatal abstinence syndrome due to maternal opioid use causes neurologic, gastrointestinal, and autonomic symptoms; irritability, tremors, diarrhea, and sneezing are classic findings.

topics.title: Placenta

pearls: β-hCG secretion begins with blastocyst implantation and syncytiotrophoblast invasion. Syncytiotrophoblast cells arise from the outer layer of the blastocyst (trophectoderm) and produce β-hCG, which maintains corpus luteum…

topics.title: Polyhydramnios
topics.summary: Polyhydramnios (excessive accumulation of amniotic fluid) presents with increased abdominal circumference out of pr…
pearls: Polyhydramnios (excessive accumulation of amniotic fluid) presents with increased abdominal circumference out of proportion to gestational age.

topics.title: Twining
topics.summary: This patient is pregnant with twins of different sexes which can only occur in dizygotic twins due to the fertiliza…
pearls: This patient is pregnant with twins of different sexes which can only occur in dizygotic twins due to the fertilization of 2 oocytes by 2 different sperm.

topics.title: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome
topics.summary: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome is caused by arteriovenous anastomoses in the chorion of monochorionic twins with re…
pearls: Twin-twin transfusion syndrome is caused by arteriovenous anastomoses in the chorion of monochorionic twins with resultant movement of red blood cells and plasma from one fetus to the other.

topics.title: Urachus
topics.summary: The urachus is a remnant of the allantois that extends from the bladder to the umbilicus. Failed obliteration of th…
pearls: The urachus is a remnant of the allantois that extends from the bladder to the umbilicus. Failed obliteration of the allantois lumen can result in a patent urachus, which presents with urinary drainage from the umbilicus in the…
Congenital anomalies of the urachus result in an abnormal connection between the bladder and the umbilicus.

topics.title: Meckel Diverticulum
topics.summary: The omphalomesenteric (or vitelline) duct is a diverticulum of the yolk sac that extends from the embryologic midgu…
pearls: The omphalomesenteric (or vitelline) duct is a diverticulum of the yolk sac that extends from the embryologic midgut to the umbilicus; it normally involutes in early gestation.

topics.title: Pharyngeal cleft
topics.summary: This patient's neck mass anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle is likely an infected branchial cleft cyst. Bra…
pearls: This patient's neck mass anterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle is likely an infected branchial cleft cyst.
Branchial cleft cysts are developmental abnormalities that result from failure of fusion of the mesodermal branchial arches and failure of obliteration of the ectodermal branchial clefts.

topics.title: Pharyngeal pouch derivatives
topics.summary: Derivatives of the third pharyngeal pouch include the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands. Disrupted development…
pearls: Derivatives of the third pharyngeal pouch include the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands.
A 22q11microdeletion underlies the spectrum of physical features seen in DiGeorge syndrome (DGS).

topics.title: Cleft lip
topics.summary: Most cases (approximately two-thirds) of cleft lip with cleft palate have multifactorial inheritance related to com…
pearls: Most cases (approximately two-thirds) of cleft lip with cleft palate have multifactorial inheritance related to complex interactions of polygenetic and environmental factors.

Cleft lip occurs due to failed fusion of the left or right maxillary prominence with the intermaxillary segment in early gestation. Cleft palate occurs primarily when the palatine shelves fail to fuse.

topics.title: Müllerian agenesis
topics.summary: This patient is most likely a 46,XX female with müllerian agenesis. During sexual differentiation in females (XX), …
pearls: This patient is most likely a 46,XX female with müllerian agenesis. During sexual differentiation in females (XX), the müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts give rise to the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina; the…
Patients with müllerian agenesis have normal ovaries, which arise embryologically from the genital ridge.

topics.title: SRY gene translocation
topics.summary: The SRY gene is located on the Y chromosome and is responsible for producing testis-determining factor, which resul…
pearls: The SRY gene is located on the Y chromosome and is responsible for producing testis-determining factor, which results in male gonadal differentiation.

topics.title: Uterine (Mullerian duct) anomalies
topics.summary: Female reproductive tract development involves the lateral/vertical fusion and involution of the paramesonephric du…
pearls: Female reproductive tract development involves the lateral/vertical fusion and involution of the paramesonephric ducts (eg, Müllerian ducts), which give rise to the fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and upper vagina.
A hysterosalpingogram is used to evaluate the structure of the uterine cavity and the patency of the fallopian tubes with fluoroscopy.

topics.title: Hypospadius
topics.summary: In males, incomplete fusion of the urethral (urogenital) folds results in hypospadias, an abnormal opening of the u…
pearls: In males, incomplete fusion of the urethral (urogenital) folds results in hypospadias, an abnormal opening of the urethra proximal to the glans penis along the ventral shaft of the penis.

topics.title: The gonadal arteries
topics.summary: Testicular torsion is due to twisting of the testis around the spermatic cord (containing the gonadal artery), whic…
pearls: Testicular torsion is due to twisting of the testis around the spermatic cord (containing the gonadal artery), which can eventually lead to ischemia. The gonadal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta.

The testicular arteries originate directly from the abdominal aorta bilaterally. They travel through the internal and external inguinal rings to reach the scrotum, where they supply blood to the epididymis and the testis.

topics.title: Venous drainage
topics.summary: Ovarian vein thrombosis (infected ovarian vein thrombus) is a rare complication associated with the postpartum peri…
pearls: Ovarian vein thrombosis (infected ovarian vein thrombus) is a rare complication associated with the postpartum period and is typically right sided.

topics.title: Lymphatic drainage
topics.summary: Due to its intra-abdominal origin, lymphatic drainage of the testis is to the para-aortic lymph nodes. In contrast,…
pearls: Due to its intra-abdominal origin, lymphatic drainage of the testis is to the para-aortic lymph nodes. In contrast, lymph drainage from the scrotum goes into the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.
Lymph from the testes drains through lymph channels directly back to the para-aortic lymph nodes. In contrast, lymph from the scrotum drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.

topics.title: Female reproductive anatomy
topics.summary: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (ie, infundibulopelvic ligament) contains the ovarian artery, ovarian vein, ly…
pearls: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (ie, infundibulopelvic ligament) contains the ovarian artery, ovarian vein, lymphatics, and nerves. The ovarian artery is the major blood supply to the ovary.
Lymph from the ovary drains to the para-aortic lymph nodes via lymphatic vessels carried in the suspensory ligament alongside the ovarian artery and vein.

topics.title: Adenexal torsion
topics.summary: Ovarian torsion typically involves twisting of the infundibulopelvic ligament, often due to the weight of a large a…
pearls: Ovarian torsion typically involves twisting of the infundibulopelvic ligament, often due to the weight of a large adnexal mass.
Ovarian torsion typically occurs in reproductive-aged women due to rotation of the ovary around the infundibulopelvic (suspensory) and uteroovarian ligaments.

topics.title: Epithelia of the female reproductive tract
topics.summary: Histologic features of endometriosis include endometrial glands (lined by columnar epithelium), endometrial stroma,…
pearls: Histologic features of endometriosis include endometrial glands (lined by columnar epithelium), endometrial stroma, and hemosiderin.

topics.title: Male reproductive anatomy

pearls: Sildenafil selectively inhibits cGMP-specific phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5), leading to an increase in nitric oxide within the corpora cavernosa (Identify on the Pic.) > D, which results in vascular dilation and tumescence of the…

topics.title: Bladder anatomy
topics.summary: The bladder is extraperitoneal. In placement of a suprapubic cystostomy, the trocar and cannula will pierce the lay…
pearls: The bladder is extraperitoneal. In placement of a suprapubic cystostomy, the trocar and cannula will pierce the layers of the abdominal wall but will not enter the peritoneum.
The bladder trigone is formed by 2 slit-like ureteric orifices and the internal urethral opening.

topics.title: Bladder injury
topics.summary: This patient's suprapubic tenderness and hematuria (ie, urine dipstick test positive for blood) in the setting of b…
pearls: This patient's suprapubic tenderness and hematuria (ie, urine dipstick test positive for blood) in the setting of blunt trauma are concerning for a bladder injury.

The dome of the bladder rises into the peritoneal cavity when distended with urine. Blunt lower abdominal trauma can abruptly increase intravesicular pressure and rupture the bladder dome, spilling urine into the intraperitoneal…

topics.title: Urethral injury
topics.summary: Pelvic fracture are frequently associated with injury to the posterior urethra, in particular the bulbomembranous j…
pearls: Pelvic fracture are frequently associated with injury to the posterior urethra, in particular the bulbomembranous junction.

topics.title: Autonomic innervation of male sexual response
topics.summary: The prostatic plexus (inferior hypogastric nerves plus pelvic and sacral splanchnic nerves) lies within the fascia …
pearls: The prostatic plexus (inferior hypogastric nerves plus pelvic and sacral splanchnic nerves) lies within the fascia of the prostate and innervates the corpus cavernosa of the penis, which facilitates penile erection.
The pelvic splanchnic nerves are efferent parasympathetic preganglionic nerves that synapse with the cavernous nerves.

topics.title: Seminiferous tubules
topics.summary: Sertoli cells also facilitate spermatogenesis within the seminiferous tubules. Impaired Sertoli cell function would…
pearls: Sertoli cells also facilitate spermatogenesis within the seminiferous tubules. Impaired Sertoli cell function would lead to decreased production of inhibin, increased FSH levels, and impaired fertility.
The blood-testis barrier is formed by tight junctions between Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules and prevents immune exposure to the developing spermatids.

topics.title: Estrogen
topics.summary: LH stimulates the theca interna cells of the ovarian follicle to produce androgens. Aromatase within the follicle's…
pearls: LH stimulates the theca interna cells of the ovarian follicle to produce androgens. Aromatase within the follicle's granulosa cells subsequently converts these androgens to estradiol under FSH stimulation.

topics.title: Progesterone
topics.summary: In pregnancy, progesterone is secreted by the corpus luteum and later by the placenta. Although prolactin secretion…
pearls: In pregnancy, progesterone is secreted by the corpus luteum and later by the placenta. Although prolactin secretion increases as pregnancy progresses, high progesterone levels inhibit lactation by preventing binding of prolactin…
Progesterone is the hormone responsible for maintaining the endometrial lining when implantation occurs. Without enough progesterone, spontaneous abortion ensues as a result of endometrial sloughing.

topics.title: Oogenesis
topics.summary: Primary oocytes are completely developed in female embryos by the fifth month of gestation, at which point they are…
pearls: Primary oocytes are completely developed in female embryos by the fifth month of gestation, at which point they are arrested in prophase of meiosis I.
Oocytes remain arrested in prophase of meiosis I until the follicle matures in preparation for ovulation. As oocytes mature, they arrest again in metaphase II until fertilization.

topics.title: Menstrual cycle
topics.summary: Progesterone is secreted during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle and transforms the endometrium from prolife…
pearls: Progesterone is secreted during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle and transforms the endometrium from proliferative to secretory.
The secretory phase of the menstrual cycle occurs between ovulation and menses, from days 15-28 of the normal menstrual cycle.

topics.title: Pregnancy
topics.summary: β-hCG is a hormone secreted by the placental syncytiotrophoblast after uterine invasion that signals the ovary to m…
pearls: β-hCG is a hormone secreted by the placental syncytiotrophoblast after uterine invasion that signals the ovary to maintain the corpus luteum, which produces progesterone in early pregnancy.

topics.title: Physiologic changes of pregnancy
topics.summary: Pregnancy is a prothrombotic state due to increased procoagulant factors (eg, fibrinogen), decreased anticoagulant …
pearls: Pregnancy is a prothrombotic state due to increased procoagulant factors (eg, fibrinogen), decreased anticoagulant factors (eg, protein S), and reduced fibrinolysis.
Gestational thrombocytopenia is common in the third trimester and is typically mild, asymptomatic, and not associated with other laboratory abnormalities.

topics.title: Human chorionic gonadotropin

pearls: This patient with coarse chin hair likely has anovulatory infertility related to polycystic ovary syndrome.

During pregnancy, progesterone is produced by the corpus luteum for the first seven to ten weeks of gestation secondary to stimulation by human chorionic gonadotropin from the placental syncytiotrophoblast, after which time it is…

pearls: Human placental lactogen creates a fetal glucose-sparing effect by increasing maternal insulin resistance during the second and third trimesters, leading to a rise in serum glucose that helps provide adequate nutrition to the…

Neonates born to mothers with poorly controlled diabetes during pregnancy are exposed to high maternal glucose levels in utero, resulting in beta cell hyperplasia followed by excessive fetal insulin production.

topics.title: Lactation
topics.summary: The breast milk content of vitamins D and K is typically insufficient for the nutritional needs of the newborn. Vit…
pearls: The breast milk content of vitamins D and K is typically insufficient for the nutritional needs of the newborn. Vitamin K is given parenterally to all newborns at birth to prevent hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.
Menopause During the menopausal transition, FSH levels increase due to resistant ovarian follicles and lack of feedback from inhibin.

topics.title: Androgens
topics.summary: Following bilateral orchiectomy, extragonadal androgen sources are inadequate to replace the loss of testosterone, …
pearls: Following bilateral orchiectomy, extragonadal androgen sources are inadequate to replace the loss of testosterone, causing a hypogonadal state.
The physis is the cartilaginous plate that lies near the end of long bones, between the epiphysis and metaphysis, that provides axial growth to the skeleton.

topics.title: Precocious & Delayed Puberty
topics.summary: Early sexual maturation, which begins as early as 8 years old (Normal), typically includes thelarche and pubarche. …
pearls: Early sexual maturation, which begins as early as 8 years old (Normal), typically includes thelarche and pubarche. Menarche usually occurs a few years after thelarche.
Idiopathic precocious puberty is characterized by early-onset, pulsatile GnRH secretion, resulting in increased estrogen production.

topics.title: Klinefelter syndrome
topics.summary: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes infertility characterized by primary hypogonadism (elevated FSH and LH, low te…
pearls: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes infertility characterized by primary hypogonadism (elevated FSH and LH, low testosterone) and azoospermia. Other findings include long lower extremities; small, firm testes; and gynecomastia.
Klinefelter syndrome is most commonly caused by a meiotic nondisjunction event during parental gametogenesis that results in a 47,XXY karyotype.

topics.title: Testosterone replacement therapy
topics.summary: Testosterone replacement therapy is indicated for men with symptomatic hypogonadism. It is associated with an incre…
pearls: Testosterone replacement therapy is indicated for men with symptomatic hypogonadism. It is associated with an increase in serum prostate-specific antigen and may raise the risk of prostate cancer.
Turner syndrome is a genetically heterogeneous condition that is most commonly due to meiotic nondisjunction during gametogenesis.

topics.title: AMH deficiency
topics.summary: Antimüllerian hormone (AMH) is produced by the testes and stimulates Müllerian duct involution so internal female s…
pearls: Antimüllerian hormone (AMH) is produced by the testes and stimulates Müllerian duct involution so internal female structures (eg, fallopian tubes, uterus) do not develop.

topics.title: Aromatase deficiency
topics.summary: Aromatase deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by high androgen (and corresponding low estro…
pearls: Aromatase deficiency is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by high androgen (and corresponding low estrogen) levels in the fetus and placenta.
This genotypically female (46,XX) infant with ambiguous genitalia was born to a mother who developed masculinizing features during pregnancy, findings which are consistent with aromatase deficiency.

topics.title: Androgen insensitivity syndrome
topics.summary: Androgen insensitivity syndrome is caused by dysfunctional androgen receptors; genotypic males (XY) have testes but…
pearls: Androgen insensitivity syndrome is caused by dysfunctional androgen receptors; genotypic males (XY) have testes but no external male genitalia or internal male genital ducts (eg, vas deferens) due to the lack of androgen effect…

Androgen receptor dysfunction in patients with partial androgen insensitivity syndrome leads to decreased facial, axillary, and pubic hair; oligospermia; gynecomastia; and undervirilization of external genitalia (eg…

topics.title: 5α-reductase type 2 deficiency

pearls: The enzyme 5-alpha reductase converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone, which drives development of external male genitalia.
5α-reductase type 2 deficiency results in diminished conversion of testosterone to DHT in the male urogenital tract.

topics.title: Kallmann syndrome
topics.summary: In Kallmann syndrome, there is an absence of GnRH secretory neurons in the hypothalamus due to defective migration …
pearls: In Kallmann syndrome, there is an absence of GnRH secretory neurons in the hypothalamus due to defective migration from the olfactory placode.

topics.summary: Placenta accreta spectrum occurs due to placental invasion into the myometrium through defects in the decidua basal…
pearls: Placenta accreta spectrum occurs due to placental invasion into the myometrium through defects in the decidua basalis.
Placenta accreta occurs due to abnormal attachment of the placenta directly onto the uterine myometrium.

topics.title: Abruptio placentae

pearls: This patient in the third trimester with painful vaginal bleeding and a tender, firm uterus has a presentation consistent with abruptio placentae (ie, premature separation of the placenta from the uterus prior to fetal delivery).
Abruptio placentae is caused by rupture of maternal vessels at the uteroplacental interface that leads to premature separation of the placenta from the myometrium.

pearls: The internal iliac artery (hypogastric artery) supplies blood to the pelvis, including the uterus via the uterine artery.

pearls: This patient has lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. In the setting of a positive pregnancy test (eg, detectable β-hCG) and an adnexal mass, her presentation is most concerning for ectopic pregnancy.
Ectopic pregnancy should be suspected in patients with a pregnancy of unknown location (ie, no visible intrauterine gestation) and abnormally rising β-hCG levels.

pearls: A complete hydatidiform mole is composed of multiple cystic edematous hydropic villi resulting from trophoblast proliferation. Serial measurements of β-hCG should be performed following evacuation of a hydatidiform mole.

topics.title: Partial mole

pearls: This patient has a partial hydatidiform mole, which typically presents in early pregnancy with vaginal bleeding and no fetal cardiac activity, similar to a miscarriage.

pearls: Gestational choriocarcinoma is a malignant tumor that arises from the trophoblast. It is most commonly preceded by a normal pregnancy but can occur following any pregnancy (molar, ectopic, aborted).

topics.summary: Preeclampsia is associated with widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction, which occurs due to increased antiangi…
pearls: Preeclampsia is associated with widespread maternal endothelial dysfunction, which occurs due to increased antiangiogenic factor release and decreased proangiogenic factor activity (eg, vascular endothelial growth factor).

pearls: HELLP (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelet count) syndrome is a thrombotic microangiopathic disorder that causes microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (eg, increased indirect bilirubin levels), thrombocytopenia, and…

vignettes.a: pyruvate dehydrogenase (converts pyruvate → acetyl-CoA of TCA cycle); described as giant complex of vitamins B1, B2, B3, B5, and lipoic acid. HY vitamins and minerals for USMLE

vignettes.q: 42M + alcoholic + high MCV; Q asks, which combination of serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine is most likely in this patient?
vignettes.a: normal methylmalonic acid (or methylmalonyl-CoA), ↑ homocysteine; diagnosis is folate (B9) deficiency. Learning point is:

vignettes.q: This is because without B9 and B12, there is less homocysteine
vignettes.a: methionine.

vignettes.q: Experiment performed showing HPV16 E6 protein causes p53 protein degradation; Q asks, which cellular enzyme will target p53 as a result of this viral protein?
vignettes.a: ubiquitin ligase; ubiquitination will target proteins for degradation by the proteasome.

vignettes.q: 31F + Pap smear shows atypical squamous cells + molecular diagnostic studies show viral E6 protein; Q asks, this protein promotes cell growth and malignancy via what mechanism?
vignettes.a: “degradation of p53”; HPV16 E6 protein targets p53; HPV18 E7 protein targets RB; both are tumor suppressor proteins; you can remember this because 16 comes before 18, as 6 comes before 7, as P comes before R.

vignettes.q: 62M + back pain + restrictive cardiomyopathy + renal failure + biopsy of kidney shows a birefringent pattern with Congo red stain; Q asks, what is the structure of the material that is stained?
vignettes.a: b-pleated sheet; diagnosis is multiple myeloma causing cardiac and renal amyloidosis; amyloid stains apple green birefringent with Congo red stain because of its b-pleated sheet structure.

vignettes.q: Neonate + several fractures occurred during birth + shortened extremities + misshapen long bones + poor skull mineralization; Q asks, this girl has a defect in which of the following?
vignettes.a: collagen; diagnosis is osteogenesis imperfecta (collagen I).

vignettes.q: Experiment with fish embryos; two pronuclei used to make embryo; results of study show that if both pronuclei are of maternal or paternal origin, the embryo fails to develop properly; why?
vignettes.a: imprinting; normally two alleles are inherited for each gene an organism has (one from each parent), but various alleles will sometimes be silenced from one parent and expressed in the other; if the allele coming from mom is silen

vignettes.q: Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS; many involved genes; mental retardation + hyperphagia) is classic maternal imprinting
vignettes.a: gene coming from mom is normally silenced; dad’s gene is supposed to be expressed but is deleted or mutated (“Willi hates his dad” because dad’s gene is deleted); even if mom’s gene is healthy, since it is normally silenced, it wi

vignettes.q: Angelman syndrome (AS; UBE3A gene on chromosome 15; “happy puppet”) is classic paternal imprinting
vignettes.a: gene coming from dad is normally silenced; mom’s gene is supposed to be expressed but is deleted or mutated (“Mom is not an angel” because mom’s gene is deleted); even if dad’s gene is healthy, since it is normally silenced, it wi

vignettes.q: 40M + pancreatic cancer due to Li-Fraumeni syndrome; Q asks, what mechanism is responsible for development of cancer in this patient?
vignettes.a: “loss of heterozygosity”; patient was born with one diseased allele in every cell (i.e., one hit); after spontaneous mutation in second allele, disease occurred. The p53 protein is a tumor suppressor that halts the cell cycle in t

vignettes.q: 44M + cognitive decline over the past six months + abnormal movement of limbs + father had similar presentation in his 50s; Q asks, what mechanism best explains this patient’s presentation?
vignettes.a: anticipation; Dx is Huntington disease (AD, chromosome 4), which is caused by 40+ trinucleotide repeats (TNR) of CAG codon; anticipation is a HY term associated with TNR disorders that refers to the disease presenting increasingly

vignettes.q: Tyrosine hydroxylase converts tyrosine --> L-DOPA. It is very rare for the USMLE to directly assess this enzyme. If it does, the answer will be obvious - i.e., "Patient has low dopamine synthesis secondary to a
vignettes.a: " --> "deficiency of tyrosine hydroxylase," where L-DOPA decarboxylase isn't listed.

vignettes.q: 43M + gets sore knees when plays basketball + pinna of left ear slightly greyish + urine sample turns dark color upon standing; what enzyme is deficient in this patient?
vignettes.a: homogentisic acid (homogentisate) oxidase; required for tyrosine breakdown into fumarate. Sometimes Q will ask which amino acid is not broken down properly; answer = tyrosine.

vignettes.q: 20M + 6-year-Hx of seizure disorder + flesh-colored papules on bridge of nose and in the nasolabial folds; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: tuberous sclerosis (TSC); AD; chromosomes 9 and 16 (hamartin and tuberin proteins); subependymal or periventricular nodules seen on MRI; hypopigmented macules (ash leaf spots); hyperpigmented velvety lesions (shagreen patches); ca

vignettes.q: Experiment is performed showing a nutrient causes increased gene products detectable by Western blotting + no change in gene products detected by Northern blotting or PCR; Q asks, what does the nutrient cause i
vignettes.a: “translation of mRNA”; Western blot detects protein; Northern blot detects RNA; Southern blot detects DNA; PCR detects DNA. Transcription is the process of DNA → RNA; translation is the process of RNA → protein. Annoying lab techn

vignettes.q: Experiment is performed visualizing changes to RNA via electron microscopy; Q asks which change occurs in the cytosol?
vignettes.a: “association with P-bodies”; DNA is transcribed to hnRNA (heteronuclear RNA); hnRNA then undergoes three main changes in the nucleus: 1) addition of poly-A tail to 3’ end, 2) addition of 7-methylguanosine cap to 5’ end, and 3) spl

vignettes.q: 28F + experiences spontaneous abortion; Q asks, what’s the most likely mechanism for this?
vignettes.a: “unbalanced chromosomal rearrangement,” which is the most common cause of spontaneous abortion.

vignettes.q: 4M + Hx of recurrent ear infections + hepatosplenomegaly + studies show deficient N- acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase + analysis of skin fibroblasts shows they secrete large amounts of acid hydrolase into
vignettes.a: lysosome; diagnosis is I-cell disease; deficient enzyme leads to inability to produce mannose-6-phosphate, which normally enables hydrolases at the Golgi to be targeted to the lysosomes; if the Q asks for the location of the defic

vignettes.q: 3M + developmental delay + ophthalmoplegia + hypotonia + hearing loss in mother + uncle had stroke-like episodes in his 20s; Q asks, which mechanism explains the findings in this family?
vignettes.a: heteroplasmy; diagnosis is a mitochondrial disorder (in this case, MELAS, which is Mitochondrial Encephalopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes); you don’t need to know MELAS specifically, but just know ear and/or eye p

vignettes.q: Neonate + marked hypopigmentation + blue irides; Q asks, this condition is caused by a defective enzyme located in which organelle?
vignettes.a: melanosome; diagnosis is albinism, which is usually caused by deficient/defective tyrosinase, a melanosomal enzyme.

vignettes.q: 27M + severe muscle cramping with exercise + venous blood sampling shows post-exercise lactic acid does not increase compared to pre-exercise levels; Q asks, which enzyme is most likely deficient?
vignettes.a: muscle glycogen phosphorylase; diagnosis is McArdle syndrome (glycogen storage disease type V).

vignettes.q: 16F + gives birth to neonate with epicanthal folds, slanted palpebral fissures, single palmar crease, and low IQ; karyotyping of the neonate shows abnormality in 100% of cells; what’s the most likely mechanism
vignettes.a: Robertsonian translocation; child has Down syndrome (trisomy 21) due to inheriting the long arm of chromosome 21 attached to chromosome 14 of one of the parents – i.e., t(14q;21q). The implication is that it is unlikely to have me

vignettes.q: Neonate born with microcephaly + prominent occiput + clenched hands + low-set ears; what chromosomal abnormality is most likely to be seen?
vignettes.a: trisomy of chromosome 18; diagnosis is Edward syndrome; presentation is microcephaly + prominent occiput + clenched hands + low-set ears; flattened facies not characteristic (that’s Down due to hypoplastic nasal bone); second trim

vignettes.q: 42F + has a tumor demonstrating G-alpha-s G-proteins that lack GTPase function; Q asks, which cellular change would be seen in this patient?
vignettes.a: increased cAMP; cleavage of GTP into GDP functions to shut off G-protein activity, so loss of GTPase function means increased activity; G-alpha-s G-proteins increase cAMP, so in this case the tumor leads to increased cAMP producti

vignettes.q: Neonate with rare disease has a mutation localized to an intron sequence; Q asks, which of the following mechanisms most likely accounts for disease in this patient?
vignettes.a: “RNA splice error”; introns are sequences that are not translated into protein; exons are sequences that can be translated into protein; a HY USMLE point regarding introns is that they play a role in post- transcriptional RNA spli

vignettes.q: 21M + ↑ serum orotic acid + hyperammonemia + ↓ blood urea nitrogen + normal RBC MCV; Dx?
vignettes.a: ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency; urea cycle disorder; X-linked recessive; orotic acid is normally produced from carbomyl phosphate (via CPS-II) in the synthesis of pyrimidines; in ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, since

vignettes.q: 21M + ↑ serum orotic acid + ↑ RBC MCV + serum B9 and B12 levels are normal; Dx?
vignettes.a: orotic aciduria; caused by deficiency of uridine monophosphate synthase, an enzyme required for pyrimidine synthesis; MCV is increased because pyrimidine synthesis is impaired; ammonia is normal (in contrast to ornithine transcarb

vignettes.q: 8-month-old girl + hyperammonemia + decreased serum citrulline + increased serum glutamine + increased serum orotic acid; which enzyme is deficient in this patient?
vignettes.a: ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency; should be noted this is X-linked recessive but Step 1 NBME gives the condition in a girl; apart from the inheritance pattern discrepancy making no sense, the only way to arrive at the answer

vignettes.q: 5M + progressive weakness and loss of muscle function + exam shows hypertrophy of calf muscles + serum CK is elevated; the most likely cause of this presentation is a defective protein in which area of muscle?
vignettes.a: cytoskeleton; diagnosis is Duchenne (XR); dystrophin protein (DMD gene) is required to connect muscle cell cytoskeleton to extracellular proteins; pseudohypertrophy results from fibroadipose tissue deposition; Gower maneuver class

vignettes.q: Girl with asthma is administered IV methylprednisolone, resulting in marked clinical improvement; what’s the mechanism via which this agent resulted in improvement?
vignettes.a: “binding to cytoplasmic receptor, translocation to nucleus, and transcriptional activation of target genes”; most steroid hormones bind to intracytoplasmic receptors, as is the case additionally for androgens, estrogens, progestin

vignettes.q: Experiment is performed where an agent inhibits histone deacetylase; this drug most likely affects which cellular process?
vignettes.a: transcription; histones are highly compacted structures of heterochromatic DNA; process of acetylation normally activates and makes DNA euchromatic (i.e., transcribable); methylation normally silences and makes DNA heterochromatic

vignettes.q: 42M + receives all-trans retinoic acid for Tx of AML M3 (APL); Q asks, which enzyme will be attracted to the retinoic acid receptor/promyelocytic leukemia fusion protein to form a pre-transcriptional complex?
vignettes.a: histone acetylase; wrong answer is histone N-methyltransferase; learning point for USMLE is that acetylation is usually associated with gene activation; methylation is usually associated with gene silencing. Epigenetics is the stu

vignettes.q: 80M + alcohol dependence + many ecchymoses + few teeth + hemorrhagic macules around hair follicles; what is most likely responsible for his poor wound healing?
vignettes.a: inadequate hydroxylation of collagen polypeptides; Dx is scurvy (vitamin C deficiency); vitamin C is necessary for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in developing collagen; perifollicular hemorrhages are a HY finding fo

vignettes.q: 30M + palpitations + weight loss + exophthalmos + tremors; Q asks, patient’s presentation is most likely due to hormonal action on which of the following receptors?
vignettes.a: “nuclear/retinoid X binding to DNA”; thyroid hormones bind intranuclear.

vignettes.q: A couple who are both healthy have two children with achondroplasia; what’s the most likely mechanism for this process?
vignettes.a: germline mosaicism; achondroplasia is an AD disorder but most cases are due to de novo mutations within one of the spermatogonia or oogonia of the parents (i.e., a % of germline cells are affected), but the somatic (body) cells of

vignettes.q: 19M + mental retardation + long face + prominent ears + large testes; analysis of patient’s DNA shows 400 CGG repeats in the FMR1 gene 5’ untranslated region; which of the following would most likely result fro
vignettes.a: “decreased transcription”; Dx is Fragile X, which is due to TNR expansion >200 repeats of CGG; expansion of untranslated region results in hypermethylation of FMR1 gene and prevents binding of transcription factors and RNA polymer

vignettes.q: 6-month-old boy + jaundice + cataracts + hepatomegaly; urine shows positive reaction to copper reduction test and negative reaction to a test agent that contains glucose oxidase; what enzyme is deficient in thi
vignettes.a: galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (classic galactosemia); if the Q mentioned cataracts alone, answer would be galactokinase deficiency; the galactose disorders appear shortly after birth because lactose in breast milk (or co

vignettes.q: Neonate has blue sclerae, hyperextensible joints, fragile bones, and dysplasia of his enamel; which mechanism accounts for the pleiotropic effects of osteogenesis imperfecta in this patient?
vignettes.a: “expression of defective gene in multiple tissues”; pleiotropy once again is one gene resulting in different unrelated phenotypes.

vignettes.q: 2F + cherry red spot on macula + deficiency of hexosaminidase A; this patient is most likely to have a buildup of what?
vignettes.a: GM2 ganglioside; Dx is Tay-Sachs.

vignettes.q: Investigator looking at mitochondrial tRNA and finds mitochondria encode their own tRNA; Q asks why?
vignettes.a: “mitochondria use a non-standard genetic code”; mitochondria have their own genes separate from chromosomal DNA.

vignettes.q: 50F + positive PPD test + negative chest x-ray + commenced on prophylactic therapy; 6 months later patient develops decreased sensation to pinprick in all extremities; Dx?
vignettes.a: vitamin B6 deficiency secondary to isoniazid.

vignettes.q: 2M + bites his fingers and lips + orange-red crystals in his diaper; which enzyme is deficient in this patient?
vignettes.a: hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT); Dx is Lesch-Nyhan syndrome; X-linked recessive; congenital cause of uric acid overproduction (gout); self-mutilation common; HGPRT is necessary for recycling of purines; if e

vignettes.q: 2F + potbelly + hypotonia + large tongue; Dx?
vignettes.a: cretinism (congenital hypothyroidism); can leads to mental retardation (thyroid hormone needed for myelin synthesis); impaired bone growth.

vignettes.q: 2F + potbelly + fed gruel; Dx?
vignettes.a: “protein-calorie malnutrition” (kwashiorkor) – i.e., sufficient calories but insufficient protein.

vignettes.q: 2F + severely underweight with wasting; Dx?
vignettes.a: “total calorie malnutrition” (marasmus).

vignettes.q: 3M + severe combined immunodeficiency + receives gene therapy delivered via lysogenic phage + treatment successful; six months later he develops leukemia; why?
vignettes.a: virus incorporated itself next to oncogene; since the treatment was successful, we know the delivered gene was successfully incorporated and transcribed, so for there to be leukemia means an oncogene may have been nearby and erron

vignettes.q: 10M + recurrent nosebleeds + bleeding time 6 minutes + platelet count 200,000 + Hb 13.5 g/dL + facial telangiectasias; Q asks, what’s the inheritance pattern of this condition?
vignettes.a: autosomal dominant; Dx is hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia; normal bleeding time and platelet count signify this is not immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

vignettes.q: 33M + non-smoker + worsening lung function + father died of alcoholic cirrhosis + younger brother is a smoker and has advanced lung disease; Q asks, the deficient enzyme in this patient normally targets what?
vignettes.a: elastase; Dx is a1-antitrypsin deficiency; codominant inheritance with varying degrees of severity; homozygous ZZ alleles cause severe presentation; a1-antitrypsin, despite the name, breaks down elastase in the lungs; deficiency l

vignettes.q: 56M + HbA1c of 12% + decreased sensation to pinprick up to the ankles; Q asks, what’s the mechanism for myelinopathy in this patient?
vignettes.a: increased activity of aldose reductase; in diabetes, glucose moves into myelin sheaths and is converted to sorbitol via aldose reductase; sorbitol causes osmotic damage due to cellular swelling.

vignettes.q: 12F + seizures + loss of vision + weakness + serum lactic acid increased + mother and maternal grandmother have hearing loss; where is the patient’s mutation?
vignettes.a: mitochondrial tRNAGlu; the point being: the kid has a mitochondrial disorder (classic findings of lactic acidosis, eye/ear problems, hypotonia/weakness), and mitochondrial tRNAGlu is the only answer that matches in this Q.

vignettes.q: Investigator looking at mutations in NF1 gene. A wildtype (healthy) sequence of 5’-ATGCCCCT-3’
vignettes.a: mutated sequence 5’-ATGGCCCT-3’; a restriction enzyme is designed to cleave the mutated sequence; what sequence will the restriction enzyme cleave at? → answer = 5’-GGCC-3’; most restriction enzymes cleave at palindromic sites (GG

vignettes.q: 69F + fractures right hip + two months later right leg has less muscle mass compared to left leg; which cellular process might explain these findings?
vignettes.a: polyubiquitination → atrophy entails protein breakdown, where ubiquitination of proteins targets them for the proteasome.

vignettes.q: 25M + undergoing chemo for leukemia; a drug is given to help prevent renal failure; Q ask which enzyme this drug inhibits; answer = xanthine oxidase
vignettes.a: allopurinol or febuxostat to prevent tumor lysis syndrome.

vignettes.q: 1M + coarse facial features + hypotonia + increased serum lysosomal enzymes; which molecule is deficient in this patient?
vignettes.a: mannose-6-phosphate (easy for I-cell disease).

vignettes.q: 40F + high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis + blurry vision + hangs around paint thinner for fun; which molecule is responsible for the patient’s change in vision?
vignettes.a: formic acid; methanol → formaldehyde → formic acid; the latter can cause blindness with methanol toxicity; methanol is part of MUDPILES for high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (Methanol, Uremia, DKA, Phenformin, Iron/INH, Lactic aci

vignettes.q: 30F + serum triglycerides 3200 mg/dL + serum appears milky; which enzyme is deficient in this patient?
vignettes.a: lipoprotein lipase (hyperchylomicronemia); if vignette also mentions lipase elevation and abdo pain, this is simply due to pancreatitis (i.e., the disease itself isn’t causing lipase elevation); hyperchylomicronemia also caused by

vignettes.q: “Decreased carnitine acyltransferase activity”
vignettes.a: enzyme required for fatty acids to enter mitochondrion from cytosol, so this enzyme is catabolic and would be increased in activity.

vignettes.q: “Synthesis of glycogen”
vignettes.a: clearly anabolic process and would not be increased in predominance of glucagon.

vignettes.q: “Increased acetyl-CoA carboxylase activity”
vignettes.a: enzyme is anabolic and converts acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA, which is a precursor to fatty acid synthesis; this would not be upregulate in catabolic state; in addition, malonyl-CoA is the allosteric inhibitor of carnitine acyltransf

vignettes.q: “Decreased ketogenesis”
vignettes.a: we would expect increased, not decreased, ketogenesis in catabolic state. Acetyl-CoAs liberated from FA breakdown are the precursors for ketones in the catabolic state.

vignettes.q: 2M + fractures at different stages of healing + genetic mutation showing a glycine residue in the collagen I gene becomes an alanine; what’s the mechanism for this patient’s condition?
vignettes.a: weakening of secondary structure of collagen; glycine is a proton; alanine is a methyl group; this means if alanine replaces glycine, there’s less hydrogen bonding between sidechains in the collagen molecule (hydrogen bonding is i

vignettes.q: Q asks about how to counsel healthy patient on good nutrition; what should be part of this patient’s diet?
vignettes.a: linoleic and linolenic acids (the two essential unsaturated fatty acids); linoleic is omega-6; linolenic is omega-3; both are C18; wrong answer is stearic acid (C18 saturated FA that shows up frequently as distractor for biochem N

vignettes.q: Q asks about impaired trafficking of vesicles into the Golgi; which would be seen on electron microscopy of the cell?
vignettes.a: rough endoplasmic reticulum dilatation; normally proteins are trafficked from RER → Golgi, so if this process cannot occur, the RER should dilate.

vignettes.q: Q asks about what kind of protein alteration will result in failure of protein transport within a cell; answer = deletion of residue from N-terminus; signal-recognition particles that enable cellular traffickin
vignettes.a: Right. Well it’s on NBME.

vignettes.q: 27F + lost in wilderness + normoglycemia even after 3 weeks; which amino acid is likely to contribute to normal serum glucose in this patient?
vignettes.a: alanine; the four main gluconeogenic substrates in humans are lactate, glycerol, alanine, glutamine.

vignettes.q: 2M + Hx of viral, fungal, bacterial, protozoal infections; investigations show a buildup of dATP in the patient’s cells; this buildup inhibits which of the following enzymes?
vignettes.a: ribonucleotide reductase; child has AR form of SCID, resulting in adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency; ADA deficiency causes a buildup of dATP, which inhibits ribonucleotide reductase (on Step 1 NBME).

vignettes.q: Girl eats a meal; what’s the mechanism of insulin secretion in her?
vignettes.a: fusion of vesicle with cell membrane; insulin secretion requires ATP-mediated closure of K channel → K builds up in the cell → depolarization → causes Ca influx → vesicles filled with insulin fuse with plasma membrane → insulin ex

vignettes.q: 5F + cystic fibrosis; Q asks, defect in which of the following is responsible for her condition
vignettes.a: protein structure; the chloride channel has defective protein structure, resulting in sequestration within the RER of the cytosol (i.e., channel is not transported to cell surface).

vignettes.q: Q asks which substrate is required to synthesize glucosamine from fructose-6-phosphate; answer = glutamine (yes, this is asked as a one-liner); F6P + glutamine
vignettes.a: glucosamine + glutamate; glucosamine is a precursor for glycoproteins, glycolipids, and proteoglycans.

vignettes.q: Albuterol
vignettes.a: beta-2 agonist → agonizes G-alpha-s → increased cAMP.

vignettes.q: Ranitidine
vignettes.a: antagonizes histamine-2 → antagonizes G-alpha-s → decreased cAMP.

vignettes.q: TATA box is mutated within a gene; what is the result of this?
vignettes.a: decreased binding of RNA polymerase; TATA box is region within the promotor region where RNA polymerase II binds to initiate transcription.

vignettes.q: 54F + temporal arteritis + IV methylprednisolone administered; how does this drug bind?
vignettes.a: cytosolic receptor with translocation to the nucleus; most steroid hormones bind cytosolic receptors, followed by translocation to the nucleus where gene transcription is upregulated.

vignettes.q: Investigator looking at organism that has incurred RNA polymerase mutation; why will this not adversely affect the species survival
vignettes.a: transcriptional errors are not transmitted to progeny.

vignettes.q: Investigator looking at plasma-membrane-associated proteins vs those that are secreted from the cell; which of the following is most likely to be observed to be different between these types of proteins
vignettes.a: transmembrane domain (present in plasma-membrane-associated proteins).

vignettes.q: Neonate + jaundice + hypoglycemia + reducing sugars seen in urine; assay for which of the following is most likely to establish the diagnosis
vignettes.a: activity of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase (classic galactosemia).

vignettes.q: G-protein signaling is disrupted in a patient; the effect of which of the following is most likely to be attenuated?
vignettes.a: epinephrine (since agonizes adrenergic receptors, which are G-protein- coupled).

vignettes.q: 3% saline is administered to a patient; what will happen to both osmolality and volume within the ECF and ICF?
vignettes.a: ↑ ECF volume; ↑ ECF osmolality; ↓ ICF volume; ↑ ICF osmolality; 3% is hypertonic (isotonic = 0.9%); ↑ osmolality of ECF will cause fluid shift out of ICF compartment, thereby increasing osmolality of ICF.

vignettes.q: Cortisol increases synthesis of which of the following enzymes?
vignettes.a: phenylethanolamine N- methyltransferase (converts NE → E); norepinephrine and cortisol share venous drainage from the medulla, where conversion to epinephrine occurs.

vignettes.q: Neonate has progressive lethargy + hypotonia + metabolic acidosis + hyperammonemia; what type of condition is most likely responsible?
vignettes.a: organic acid metabolism disorder; common type is methylmalonic acidemia; organic acids, such as methylmalonic acid, can disrupt urea cycle (↓ conversion of ammonia to urea); the acids themselves ↓ pH.

vignettes.q: How to overcome methotrexate toxicity?
vignettes.a: leucovorin rescue (folinic acid; not folic acid).

vignettes.q: How to overcome 5-FU toxicity
vignettes.a: oral thymidine or uridine.

vignettes.q: What two substrates are required for heme synthesis?
vignettes.a: glycine and succinyl-CoA (combine via B6 and delta-ALA synthase → delta-ALA as first step in heme synthesis).

vignettes.q: What best explains altered mental status in diabetic ketoacidosis?
vignettes.a: dehydration both intra- and extracellularly (polyuria causing fluid depletion).

vignettes.q: Investigator looking at a protein that serves as a precursor for various hormones; which of the following molecular processes is required in order to generate the hormones from the precursor protein?
vignettes.a: post-translational modification.

vignettes.q: Patient with terminal ileectomy; which of the following molecular processes is most likely to be disrupted?
vignettes.a: conversion of N5 -methyltetrahydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate; vitamin B12 is required for conversion of uracil → thymine, as a methyl group is transferred to uracil in order to make thymine.

vignettes.q: 1) Homocysteine + 5-methyl-THF, via B12
vignettes.a: methionine + THF

vignettes.q: Neonate + jaundice + increased LFTs + increased serum very-long-chain fatty acids; which organelle is the site of the defect?
vignettes.a: peroxisome (required for very-long-chain and branched-chain FA breakdown).

vignettes.q: Which phase of the cell cycle are mitotic cyclins synthesized?
vignettes.a: G2 (preparation for mitosis). Cell cycle phases are G1, S, G2, M. Interphase comprises G1, S, G2; mitotic phase is M.

vignettes.q: G1
vignettes.a: cellular contents (excluding chromosomes) are duplicated.

vignettes.q: S
vignettes.a: DNA synthesis (46 chromosomes duplicated by the cell).

vignettes.q: G2
vignettes.a: more cell growth + mitotic cyclin synthesis.

vignettes.q: M
vignettes.a: mitosis + cytokinesis; nuclear envelope proteins phosphorylated during cytokinesis.

vignettes.q: Neonate + lactic acidosis + ketonemia + hypoglycemia; fructose + glycerol fail to increase glucose levels; galactose does increase glucose levels; what kind of defect does this patient have?
vignettes.a: defect in gluconeogenesis; galactose ß→ galactose-1-phosphate ß→ galactose-6-phosphate ß→ glucose-6-phosphate; the latter, via glucose-6-phosphatase → glucose.

vignettes.q: Glycerol
vignettes.a: dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) ß→ F-1,6-BP →→ glucose.

vignettes.q: Fructose
vignettes.a: F-1-phosphate → dihydroxyacetone phosphate ß→ F-1,6-BP →→ glucose.

vignettes.q: Marfan or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
vignettes.a: MVP or aortic regurg

vignettes.q: Refeeding syndrome
vignettes.a: worry about hypophosphatemia

vignettes.q: Methotrexate MOA
vignettes.a: dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor

vignettes.q: What is main function of vWF?
vignettes.a: bridges platelet GpIb to underlying collagen (adhesion, not aggregation)

vignettes.q: Vitamin K deficiency heme parameters?
vignettes.a: Increased PT + aPTT; bleeding time normal

vignettes.q: Cause of vitamin K deficiency in adults
vignettes.a: chronic Abx knock out colonic flora

vignettes.q: Mechanism of metformin
vignettes.a: “increases glycolysis; decreases gluconeogenesis”

vignettes.q: 46M + alcoholic + Q shows you hypersegmented neutrophil; what’s the vitamin deficiency?
vignettes.a: folate (B9); most common vitamin deficiency; B9 deficiency also the answer for history of tea and toast diet for 6 months, and anti-epileptic use (i.e., valproic acid, phenytoin, carbamazepine); B12 is the answer for veganism, str

vignettes.q: 18M + gets lost hiking in woods for 3 weeks + BMI 27; what electrolyte are we worried about upon restoration of oral intake?
vignettes.a: hypophosphatemia; refeeding syndrome can cause various electrolytes to be low, but phosphate is the main one; mechanism is rapid sequestration of phosphate by glycolytic intermediates as glycolysis resumes.

vignettes.q: 24M + cuts his arm while scraping the BBQ in the backyard; which cell infiltrating into the area of the wound in the acute setting will most likely decrease his risk of a bacterial infection?
vignettes.a: neutrophils; present in acute inflammation; part of innate immunity; phagocytose and kill bacteria via lysosomal hydrolases and H2O2 production.

vignettes.q: 23M + lost in woods for 3 weeks without food + given big meal following rescue + develops arrhythmia; Q wants Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: refeeding syndrome; presents as hypophosphatemia causing arrhythmia; patient can have normal BMI; being given food after a long time without can cause a surge production of glycolytic intermediates that trap phosphate within the l

vignettes.q: 35F + pregnant + high AFP measurement despite correct dates; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: likely neural tube defect (i.e., spina bifida) due to folate (B9) deficiency; B9 required during first 3-4 weeks of gestation for neural tube development; high AFP can also be due to anencephaly, multiple-gestation pregnancy, omph

vignettes.q: 44M + Hx of epistaxis since adolescence + they show you pic of a tongue with a red dot on it + dyspnea + high ejection fraction (75-80%); Dx?
vignettes.a: answer on NBME = pulmonary arteriovenous malformation → presentation is hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu) → USMLE will always show you a red dot on the tongue or fingernail → Q may also mention fatigue (GI

vignettes.q: Postmenopausal woman + stress factor + bulging of LV on echo + hypercontractile LV base; Dx?
vignettes.a: Takotsubo cardiomyopathy → “ballooning of LV” → once again, weird Dx but USMLE likes it.

vignettes.q: Atherosclerosis; where does the process start?
vignettes.a: USMLE answer = endothelial cell, not adipocyte.

vignettes.q: Congenital heart block; Dx in the mom?
vignettes.a: SLE → 1-5% of SLE mothers will have kid with CHB.

vignettes.q: Neonate with supravalvular aortic stenosis; Dx?
vignettes.a: kid has William syndrome (chromosome 7, AD; elfin-like facies; hypercalcemia due to increased vitamin D sensitivity; well-developed verbal skills).

vignettes.q: Left ventricular hypertrophy; USMLE asks arrow Q
vignettes.a: answer = transcription factor c-Jun activity is increased; beta-myosin heavy chain gene expression is increased; endothelin is increased.

vignettes.q: 65M + 2-3-day Hx of severe chest pain + dyspnea + visible pulsation above manubrium + tracheal deviation + murmur in 2nd intercostal space on the right; Dx?
vignettes.a: USMLE answer = aortic aneurysm.

vignettes.q: Dysphagia and/or hoarseness caused by dilated cardiac structure; which structure is dilated?
vignettes.a: answer = left atrium → the hoarseness is due to recurrent laryngeal nerve impingement by LA (Ortner syndrome).

vignettes.q: Location of SA node?
vignettes.a: answer on NBME = “junction of superior vena cava and right atrium.”

vignettes.q: Location of AV node?
vignettes.a: answer on NBME = “inferior to the opening of the coronary sinus” → it is located on the posteroinferior interatrial septum near the coronary sinus.

vignettes.q: Location of coronary sinus?
vignettes.a: answer = “between the opening of the IVC and the tricuspid valve.”

vignettes.q: Neonate with truncus arteriosus; Q is which of the following populations of cells was most likely absent during cardiac development?
vignettes.a: USMLE answer = “ectodermal neural crest” cells.

vignettes.q: Fetal alcohol syndrome + heart/lung fistula; mechanism?
vignettes.a: answer = “failure of migration of neural crest cells.”

vignettes.q: Most common cause of death due to fall or MVA?
vignettes.a: traumatic rupture of the aorta (thoracic).

vignettes.q: Where does rupture of the aorta occur?
vignettes.a: where the ligamentum arteriosum wraps around the top of the descending arch → ligament is taut but arch is more mobile → leads to shearing.

vignettes.q: What will the NBME/USMLE Q say for traumatic rupture
vignettes.a: MVA or fall followed by “widening of the mediastinum on CXR.”

vignettes.q: Tx for traumatic rupture?
vignettes.a: if ascending arch: labetalol + surgery; if descending arch: labetalol only.

vignettes.q: BP different between the arms; Dx?
vignettes.a: aortic dissection or subclavian steal syndrome.

vignettes.q: Most likely cause of dissection?
vignettes.a: HTN, but connective tissue disorders (e.g., Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, MYH11 mutations) also important.

vignettes.q: Tx for dissection?
vignettes.a: if ascending aortic arch, answer = labetalol + surgery; if descending arch, answer = labetalol only (HY, since everyone chooses surgery) → do not choose sodium nitroprusside here.

vignettes.q: High TGAs + high chylomicrons on lab report; Dx + mechanism?
vignettes.a: familial hyperchylomicronemia; answer on USMLE = “deficiency of apolipoprotein C-II” or “deficiency of lipoprotein lipase.”

vignettes.q: Normal TGAs + high LDL on lab report; Dx + mechanism?
vignettes.a: familial hypercholesterolemia; answer on USMLE = “deficiency of LDL receptor.” If total cholesterol is ~3-500s mg/dL, USMLE wants “deficiency”; if total is ~700-1000 mg/dL, the answer = “absence of functional LDL receptors on hepa

vignettes.q: High TGAs + normal LDL on lab report; Dx + mechanism?
vignettes.a: familial hypertriglyceridemia; answer on USMLE = “increased hepatic production of VLDL.”

vignettes.q: “Creamy plasma” on laboratory inspection. Dx?
vignettes.a: familial hyperchylomicronemia.

vignettes.q: Confused old man + temp of 96F + CO high + PCWP low + TPR low; Dx?
vignettes.a: septic shock → dementia increases risk of aspiration pneumonia due to diminished gag reflex (important cause of sepsis) → by all means the vignette might say urinary retention in BPH, or tell you there’s a catheter → also importan

vignettes.q: Patient with infective endocarditis + now has limb weakness or sensory findings; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: septic embolus → answer = give immediate IV antibiotics.

vignettes.q: Patient with alternating tachycardia + bradycardia; Dx?
vignettes.a: sick sinus syndrome → caused by damage to SA node (i.e., due to coronary artery or valvular disease, or autoimmunity, e.g., sarcoidosis) → Tx with atrial pacemaker.

vignettes.q: Diffuse ST-segment elevations on ECG; Dx?
vignettes.a: pericarditis.

vignettes.q: If infective, most likely etiology of pericarditis? (answers are bacteria, parasitic, fungal, etc.); answer = viral
vignettes.a: viruses can cause serous pericarditis.

vignettes.q: 22M after night of heavy partying + central chest pain worse when leaning back + better when leaning forward; Dx?
vignettes.a: serous pericarditis caused by cocaine.

vignettes.q: 68F diabetic + high K + high BUN + high Cr + friction rub in central chest; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: uremic pericarditis → answer on USMLE = immediate hemodialysis.

vignettes.q: 72M + had STEMI two days ago + now has central friction rub; Dx?
vignettes.a: post-MI fibrinous pericarditis.

vignettes.q: 72M + had STEMI 2-6 weeks ago + now has central friction rub; Dx?
vignettes.a: Dressler syndrome (autoantibodies causing fibrinous pericarditis).

vignettes.q: 34F + ulnar deviation + MCP/PIP pain + heart problem; Dx?
vignettes.a: pericarditis → autoimmune diseases like RA and SLE cause serous pericarditis.

vignettes.q: 34F + anti-Scl70 (topoisomerase I) Abs + heart issue; Dx?
vignettes.a: pericardial fibrosis due to systemic sclerosis.

vignettes.q: High-Yield Pearl #36
vignettes.a: Kid + heart tumor = cardiac rhabdomyoma until proven otherwise (usually tuberous sclerosis).

vignettes.q: Adult + heart tumor = cardiac myxoma until proven otherwise (ball-in-valve tumor in the left atrium
vignettes.a: causes murmur that abates when patient is positioned in an unusual way, e.g., on his right side while leaning diagonally).

vignettes.q: 2-year-old boy has cardiac myxoma (correct, not rhabdomyoma) + perioral melanosis (sophisticated way of saying hyperpigmentation around the mouth/lips) + hyperthyroidism; Dx?
vignettes.a: answer = Carney complex → this is asked on the USMLE → classically triad of cardiac myxoma + perioral melanosis + endocrine hypersecretion (classically bilateral pigmented zona fasciculata hyperplasia resulting Cushing syndrome, b

vignettes.q: What does S1 heart sound mean?
vignettes.a: closure of atrioventricular valves (mitral + tricuspid), signifying onset of systole.

vignettes.q: What does S2 heart sound mean?
vignettes.a: closure of semilunar valves (aortic + pulmonic), signifying onset of diastole.

vignettes.q: What does S3 heart sound mean?
vignettes.a: early-diastolic reverberation caused by dilated left ventricle → often synonymous with dilated cardiomyopathy on the USMLE; yes, it can be seen sometimes incidentally in pregnancy and young athletes (due to increased preload), but

vignettes.q: What is a parasternal heave?
vignettes.a: a parasternal heave means the heartbeat can be felt (or sometimes seen) along the left sternal border, usually due to RVH (since the RV is most anterior) → RVH can be seen in ventricular septal defect (VSD), so parasternal heave c

vignettes.q: What is a palpable thrill?
vignettes.a: a palpable thrill is merely a palpable murmur; it carries no additional diagnostic significance; a thrill is seen in grades 4-6 of the heart sounds.

vignettes.q: What are the 6 grades of heart sounds? (not asked on USMLE, but just for your own knowledge with respect to this document)
vignettes.a: 1: very faint; not heard in all positions (“cardiologist only”); 2: faint; heard in all positions; 3: loud, with no thrill; 4: loud with palpable thrill; 5: loud with palpable thrill + can be heard with stethoscope partially off c

vignettes.q: Which murmurs are holosystolic (aka pansystolic)?
vignettes.a: mitral regurgitation (mitral insufficiency; MR) + tricuspid regurgitation (tricuspid insufficiency; TR); ventricular septal defect (VSD).

vignettes.q: Which murmurs are mid-systolic (crescendo-decrescendo systolic)?
vignettes.a: aortic stenosis (AS) + hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (HOCM) + pulmonic stenosis (PS).

vignettes.q: Which murmur has a diastolic opening snap?
vignettes.a: mitral stenosis (MS) → has diastolic opening snap, followed by a mid-late decrescendo diastolic murmur.

vignettes.q: Which murmur has a mid-systolic click?
vignettes.a: mitral valve prolapse (MVP).

vignettes.q: Which murmur can also be described as a late-peaking systolic murmur with an ejection click?
vignettes.a: AS.

vignettes.q: Which murmur is continuous machinery-like?
vignettes.a: patent ductus arteriosus (PDA); can also be AV fistulae.

vignettes.q: Which murmur is pansystolic-pandiastolic?
vignettes.a: PDA (same as continuous machinery-like).

vignettes.q: Which murmur is to-and-fro?
vignettes.a: PDA; same as continuous or pansystolic-pandiastolic.

vignettes.q: Which murmur is fixed splitting of S2?
vignettes.a: atrial septal defect (ASD).

vignettes.q: Which murmurs are holodiastolic (pandiastolic)?
vignettes.a: aortic regurgitation (aortic insufficiency; AR) + pulmonic regurgitation (pulmonic insufficiency; PR).

vignettes.q: Which murmur is pandiastolic and loudest in early-diastole?
vignettes.a: classically AR (decrescendo holodiastolic murmur).
