vignettes.q: Young child + hypocalcemia + harsh systolic murmur at left sternal border; Dx?
vignettes.a: DiGeorge syndrome associated with tetralogy of Fallot → on the USMLE, you should essentially think of ToF and DiGeorge syndrome as interchangeable → you can by all means get other heart defects in DiGeorge, e.g., truncus arteriosu

vignettes.q: How do the heart murmurs change with volume in the heart (i.e., do they get louder/softer with more/less volume)?
vignettes.a: all will get worse / more prominent with more volume in the heart, however MVP and HOCM are the odd ones out; they’ll get worse with less volume in the heart. No change = softer on USMLE. So for example, AS will be no change or so

vignettes.q: 8F + sickle cell + fever + HR of 120 + normal BP + 2/6 mid-systolic murmur at upper right sternal border; Dx?
vignettes.a: transient, functional high-flow murmur secondary to tachycardia → called functional because murmur will subside once HR returns to baseline.

vignettes.q: 13F + Hb of 7 g/dL + HR of 120 + normal BP + 2/6 mid-systolic murmur at upper right sternal border; Dx?
vignettes.a: once again, transient, functional flow murmur → I point this out because students often erroneously think there’s some heart abnormality when they see this type of murmur.

vignettes.q: Aortic stenosis (AS) – what will you auscultate?
vignettes.a: mid-systolic (crescendo-decrescendo systolic) murmur classically at 2nd intercostal space, right sternal border, with radiation to the carotids; however will also show up as “late-peaking systolic murmur with an ejection click.” →

vignettes.q: Who gets AS?
vignettes.a: classically bicuspid aortic valve → can be familial autosomal dominant; also seen in Turner syndrome (45XO) → leads to early calcification of valve in the 40s onward; however a young patient without significant calcification can e

vignettes.q: What about if the patient doesn’t have bicuspid valve?
vignettes.a: AS can still occur in the general population with normal senile calcification seen typically age 70s-80s onward (i.e., incidental 1/6 or 2/6 mid-systolic murmur in otherwise healthy elderly patient).

vignettes.q: How does AS classically present Sx-wise?
vignettes.a: SAD → Syncope, Angina, Dyspnea.

vignettes.q: AS causes what kind of LVH?
vignettes.a: concentric hypertrophy due to pressure overload → can also cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with an S4 heart sound (stiff LV). This is in contrast to aortic regurgitation (aortic insufficiency), which causes eccentric hypertrophy

vignettes.q: What kind of pulse is seen in AS?
vignettes.a: slow-rising pulse (“pulsus parvus et tardus”). Don’t confuse this with AR, which causes bounding pulses with head-bobbing (Q will often say for AR: “pulse has brisk upstroke with precipitous downstroke.”).

vignettes.q: Any weird factoid about AS?
vignettes.a: Heyde syndrome is the combo of AS + angiodysplasia (painless rectal bleeding in elderly due to superficial tortuous vessels on the bowel wall) → shows up on NBME.

vignettes.q: What does HOCM sound like?
vignettes.a: same as AS (mid-systolic murmur, aka crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur).

vignettes.q: What causes HOCM?
vignettes.a: autosomal dominant mutation in beta-myosin heavy-chain gene.

vignettes.q: What’s the structural change in the heart with HOCM?
vignettes.a: asymmetric septal hypertrophy that causes the anterior mitral valve leaflet to block off the LV outflow tract under states of lesser preload → student says, “if the LV outflow tract is blocked off (i.e., where the aortic valve is)

vignettes.q: What’s the cause of death in HOCM?
vignettes.a: ventricular fibrillation due to acute left-heart strain → the “sudden death in young athlete” is not due to an MI → i.e., the patient has clean coronary arteries → do not select coronary artery occlusion as the answer.

vignettes.q: What about if the vignette is sudden death in middle-aged patient with heart disease?
vignettes.a: answer = ischemic heart disease (MI), not HOCM.

vignettes.q: 18M athlete + 2/6 mid-systolic murmur at right sternal border 2nd intercostal space + there is paradoxical splitting of S2 + there is no change in the murmur with Valsalva; Dx?
vignettes.a: ”bicuspid aortic valve” (AS), not HOCM → students say “oh em gee young athlete! HOCM!” → the USMLE will slam you on this and wants you to know that the key way to distinguish between AS and HOCM murmurs is that HOCM gets worse wit

vignettes.q: How to Tx HOCM
vignettes.a: can give propranolol to keep HR from getting too fast (the slower the HR, the more time the heart spends in diastole → more diastolic filling → greater preload → less occlusion of LV outflow tract) → should be noted tangentially t

vignettes.q: Can you explain “splitting of S2”? What does that even mean?
vignettes.a: the aortic valve normally shuts (A2) just before the pulmonic valve (P2), so A2 will occur slightly before P2 → when we talk about changes in splitting of the S2 heart sound (i.e., wide splitting, paradoxical splitting, etc.), if

vignettes.q: What is fixed splitting of S2?
vignettes.a: Super HY for atrial septal defect (ASD) → sometimes can be written as “wide, fixed splitting of S2” → it’s not the “wide” that matters; you need to remember fixed splitting. Wide splitting just means RVH, which can occur due to ch

vignettes.q: What does “splitting of S1 mean”?
vignettes.a: highly unlikely to show up on the USMLE, don’t worry, but for the sake of some people who’d ask, it’s usually seen in right bundle branch block (BBB), which causes delayed closure of the tricuspid valve.

vignettes.q: Maneuvers that decrease blood in the heart
vignettes.a: Valsalva; standing up from seated position; sitting up from supine position; administration of nitrates → any of these will cause MVP + HOCM to get worse; all other murmurs will soften or not change.

vignettes.q: Maneuvers that increase blood in the heart
vignettes.a: Lying down; leg raise while supine; squatting; hand-grip.

vignettes.q: How does Valsalva decrease blood in the heart?
vignettes.a: attempted exhalation against a closed glottis → robust increase in intrathoracic pressure → decreased venous return → decreased cardiac preload.

vignettes.q: How do nitrates decrease blood in the heart?
vignettes.a: Increased venodilation + venous pooling → decreased venous return to the right heart → decreased cardiac preload.

vignettes.q: How does hand-grip increase blood in the heart?
vignettes.a: hand-grip increases afterload → LV cannot eject blood as readily → greater volume of blood left in the LV; it should be pointed out, however, that it would be incorrect to say hand-grip increases preload, as this effect is indirec

vignettes.q: Exceptions regarding handgrip in terms of murmur intensities?
vignettes.a: decreases intensity of aortic stenosis (same as HOCM) + increases intensity of mitral stenosis (in an NBME vignette).

vignettes.q: How does respiration relate to left- vs right-sided murmurs?
vignettes.a: inspiration makes right-sided murmurs worse; exhalation makes left-sided murmurs worse.

vignettes.q: Why does inspiration make right-sided murmurs worse?
vignettes.a: inspiration → decreased intrathoracic pressure → easier for blood to return to the RA → increased venous return → more preload in right heart → worsening of TR, TS, PR, PS.

vignettes.q: Why does inspiration soften left-sided murmurs?
vignettes.a: decreased intrathoracic pressure → increased pulmonary vascular compliance → transient decrease in pulmonary venous return to the LA → decreased LA preload; it should be noted that although RA preload increases, this effect does n

vignettes.q: Why does expiration soften right-sided murmurs?
vignettes.a: expiration → increased intrathoracic pressure → harder for blood to return to the RA → decreased venous return → less preload in right heart → softening of TR, TS, PR, PS.

vignettes.q: Why does expiration intensify left-sided murmurs?
vignettes.a: expiration → increased intrathoracic pressure → decreased pulmonary vascular compliance → transient increase in pulmonary venous return to the LA → increased LA preload; it should be noted that although RA preload decreases, this

vignettes.q: What does VSD sound like?
vignettes.a: Holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border. Can sometimes be described as having palpable thrill or heave. Q can also mention a diastolic rumble in addition to the holosystolic murmur due to volume reverberations (I've s

vignettes.q: If you patch/repair a VSD, what will happen to pressure in the LV, RV, and LA? (up or down arrows)
vignettes.a: repairing a VSD will cause up LV, down RV, down LA → the down LA always confuses people → repair of VSD means less blood entering RV → less blood going back through the lungs to the LA.

vignettes.q: Who gets AVSD (atrioventricular septal defect)?
vignettes.a: Down syndrome (aka endocardial cushion defect).

vignettes.q: What does ASD sound like and why?
vignettes.a: as discussed earlier, fixed splitting of S2 → when you’ve got an ASD, blood is constantly moving L –> R from LA –> RA (pressure is always greater on the left side). So the effects of inhalation/exhalation are minimized in terms of

vignettes.q: What is the fossa ovalis?
vignettes.a: impression in the interatrial septum following closure of the wall during embryological development. Failure of closure leads to patent foramen ovale, which is a type of ASD.

vignettes.q: ASD/VSD in relation to blood pO2?
vignettes.a: USMLE loves making you guess whether you have an ASD or VSD based on info they give you about blood pO2. If they say pO2 increases from SVC to RA, you know the answer is ASD. If they say pO2 increases from RA to RV, you know VSD i

vignettes.q: What does MVP sound like?
vignettes.a: as mentioned earlier, mid-systolic click, over 4th intercostal space, left mid-clavicular line.

vignettes.q: Who gets MVP?
vignettes.a: most common heart murmur; polygenic; usually benign + incidental; can also get in connective tissue disorders (i.e., Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos).

vignettes.q: Murmurs seen in connective tissue disorders
vignettes.a: MVP or AR.

vignettes.q: What does myxomatous degeneration mean?
vignettes.a: answer = MVP → connective tissue degeneration.

vignettes.q: What does MR sound like?
vignettes.a: holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur over 4th intercostal space, left mid-clavicular line; classically radiates to the axilla but by all means doesn’t have to.

vignettes.q: Most common cause of MR?
vignettes.a: ischemia; student says “what do you mean?” → atherosclerosis (i.e., due to diabetes, smoking, HTN, familial) → ischemia → structural heart change (LVH + LV dilatation) + papillary muscle weakening → MVP. This is not the same thing

vignettes.q: 68M + T2DM + dilated heart on CXR + S3 heart sound + 2/6 holosystolic murmur over left chest; Dx?
vignettes.a: MR due to ischemia from atherosclerosis.

vignettes.q: 68M + T2DM + crushing central chest pain + 3 days later has sudden-onset 4/6 holosystolic murmur over left chest; Dx?
vignettes.a: MR from papillary muscle rupture.

vignettes.q: 22M + obvious Marfan syndrome in vignette + stethoscope Q where it starts hovering over aortic valve region; what do you do?
vignettes.a: you’re listening for either AR or MVP, so if you don’t hear anything, just move the stethoscope to the mitral area and you’ll hear the mid-systolic click.

vignettes.q: What does mitral stenosis sound like?
vignettes.a: diastolic opening snap with a decrescendo mid-late diastolic murmur.

vignettes.q: Who gets MS?
vignettes.a: 99% due to previous rheumatic fever as a kid.

vignettes.q: What is mechanism for rheumatic fever?
vignettes.a: type II hypersensitivity against M-protein of Group A Strep (S. pyogenes) → immune system makes antibodies against Group A Strep M-protein that cross-react with the mitral valve (molecular mimicry).

vignettes.q: How does rheumatic fever present?
vignettes.a: JONES (J©NES) → Joints (polyarthritis) + © (myocarditis / mitral valve disease) + Nodules (subcutaneous nodules over bony prominences) + Erythema marginatum (appears annular [ring-like] and serpiginous [snake-like]; important voca

vignettes.q: 12F + red tongue + salmon body rash; Dx and Tx?
vignettes.a: scarlet fever caused by Group A Strep. Must give penicillin to prevent RF.

vignettes.q: RF caused by cutaneous Group A Strep?
vignettes.a: No. Cutaneous infections (i.e., impetigo, erysipelas, cellulitis) can cause post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN), but not RF. RF is caused by pharyngitis / scarlet fever (pharyngitis + body rash).

vignettes.q: 40M + Hx of rheumatic fever as a child; what murmur does he most likely have now?
vignettes.a: MS.

vignettes.q: 40M + Hx of rheumatic fever as a child + rumbling diastolic murmur; which of the following is most likely part of his Hx as a child?
vignettes.a: mitral regurgitation. → this is exceedingly HY → RF causes MR acutely in the child but will cause MS later in life as the valve scars over.

vignettes.q: 12M + fever + sore throat + painful joints + annular skin rash + heart murmur; most likely murmur that he has?
vignettes.a: MR, not MS.

vignettes.q: 12M + fever + sore throat + painful joints + annular skin rash + 2/6 holosystolic murmur over left chest; as an adult, what might we expect in this patient?
vignettes.a: answer = diastolic rumbling murmur with opening snap (MS); even though right now he has MR, later in life it will become MS.

vignettes.q: 33F + pregnant at 20 weeks + new-onset dyspnea + crackles in both lung fields + diastolic rumbling murmur; Dx?
vignettes.a: mitral stenosis presenting symptomatically now that plasma volume has increased ~50% in pregnancy.

vignettes.q: 33F + pregnant at 38 weeks + prominent bilateral ankle pitting edema + dyspnea; Dx?
vignettes.a: peripartum dilated cardiomyopathy (antibody-mediated; idiopathic).

vignettes.q: 33F + pregnant at 32 weeks + mild ankle edema; Dx?
vignettes.a: normal edema seen in pregnancy.

vignettes.q: Does peripartum dilated cardiomyopathy come back in subsequent pregnancies?
vignettes.a: Yes, and it gets worse.

vignettes.q: 33F + peripartum dilated cardiomyopathy; best way to predict prognosis if she goes on to have a future pregnancy?
vignettes.a: TTE (ejection fraction predicts prognosis for future pregnancy).

vignettes.q: If 99% of MS is due to Hx of rheumatic fever, what else can cause it?
vignettes.a: Libman-Sacks endocarditis in SLE is associated with MS. 60% of those with LS endocarditis have anti-phospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant).

vignettes.q: 32F + SLE + diastolic rumbling murmur; most likely characteristic of valvular lesion?
vignettes.a: answer = “verrucous vegetations on both sides of the mitral valve” for LS endocarditis.

vignettes.q: 28M IV drug user + 2/6 holosystolic murmur at left sternal border that increases with inspiration + fever; most likely characteristic of valvular lesion?
vignettes.a: “large, friable, floppy vegetation” → bacterial endocarditis (tricuspid regurg in this case bc IV drug user).

vignettes.q: New-onset murmur + fever; Dx?
vignettes.a: infective endocarditis (IE) until proven otherwise. Unlike rheumatic fever, this is actual bacterial colonization of a heart valve + production of vegetation; RF is a mere antibody response.

vignettes.q: What is acute endocarditis?
vignettes.a: no Hx of valve abnormality; caused almost always by S. aureus; classically seen in IV drug users); classic new-onset murmur + fever presentation.

vignettes.q: What is subacute endocarditis?
vignettes.a: Hx of valve abnormality, i.e., congenital defect, Hx of RF; classically occurs following dental procedures; S. viridans (same thing as S. sanguinis or S. mutans) is classic cause; USMLE wants you to know S. viridan’s production of

vignettes.q: What is HACEK?
vignettes.a: Gram (-) organisms that can cause endocarditis – Hemophilus species, Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans, Cardiobacterium hominis, Eikenella corrodens, and Kingella kingae – the yield on the USMLE is extremely low so you do not

vignettes.q: For IE, blood cultures before Abx, or Abx before blood cultures?
vignettes.a: Always blood cultures (draw three tubes of blood) before giving Abx.

vignettes.q: Empiric Tx for endocarditis?
vignettes.a: Gentamicin (aminoglycoside) PLUS either vancomycin or ampicillin/sulbactam. Add rifampin if patient has prosthetic valve.

vignettes.q: If culture comes back positive for MSSA (not MRSA)?
vignettes.a: switch to six weeks nafcillin (highly simplified, but the bottom line is if MSSA is confirmed, USMLE answer is you switch to the beta-lactam).

vignettes.q: Why switch to beta-lactam if MSSA? Why not just stay on vanc?
vignettes.a: Beta-lactams are way more efficacious than vanc → vanc is actually not a very good drug, but if the organism causing IE is MRSA, it’s first-line.

vignettes.q: Who gets pulmonic stenosis and what does it sound like?
vignettes.a: sounds like aortic stenosis (midsystolic murmur) but increases in intensity with inspiration because it’s right-sided; classically seen as part of tetralogy of Fallot in DiGeorge syndrome; also seen classically in Noonan syndrome

vignettes.q: Who gets pulmonic regurg and what does it sound like?
vignettes.a: sounds like aortic regurg (holodiastolic) but increases with inspiration; rare, but can be seen in endocarditis in IV drug users.

vignettes.q: Who gets tricuspid regurg and what does it sound like?
vignettes.a: same as mitral regurg (holosystolic murmur) but gets louder with inspiration; highest yield cause on USMLE is pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonale (these don't cause pulmonic regurg, so sounds a bit weird). Can also be seen in I

vignettes.q: Who gets tricuspid stenosis and what does it sound like?
vignettes.a: sounds like mitral stenosis presumably (diastolic rumbling murmur, with or without opening snap; but would increase in intensity with inspiration in theory); very rare; I’ve never seen this in any USMLE question.

vignettes.q: How does isolated left heart failure present?
vignettes.a: fluid in the lungs (pulmonary edema) +/- pleural effusion; orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND); depending on the etiology of the heart failure, the structure of the heart will take on different characteristics, but the i

vignettes.q: What is PCWP?
vignettes.a: equal to left atrial pressure; if you stick a catheter through the venous circulation all the way back to the right heart, and then into the pulmonary circulation, and then into a distal pulmonary capillary such that it can’t go a

vignettes.q: What is orthopnea?
vignettes.a: reflective of LH decompensation → requirement to sleep on multiple pillows when supine to prevent fluid buildup in lungs; when supine, there’s greater venous return → greater preload → worsening of dyspnea because the heart cannot

vignettes.q: What is paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND)?
vignettes.a: like orthopnea, reflective of LH decompensation → severe dyspnea that occurs while sleeping due to redistribution of fluid into the lungs; unlike orthopnea, does not immediately subside when sitting up.

vignettes.q: How does isolated right heart failure present?
vignettes.a: right ventricular hypertrophy (unless tricuspid pathology), jugular venous distension (JVD), peripheral edema, hepatosplenomegaly (late).

vignettes.q: What is congestive heart failure (CHF)?
vignettes.a: right heart failure + left heart failure.

vignettes.q: What causes left heart failure?
vignettes.a: systemic HTN, ischemia (atherosclerosis), valvular abnormalities.

vignettes.q: Since left heart failure is the most common cause of right heart failure, what usually causes isolated right heart failure?
vignettes.a: lung pathology → when you have lung pathology causing RH failure, that’s called cor pulmonale.

vignettes.q: “Wait, can you explain cor pulmonale a little more. I’ve heard that a lot but don’t really understand it.”
vignettes.a: when you have a lung condition like COPD, cystic fibrosis, chronic asthma, etc., that leads to RH failure, we call that cor pulmonale. Probably the most important piece of info regarding this condition is that PCWP is normal, whic

vignettes.q: 45M + 70-pack-year Hx of smoking + JVD + peripheral edema; Dx?
vignettes.a: cor pulmonale → signs of RH failure in someone who has lung disease.

vignettes.q: 45M + 70-pack-year Hx of smoking + systemic HTN + JVD + peripheral edema + has crackles in lungs + dilated heart on CXR; Dx?
vignettes.a: congestive heart failure; patient has combo of left and right heart failure signs.

vignettes.q: 25M + cystic fibrosis + JVD + peripheral edema + crackles in lungs; Dx?
vignettes.a: cor pulmonale → crackles due to CF, not LH failure.

vignettes.q: If USMLE asks you for the mechanism of cor pulmonale, what’s the answer?
vignettes.a: pulmonary hypertension → hypoxic vasoconstriction (e.g., in chronic bronchitis, CF) or obliteration of pulmonary parenchyma (emphysema) will cause a backup of blood and pulmonary HTN → increased afterload on RV → starts the proces

vignettes.q: How will USMLE describe pulmonary HTN?
vignettes.a: Increased pulmonary vascular markings; loud P2; tricuspid regurg. Loud P2 means valve slams shut due to high pressure distal to it. Highest yield cause of tricuspid regurg on USMLE is pulmonary hypertension / cor pulmonale..

vignettes.q: 28F + non-smoker + dyspnea + JVD + increased pulmonary vascular markings; Dx?
vignettes.a: primary pulmonary hypertension.

vignettes.q: What is primary pulmonary HTN?
vignettes.a: mutation in BMPR2 gene leading to narrowing of pulmonary vessels + RH failure.

vignettes.q: Tx for pulmonary HTN
vignettes.a: most patients will respond to dihydropyridine CCBs; if fail, can use agents like bosentan (endothelin-1 receptor antagonist), prostaglandins (i.e., epoprostenol), or sildenafil (yes, Viagra).

vignettes.q: 28F + non-smoker + dyspnea + JVD + increased pulmonary vascular markings; which of the following might describe her condition?
vignettes.a: USMLE answer = increased endothelin-1 expression (which makes sense as we know bosentan is a Tx).

vignettes.q: What is dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) + what are the causes?
vignettes.a: heart failure with dilatation of the LV cavity + systolic dysfunction with decreased ejection fraction; classic causes are systemic HTN and ischemia (coronary atherosclerosis), but may also be due to ABCD → Alcohol (EtOH directly

vignettes.q: How does DCM present?
vignettes.a: enlarged cardiac silhouette on CXR (dilated heart), lateralized apex beat (dilated heart); sometimes S3 heart sound; fluid in the lungs (pulmonary edema) +/- pleural effusion; can present with orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspn

vignettes.q: Is HOCM the same thing as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)?
vignettes.a: Once again, no. HOCM is an AD condition (as discussed earlier). HCM is the diastolic dysfunction of the LV that ensues secondary to increased LV afterload (i.e., from systemic HTN, AS, or HOCM) → the USMLE will often give you an S

vignettes.q: What about restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM)?
vignettes.a: diastolic dysfunction with failure of the heart to expand; causes are fibrosis, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, scleroderma, prior radiation, etc.

vignettes.q: What are the important arrows for systolic dysfunction?
vignettes.a: Ejection fraction – decreased; LV pressure – increased; LV volume – increased.

vignettes.q: What are the important arrows for diastolic dysfunction?
vignettes.a: Ejection fraction – normal; LV pressure – increased; LV volume – normal.

vignettes.q: “Can you explain restrictive cardiomyopathy vs constrictive pericarditis?”
vignettes.a: both are characterized by diastolic dysfunction (decreased ability of heart to expand), but in RCM this is due to myocardial stiffness / inelasticity, whereas in CP, the etiology is strictly pericardial, with TB being the most com

vignettes.q: 22M + stab wound to left chest + JVD + muffled heart sounds + hypotension; Dx?
vignettes.a: cardiac tamponade → Beck triad always seen in USMLE Qs = JVD + muffled heart sounds + hypotension; also associated with pulsus paradoxus.

vignettes.q: What is pulsus paradoxus?
vignettes.a: drop in BP of >10 mm Hg on inspiration → reflects inability of the heart to fill → seen in cardiac tamponade, severe lung disease (i.e., severe asthma, COPD), and sometimes severe sleep apnea → my observation is students love to f

vignettes.q: What’s the difference between pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade?
vignettes.a: all tamponades are effusions, but not all effusions are tamponades → a tamponade is merely a pericardial effusion that is associated with hemodynamic decompensation (low BP).

vignettes.q: What determines whether a pericardial effusion becomes a tamponade?
vignettes.a: acuteness of fluid accumulation → tamponades can be a small volume that accumulates quickly, i.e., from a stab wound or post-MI LV free-wall rupture; whereas we could have, e.g., a slowly accumulating chylous or serosanguinous acc

vignettes.q: USMLE asks where pericardial fluid is secreted into (Step 1)
vignettes.a: between the visceral and parietal serous layers → the pericardium = visceral + parietal serous layers + an outer fibrous layer.

vignettes.q: 6M + strong radial pulses + cold lower extremities; Dx?
vignettes.a: coarctation of the aorta; coarctation need not only occur in Turner syndrome.

vignettes.q: What is pre-ductal vs post-ductal coarctation?
vignettes.a: if the coarctation occurs proximal to the ductus arteriosus insertion on the descending aortic arch, it’s called pre-ductal; this will be a very sick/cyanotic baby. In contrast, post-ductal will be the answer for a school-age chil

vignettes.q: Congenital rubella syndrome + cardiovascular defect; Dx?
vignettes.a: PDA → continuous machinery-like murmur, pansystolic-pandiastolic, or to-and-fro; can also present with bounding pulses similar to AR.

vignettes.q: How to close PDA?
vignettes.a: indomethacin (NSAID).

vignettes.q: How to keep PDA open?
vignettes.a: prostaglandin.

vignettes.q: Kid is cyanotic at birth; before surgery, what should be given?
vignettes.a: prostaglandin → open PDA can mask and/or mitigate the effects of cyanotic congenital heart disease.

vignettes.q: Bile acid sequestrants; important info?
vignettes.a: colestipol, cholestyramine, colesevelam → decrease enterohepatic circulation of bile acids → liver needs to make more → liver pulls cholesterol out of the blood in order to convert it to more bile acids → decreases serum LDL → may

vignettes.q: Ezetimibe; mechanism?
vignettes.a: inhibits absorption of cholesterol through the small bowel wall at brush border → does not decrease mortality → just be aware of this drug name + MOA for Step 1.

vignettes.q: Fibrates; important info?
vignettes.a: gemfibrozil, fenofibrate → upregulate lipoprotein lipase (LPL) → increases TGA clearance out of blood → answer on the USMLE is TGAs >300 mg/dL; first-line agent to treat severe hyper-TGAs → also upregulates PPAR-alpha, which incre

vignettes.q: Why is myositis/rhabdomyolysis more likely when fibrates are combined with statins?
vignettes.a: USMLE wants “inhibition of P-450 enzymes” as the answer (fibrates inhibit P-450).

vignettes.q: Statins; mechanism?
vignettes.a: competitive, reversible inhibition of HMG-CoA reductase → this secondarily causes upregulation of hepatic LDL receptors → both mechanisms decrease serum LDL → statins decrease morality, not because of their LDL-lowering effect (be

vignettes.q: Orlistat; MOA
vignettes.a: pancreatic lipase inhibitor → sometimes used to Tx obesity → can cause fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies + steatorrhea.

vignettes.q: Evolocumab + alirocumab; MOA?
vignettes.a: PCSK9 inhibitors → Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 is an enzyme that breaks down LDL receptors → therefore these drugs prevent breakdown of LDL receptors and decrease LDL cholesterol by enabling greater clearance → t

vignettes.q: Digoxin; MOA?
vignettes.a: inhibits Na/K-ATPase pump → leads to buildup of Na inside the cardiac myocyte → leads to indirect inhibition of Na/Ca-ATPase pump bc the buildup of intracellular Na disfavors the inward movement of Na via this latter pump → theref

vignettes.q: Yellow wavy vision + drug OD? Dx?
vignettes.a: digoxin toxicity.

vignettes.q: How to Tx digoxin toxicity?
vignettes.a: normalize potassium + give anti-digoxin Fab fragments + give Mg.

vignettes.q: Electrolyte disturbance causing digoxin toxicity?
vignettes.a: hypokalemia (digoxin normally binds to extracellular K+ binding site on the cell, so low K+ means more digoxin binding).

vignettes.q: What are the Ia Na channel blockers?
vignettes.a: “the Queen Proclaims Diso’s pyramid.” → Quinidine, Procainamide, Disopyramide → you need to know quinidine causes cinchonism (think “quinchonism”), which is tinnitus + headache → procainamide causes DILE (drug-induced lupus erythe

vignettes.q: What are the Ib Na channel blockers?
vignettes.a: “I’d buy Liddy’s Mexican Tacos.” → Lidocaine, Mexiletine, Tocainide → highest yield detail is that they cause “CNS stimulation/depression”; in other words, you’ll get a Q where a patient was started on an anti-arrhythmic and gets,

vignettes.q: What are the Ic Na channel blockers?
vignettes.a: Flecainide, Encainide, Propafenone → highest yield detail is that flecainide is the first-line anti-arrhythmic to Tx atrial fibrillation in the absence of structural or coronary artery disease → Ics do not change action potential

vignettes.q: What are the type II anti-arrhythmics?
vignettes.a: beta-blockers → HY mnemonic for agents that antagonize beta-1 only are “A BEAM of beta-blockers” → Atenolol, Bisoprolol, Esmolol, Acebutolol, Metoprolol → metoprolol used largely as rate control for atrial fibrillation + flutter.

vignettes.q: What are the beta-blockers that also act on alpha-receptors?
vignettes.a: carvedilol + labetalol antagonize both alpha- and beta-receptors.

vignettes.q: Which beta-blockers decrease mortality in heart failure?
vignettes.a: nebivolol, carvedilol, bisoprolol, metoprolol XR.

vignettes.q: Notable use of timolol?
vignettes.a: topical solution used for glaucoma → decreases aqueous humour production.

vignettes.q: Notable side-effects of beta-blockers?
vignettes.a: patients with depression + sexual dysfunction.

vignettes.q: Contraindications to beta-blockers
vignettes.a: severe lung disease (asthma w/ Hx of hospitalization or O2 use; COPD); severe or psychotic depression; 2nd or 3rd degree heart block; symptomatic bradycardia; use cautiously in severe diabetes due to masking of hypoglycemic events

vignettes.q: Tx for beta-blocker overdose?
vignettes.a: glucagon.

vignettes.q: Important point about BB in relation to pheochromocytoma?
vignettes.a: Never give beta-blocker before alpha-blocker; always give phenoxybenzamine (irreversible alpha-blocker) before beta-blocker in pheo.

vignettes.q: What are the type III anti-arrhythmics?
vignettes.a: potassium channel blockers → amiodarone, dronedarone, sotalol, ibutilide, dofetilide → often used in ventricular arrhythmias and in patients being defibrillated unsuccessfully → can be used in atrial fibrillation for rhythm contro

vignettes.q: Points about amiodarone?
vignettes.a: causes TdP, pulmonary fibrosis, drug-induced thyroid dysfunction (~40% iodine by weight), corneal deposits, blue-grey skin discoloration → do PFTs, TFTs, LFTs before commencing amiodarone.

vignettes.q: What are the type IV anti-arrhythmics?
vignettes.a: non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers → verapamil, diltiazem → verapamil is aka non-dihydropyridine CCB → acts selectively on cardiac (nodal) tissue; in contrast, dihydropyridines like nifedipine act on vascular smooth musc

vignettes.q: What is ivabradine?
vignettes.a: inhibits myocardial “funny” Na channels (phase IV of AP) → may be attempted in select patients with stable angina who cannot take beta-blockers → can cause “luminous phenomenon,” which is brightness in an area of the visual field.

vignettes.q: What is sacubitril?
vignettes.a: neprilysin inhibitor → neprilysin is an enzyme that breaks down ANP and BNP → therefore sacubitril can be used as an antihypertensive to allow the kidney to excrete sodium and water → sacubitril usually used in combination with va

vignettes.q: Tx of heart failure?
vignettes.a: Start with ACEi, ARB, or sacubitril + ACEi/ARB (beta-blocker first is wrong answer on USMLE) → then make sure patient is euvolemic with furosemide → then add beta-blocker (metoprolol XR, bisoprolol, carvedilol, or nebivolol; these

vignettes.q: Super important point about above sequence?
vignettes.a: Digoxin and furosemide DO NOT decrease mortality (USMLE is obsessed with that point).

vignettes.q: What is ranolazine?
vignettes.a: sodium channel blocker used rarely for angina.

vignettes.q: Mechanism of nitrates?
vignettes.a: NO activates guanylyl cyclase → increased cGMP production → increased protein kinase G → increased dephosphorylation of myosin light-chain kinase → vascular smooth muscle relaxation → work on veins >> arteries → venodilatation is

vignettes.q: What about sodium nitroprusside?
vignettes.a: works on both arteries and veins → used in hypertensive emergencies → can cause cyanide toxicity → if patient with HTN emergency gets confusion after administration of SN, the answer = cyanide toxicity; if patient has confusion be

vignettes.q: What is fenoldopam?
vignettes.a: dopamine 1 (D1) receptor agonist → dilates both renal afferent and efferent arterioles → used to maintain renal perfusion in hypertensive emergency.

vignettes.q: 66M + back pain + hypercalcemia + renal insufficiency + Q shows you a pic of a white, fibrotic-appearing heart; Dx?
vignettes.a: answer = cardiac amyloidosis → seen classically in multiple myeloma (renal insufficiency is often renal amyloidosis).

vignettes.q: Hypovolemic shock arrows
vignettes.a: CO down, VR down, TPR up, PCWP down (or normal).

vignettes.q: Cardiogenic shock arrows
vignettes.a: CO down, VR down, TPR up, PCWP up.

vignettes.q: Septic + anaphylactic shock arrows
vignettes.a: CO up, VR up, TPR down, PCWP normal.

vignettes.q: Neurogenic shock + adrenal crisis arrows
vignettes.a: CO down, VR down, TPR down, PCWP normal.

vignettes.q: “Can you explain ‘autoregulation’?”
vignettes.a: Carotid sinus baroreceptors (think “sinus pressure”) are stretch-dependent (higher BP = more stretch = more firing of CN IX; lower BP = less stretch = less firing of IX) → so if, for instance, there is high BP, we get increased CN

vignettes.q: “I’m still a little confused though. If patient is hypovolemic, then what happens in terms of autoregulation?”
vignettes.a: decreased stretch of carotid sinus baroreceptors → DECREASED afferent firing of CN IX → decreased efferent CN X firing → decreased ACh binding to M2 receptors at atria + increased sympathetic outflow → HR increases.

vignettes.q: Mediator that causes cardiac pain?
vignettes.a: Adenosine. Produced from ATP breakdown. In the setting of ischemia, adenosine builds up, causing cardiac pain.

vignettes.q: Main regulators of coronary blood flow?
vignettes.a: O2, CO2, adenosine, NO. But adenosine is most important. Q will tell you norepinephrine was administered, resulting in reduced coronary artery blood flow. Then very soon after blood flow drastically increases. They ask what’s resp

vignettes.q: Main regulators of skeletal muscle blood flow?
vignettes.a: “CHALK” → CO2, H+, adenosine, lactate, K+.

vignettes.q: Q asks if coronary blood flow is greater or equal during systole or diastole when person is at rest vs exercising
vignettes.a: answer = coronary blood flow is: diastole > systole regardless if patient is at rest or exercising.

vignettes.q: ST-elevations in leads II, III, aVF; which vessel is affected?
vignettes.a: answer = posterior descending artery → supplies inferior portion of the heart → sometimes the answer will just be straight-up “right coronary artery” (~70-80% of the time the PDA comes off the RCA).

vignettes.q: ST-elevations in leads V1, V2, V3; which vessel is affected?
vignettes.a: left anterior descending artery (LAD; aka anterior interventricular artery) → supplies anterior heart.

vignettes.q: ST-depressions in leads V1, V2, V3; which vessel is affected?
vignettes.a: posterior descending artery → posterior infarcts can present as reciprocal ST-depression in the anterior leads.

vignettes.q: ST-elevations in V4, V5, V6; which vessel is affected?
vignettes.a: left circumflex artery (LCx) → supplies left lateral heart.

vignettes.q: Hypokinesis of the apex of the heart on echo; which vessel is affected?
vignettes.a: LAD → supplies apex.

vignettes.q: Wide-complex tachycardia
vignettes.a: ventricular tachycardia (VT).

vignettes.q: Tx for SVT
vignettes.a: vagal/carotid massage (“vagal maneuvers”) first; if doesn’t work, then adenosine.

vignettes.q: Tx of VT
vignettes.a: anti-arrhythmics, e.g., amiodarone.

vignettes.q: Tx of SVT or VT in setting of coma or low BP
vignettes.a: direct-current countershock.

vignettes.q: Tx of first-degree heart-block or second-degree Mobitz I (Wenckebach)
vignettes.a: observe.

vignettes.q: Tx of second-degree Mobitz II or third-degree heart block
vignettes.a: pacemaker.

vignettes.q: First-degree heart-block
vignettes.a: PR-interval >200 milliseconds.

vignettes.q: Mobitz I
vignettes.a: gradually prolonging PR-interval before a QRS drops.

vignettes.q: Mobitz II
vignettes.a: no gradual prolongation of PR-interval; QRS randomly drops.

vignettes.q: Third-degree
vignettes.a: HR super slow at 30-40; no relation between p-waves and QRS complexes.

vignettes.q: Infective causes of third-degree
vignettes.a: Lyme disease, congenital lupus, diphtheria.

vignettes.q: Mechanism of Goodpasture syndrome?
vignettes.a: antibodies against type IV collagen → “2, 3, 4… 2, 3, 4… 2, 3, 4. The Goodpasture is marching in the field, 2, 3, 4!”→ Type 2 hypersensitivity against the alpha-3 chains of type 4 collagen. Presents as male 20s-40s with hemoptysis

vignettes.q: Hematuria + hemoptysis + “head-itis” (mastoiditis, sinusitis, otitis, nasal septal perforation)
vignettes.a: Wegener granulomatosis.

vignettes.q: Annoying new name for Wegener
vignettes.a: granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

vignettes.q: Dx of Wegener
vignettes.a: c-ANCA (anti-PR3; anti-proteinase 3).

vignettes.q: Asthma + eosinophilia
vignettes.a: Churg-Strauss.

vignettes.q: Annoying new name for CS
vignettes.a: eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

vignettes.q: Dx of CS
vignettes.a: p-ANCA (anti-MPO; anti-myeloperoxidase).

vignettes.q: Hematuria in isolation + p-ANCA in serum
vignettes.a: microscopic polyangiitis (MP).

vignettes.q: Severe renal disease in Wegener or Goodpasture or MP
vignettes.a: rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (crescentic).

vignettes.q: 44M + hematuria + hemoptysis
vignettes.a: Goodpasture syndrome.

vignettes.q: 44M + hematuria + hemopytisis + head-itis
vignettes.a: Wegener.

vignettes.q: What is polyarteritis nodosa
vignettes.a: medium-vessel vasculitis characterized by immune complex deposition in vascular walls + fibrinoid necrosis (can be described as “segmental, ischemic necrosis”).

vignettes.q: Polyarteritis nodosa is associated with what infection?
vignettes.a: 30% of patients are HepB positive.

vignettes.q: What do you see on renal artery angiogram in PN
vignettes.a: “beads on a string” (similar to fibromuscular dysplasia, although completely unrelated diseases).

vignettes.q: Kid jumps into cold lake; what happens to (arrows) central blood volume, ADH, and ANP levels?
vignettes.a: answer = central blood volume increases, ADH decreases, ANP increases → cold means increased alpha-1 agonism in arterioles to constrict distally to retain heat → increased blood volume in larger vessels → increased right atrial fi

vignettes.q: Medial malleolus ulcer + hyperpigmentation of lower legs; Dx?
vignettes.a: chronic venous insufficiency

vignettes.q: Punched-out ulcer on foot + intermittent claudication; Dx?
vignettes.a: arterial insufficiency (peripheral vascular disease)

vignettes.q: What causes venous insufficiency?
vignettes.a: valvular incompetence (most commonly familial), resulting in venous reflux + insufficiency. Patient need not have varicose veins. Venous insufficiency can present as hyperpigmentation due to hemosiderin deposition and Hx of DVT.

vignettes.q: What causes arterial insufficiency
vignettes.a: atherosclerosis (diabetes, followed by smoking, are the two most acceleratory risk factors; hypertension is the most common risk factor)

vignettes.q: Varicose veins and venous insufficiency same thing?
vignettes.a: varicose veins are one of the mere presentations of venous insufficiency, so yes, patients with varicose veins have venous insufficiency.

vignettes.q: Tx for arterial insufficiency
vignettes.a: exercise regimen first, THEN cilostazol (phosphodiesterase 3 inhibitor)

vignettes.q: What must you do before starting the exercise regimen in the Tx of arterial insufficiency
vignettes.a: ECG stress test to ascertain patient’s exercise tolerance.

vignettes.q: What if patient has abnormal baseline ECG (e.g., BBB)
vignettes.a: do echo stress test instead.

vignettes.q: Patient with CVD is on various medications + has hyperkalemia; why?
vignettes.a: ACEi, ARB, and spironolactone all can cause hyperkalemia.

vignettes.q: Patient with CVD is on various medications + hypokalemia; why?
vignettes.a: furosemide (Loop diuretic)

vignettes.q: When do we start patients on furosemide?
vignettes.a: to fluid unload (dyspnea in heart failure or peripheral edema)

vignettes.q: Patient is started on furosemide + still has fluid overload; what’s the next diuretic to use
vignettes.a: spironolactone → essentially furosemide causes increased K wasting, so we must give a potassium-sparing diuretic to balance the effect (spironolactone).

vignettes.q: What’s the MOA of spironolactone
vignettes.a: aldosterone receptor antagonist.

vignettes.q: Side-effects of spironolactone
vignettes.a: hyperkalemia; gynecomastia.

vignettes.q: When do we give patients spironolactone apart from as a step-up from Loops?
vignettes.a: added onto heart failure management after a patient is already on ACEi (or ARB) + beta-blocker. In other words, for heart failure: give ACEi (or ARB) first, then add beta-blocker, then add spironolactone.

vignettes.q: Major side-effects of beta-blockers
vignettes.a: depression + sexual dysfunction (avoid in these patients)

vignettes.q: Major side-effect of naproxen
vignettes.a: fluid retention (edema) due to increased renal retention of sodium.

vignettes.q: What is naproxen?
vignettes.a: NSAID that the USMLE is obsessed with for some reason.

vignettes.q: Why might NSAIDs cause fluid retention / renal retention of sodium?
vignettes.a: knocking out COX → decreased prostaglandin synthesis → decreased renal afferent arteriolar dilatation → decreased renal blood flow → PCT of kidney compensates for perceived low blood volume by increasing Na reabsorption → water fo

vignettes.q: Most common cause of carotid plaques?
vignettes.a: HTN → the strong systolic impulse from the heart pounds the carotids --> endothelial damage --> atherosclerosis.

vignettes.q: What % of people over age 80 have AF?
vignettes.a: 8% of people over age 80 have AF, which is why age is a huge risk factor. In other words, if the vignette says the guy is 58, AF is probably less likely just based on shear probability, regardless of hypertensive status." And, onc

vignettes.q: High-Yield Pearl #267
vignettes.a: For the actual Tx of the AF, we do rate control before rhythm control (the management is actually heavily involved, but for the USMLE know the following): o Rate control: beta-blocker first-line (metoprolol). If beta-blocker avoid

vignettes.q: 68F + diabetic + diffuse, dull abdo pain 1-2 hours after meals; Dx?
vignettes.a: chronic mesenteric ischemia due to atherosclerosis of SMA or IMA, not duodenal ulcer (if they want the latter, they’ll say 29M from Indonesia) → essentially stable angina of the bowel.

vignettes.q: 68F + Hx of intermittent claudication + CABG + abdo pain 1-2 hours after eating meals; Dx?
vignettes.a: chronic mesenteric ischemia.

vignettes.q: 78M + Hx of AF + acute-onset severe abdo pain “out of proportion to physical exam”; Dx?
vignettes.a: acute mesenteric ischemia due to embolus (LA mural thrombus that’s launched off to SMA or IMA).

vignettes.q: 66F + has episode of ventricular fibrillation + defibrillated + now has severe abdo pain; Dx?
vignettes.a: acute mesenteric ischemia → defibrillation likely launched off LA mural thrombus the patient had (even if no overt Afib).

vignettes.q: 68F + diabetic + Hx of diffuse, dull abdo pain 1-2 hours after meals + now has 2-day Hx of severe abdo pain out of proportion to physical exam; Dx?
vignettes.a: acute on chronic mesenteric ischemia due to ruptured atherosclerotic plaque (akin to an “MI” of the bowel).

vignettes.q: Dx of acute + chronic mesenteric ischemia?
vignettes.a: USMLE answer = mesenteric angiography.

vignettes.q: 45M + has FHx of DCM + cirrhosis + generalized hyperpigmentation; his heart may show accumulation of what?
vignettes.a: answer = Iron. Diagnosis is hereditary hemochromatosis, which can present as “bronze diabetes” → 1) increased glucose levels + 2) hyperpigmentation + 3) other miscellaneous finding like cardiomyopathy, or pseudogout, or infertilit

vignettes.q: 92F dies in her sleep; heart is most likely to show what on biopsy?
vignettes.a: lipofuscin → yellow-brown “age pigment” that reflects autodigestion of intracellular lipid residues by lysosomal enzymes.

vignettes.q: Post-MI dyspnea; mechanism for fluid in lungs?
vignettes.a: answer = “increased pulmonary capillary pressure” → the wrong answer is “increased permeability of pulmonary capillaries.” The former refers to transudate; the latter refers to exudate.

vignettes.q: Left dominant coronary circulation in someone with STEMI in leads II, III, and aVF; what is the pathway of vessels here?
vignettes.a: firstly, need to identify this as inferior infarct; then identify that the posterior descending artery (PDA) supplies the inferior portion of the heart; Q gives you “LCA,” “LCx” and “PDA” as answers in different order; answer = LC

vignettes.q: Patient has end-systolic volume of 100 mL + end-diastolic volume is 150 mL; what’s the ejection fraction in terms of %?
vignettes.a: answer = (EDV – ESV / EDV) = (150 – 100 / 150) = 50/150 = 33.3% → USMLE will ask you to calculate.

vignettes.q: What is normal ejection fraction?
When might the Q say the EF is high?
vignettes.a: sometimes in high-output cardiac failure due to AV shunts, i.e., in Paget disease of bone, hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (pulmonary AVM), or patient with previous dialysis + shunt.

vignettes.q: 29F + SOB with exertion + S3 heart sound + laterally displaced apex beat + CXR shows cardiomegaly + Kerley B lines + TTE shows EF of 30%; Dx?
vignettes.a: answer = CHF → you’re supposed to say, “Wait, in a young patient without any specific disorder? And they don’t mention pregnancy either?” → but the rest of the presentation is overwhelming, so you need to know this is ultra-classi

vignettes.q: NBME Q on CHF asks for (up or down) for LV stroke volume, LA pressure, and TPR
vignettes.a: answer = LV stroke volume down; LA pressure up; TPR up.

vignettes.q: 56M + MI + has coronary angioplasty to restore blood flow + now has idioventricular arrhythmia; why?
vignettes.a: answer = “generation of reactive oxygen species”; this refers to reperfusion injury.

vignettes.q: 32F + abdominal bruit + BP of 160/100. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑ or ↓) for Na+, K+, pH, bicarb, and CO2?
vignettes.a: ↑ Na+ , ↓ K+ , ↑ pH, ↑ bicarb, ↑ CO2. — Diagnosis is fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD), which is tunica media proliferation, generally in women 20s-50s. This results in decreased renal perfusion → renin secretion by JGC → RAAS activat

vignettes.a: ↓ Carotid sinus baroreceptor firing rate, ↓ vagus nerve firing rate, ↑ sinoatrial sympathetic activity. — The feedback loop for autoregulation is: • Carotid sinus baroreceptors (sense blood pressure/volume) → afferent cranial nerv

vignettes.a: ↔ PCWP, ↑ endothelin-1, ↑ pulmonary vascular resistance, ↔ systemic vascular resistance. — Diagnosis is primary pulmonary hypertension, usually caused by mutations in BMPR2. • Vignette will usually be a female in her 20s-30s who’s

vignettes.a: ↑ Left ventricular pressure, ↓ right ventricular pressure, ↓ left atrial pressure. — When a VSD is repaired, less blood is leaving the left ventricle for the right ventricle, so left ventricular pressure increases and right ventri

vignettes.a: ↔ Superior vena cava pO2, ↔ right atrial pO2, ↑ right ventricular pO2, ↔ left ventricular pO2, pulmonary artery pO2. — The diagnosis is VSD. It is classically described as a holosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border. •

vignettes.a: ↓ Venous return, ↓ carotid sinus baroreceptor activity, ↓ cerebral blood flow. — Moving from supine to standing / sitting up decreases venous return (due to increased venous pooling). • This means less central blood volume and les

vignettes.a: ↑ Left ventricular end-diastolic volume, ↓ cardiac output, ↑ systemic vascular resistance. — Propranolol is a non-specific beta-blocker at both b1 and b2 receptors. • b1 blockade results in lower heart rate (chronotropy) and contr

vignettes.a: ↓ Systemic vascular resistance, ↑ heart rate, ↑ left ventricular ejection fraction. — In contrast to nitrates, which dilate veins, nifedipine, a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, dilates peripheral arterioles. • Dilation of

vignettes.a: ↓ LV ejection fraction, ↑ LV end-diastolic pressure, ↑ LV end-diastolic volume. — The patient has dilated cardiomyopathy and systolic dysfunction. • S3 = dilated left ventricle = volume overload (preload) = systolic dysfunction (i

vignettes.a: ↑ cardiac output, ↓ systemic vascular resistance, ↓ PCWP. — Diagnosis is anaphylactic shock, a type I hypersensitivity response. • What I’ve seen in NBME Qs is: they want IgE crosslinking on surface of mast cells and basophils → c

vignettes.a: ↑ cardiac output, ↓ systemic vascular resistance, ↓ PCWP. — Diagnosis is septic shock. • Systemic vascular resistance is decreased due to TNFa-mediated peripheral vasodilation. • Fever is due to interleukin-1. • PCWP can be low or

vignettes.q: 22M + bleeding from gunshot wound + drowsy. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑ or ↓) for cardiac output, systemic vascular resistance, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure?
vignettes.a: ↓ cardiac output, ↑ systemic vascular resistance, ↓ PCWP. — Diagnosis is hypovolemic shock. • Loss of blood volume → low cardiac output → decreased stretch of carotid sinus baroreceptors → decreased CN IX (glossopharyngeal) firing

vignettes.q: 9M + viral infection + low blood pressure + HR 120 + chest x-ray shows enlarged heart and hazy lung fields + red urine. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑ or ↓) for cardiac output, systemic vascular resistance, and p
vignettes.a: ↓ cardiac output, ↑ systemic vascular resistance, ↑ PCWP. — Diagnosis is cardiogenic shock secondary to dilated cardiomyopathy due to coxsackie B virus. • I’m really reinforcing PCWP in relation to shock here. • Patien

vignettes.q: ECG shows diffuse ST-segment elevations
vignettes.a: pericarditis

vignettes.q: Pericarditis Tx
vignettes.a: NSAID, or steroid, or colchicine

vignettes.q: Central chest pain worse when supine; better when leaning forward
vignettes.a: pericarditis

vignettes.a: pericardial tamponade / pericardial effusion

vignettes.q: Pulsus paradoxus (drop in systolic BP >10 mm with inspiration)
vignettes.a: cardiac tamponade or severe asthma

vignettes.q: Beck triad
vignettes.a: hypotension + muffled heart sounds + JVD → pericardial tamponade

vignettes.q: Tx of tamponade
vignettes.a: pericardiocentesis or pericardial window

vignettes.q: Tamponade
vignettes.a: do echo before pericardiocentesis if both listed

vignettes.q: Tx for TCA toxicity
vignettes.a: sodium bicarb → dissociates drug from myocardial sodium channels

vignettes.q: Hx of hypertension + dementia + sensory/motor disturbance
vignettes.a: vascular dementia

vignettes.q: New-onset murmur + fever
vignettes.a: endocarditis till proven otherwise

vignettes.q: Empiric Tx for endocarditis
vignettes.a: vancomycin or ampicillin/sulbactam, PLUS gentamicin

vignettes.a: VSD

vignettes.q: Holosystolic murmur at left sternal border PLUS diastolic rumble
vignettes.a: also VSD

vignettes.q: To-and-fro murmur
vignettes.a: PDA

vignettes.q: Continuous, machinery-like murmur
vignettes.a: PDA

vignettes.q: Congenital rubella syndrome
vignettes.a: PDA

vignettes.q: Heart problem in William syndrome
vignettes.a: supravalvular aortic stenosis

vignettes.q: Bicuspid aortic valve
vignettes.a: aortic stenosis

vignettes.q: Mid-systolic (crescendo-decrescendo) murmur + gets worse with Valsalva
vignettes.a: HOCM

vignettes.q: Mid-systolic (crescendo-decrescendo) murmur + no change or softens with Valsalva
vignettes.a: aortic stenosis

vignettes.q: Myxomatous degeneration of mitral valve
vignettes.a: mitral valve prolapse

vignettes.q: Rheumatic heart disease acutely (onset of Group A Strep infection)
vignettes.a: mitral regurg

vignettes.q: Rheumatic heart disease later on (years after infection)
vignettes.a: mitral stenosis

vignettes.q: Late-peaking systolic murmur with ejection click
vignettes.a: another way they describe aortic stenosis

vignettes.q: Bounding pulses + massively wide pulse pressure
vignettes.a: aortic regurg

vignettes.q: Brisk upstroke + precipitous downstroke of pulse
vignettes.a: aortic regurg

vignettes.q: Syncope + angina + dyspnea (SAD)
vignettes.a: aortic stenosis

vignettes.q: Dyspnea in second trimester of pregnancy
vignettes.a: mitral stenosis

vignettes.q: Dyspnea late in pregnancy
vignettes.a: peripartum cardiomyopathy

vignettes.q: Tx of oropharyngeal candida
vignettes.a: nystatin mouthwash

vignettes.q: Tx of esophageal candidiasis
vignettes.a: oral azole, not nystatin mouthwash

vignettes.q: Tx of vaginal candidiasis
vignettes.a: topical nystatin before trying oral azole

vignettes.q: CREST syndrome lung pathology?
vignettes.a: can cause pulmonary fibrosis → pulmonary hypertension

vignettes.q: Normotensive old pt + TIA or stroke or retinal artery occlusion
vignettes.a: atrial fibrillation

vignettes.q: ADPKD
vignettes.a: which do we do for screening, MR angiogram circle of Willis, or serial blood pressure checks? → answer = serial blood pressure checks → don’t do MR angiogram screening unless FHx of aneurysm → most patients get high blood pressure

vignettes.q: MVA + bruising/pain over the sternum +/- rib fractures
vignettes.a: myocardial contusion

vignettes.q: MVA + bruising/pain over sternum + pulmonary infiltrates + O2 sats get worse when saline is given
vignettes.a: myocardial contusion

vignettes.q: Important point about Mx of myocardial contusion
vignettes.a: do troponins + must monitor for arrhythmia

vignettes.q: Pt has tachy + diaphoresis + diarrhea + tricuspid valve lesion
vignettes.a: carcinoid syndrome

vignettes.q: Which decreases risk of stroke more, smoking cessation or BP control?
vignettes.a: BP control (USMLE wants lisinopril as the answer, not smoking cessation); for stroke, answer is always hypertension as worse risk factor

vignettes.q: How do you Dx venous insufficiency?
vignettes.a: duplex ultrasound of the calves showing stasis and/or occlusive disease (the latter may result from venous insufficiency or cause it)

vignettes.q: Tx for venous insufficiency
vignettes.a: compression stockings

vignettes.q: What if the patient gets stable angina after merely walking up a flight of stairs
vignettes.a: skip stress test and go straight to myocardial perfusion scan (myocardial scintigraphic assay); this is answer on the NBME.

vignettes.q: Patient has severe ischemia on stress test or myocardial perfusion scan
vignettes.a: do coronary angiography → then do coronary artery bypass grafting if three-vessel disease, OR two-vessel disease + diabetic, OR single-vessel disease if it’s the left main coronary.

vignettes.q: When do we use “regular” metoprolol
vignettes.a: classically first-line for atrial fibrillation rate control.

vignettes.q: When do we use propranolol
vignettes.a: migraine prophylaxis, tachycardia in hyperthyroidism (decreases peripheral conversion of T4 to T3), esophageal varices prophylaxis, akathisia caused by anti- psychotics, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to increase preload (HOCM and MV

vignettes.q: 72M + intermittent claudication + absent distal pulses + Hx of coronary artery bypass grafting + high BP that’s been gradually increasing past two years; Dx?
vignettes.a: renal artery stenosis

vignettes.q: Tx for hypertension?
vignettes.a: if patient has pre-diabetes, diabetes, or any cardiovascular/cerebrovascular disease of any kind → answer = ACEi or ARB first. These agents decrease morbidity and mortality in these patient groups. If patient has none of the above

vignettes.q: Tx for pulmonary hypertension
vignettes.a: most patients respond to dihydropyridine CCBs (e.g., nifedipine).

vignettes.q: 28F non-smoker has loud P2 + RVH; Dx?
vignettes.a: primary pulmonary hypertension

vignettes.q: VSD is repaired with a prosthetic patch; how will LV, RV, and LA pressures change?
vignettes.a: LV pressure goes up, RV pressure goes down, LA pressure goes down. → student says “the LA one is weird tho why is that?” Because if you decrease the LV → RV shunt, then there’s less blood circulating back to the LA → decreased LA

vignettes.a: cilostazol; both cilostazol and dipyridamole inhibit platelet phosphodiesterase; cilostazol used for intermittent claudication after exercise regimen fails; dipyridamole-thallium is a type of pharmacologic stress test (answer on U

vignettes.q: 40F + goes for run; which of the following regarding diastole and systole represent her coronary artery filling pressure at rest vs while running?
vignettes.a: at rest: diastole > systole; while running: diastole > systole; answer is the same for both; the coronary arteries fill during diastole irrespective of how fast the HR is.

vignettes.a: costochrondritis → MSK because changes with position (pericarditis only exception when cardiac).

vignettes.q: 80M + atrial fibrillation + severe abdominal pain + physical exam shows mild tenderness to palpation; Dx?
vignettes.a: acute mesenteric ischemia; pain out of proportion to physical exam is characteristic; left atrial mural thrombus from AF launched off to SMA or IMA.

vignettes.a: When in doubt, “smoking cessation” is the most common overall answer on NBME/USMLE for the #1 way to improve general health. The stem might be a long, rambling vignette where the dude is overweight, smokes, has high blood pressure

vignettes.a: smoking. As we said above, the order of importance for atherosclerosis leading to MI is diabetes → smoking → HTN. This is asked on one of the NBME exams, where it’s a 1-2-liner Q followed by smoking being correct over HTN.

vignettes.q: 60F + diabetic + HTN + smoker + about to undergo hip surgery; Q asks for the best way to reduce perioperative MI risk
vignettes.a: smoking cessation. As mentioned above, smoking cessation is #1 way to reduce peri- and post-operative MI risk, since acute smoking cessation improves myocardial oxygenation and coronary autoregulation.

vignettes.q: 65F + 80-pack-year Hx of smoking + CXR shows hyperinflation + loud P2 on auscultation + JVD + ECG shows right-axis deviation + 2-year Hx of type II diabetes; Q asks what is most likely to reduce MI risk in this
vignettes.a: smoking cessation. Inflated lung fields mean COPD. Loud P2 means pulmonary hypertension (pulmonic valve slams shut due to high distal pressure). JVD means impaired right-heart filling. Right-axis deviation means right ventricular

vignettes.q: 60F + Hx of MI 5 years ago + diabetic + smoker + HTN; Q asks number-one risk factor for an MI occurring in this patient
vignettes.a: “Hx of myocardial infarction.” Not complicated. Akin to psych questions that want you to know biggest risk factor for suicide is Hx of previous suicide attempt.

vignettes.q: 55M + gangrene of the fingers + HTN + drinks alcohol and smokes; Q wants to know #1 way to improve this patient’s condition
vignettes.a: smoking cessation; diagnosis is Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans), which is idiopathic digital gangrene, generally in middle-age men who are heavy smokers.

vignettes.a: Since HTN is biggest risk factor for stroke (in patients without Afib), and the best way to decrease BP is weight loss, this means weight reduction is crucial for decreasing stroke risk.

vignettes.q: 50M + undergoing dental procedure; Q asks about risk for endocarditis and if prophylaxis is indicated

vignettes.q: 38M + diabetic + no proteinuria + LDL 110 mg/dL + BP 120/80 + HbA1c of 7%; Q asks what is most likely to decrease morbidity in this patient?
vignettes.a: statin. LDL should be under 100 mg/dL in diabetics on NBME (the literature says <70-100 depending on the source, but I’ve seen NBME Qs where 95 mg/dL LDL is written in vignette and statin isn’t indicated).

vignettes.a: Since PAD is caused by atherosclerosis, we’d have the same risk factors as before – i.e., diabetes > smoking > HTN, with the caveat being that if the vignette hyper-emphasizes / pushes one risk factor onto you (e.g., they give you

vignettes.a: achalasia; loss of myenteric plexus; often idiopathic; can be due to Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas disease) as risk factor; latter can also cause dilated cardiomyopathy.
