vignettes.a: chronic mesenteric ischemia due to atherosclerosis of SMA/IMA; don’t confuse with duodenal ulcers; will sound like duodenal ulcer except will be an older patient with extensive cardiovascular history. The abdo pain is angina of th

vignettes.q: 55F + started on new medication regimen + now has hypothyroidism; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: drug- induced thyroiditis; lithium and amiodarone are HY causes.

vignettes.q: 67 + chest pain when arguing with wife + blood in stool; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: angiodysplasia; risk factor is aortic stenosis (combo of angiodysplasia + aortic stenosis + acquired vWD = Heyde syndrome); angiodysplasia is tortuosity of superficial vessels within the colon that are prone to painlessly bleed; t

vignettes.q: 26F + IV drug user + recently treated with 6 weeks of nafcillin for MSSA endocarditis + now has rash and eosinophils in the urine; Dx + risk factor for renal condition?
vignettes.a: interstitial nephropathy (aka tubulointerstitial nephropathy/-nephritis); risk factor is beta-lactam, cephalosporin, or NSAID; answer on USMLE if patient gets WBCs (eosinophils) in urine +/- maculopapular rash following any of the

vignettes.q: 26F + IV drug user + develops oliguria following gentamicin and vancomycin empiric Tx for endocarditis; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: acute tubular necrosis due to gentamicin (aminoglycoside).

vignettes.q: Student Q showed 10M with scalp lesion similar to below, then the Q asked for the treatment:
vignettes.a: oral griseofulvin for patient only; wrong answer = “oral griseofulvin for patient and classmates”; Dx is tinea capitis; note alopecia and circular/scaly appearance of lesion; cause is dermatophytes (i.e., Microsporum; Trichophyton

vignettes.q: 24M + itchy patches and greasy scales along the hairline; Q asks for the diagnosis:
vignettes.a: seborrheic dermatitis (dandruff); treatment = topical selenium or ketoconazole shampoo; does not cause circular area of alopecia as with tinea capitis; more common in adults (tinea capitis more common in children); cause is inflam

vignettes.q: 46F + has three dogs at home; the following lesion from her forearm is shown; Q asks treatment:
vignettes.a: topical miconazole or clotrimazole; diagnosis = tinea corporis (ringworm); Q will often mention dogs or use of yoga mats at the gym.

vignettes.q: 35F + BMI of 55 + type II diabetes + red, moist 8x12-cm ellipse under right breast; Q asks biggest risk factor for her condition?
vignettes.a: insulin resistance (increases risk for cutaneous Candida); obesity is wrong answer; diagnosis is cutaneous Candida; treat with oral fluconazole.

vignettes.q: 27F + white, cheese-like discharge per vaginum; Q asks what oral treatment she needs; answer = fluconazole; some students say, “Wait, I thought we use topical nystatin”
vignettes.a: either oral fluconazole or topical nystatin can be used; there’s an NBME Q for Step 1 where they specify “oral” treatment; fluconazole is correct and nystatin isn’t listed.

vignettes.q: 32M + fever 101 F + red, itchy, scaly area between his 1st and 2nd toes + the redness/scaling extends up dorsum of foot and onto ankle; Q asks most likely causal organism for his fever; answer = Staph aureus; T
vignettes.a: Tx for tinea pedis on USMLE is topical terbinafine or -azole (i.e., clotrimazole/miconazole).

vignettes.q: 40F + diabetic foot ulcer; sterile probe to base of lesion is likely to show what?
vignettes.a: correct answer on new NBME exam = “polymicrobial”; wrong answers are Staph aureus and Pseudomonas. This is an extremely important Q from NBME because people have long debated Staph vs Pseudomonas for diabetic foot ulcers.

vignettes.q: 60M + farmer + thickened yellow nailbed of left big toe; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: onychomycosis (fungus of nails); Tx = oral terbinafine (if not listed, choose griseofulvin).

vignettes.q: 17F + Candida skin infections since childhood + 2-year Hx of type I diabetes mellitus + 1-yr Hx of autoimmune thyroiditis; Q asks mechanism for patient’s condition
vignettes.a: “deficiency of cell- mediated immunity”; diagnosis is chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis; USMLE wants you to know this is a T cell problem; autoimmune conditions go together (i.e., increased risk of one → increased risk of another)

vignettes.q: 31M + gardener + has presentation shown below; Q asks the mechanism for this patient’s condition:
vignettes.a: lymphangitis; diagnosis is lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis (Sporothrix schenckii); this image of erythematous lesions streaking toward the axilla is exceedingly HY for lymphangitis; sometimes the image can just be a fine pink strea

vignettes.q: 19M + plays soccer and goes to beach; has condition in image shown below; what is treatment?
vignettes.a: topical selenium; diagnosis is tinea versicolor (Malassezia furfur); fungus causes degradation of fatty acids within the skin leading to hypopigmentation; this image is all over the NBMEs for USMLE Step 1.

vignettes.q: 2-month-old girl + red papules in groin area and intergluteal cleft; family has Hx of asthma; what’s the diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Candida (diaper rash); not atopic dermatitis; the latter can occur in babies but is more often on trunk, dorsa of hands, and face. Treat Candida diaper rash with topical -azoles or nystatin.

vignettes.q: 48M + IV drug user + treated for 6 weeks in hospital on broad-spectrum antibiotics; intertriginous red rash is seen; organisms are cultured as purple-budding organisms; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Candida; broad-spectrum antibiotics → increased risk of Candida infections.

vignettes.q: 42M + fever 100.8 F + diffuse, pink lesion shown on leg below; Q asks most appropriate treatment:
vignettes.a: oral dicloxacillin, cephalexin, or Augmentin (amoxicillin + clavulanate); diagnosis is cellulitis (infection of the dermis and hypodermis [subcutaneous fat]); Staph aureus exceeds Strep pyogenes (Group A Strep) as causal organism;

vignettes.q: 35M + fever 100.5 F + leg has lesion shown + Q asks most likely causal organism:
vignettes.a: Answer on NBME = Strep pyogenes (Group A Strep); diagnosis is erysipelas (infection of upper dermis and superficial lymphatics); Group A Strep eclipses Staph aureus for erysipelas; looks worse than cellulitis but is more superfici

vignettes.q: 7M + presentation shown; Q asks for the treatment:
vignettes.a: topical mupirocin; diagnosis is impetigo (school sores); Staph aureus exceeds Group A Strep for both bullous and non-bullous types (bullous generally implies Staph); if orals given, use dicloxacillin or cephalexin, but USMLE loves

vignettes.q: 16M + cellulitis + BP of 80/40; Q asks which immunologic receptor(s) is/are bound in this patient’s condition → answer = MHC-II and T-cell receptor; diagnosis is toxic shock-like syndrome caused by exotoxin A (
vignettes.a: Toxic shock syndrome Qs will mention low BP in someone with cotton nasal packing or tampons → answer is “MHC-II and TCR” bound by TSST of Staph aureus. In contrast, cellulitis causing shock, the answer will be Strep pyogenes (Stap

vignettes.q: 12F + fever + sore throat + red tongue + pink maculopapular body rash; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: scarlet fever caused by Strep pyogenes; presents with “strawberry tongue” and salmon-pink body rash; Tx with penicillin to prevent rheumatic heart disease.

vignettes.q: 14M + fever + rapid, irregular, jerking movements of limbs + following rash on legs as shown; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: erythema marginatum as seen in rheumatic fever; treatment is penicillin; erythema marginatum is annular (ring-like) and serpiginous (serpent-/snake-like); movements are Sydenham chorea (autoimmune attack against basal ganglia).

vignettes.q: 10M + “yellow crusties” on his forearm for the past week + red urine; what’s the diagnosis? → answer = post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) secondary to Strep impetigo. USMLE can sometimes write answer
vignettes.a: Proliferative glomerulonephritis = PSGN. Do not confuse this with diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (DPGN, which is red urine in SLE), or membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN, which is red urine in HepC or maligna

vignettes.q: 19M + burned leg playing with firecrackers + while in hospital develops infection of burn site that has a yellow color; Dx?
vignettes.a: Staph aureus (golden staph); wrong answer is Pseudomonas. Although this is HY organism in burns patients, it produces a blue-green color due to pyocyanin, not a yellow color, which is instead golden Staph. So USMLE likes to be tri

vignettes.q: 25F + breastfeeding + red, cracked, fissured nipple; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: mastitis; usually caused by Staph aureus; Tx is oral dicloxacillin + continue breastfeeding through the affected breast.

vignettes.q: 25F + recently stopped breastfeeding + tender, fluctuant mass lateral to the nipple; patient is afebrile; mass is not warm or red; Dx?
vignettes.a: galactocele (milk retention cyst); can sometimes be confused with abscess since it is fluctuant and can be tender; if abscess, however, they will say red/warm +/- fever.

vignettes.q: 42F + inverted nipple + patient is worried because family Hx of breast cancer; Dx?
vignettes.a: ductal ectasia; benign condition; as name implies, simply dilation/widening of lactiferous duct.

vignettes.q: 65F + red, eczematoid-appearing nipple + mass palpable beneath nipple; Dx?
vignettes.a: Paget disease of breast; often associated with underlying ductal carcinoma in situ.

vignettes.q: 65F + peau d’orange of left breast + erythematous; Dx?
vignettes.a: inflammatory breast cancer; peau d’orange appearance due to Coopers ligaments of breast (on NBME).

vignettes.q: 17M + presents as per image shown; what’s the diagnosis? (answers are either Propionibacterium acnes or tinea faciei):
vignettes.a: acne; Propionibacterium acnes; not difficult, but I’ve seen enough students select tinea faciei. First-line Tx for acne on USMLE is topical retinoids (i.e., topical tretinoin; not oral isotretinoin; latter is only for severe acne)

vignettes.q: 20F + being treated for acne with both topical + oral medications; her forehead is shown below; what is the most appropriate recommendation for this patient?
vignettes.a: “avoidance of sun exposure”; above rash is classic photosensitivity caused by topical retinoids; tetracycline photosensitivity tends to be blistering; do not choose answers such as “avoidance of spicy/sweet foods” for acne questio

vignettes.q: 16M + face shown in following image; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Dx is tinea faciei; Tx = topical -azoles (clotrimazole, miconazole).

vignettes.q: 3M + fever of 103 F + stiff neck + low BP; following image of patient’s leg is shown. What is the most likely causal organism?
vignettes.a: gram-negative diplococci; Dx is meningitis + characteristic non-blanching rash caused by Neisseria meningitidis. Low BP can be endotoxic shock, but student should bear in mind Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is often asked; give

vignettes.q: 23M + 2-day Hx of soreness of left knee and right elbow + positive Finkelstein test on right hand + cutaneous papules visualized on right wrist; Dx?
vignettes.a: gonococcal arthritis; will present one of two ways on USMLE; 1) monoarthritis of large joint, such as the knee; 2) polyarthritis + tenosynovitis (e.g., deQuervain) + cutaneous papules/vesicopustules. The USMLE will sometimes just

vignettes.q: 40F + penetrating trauma to thigh one week ago + skin has black appearance and crepitus on exam; the most likely causal organism can also cause what?
vignettes.a: watery diarrhea; Dx is gas gangrene due to Clostridium perfringens, resulting in subcutaneous emphysema (crunching of skin due to underlying CO2 gas); this is due to production of lecithinase (phospholipase); C. perfringens also c

vignettes.q: 56F + poorly controlled diabetes + Pseudomonal sepsis + following image is shown; Dx?
vignettes.a: ecthyma gangrenosum; uncommon cutaneous infection seen in patients with severe Pseudomonal infections.

vignettes.q: 23F + works as postal worker + horticulturist + has many pet birds; following image is shown + Q describes lesion as an eschar with surrounding edema; Dx?
vignettes.a: Bacillus anthracis (anthrax); cutaneous anthrax can present classically with a black, eschar lesion; the gram (+) rod increases cAMP and produces edema factor.

vignettes.q: 28F gives birth to stillborn neonate + she ate soft cheeses and deli meat while pregnant + stillborn has diffuse granulomas on body; which of the following best describes the most likely causal organism?
vignettes.a: gram (+) rods; Listeria can cause granulomatosis infantiseptica (severe intrauterine infection often resulting in fetal demise + diffuse cutaneous granulomas).

vignettes.q: 39M + bilateral pneumonia + skin ulcer on back of hand (image shown) + low-grade fever + has many pet rabbits; what’s the diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Francisella tularensis; cutaneous tularemia can present as ulcerative lesions; can also cause bilateral atypical pneumonia; rabbits are classic source.

vignettes.q: 54M + type II diabetic + red rash under right axilla + rash appears bright coral red under Woods lamp (image shown); Dx?
vignettes.a: erythrasma, caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum; skin infection of intertriginous areas that shines/glows coral red under Woods lamp.

vignettes.q: 40M + painful erythematous lesions in her axillae; an image is shown below; what’s the best treatment for this patient?
vignettes.a: NBME answer = “surgical excision of lesions”; diagnosis is hidradenitis suppurativa, a skin condition characterized by painful abscesses and sinus tracts, most commonly in the groin, axilla, and under the breasts; frequently affec

vignettes.q: 17M + athlete + strong body odor when finished with sports; Q asks what type of gland is responsible → answer = apocrine; Types of glands:
vignettes.a: USMLE wants you to know apocrine glands are found in the groin and axilla and are responsible for body odor. Part of the plasma membrane buds off with the substance secreted by the cell. “Apocrine metaplasia,” is a term sometimes

vignettes.q: 43F + recent penetrating trauma to leg + necrotic tissue that on examination appears to spread along fascial planes; what’s the most likely diagnosis?
vignettes.a: necrotizing fasciitis; Tx = IV antibiotics + debridement of necrotic tissue.

vignettes.q: 27F + painful 1-cm lump in labia majora; what’s the most likely causal organism?
vignettes.a: polymicrobial; diagnosis is Bartholin gland cyst/abscess; uncomplicated cysts → treatment = warm compresses or sitz bath; overt abscess → Tx answer = drainage.

vignettes.q: 8M + fever for 5 days + palms and soles desquamation + edema of dorsa of hands + cervical lymphadenopathy + injection of conjunctiva and lips; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Kawasaki disease; 5+ days of fever is HY; Tx = aspirin + IVIG (never give aspirin to kids for other purposes because of Reye syndrome).

vignettes.q: 24F + lives in Connecticut + went hiking five days ago + rash of wrists and ankles + rash migrates in toward chest; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia rickettsii); classically palms and soles rash, but USMLE also sometimes says wrists + ankles; student should be aware rash is centripetal (i.e., starts at palms/soles, or wrists/ankles, and

vignettes.q: 6M + vesicular eruption on bottoms of feet, palms, and periorally; most likely causal organism?
vignettes.a: “RNA virus; non-enveloped; non-segmented”; diagnosis is hand-foot-mouth disease caused by Coxsackie A virus; this virus can also cause herpangina (posterior oropharyngeal vesicles).

vignettes.q: 24M + recently returned home from military service + fever of 101 F + cervical lymphadenopathy + posterior oropharyngeal vesicles + painful vesicles inside the lip (nothing on outside of mouth/lips); Q asks nex
vignettes.a: “PCR testing of vesicles”; viral culture is wrong answer; diagnosis is HSV1/2; do not confuse with herpangina; HSV primary infection will classically present with fever and lymphadenopathy.

vignettes.q: 54F + image shown below; Q asks most likely organism in terms of viral structure (i.e., DNA vs RNA; enveloped vs non-enveloped; circular vs linear):
vignettes.a: DNA, enveloped, linear; Dx is HSV1/2; herpes labialis.

vignettes.q: 40F + works as dentist + image as shown below; what’s the MOA of the treatment?
vignettes.a: Treatment = DNA polymerase inhibitor (causes “chain termination”); acyclovir (or valacyclovir); Dx is herpetic whitlow, which is an HSV1/2 infection of the finger, often caused by inoculation from a cold sore; increased prevalence

vignettes.q: 40M + gardener + photo is shown; this is due to what type of toxicity?
vignettes.a: NBME answer = arsenic; Mees lines are white lines seen on fingernails in arsenic toxicity; arsenic is present in small amounts in fertilizers, which causes plants to flourish; gardeners + landscapers at increased risk; arsenic can

vignettes.q: 8M + recent paranasal sinus infection + now presents with fever 103 F + painful, swollen eye as shown below; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Dx is orbital cellulitis (infection involving tissues posterior to orbital septum); Staph aureus most common cause; rare sequela of adjacent infection, e.g., from the paranasal sinus; medical emergency; requires IV antibiotics; pr

vignettes.q: 30F + painful, red bump on upper eyelid; image shown; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Dx is hordeolum (stye); Staph aureus infection of sweat gland or oil duct; treat with warm compresses.

vignettes.q: 24M + painless ulcer on his penile shaft; Dx + Tx? → answer = primary syphilis (chancre sore described); organism is Treponema pallidum; diagnose with darkfield microscopy to visualize spirochetes; Tx with peni
vignettes.a: Do not confuse with chancroid, which is a painful ulcer caused by Haemophilus ducreyi.

vignettes.q: 24M + Hx of unprotected intercourse + rash as shown in image below; KOH prep is negative; Q asks what is most likely to confirm diagnosis:
vignettes.a: Answer on USMLE = fluorescent treponemal antibody(FTA); Dx is secondary syphilis showing characteristic maculopapular/nodular body rash; negative KOH means it's not tinea versicolor; palms and soles are classically affected in sec

vignettes.q: 24M + Hx of unprotected intercourse + recently immigrated to US from Egypt + presents with below image of lesion on forehead + 2/6 decrescendo holo-diastolic murmur auscultated on exam; the most likely causal o
vignettes.a: Leptospira interrogans; diagnosis in image above is gumma of tertiary syphilis; syphilis is a spirochete, as are Leptospira, Borellia burgdorferi (Lyme disease), and Borrelia recurrentis (relapsing fever). Tertiary syphilis can ca

vignettes.q: 7M + from Massachusetts + family has pet dog + has rash as shown below; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Lyme disease; rash is erythema chronicum migrans (classic target rash); the rash need not be a target on USMLE; it can merely be circular with no clearing; but the target is classic; USMLE can give two side by side images: 1) circ

vignettes.q: 24F + pregnant + Bells palsy + target rash; Q asks for treatment (answers are steroids, doxycycline, ceftriaxone)
vignettes.a: ceftriaxone; doxycycline not given to pregnant women or children under age 8; student says, “Wait, but I thought you just said ceftriaxone is for severe Lyme; her presentation is simple” → Yes, I agree, ceftriaxone is classically

vignettes.q: 25M + sleeps with pet dog + tick found on the dog + circular rash on arm + blood smear shows phagocytes with intracellular berry cluster organisms; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Ehrlichiosis (Ehrlichia chaffeensis); bacterium spread by Ixodes tick (same as Lyme disease, Babesia, and Anaplasma); will not cause target rash; “berry cluster organisms” or intracellular “morulae” may be seen.

vignettes.q: 40M + living in homeless shelter for past 4 months + itchy hands + image shown below + topical antifungals were attempted but not effective; Q asks for the treatment:
vignettes.a: topical permethrin; Dx is scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei); lesions classically described as “linear burrows”; can become superinfected with Staph aureus. Disseminated scabies can occur in HIV patients; Tx is oral ivermectin. Topical p

vignettes.q: 19F + recent travel through southern US + stayed at dodgy AF motel on the side of the highway next to a Denny’s and a Sonic + itchy lesions on arm as shown in image below; Q asks for organism:
vignettes.a: Answer on NBME = bed bugs; caused by an insect called Cimex.

vignettes.q: 6M + family recently immigrated to US from Albania + diffuse maculopapular rash + photograph of buccal mucosa is shown below; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Dx = measles (rubeola); Tx is supportive; image shows Koplik spots (pathognomonic whiteish lesions on buccal mucosa); immigrant Hx on USMLE sometimes implies unvaccinated status.

vignettes.q: 6M + diffuse maculopapular rash + tenderness at base of occiput and behind the ears; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Dx is rubella (German measles); Tx is supportive; suboccipital and post-auricular lymphadenopathy are characteristic.

vignettes.q: 4M + fever + image shown below; what is the most likely causal organism (DNA vs RNA; enveloped vs non-enveloped; segmented vs non-segmented)?
vignettes.a: Dx is mumps → causes POM → Parotitis, Orchitis, Meningitis; virus is RNA, enveloped, non- segmented.

vignettes.q: Neonate + intracranial calcifications + hepatomegaly + rash as shown in image below; no murmurs; Q asks most likely causal organism:
vignettes.a: congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV); image shows blueberry muffin rash; no murmurs implies not rubella (causes patent ductus arteriosus).

vignettes.q: 5M + fever 2-3 days ago + brought in by mother to emergency with appearance as shown below; the most likely causal organism can also cause what?
vignettes.a: aplastic anemia; Dx = Parvovirus B19 (Fifth disease); image shows classic “slapped cheek” appearance; next best step in Dx = Parvovirus B19 IgM titers. If IgM titers are not listed and the child has aplastic anemia, choose bone ma

vignettes.q: 26F + works at daycare center + fever + rash as shown in image below; next best step in diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Parvovirus IgM titers. Viral infections in general can present with exanthem (rash). If they say "daycare center," this is hyper buzzy for Parvo on USMLE.

vignettes.q: 17M + high school wrestler + Hx of atopy + has burning, painful rash on trunk + lymphadenopathy + fever; image shown below; Q asks what’s the treatment?
vignettes.a: oral acyclovir (or valacyclovir); diagnosis is eczema herpeticum → HSV1/2 infection superimposed on eczema; often self-inoculated from touching cold sore then cracked skin of eczema; herpes infection can present with fever, lympha

vignettes.q: 3M + undergoing chemotherapy for ALL + has rash as shown below; what’s the diagnosis?
vignettes.a: shingles; yes, pediatric shingles “is a thing”; patient is immunocompromised due to chemotherapy. Shingles is aka “herpes zoster” and is caused by varicella zoster virus (VZV); herpes zoster is not a virus name; herpes zoster lite

vignettes.q: 18F + immigrated to US from Mexico in elementary school + presents with crops of pruritic vesicles on the trunk at different stages of healing; Dx?
vignettes.a: varicella (chickenpox); immigrant status implies unvaccinated status; “crops of vesicles at different stages of healing” = buzzy for VZV.

vignettes.q: 2M + fever of 103-4 F for 3 days; fever abruptly subsides, followed by rash as shown below; patient’s vaccination Hx is up to date; what’s the diagnosis?
vignettes.a: roseola (HHV6); described as “spiking fever followed by a rash”; child will have high fever for 2-3 days, followed by a rash.

vignettes.q: 22F + no past medical history + afebrile + itchy rash on back for past week as shown below; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Dx = pityriasis rosea; caused by HHV6 or 7; self-limiting; starts as Herald patch (larger pink ellipse above), usually on the back or trunk, then spreads upward onto the shoulder blades (“Christmas tree distribution”); USMLE will

vignettes.q: 50M + Hx of IV drug use + violaceous skin lesions as shown below; what’s the diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Kaposi sarcoma; usually caused by HHV8 (Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpes virus) in immunocompromised patients (i.e., AIDS, chemotherapy); Kaposi sarcoma presents as tumorous lesions of vascular-lymphatic origin.

vignettes.q: 12M + undergoing chemotherapy for ALL + skin lesions as shown in image below; Q asks you to pick the organism that causes it, but you see answers are all bacteria (i.e., HHV8 not listed):
vignettes.a: Bartonella henselae; Dx is bacillary angiomatosis; bacterium causes cat scratch disease but is also known to cause Kaposi-sarcoma like lesions in immunocompromised patients.

vignettes.q: 7F + has pet cat + papules on hand + lymph node biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation + organism can be visualized using silver stain; Dx?
vignettes.a: cat scratch disease.

vignettes.q: 6M + went to pool party a week ago + has lesions on trunk as shown in image below; what’s the most likely causal organism?”
vignettes.a: poxvirus (molloscum contagiosum); largest DNA virus; classically skin-colored or reddish papules with central umbilication. Classically acquired from fomites (inanimate objects like metal railings of a pool).

vignettes.q: 9M + comes to your clinic in Brazil + black ulcer on arm + vision loss + patient is successfully treated with ivermectin; what’s the most likely diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Onchocerciasis (Onchocerca volvulus); nematode (roundworm helminth) transmitted by black fly; second most common cause of blindness worldwide after trachoma (Chlamydia A-C).

vignettes.q: 9M + lives in South America + swollen eyebrow + shortness of breath on exertion + S3 heart sound on examination; what’s the most likely organism?
vignettes.a: Trypanasoma cruzi (Chagas disease); protozoan; unicellular eukaryote; spread by Reduviid bug (“kissing bug” because bite is painless); can cause dilated cardiomyopathy and achalasia; swollen eyebrow is referred to as Romaña sign.

vignettes.q: 40F + traveled to Middle East for one month + has lesion on hand as shown below + elevated liver enzymes + pancytopenia; the organism is transmitted by sandfly; what’s the most likely diagnosis?
vignettes.a: leishmaniasis; Leishmania donovani; protozoan; unicellular eukaryote; can cause visceral disease known as kala azar, which is associated with ↑ LFTs and pancytopenia.

vignettes.q: 39M + works at aquarium + presents with lesions as shown below; what’s the diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Mycobacterium marinum; causes red ulcers/blisters on hand/arm of those who are exposed to aquatics. Do not choose Staph aureus if they specifically say aquarium / waterpark in the question.

vignettes.q: 7M + received renal transplant last year + has preauricular reddish lesion shown below; Dx?
vignettes.a: Answer on USMLE = Mycobacterium avium intracellulare (MAI); can cause lymphadenitis with classic reddish/violaceous lesion on the neck or preauricularly; MAI classically causes lung disease in older women (Lady Windermere syndrome

vignettes.q: 45M + recently immigrated to US from Libya with adult children + hypoesthesia of hands to pain and temperature + nodularity of fingers and nose; the most likely causal organism most likely bears what characteri
vignettes.a: “temperature sensitivity”; Dx = leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae); grows at cooler temperatures, so can affect the peripheral nerves and nose → can cause neuropathy and disfiguration of face (leonine facies) and limbs.

vignettes.q: 17M + Hx of Celiac disease + lesions on elbows as shown in below photo; what is most likely to be seen on skin biopsy?
vignettes.a: IgA deposition at dermal papillae; diagnosis is dermatitis herpetiformis (not actual herpes, in contrast to eczema herpeticum; don’t confuse these conditions); this is a cutaneous eruption that can occur in patients with Celiac.

vignettes.q: 35M + Hx of ulcerative colitis + lesion on forearm as shown in below photo; what’s the diagnosis?
vignettes.a: pyoderma gangrenosum; described as ulcer with necrotic debris; rare cutaneous manifestation in IBD (usually ulcerative colitis).

vignettes.q: 32F + African-American + high serum calcium + image shown + biopsy of lung tissue shows non- caseating granulomas; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Image is erythema nodosum. Patient has sarcoidosis. Erythema nodosum is a panniculitis (inflammation of subcutaneous fat); can be caused by autoimmune diseases like sarcoidosis and Crohn, as well as part of serum sickness due to m

vignettes.q: 16M + episodes of bloody stool over past two years + perianal abscesses/fistulae seen on physical examination; Dx?
vignettes.a: Crohn disease; increased risk since transmural inflammation in Crohn.

vignettes.q: 46M + pain during defecation + perianal skin tag visualized on physical exam + patient won’t allow rectal exam due to exquisite pain; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: anal fissure; usually posterior in the midline; NBME answer is Sitz bath for treatment.

vignettes.q: 16M + painful 2-cm mass located at superior aspect of gluteal cleft; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: pilonidal cyst/abscess; Tx = surgical closure.

vignettes.q: 20F + receives IM ceftriaxone + oral azithromycin for pelvic inflammatory disease; 3-5 days later she has red rash in area of injection; diagnosis? → answer = Arthus reaction; type III hypersensitivity; can be
vignettes.a: 20F + receives IM ceftriaxone + gets polyarthritis a few days later; Dx? → answer = serum sickness; type III hypersensitivity. Arthus reaction = redness at injection site 3-5 days later. Serum sickness = polyarthritis 3-5 days aft

vignettes.q: 34F with image shown below; Q asks which other condition is most immunologically similar:
vignettes.a: Image shows malar rash of SLE; answer = serum sickness, Arthus reaction, or PSGN; all four presentations are type III hypersensitivities (the correct answer is any type III hypersensitivity listed in Q answer choices; the point is

vignettes.q: 52F + increased serum creatine kinase + 3/5 strength of hips on physical exam; images as shown below; what type of antibodies are classically seen in this condition?
vignettes.a: Anti-Jo1 antibodies; diagnosis is dermatomyositis; left image shows heliotrope rash; often described as violaceous eyelids; do not confuse with malar rash of SLE; right image shows shawl sign/rash; both dermatomyositis and polymyo

vignettes.q: 50F + proximal muscle weakness + image shown below; Q asks for diagnosis:
vignettes.a: Dx = dermatomyositis; image shows Gottron papules, which is a HY cutaneous finding; patients can also have “mechanics hands,” which are rough-surfaced / scaly-appearing hands; do not go chasing fungal infections here.

vignettes.q: 6F + fever 102 F + pain, erythema, and warmth of left knee + Hx of several episodes of joint pains past few years + Hb of 10.1 g/dL + MCV 72; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA), aka juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA); HY for Peds; patients are susceptible to septic arthritis (as with this patient), but will often have Hx of several episodes of non-septic joint pain; a

vignettes.q: 25F + hands shown in image below; Q asks melanocyte # and melanin production in following condition (i.e., ↑, ↓, or no change):
vignettes.a: ↓ melanocyte #; ↓ melanin production; diagnosis is vitiligo; T cell-mediated destruction of melanocytes; can be associated with other autoimmune polyglandular syndromes, as well as IgA deficiency.

vignettes.q: 69F + lesion on zygoma as shown below; Q asks for for melanocyte # and melanin production:
vignettes.a: ↑ melanocyte #; no change melanin production; diagnosis is lentigo (age spot; plural = lentigines).

vignettes.q: 34M + dark complexion + skin sample mixed up in lab with fair-skinned individual; Q asks melanocyte # and melanosome # in dark-skinned individual
vignettes.a: no change melanocyte #; ↑ melanosome #; melanosomes are organelles within melanocytes that produce melanin. Differences in skin pigmentation between individuals is due to more or less melanin, while melanocyte number is the same f

vignettes.q: 25F + Hx of gastroesophageal reflux + hands shown in image below; Q asks for what condition this patient is most likely to develop:
vignettes.a: pulmonary hypertension (secondary to pulmonary fibrosis); diagnosis is limited scleroderma (CREST syndrome); left image shows Raynaud phenomenon, which is color change due to vascular spasm and reactive hyperemia; the right image

vignettes.q: 42F + dysphagia + cracked corners of the mouth; image of nail shown below; Q asks for what is most likely to be seen in this patient:
vignettes.a: low MCV; Dx is Plummer-Vinson syndrome, which is the triad of 1) esophageal webs (dysphagia), 2) angular cheilosis (cracked corners of mouth), and 3) iron deficiency anemia (severe cases can present with koilonychia [spoon-shaped

vignettes.q: 16F + blood in stool + arthritis + erythematous/silvery scaling lesions on forehead, above upper lip, and on elbows; attempting to remove one of the skin lesions causes bleeding; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: psoriasis; patient here also has IBD; HLA-B27 sometimes associated (PAIR → Psoriasis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD, Reactive arthritis); Auspitz sign is bleeding of psoriatic scales with attempted removal; psoriatic lesions classic

vignettes.q: 8F + excoriations visible in flexor creases + occasional dry cough worse in winter; image of elbow shown below; Q asks what type of hypersensitivity is most likely responsible for this patient’s presentation:
vignettes.a: type I (immediate); diagnosis is atopy; image shows eczema (atopic dermatitis); patient has cough-variant asthma (1/3 of asthma patients only have dry cough, usually worse in the winter or with exercise); treat with oil-based emol

vignettes.q: 18F + history of eczema + area over elbow is red, inflamed, and oozing; 6-year-old sister recently had weeping papules on face; Dx in the 18-year-old?
vignettes.a: Staph aureus or Group A Strep superinfection over eczema; likely inoculated from younger sister’s impetigo.

vignettes.q: 22M + recently treated with azithromycin for chlamydial urethritis; forearm is shown in below photo; Dx?
vignettes.a: urticaria (hives); type I hypersensitivity; can be precipitated by various allergens, including pollen, pet dander, and drugs.

vignettes.q: 39M + went hiking + used sunscreen over body + has linear vesicles on legs; Q asks best way to prevent this condition; Dx?
vignettes.a: “avoidance of contact with weeds”; diagnosis is contact dermatitis due to poison ivy/sumac; linear vesicles is hugely HY descriptor for poison ivy/oak/sumac; sunscreen will be the answer if they say rash on dorsa of hands, arms, a

vignettes.q: 38F + recently treated with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole for simple UTI + develops sloughing skin over her arms; image shown below; Dx?
vignettes.a: Stevens-Johnson syndrome → autoimmune type IV hypersensitivity (T cell response) resulting in detachment of skin covering <10% surface area of body; Nikolsky sign is (+), which is sloughing of the skin with friction. Toxic epiderm

vignettes.q: 24F + tattoo a couple days ago + image shown below; Q asks for Dx:
vignettes.a: contact dermatitis from tattoo ink; asked on USMLE.

vignettes.q: 24F + nurse + allergic to bananas + image of hands shown below; Q asks diagnosis:
vignettes.a: Latex allergy (contact dermatitis; type IV hypersensitivity); patients who are allergic to bananas are often allergic to latex; contact dermatitis secondary to medical adhesives (i.e., bandages) can also occur, causing well-demarc

vignettes.q: 38F + chronic dry skin on the legs + scratches same area repeatedly; no other past medical history; image shown below; Dx?
vignettes.a: lichen simplex chronicus; dry, excoriated skin due to repeated scratching; dry, excoriated skin due to repeated scratching. The word excoriated means scratched. It's an important vocab word for Derm.

vignettes.q: 23M + painful vesicular lesions on the lip + fever + lymphadenopathy + presents with rash on arms as shown in below photo; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Erythema multiforme; immune complex-mediated rash (type III hypersensitivity) with many etiologies; HSV1/2 is classic cause; can also be caused by drugs (e.g., sulfa).

vignettes.q: 21M + blistering skin lesions + oral involvement + no mention of medications recently taken + Nikolsky sign (+); Q asks for the molecular target of the antibodies seen in this condition?
vignettes.a: desmosomes (desmoglein proteins), which mediate adjacent keratinocyte adhesion; diagnosis is pemphigus vulgaris, which is a blistering autoimmune skin condition caused by antibodies against desmosomes; oral involvement is common;

vignettes.q: 21M + blistering skin lesions + no oral involvement + no mention of medications recently taken + Nikolsky sign negative; Q asks for the molecular target of the antibodies seen in this condition?
vignettes.a: hemidesmosomes, which stabilize basal epithelial cells to the basement membrane; diagnosis is bullous pemphigoid; less severe than pemphigus vulgaris; usually no oral involvement; Nikolsky is negative; immunofluorescence shows a l

vignettes.q: 21M + formation of skin blisters with minor trauma; Q asks for what type of cell-cell interaction is disrupted in this patient?
vignettes.a: “basal:suprabasal” → Weird answer, but on NBME they write it just like that with the colon separating the words; diagnosis is epidermolysis bullosa, which is due to mutations (not antibodies, as with the aforementioned PV and BP)

vignettes.q: 26M + oral + genital ulcers + high ESR; Dx?
vignettes.a: Behcet disease.

vignettes.q: 63M + patchy facial erythema that worsens with spicy foods and alcohol; slight pain of rash in cold weather; image of patient is below; Q asks simply for diagnosis:
vignettes.a: rosacea; multifactorial etiology; described as mix of itchy and painful facial rash in middle age patient that gets worse with things like cold weather, alcohol, and spicy food; topical metronidazole sometimes effective, as with a

vignettes.q: 46M + high serum calcium + CXR shows bilar lymphadenopathy + image of face is shown below; Dx?
vignettes.a: lupus pernio (a cutaneous manifestation of sarcoidosis, not SLE, despite the name).

vignettes.q: 26F + presents during winter + painful/itchy toes + topical antifungals not effective; Dx?
vignettes.a: perniosis (chilblains); painful inflammation of distal capillaries due to repeated exposure to cold air, followed by immersion in hot water (i.e., from bath/shower). This is different from frostnip and frostbite. Frostnip is cold-

vignettes.q: 28F + occasional painful single mouth ulcers (image shown below); Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Dx = aphthous ulcers (aphthous stomatitis); no Tx necessary; not related to HSV1/2; etiology is multifactorial; can be precipitated by allergens such as spice; T cell-mediated.

vignettes.q: 35F + mouth ulcers + fever + treated two days ago for hyperthyroidism in hospital; Dx?
vignettes.a: Drug-induced neutropenia. Propylthiouracil and methimazole are thionamides (anti-thyroid drugs) that can both cause neutropenia (aka agranulocytosis), which can present as mouth ulcers (mucositis). Propylthiouracil is one of the d

vignettes.q: 37M + occasional itchy bumps on hands; sometimes in ring-like pattern; Dx?
vignettes.a: Dx = granuloma annulare; caused by cutaneous T cell response; occurs in young, healthy patients; may present as small bumps that progress to annular/ring-like pattern; self- resolving + no Tx necessary.

vignettes.q: 45F + hepatitis C positive + purple, pruritic skin lesions; image shown below; Dx?
vignettes.a: lichen planus; classically described as “The Ps” → purple, pruritic, polygonal papules; however Qs need not mention they’re pruritic; hepatitis C + red/purple skin lesions = lichen planus. I've also seen it occur idiopathically on

vignettes.q: 28F + thrombocytopenia + polyarthritis + chronic sores of the cheeks and scalp + anti-Smith antibody positive; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: SLE; dermatologic component is discoid lupus, which is a severe cutaneous presentation seen sometimes in SLE patients, with sores/scarring of the face, scalp, and ears; thrombocytopenia (and leuko-/erythropenia) is seen in many SL

vignettes.q: Neonate born to mother who took methimazole during first trimester; photo of child is shown; what’s the diagnosis?
vignettes.a: aplasia cutis congenita; absence of skin on an area of scalp; can be caused by teratogens such as methimazole.

vignettes.q: 5M + second episode of edema of face, hands, and arms; patient is prescribed danazol; image of patient is shown below; what is the most likely mechanism for this condition?
vignettes.a: deficiency of C1 esterase inhibitor (not C1 esterase alone); diagnosis is hereditary angioedema; condition characterized by recurrent swelling of various bodily regions; danazol (androgen receptor partial agonist) causes liver to

vignettes.q: 33F + third trimester of pregnancy + itchy rash around umbilicus + stretch marks not involved; image is shown below; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Dx is gestational pemphigoid; does not involve stretchmarks (unlike PUPPP); cause is sporadic/multifactorial; Tx is oral or topical steroids.

vignettes.q: 33F + third trimester of pregnancy + intense, diffuse pruritis, especially on palms + soles; no skin rash; serum bile acids are elevated; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy; Dx by measuring increased serum bile acids; Tx is ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol).

vignettes.q: 12M + nosebleeds for the past week + petechial rash + bleeding time 9 minutes + platelet count 90,000/uL; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: idiopathic (immune) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP); cause is antibodies against GpIIb/IIIa on platelets (type II HS); Dx with decreased platelet count (answer on NBME; increased bleeding time for Dx is wrong answer). Tx = steroids

vignettes.q: 67M + lesion shown on nose in photo below; Q simply asks the diagnosis:
vignettes.a: basal cell carcinoma (BCC); on USMLE, classically pearlescent / slightly translucent; talengiectasias common; can be described as having “heaped up borders” or “rolled edges”; may or may not be ulcerated. Treatment for skin cancer

vignettes.q: 30F + atypical skin lesion on neck + biopsy shows clusters of basophilic cells (shown below); Q asks for the diagnosis:
vignettes.a: BCC; histo shows clusters of basophilic (purple) cells.

vignettes.q: 42M + receives topical immunomodulator for confirmed BCC; what is the drug he received?
vignettes.a: imiquimod; stimulates toll-like receptor-7 (TLR-7).

vignettes.q: 62F + farmer + lesions on forearm/hand shown below; Q asks diagnosis:
vignettes.a: actinic keratoses (aka solar keratoses); precursor to squamous cell carcinoma (SCC); classically described as red/scaly lesions on forehead, ear, or arms of fisherman, farmers, or construction workers. Can also appear as rough whi

vignettes.q: 74M + fisherman; forehead and ear are shown below; Q asks for the diagnosis of the ear lesion:
vignettes.a: Forehead shows actinic keratoses. Ear shows squamous cell carcinoma; actinic keratoses can classically progress to SCC; patient has many actinic keratoses and was likely at risk of developing SCC, as with the ear lesion; on USMLE,

vignettes.q: 60M + 2 packs cigarettes daily for 30 years + lesion on back; biopsy is shown below; Q asks Dx:
vignettes.a: SCC; histo shows keratin pearls (pink circles), which are classic for SCC; USMLE wants you to know “keratin pearls + intercellular bridges” = SCC. Smoking + immunodeficiency (e.g., HIV) are HY risk factors for SCC.

vignettes.q: 68F + rough-surfaced grey/white lesion on labia majora; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: lichen sclerosus; described as rough, white/grey, patchy, and/or itchy area on vulva or perineum; must do biopsy to rule out SCC before topical steroids; the latter are effective treatment. If the Q gives an overtly ulcerated lesi

vignettes.q: 65F + lesion on face shown below; Q asks for the diagnosis:
vignettes.a: keratoacanthoma; can be confused with SCC; described as fast-growing and dome- shaped with a hyperkeratotic core, surrounded by a wall of inflamed skin; can sometimes self-regress, but Tx is still surgical excision.

vignettes.q: 32F + confirmed melanoma + receives aldesleukin; Q asks which cytokine this relates to?
vignettes.a: IL-2; aldesleukin is a recombinant interleukin-2 that can be used in the treatment of melanoma and RCC; IL-2 normally functions to stimulate T cells.

vignettes.q: 30F + African-American + lesion on foot as shown below; what’s the diagnosis?
vignettes.a: acral lentiginous melanoma; melanoma of palms/soles (areas not usually exposed to sun); more common in persons of African and Asian descent.

vignettes.q: 34F + Asian-American + fingernail shown in photo below; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: acral lentiginous melanoma; USMLE will show you image of ALM on the palm/sole, or it can be subungual (as shown here).

vignettes.q: 29M + nailbed lesion + radiating pain incited by cold temperature; Dx?
vignettes.a: glomus tumor; The glomus body is a type of modified smooth muscle cell in fingers/toes that assists in thermoregulation. Sounds arcane/weird, but for some magical reason exists on USMLE.

vignettes.q: 67M + lesion on face as shown in photo below; biopsy shows malignant cells growing laterally along the basement membrane without dermal invasion; Q asks diagnosis:
vignettes.a: lentigo maligña; considered melanoma in situ; starts as black/brown “stain” that grows laterally within stratum basale without penetration; once it invades, it is called lentigo maligña melanoma (Hutchinson melanotic freckle); the

vignettes.q: 37F + confirmed melanoma + two other first-degree family members also had melanoma; Q asks for which gene is most likely associated in this patient
vignettes.a: BRAF; proto-oncogene, not a tumor suppressor; BRAF codes for BRAF serine-threonine kinase. You do not need to know vemurafenib (targets BRAF kinase) for USMLE, but some students have asked about it.

vignettes.q: 83F + facial lesions shown in photo below; Q asks for diagnosis:
vignettes.a: seborrheic keratoses; sun exposure and old age are biggest risk factors; described as “greasy,” or waxy, skin growths that appear like they can be “peeled off”; not malignant. Sign of Leser-Trélat = sudden, eruptive seborrheic ker

vignettes.q: 15M + mouth shown in photo below; Q asks for what kind of polyps he most likely has:
vignettes.a: hamartomatous; Dx is Peutz-Jeghers syndrome; combination of perioral melanosis (sophisticated way of saying hyperpigmentation around the mouth/lips) and hamartomatous colonic polyps. Perioral melanosis also seen in Carney complex

vignettes.q: 6M + jaw lesion as shown in photo below; Q asks for molecular function of gene involved:
vignettes.a: transcription factor; Dx is Burkitt lymphoma; usually t(8;14) translocation; c-MYC gene; codes for transcription factor; “starry sky” appearance on histo. Focus here isn’t heme/onc, but HY contrasting point: do not confuse with fo

vignettes.q: 49M + smoker + rough, white lesion on lateral aspect of tongue that does not scrape off; Dx?
vignettes.a: leukoplakia; precancerous lesion to SCC; caused by smoking / chewing tobacco.

vignettes.q: 32M + HIV positive + white lesions on lateral tongue that do not scrape off; Q asks for the viral etiology
vignettes.a: EBV; Dx is oral hairy leukoplakia; not precancerous; caused by hyperkeratosis (excessive skin proliferation); one of the most common presentations of HIV (in addition to oropharyngeal candidiasis).

vignettes.q: 54M + IV drug-user + lesion on leg shown in photo below + biopsy shows malignant T cells with cerebriform nuclei; Q asks which virus is most likely responsible:
vignettes.a: Human T cell lymphotropic virus (HTLV-1/2); diagnosis is mycosis fungoides, which is a cutaneous T cell lymphoma; T cells have nuclei with classic “cerebriform” appearance; Pautrier microabscesses are atypical T cells in epidermis

vignettes.q: 54M + Hx of IV drug-use + diffuse red body rash as shown in photo below + blood smear shows leukemic T cells with cerebriform nuclei; Q asks for structure of viral etiology (i.e., RNA vs DNA; enveloped vs non-e
vignettes.a: RNA, enveloped; virus is HTLV-1/2; diagnosis is Sezary syndrome; T cell leukemic extension of mycosis fungoides; diffuse exfoliative erythroderma is classic.

vignettes.q: 82F + had gallbladder removed at age 58 + afebrile + abdomen shown below; Q asks next best step in diagnosis?
vignettes.a: CT of abdomen with contrast; Dx is pancreatic cancer; image shows jaundice (yes, I jacked up the saturation to make the patient yellow AF); remote cholecystectomy denotes impossibility of choledocholithiasis; this Q asked on Surg

vignettes.q: 40M + history of shooting groin pain + elevated serum glucose + red rash on abdomen; Q asks for which pancreatic cancer type is the Dx
vignettes.a: glucagonoma → can cause ↑ glucose + necrolytic migratory erythema (rash). Patient has MEN1 (pancreas, parathyroid, pituitary); shooting groin pain = ureterolithiasis; hyperparathyroidism → high Ca2+ → stones.

vignettes.q: 40M + flushing of face + diarrhea + low serum potassium; Dx?
vignettes.a: VIPoma; classically WDHA syndrome → Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia, Achlorhydria; can also cause facial flushing.

vignettes.q: 27F + 20 weeks’ gestation + scattered skin lesions on trunk and arms, as shown in photo below; patient also has axillary/groin freckling; Q asks inheritance pattern:
vignettes.a: autosomal dominant; Dx is neurofibromatosis type I (NF1); image shows café au lait spot; one of the phakomatoses (neurocutaneous disorders → NF1/2, VHL, TSC, Sturge- Weber); NF1 → café au lait spots, neurofibromas, axillary/groin

vignettes.q: 7M + lesions shown on face in image below; Q asks inheritance pattern:
vignettes.a: autosomal dominant; Dx is tuberous sclerosis (TSC); image shows adenoma sebaceum (angiofibromas); one of the phakomatoses; in TSC we see intracranial / periventricular nodules (tubers, aka cortical hamartomas), adenoma sebaceum, c

vignettes.q: 17M + Hx of epilepsy + physical examination shows violaceous papules in a temporal distribution; Dx? → answer = Sturge-Weber; classically Port Wine-stain birthmark (nevus flammeus) in textbooks, but USMLE can d
vignettes.a: Classic Port wine stain birthmark, as seen in Sturge-Weber; condition is not inherited and is due to somatic mosaicism.

vignettes.q: 3M + deficiency of a-galactosidase A + buildup of ceramide trihexoside + heart/kidney issues + red lesions on skin shown in image below; Q asks diagnosis:
vignettes.a: Fabry disease; lysosomal storage disease; X-linked recessive; image shows angiokeratomas, which are dilated capillaries forming papules.

vignettes.q: 6M + skin lesions as shown in image below + polyostotic fibrous dysplasia + testes large for gestational age; Dx?
vignettes.a: McCune-Albright syndrome → triad of “coast of Maine” café au lait spots (above image), polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (bone is replaced by fibrous tissue), and endocrine hypersecretion (classically precocious puberty).

vignettes.q: 3M + retained primary teeth + eczema + recurrent Staphylococcal abscesses; Dx?
vignettes.a: hyper- IgE syndrome (Job syndrome) → FATED → coarse Facies, Staphylococcal Abscesses, retained primary Teeth, hyper-IgE, Dermatologic abnormalities (eczema).

vignettes.q: 3M + delayed separation of umbilical cord at birth + recurrent skin infections without pus + biopsy shows decreased neutrophils at sites of skin infection; Dx?
vignettes.a: leukocyte adhesion deficiency; defective LFA-1/CD18 integrin.

vignettes.q: Neonatal male + family recently immigrated to US from China; back is shown in image below; Dx?
vignettes.a: Diagnosis is Mongolian spot (blue nevus), a form of benign birthmark where dermal melanocytes fail to migrate superficially to stratum basale. Often mistaken for child abuse. Schedule routine follow-up. Wrong answer is contacting

vignettes.q: 22M + BMI 36 + neck shown in image below; what is most likely to be seen in this patient?
vignettes.a: hyperinsulinemia; image is acanthosis nigricans (brown/black velvety skin, usually along nape of neck); associated with hyperinsulinemia and type II diabetes; can also rarely be seen in patients with underlying, visceral malignanc

vignettes.q: 42M + lantern jaw + increased hat/shoe size + high BP + image shown below; Q asks next best step in diagnosis:
vignettes.a: measure serum insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-1); wrong answer is measure serum growth hormone; diagnosis is acromegaly; GH causes liver to secrete IGF-1, which in turn promotes growth of tissues; skin tags can be seen secondary

vignettes.q: 3M + coloboma of the iris + ventricular septal defect + ear is shown below; Q asks what else is likely to be seen in this patient?
vignettes.a: atresia of the choanae; Dx is CHARGE syndrome → Coloboma of the iris, Heart defects, Atresia of the choanae (baby turns blue during breastfeeding and pink when crying; Dx by inserting nasogastric tube), Retardation of growth/devel

vignettes.q: 7M + hole seen on preauricular aspect of ear bilaterally; patient is asymptomatic; Q asks treatment:
vignettes.a: no Tx necessary; preauricular pits are benign finding, usually not associated with any congenital disorder; can become infected; surgical closure if frequent infections.

vignettes.q: Neonate + lesion superior to pinna in image shown below; Dx+ Tx?
vignettes.a: Dx is strawberry hemangioma; benign capillary tumor in neonates that will grow slightly then regress spontaneously within a few years; no Tx necessary unless causing functional impairment.

vignettes.q: 50F + photo of lesions on neck shown below; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: cherry hemangiomas; no Tx necessary; benign capillary tumors caused by UV light; greater prevalence with increasing age. Students confuse with strawberry hemangioma in peds.

vignettes.q: Neonate + tuft of hair seen on lower back; Dx?
vignettes.a: spina bifida occulta; NBME exam has one answer written as “spinal dysraphism,” rather than spina bifida.

vignettes.q: 50M + long-standing Hx of ulcerative colitis managed with multiple medications; abdomen shown in image below. What is causing this skin presentation:
vignettes.a: Cushing syndrome due to exogenous prednisone used in autoimmune disease; USMLE wants you to know purple striae are classically Cushing. This is due to weakening of dermal collagen and capillary walls, with micro bleeding into skin

vignettes.q: 41M + serum glucose 130 mg/dL + sore hands + hand x-ray shows Heberden nodes; physical exam shows darkening of the skin of the forearms; Q asks next best step in diagnosis?
vignettes.a: check serum ferritin; Dx is hereditary hemochromatosis; can present as “bronze diabetes” → diabetes due to deposition of iron in tail of pancreas; hemosiderin deposition in skin causes hyperpigmentation (hemosiderosis); arthritis

vignettes.q: 30M + 6-month-Hx of fatigue + serum potassium 6.0 mEq/L, sodium 130 mEq/L, bicarb 20 mEq/L + eosinophils 23% + hyperpigmentation of forearms; Q asks which diagnostic test should be performed?
vignettes.a: ACTH stimulation test; Dx is Addison disease (primary hypoadrenalism); classically low sodium, high potassium, and low bicarb when aldosterone is low; low cortisol can cause eosinophilia; do not go chasing stool ova and parasites;

vignettes.q: 3M + brought in by mother for pain in right arm after falling off swing on playground; x-ray shows fracture of the humerus; photo of hand shown below; Q asks next best step?
vignettes.a: contact child protect services; photo shows classic circular appearance of cigarette burn; can also be on face / resemble impetigo if at different stages of healing; humerus fractures uncommon and can be from blunt-force trauma; c

vignettes.q: 22F + lesions on ear shown in image below + occurred following removal of ear piercings several weeks ago; Dx?
vignettes.a: keloid scars; disorganized growth of collagen type I and III; scar grows beyond boundaries of original wound; In contrast, hypertrophic scars may resemble keloids but do not grow beyond boundaries of original wound; Tx is surgical

vignettes.q: 22M + face shown in photo below; vitals normal; no past medical Hx; Dx?
vignettes.a: pseudofolliculitis barbae (razor bumps); increased prevalence in African descent; curly beard hair grows back into the skin; Tx is to allow the beard to grow; USMLE Q will show you image and just ask the spot-Dx.

vignettes.q: 65F + Hx of pain in buttocks/thighs when walking his dog + image of foot shown; what’s the most likely cause of this finding?
vignettes.a: arterial insufficiency; image shows arterial ulcer; often punched-out in appearance, well-demarcated; usually tops/bottoms of feet/toes; patients will frequently have Hx of intermittent claudication, diabetes, CABG, etc. Periphera

vignettes.q: 50F + image shown below; what’s the most likely cause of this finding?
vignettes.a: chronic venous insufficiency; image shows venous ulcer; classically large, sloughy lesion around the ankle / medial malleolus; hyperpigmentation common in venous disease due to congestion and hemosiderin extravasation (“brawny ede

vignettes.q: 54M + leg shown below; no other past medical Hx; Q asks for next best step in Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Image shows varicose veins; Dx → Duplex venous ultrasonography for venous disease / valvular insufficiency; Tx is compression stockings; do not choose surgical interventions for varicose veins on USMLE.

vignettes.q: 50M + 1-cm painful, palpable “cord” around the ankle / tracks up toward the knee; image is shown below; Q asks for Tx:
vignettes.a: Answer on NBME = subcutaneous enoxaparin; Dx is superficial thrombophlebitis; similar to DVT, but in more superficial vein; treated with heparin; wrong answer is compression stockings; difficult Q since compression stockings commo

vignettes.q: 48M + heavy smoker + hands shown below + no other significant past medical history; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Dx = thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease); Tx = smoking cessation; presents as digital gangrene in males who are heavy smokers.

vignettes.q: 66F + type II diabetes + HbA1c 9.8% + metoclopramide is one of her meds; image of foot shown below; x-ray of the foot shows disorganization of the tarsals/metatarsals; Q asks most likely cause of the lesion sho
vignettes.a: “lack of appropriate joint sensation”; Dx = Charcot joint (neuropathic joint); patient cannot feel her feet due to peripheral neuropathy; vignette description points away from pure arterial ulcer (plus arterial ulcers are more dis

vignettes.q: 62M + hepatitis C + decreased serum C4 + legs shown in image below; Dx?

vignettes.a: ↑ 7-dehydrocholesterol, ↓ cholecalciferol, ↓ 25-OH-D3, ↓ 1,25-(OH)2-D3. — UV-B radiation is required to convert 7-dehydrocholesterol in the stratum basale of the epidermis into cholecalciferol. • If the USMLE mentions a patient wh

vignettes.a: ↓ LH, ↓ FSH, ↓ ACTH, ↓ growth hormone, ↓ TSH, ↑ prolactin. — The pituitary stalk is what enables hormonal signaling between the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. • GnRH stimulates LH and FSH. • CRH stimulates ACTH. • GHRH stimu

vignettes.a: ↑ Serum K+ , ↓ Na+ , ↓ pH, ↓ HCO3- , ↓ glucose. — Diagnosis is 21-hydroxylase deficiency. • Congenital adrenal hyperplasia refers to 21-, 11-, or 17-hydroxylase deficiency. • Do not freak out about memorizing the flow chart of all

vignettes.a: ↓ pH, ↓ HCO3- , ↓ CO2. — Diagnosis is diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). • Etiology is classically recent viral infection (usually Coxsackie B) followed by polyuria and polydipsia. • Lack of insulin production by the pancreas results in

vignettes.q: ADH is produced by both the supraoptic nucleus and paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus
vignettes.a: stored in posterior pituitary.

vignettes.q: If ADH is ↑, we get ↑ free water reabsorption and dilution of our serum
vignettes.a: serum sodium and osmolality ↓. Likewise, our urine becomes more concentrated, meaning urine osmolality and specific gravity ↑.

vignettes.q: If ADH is ↓, we get ↓ free water reabsorption and concentration of our serum
vignettes.a: serum sodium and osmolality ↑. Likewise, our urine becomes more dilute, meaning urine osmolality and specific gravity ↓.

vignettes.q: An increase in serum osmolality will trigger ADH release, which in turn will reabsorb more free water in the medullary collecting duct of the kidney to help re-dilute the serum back to original osmolality.
vignettes.a: ↑ serum tonicity + osmolality → ↑ ADH release → dilutes serum back to normal. ↓ serum tonicity + osmolality → ↓ ADH release → concentrates serum back to normal.

vignettes.q: Estrogen causes ↑ thyroid-binding globulin (TBG) production by the liver. TBG is the protein carrier molecule for thyroid hormone in the blood. An NBME Q asks for which hormone causes the ↑ TBG in pregnancy
vignettes.a: estrogen; progesterone is wrong answer.

vignettes.a: .” It’s because the bold arrows are what the USMLE wants. Pregnant women who are euthyroid will have normal free-T4 and increased total T4, and their TSH will be normal. The changes due to TBG rising are likely synchronous and slo

vignettes.q: - Q will tell you patient has SLE treated with prednisone who goes into surgery and gets a ↓↓ drop in BP to 80/40 + fluids and pressors don’t help; Q asks next best step
vignettes.a: IV hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone. What we are doing is replenishing the glucocorticoid. “Pressors” can refer to NE, E, or even desmopressin.

vignettes.q: - The Q can also tell you patient being treated with prednisone for SLE or RA experiences an acute thyroiditis (remember autoimmune diseases go together) and gets ↓↓ in BP
vignettes.a: hydrocortisone (after fluids). Or patient with autoimmune disease gets an infection + ↓↓ in BP → answer = hydrocortisone (after fluids).

vignettes.q: - ACTH is ↑ in all three types. This is the mechanism USMLE wants for the hyperplasia. That is, cortisol production is impaired in all three, so ACTH goes ↑ to compensate
vignettes.a: stimulates hyperplasia of adrenals.

vignettes.q: - The USMLE will give a vignette of CAH, followed by “which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?”
vignettes.a: “Increased ACTH secretion.” Sounds weird, but it’s on NBME.

vignettes.q: - For both 21- AND 11-hydroxylase deficiencies:
vignettes.a: ↑ 17-OH substrates (i.e., 17-OH-progesterone and 17-OH-pregnenolone). ↑ DHEA-S, ↑ androstenedione. If you see any of these up in the Q, you know right away answer is either 21- or 11-deficiency. This is because it’s impossible to

vignettes.a: Predicted pCO2 = (1.5xHCO3) + 8 +/- 2.
