vignettes.q: - Acute asthma attack and PE: ↓ pCO2, no change HCO3- , ↑ pH,
vignettes.a: The key here is that these conditions cause acute respiratory alkalosis, not acidosis, as I mentioned in above table. Students normally this up and think pCO2 is high. pCO2 only goes ↑ if the patient becomes tired as an asthma att

vignettes.q: - Patients with COPD and obstructive sleep apnea are chronic CO2 retainers, where we have:
vignettes.a: ↑ pCO2, ↑ HCO3- , ↓ pH. Bicarb goes up to compensate. Miscellaneous HY acid/base

vignettes.q: Acid-base role of aldosterone
vignettes.a: causes direct proton secretion at apical membrane of cortical collecting duct

vignettes.q: How does aldosterone relate to ENac?
vignettes.a: increased reabsorption of Na at basolateral membrane means decreased intracellular Na → favorable high-low gradient of Na from urine into tubular cell → ENac upregulates on apical membrane to increase movement of Na into tubular c

vignettes.q: Acid-base / biochemical disturbance in Addison
vignettes.a: low Na, high K, low bicarb, low pH (metabolic acidosis)

vignettes.q: Fatigued patient + hyperpigmentation + low BP
vignettes.a: Addison disease (primary hypoadrenalism; low aldosterone + low cortisol)

vignettes.q: Infective cause of Addison
vignettes.a: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (WFS)

vignettes.q: What is WFS
vignettes.a: hemorrhagic (not ischemic) necrosis of adrenal glands

vignettes.q: Cause of WFS
vignettes.a: meningococcal septicemia (non-blanching rash)

vignettes.q: Low BP in WFS + fluids are given; next best step?
vignettes.a: give dexamethasone to compensate for low cortisol

vignettes.q: If WFS is hemorrhagic necrosis, what HY scenario contrasts
vignettes.a: Sheehan syndrome is ischemic necrosis of anterior pituitary following labor

vignettes.q: Cause of Sheehan
vignettes.a: anterior pituitary doubles in size during pregnancy to increase prolactin secretion; blood loss during labor → ischemic infarction

vignettes.q: USMLE arrow Q for Sheehan
vignettes.a: down ACTH, down TSH, down prolactin, up aldosterone (NBME exam)

vignettes.q: How do you Dx Addison disease
vignettes.a: ACTH stimulation test (if cortisol doesn’t go up appreciably, Dx confirmed)

vignettes.q: Weird hematologic finding in Addison
vignettes.a: eosinophilia (don’t go chasing ova, stool, parasites)

vignettes.q: Why fatigue in Addison
vignettes.a: low cortisol causes chronic fatigue syndrome

vignettes.q: Why hyperpigmentation in Addison
vignettes.a: low cortisol, so less negative feedback at hypothalamus + anterior pituitary → increase in CRH → increase in POMC (precursor to ACTH and alpha-MSH)

vignettes.q: Tx for Addison
vignettes.a: fludrocortisone

vignettes.q: Important point about fludrocortisone
vignettes.a: corticosteroid with high mineralocorticoid effect (acts like aldosterone) → can be used to overcome low aldosterone + low cortisol caused by Addison

vignettes.q: Important point about prednisone + hydrocortisone + dexamethasone
vignettes.a: glucocorticoids with very low mineralocorticoid effect (do not act like aldosterone) → hydrocortisone classically used to treat secondary hypoadrenalism (only decreased cortisol)

vignettes.q: Cause of Addison
vignettes.a: autoimmune, typically part of polyglandular syndrome

vignettes.q: Cause of secondary hypoadrenalism
vignettes.a: decreased ACTH production → usually due to impingement by pituitary tumor (e.g, prolactinoma); can also be caused by Sheehan syndrome

vignettes.q: ACTH levels in Addison vs secondary hypoadrenalism
vignettes.a: high in Addison; low in secondary

vignettes.q: Potassium levels in secondary hypoadrenalism?
vignettes.a: normal because aldosterone intact through RAAS; cause is merely decreased ACTH

vignettes.q: Primary hyperaldosteronism
vignettes.a: Conn syndrome (tumor) or diffuse hyperplasia (autoimmune)

vignettes.q: High BP + high renin/aldosterone ratio in young woman
vignettes.a: fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD)

vignettes.q: Dx of fibromuscular dysplasia?
vignettes.a: MR angiography of renal arteries

vignettes.q: High BP + high renin/aldosterone ratio in older patient with cardiovascular disease
vignettes.a: renal artery stenosis

vignettes.q: Cause of renal artery stenosis
vignettes.a: atherosclerosis

vignettes.q: Patient with high BP + given ACEi + now creatinine increases; Dx?
vignettes.a: renal artery stenosis or FMD

vignettes.q: Acid-base / biochemical disturbance in RAS or FMD
vignettes.a: high Na, low K, high bicarb, high pH (metabolic alkalosis)

vignettes.q: How does RAAS work?
vignettes.a: Low blood volume → JGC secrete renin → renin cleaves angiotensinogen (produced by the liver) in the plasma into angiotensin I → AT-I goes to lungs and is cleaved by ACE into AT-II → AT-II goes to zona glomerulosa of adrenal cortex

vignettes.q: Important functions of AT-II unrelated to aldosterone?
vignettes.a: potent vasoconstrictor on systemic arterioles (increases afterload) + renal efferent arterioles (increases filtration fraction [GFR/RPF] in setting of low blood volume, meaning that GFR is maintained despite low renal plasma flow)

vignettes.q: Why is AT-II-mediated PCT reabsorption of Na important?
vignettes.a: water follows Na; mechanism to increase fluid retention in setting of low blood volume

vignettes.q: Effect of giving ACEi on efferent arteriolar diameter
vignettes.a: increases diameter

vignettes.q: ACEi (e.g., enalapril) effect on RAAS
vignettes.a: increases renin, increases AT-I, decreases AT-II, decreases aldosterone

vignettes.q: ARB (e.g., valsartan) effect on RAAS
vignettes.a: increases renin, increases AT-I, increases AT-II, decreases aldosterone

vignettes.q: Spironolactone effect on RAAS
vignettes.a: increases renin, increases AT-I, increases AT-II, increases aldosterone

vignettes.q: Eplerenone vs spironolactone
vignettes.a: eplerenone way less likely to cause gynecomastia

vignettes.q: If suspected Dx of Conn syndrome
vignettes.a: CT abdomen

vignettes.q: If CT abdomen negative (hyperplasia not tumor)
vignettes.a: adrenal venous sampling to confirm

vignettes.q: What is pheochromocytoma
vignettes.a: catecholamine-secreting tumor of adrenal medulla

vignettes.q: Paroxysmal headaches/palpitations (high BP) + normal electrolytes
vignettes.a: pheochromocytoma (PCC)

vignettes.q: Paroxysmal headaches/palpitations (high BP) + high glucose
vignettes.a: PCC (catecholamines cause liver to make glucose)

vignettes.q: Tx for PCC
vignettes.a: phenoxybenzamine first (irreversible alpha-1 blocker); never beta-blocker first

vignettes.q: Why phenoxybenzamine first to treat PCC
vignettes.a: if you give beta-blocker first, you get “unopposed alpha,” meaning all of the NE + E (catecholamines) floating around bind to alpha-1, causing massive arteriolar vasoconstriction, shooting BP through the roof

vignettes.q: Dx of PCC
vignettes.a: urinary or serum metanephrines

vignettes.q: Who gets PCC
vignettes.a: NF1, MEN2A/2B (ret gene)

vignettes.q: PCC adults or kids?
vignettes.a: adults

vignettes.q: PCC-like presentation in kids?
vignettes.a: neuroblastoma (n-myc gene)

vignettes.q: Dancing eyes + high BP + midline mass in kid
vignettes.a: neuroblastoma

vignettes.q: Dancing eyes? ?
vignettes.a: opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome (seen in neuroblastoma; yes, weird)

vignettes.q: Dx of neuroblastoma
vignettes.a: abdominal ultrasound

vignettes.q: Kid with painless flank mass that doesn’t cross midline
vignettes.a: Wilms tumor

vignettes.q: Dx of Wilms tumor
vignettes.a: renal ultrasound

vignettes.q: Neonatal boy with midline suprapubic mass
vignettes.a: posterior urethral valves

vignettes.q: Dx of posterior urethral valves
vignettes.a: voiding cystourethrogram

vignettes.q: Cushing syndrome vs Cushing disease
vignettes.a: syndrome = what you look like + refers to any cause of Cushingoid appearance; Cushing disease only = anterior pituitary ACTH-secreting tumor; in other words, Cushing disease is a cause of Cushing syndrome

vignettes.q: Most common cause of Cushing syndrome
vignettes.a: exogenous glucocorticoids (e.g., prednisone)

vignettes.q: Pt not on exogenous steroids + Cushingoid; most common cause?
vignettes.a: Cushing disease most common cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome

vignettes.q: Main causes of Cushing syndrome
vignettes.a: exogenous steroids (most common overall), Cushing disease (most common endogenous), small cell bronchogenic carcinoma (ectopic ACTH), cortisol-secreting tumor (or diffuse hyperplasia) of zona fasciculata of adrenal cortex; CRH tum

vignettes.q: Patient with chronic disease (i.e., IBD, SLE, RA) + Cushingoid; what are the ACTH + cortisol levels
vignettes.a: need to know this means patient is taking prednisone → low ACTH + low cortisol (prednisone is NOT the same thing as cortisol) → prednisone suppresses CRH and ACTH secretion at hypothalamus and anterior pituitary → decreased endoge

vignettes.q: Patient with Cushing disease; ACTH + cortisol levels?
vignettes.a: high ACTH + high cortisol

vignettes.q: Smoker + Cushingoid
vignettes.a: small cell bronchogenic carcinoma

vignettes.q: Smoker + Cushingoid; ACTH + cortisol levels?
vignettes.a: high ACTH (ectopic) + high cortisol

vignettes.q: When to do dexamethasone suppression test
vignettes.a: Cushingoid patient not on exogenous glucocorticoids and has high serum cortisol

vignettes.q: Low-dose dexamethasone suppression test
vignettes.a: tells us yes or no, patient has pathologic cause of Cushing syndrome (i.e., Cushing disease, or SCC of lung, or cortisol-secreting tumor), but we can’t establish the causation from this; if cortisol doesn’t suppress → yes, patient

vignettes.q: High-dose dex
vignettes.a: only cause of Cushing syndrome that will suppress in response is Cushing disease

vignettes.q: Pt has no suppression to low-dose dex + suppresses to high-dose
vignettes.a: Dx = Cushing disease (ACTH secreting tumor of anterior pituitary)

vignettes.q: Pt has no suppression to low- or high-dose dex
vignettes.a: ACTH high? → Yes, answer = SCC of lung; No → answer = cortisol-secreting tumor (or diffuse hyperplasia) of adrenal cortex

vignettes.q: Cushingoid + low ACTH + low cortisol
vignettes.a: exogenous steroids

vignettes.q: Cushingoid + low ACTH + high cortisol
vignettes.a: cortisol-secreting tumor (or diffuse hyperplasia) of adrenal cortex

vignettes.q: Cushingoid + high ACTH + high cortisol
vignettes.a: Cushing disease

vignettes.q: Most accurate test for Dx Cushing syndrome
vignettes.a: 24-hour urine cortisol

vignettes.q: Why dex test not most accurate?
vignettes.a: false-positives in e.g., depression, alcoholism

vignettes.q: Acanthosis nigricans + low K + hyperpigmentation
vignettes.a: Cushing syndrome

vignettes.q: Why acanthosis nigricans
vignettes.a: caused by insulin resistance (unrelated: also can be caused by visceral malignancies)

vignettes.q: Why low K in Cushing syndrome
vignettes.a: chronic elevation of glucocorticoid effect at kidney can push out potassium similar to aldosterone

vignettes.q: Why hyperpigmentation
vignettes.a: high ACTH secretion means POMC is high → high alpha-MSH as well

vignettes.q: Purple striae in obese patient
vignettes.a: Cushing syndrome

vignettes.q: Why purple striae
vignettes.a: glucocorticoids weaken collagen → micro bleeding into skin

vignettes.q: Why hypertension in Cushing syndrome
vignettes.a: cortisol upregulates alpha-1 receptors on arterioles, thereby allowing NE and E to do their job

vignettes.q: Graph shows you two scenarios: 1) NE given alone, then BP increases a little; 2) NE + cortisol given together, then BP increases a lot; why the difference?
vignettes.a: cortisol is permissive of the effects of catecholamines (don’t choose synergistic or additive); once again, cortisol merely allows NE and E to do their job; cortisol isn’t directly increasing BP

vignettes.q: Why normally ratio of E to NE in the blood is 80/20?
vignettes.a: NE draining venously out of the adrenal medulla passes through the adrenal cortex → cortisol upregulates PNMT (converts NE to E)

vignettes.q: What does low cortisol cause?
vignettes.a: chronic fatigue syndrome (as mentioned earlier but super important)

vignettes.q: Function of PTH
vignettes.a: increases blood Ca + decreases blood PO4

vignettes.q: Function of PTH at bone
vignettes.a: increases bone resorption

vignettes.q: Cell PTH binds to at bone
vignettes.a: osteoblast, not -clast

vignettes.q: If PTH causes bone resorption, why the would it bind to osteoblasts (which build bone)
vignettes.a: because PTH causes osteoblasts to express RANK-Ligand on their cell surface → binds to RANK receptor on osteoclasts → bone resorption

vignettes.q: How do osteoclasts resorb bone
vignettes.a: intracellular carbonic anhydrase II (CAH-II) → creates H2CO3 from H2O and CO2; then the H2CO3 → bicarb + proton → protons accumulate at bone-osteoclast interface → surface for resorption

vignettes.q: What is teriparatide
vignettes.a: N-terminus PTH analogue that binds to osteoblasts, and then rather than causing bone resorption, actually stimulates bone growth (difference in mechanism not well elucidated) → used in advanced osteoporosis

vignettes.q: Avoid teriparatide in whom?
vignettes.a: Paget disease of bone patients; Hx of osteosarcoma

vignettes.q: Three effects of PTH at the kidney?
vignettes.a: 1) it upregulates 1-alpha hydroxylase activity in the PCT (converts inactive 25-OH-D3 into active 1,25-(OH)2-D3; 2) decreases PO4 reabsorption in PCT by downregulating three types of apical membrane brush-border sodium-phosphate s

vignettes.q: What does secretion in kidney terms mean
vignettes.a: excretion through the tubular wall (excretion is umbrella term → filtration = excretion through Bowman capsule; secretion = through tubular wall)

vignettes.q: Primary hyperparathyroidism biochemical disturbance?
vignettes.a: high Ca, low PO4, high ALP, high PTH

vignettes.q: Why is ALP high
vignettes.a: ALP reflects osteoblast activity; if PTH high, then ALP also high (but annoyingly, if PTH is low, ALP will be normal, not low)

vignettes.q: Who gets primary hyperPTH
vignettes.a: usually parathyroid adenoma (e.g., 22 yr old girl with nodule)

vignettes.q: Who else gets primaryPTH
vignettes.a: MEN1 + MEN2A (can be diffuse 4-gland hyperplasia in MEN patients)

vignettes.q: , what are the MEN syndromes again?
vignettes.a: Relax. MEN1 = parathyroid, pituitary, pancreas; MEN2A = parathyroid, PCC, medullary thyroid carcinoma; MEN2B = PCC, medullary thyroid carcinoma, mucosal neuromas, and Marfanoid body habitus (“oid” means looks like but ain’t)

vignettes.q: Question says girl has high Ca + low PO4 + nodule of left, superior parathyroid gland; what’s the embryo derivative?
vignettes.a: 4th pharyngeal pouch

vignettes.q: Other weird info I need to know for primaryPTH?
vignettes.a: Yeah, firstly, urinary Ca is high, not low.

vignettes.q: , how is that possible if PTH reabsorbs Ca from urine
vignettes.a: because serum Ca is high, so the net amount in the urine is still high (this is a HY arrow Q that everyone gets wrong); in other words, on the USMLE, in primaryPTH → serum Ca up; serum PO4 down; serum ALP up; urinary Ca up (oh wow

vignettes.q: Second weird factoid about primaryPTH
vignettes.a: urinary cAMP is elevated (USMLE likes this for some magical reason)

vignettes.q: What is the biochemical disturbance in secondary hyperparathyroidism?
vignettes.a: Ca and PO4 opposite of primary → low Ca; high PO4, high ALP + high PTH

vignettes.q: Who gets secondaryPTH
vignettes.a: chronic renal failure

vignettes.q: Why does chronic renal failure cause secondaryPTH
vignettes.a: inability to activate vitamin D3 in PCT → decreased Ca absorption through small bowel → low serum Ca → stimulates PTH release; kidney also simply cannot reabsorb Ca as well, further decreasing serum Ca and stimulating PTH release

vignettes.q: What about low Ca in acute renal failure; doesn’t it take a while for vitamin D effects to occur
vignettes.a: if low Ca in acute, due to mere inability to reabsorb from urine

vignettes.q: Why high PO4 in renal disease
vignettes.a: kidney can’t filter it out; even though there’s less activated D3 and PO4 absorption through small bowel is also decreased, the inability of the kidney to excrete it “wins”

vignettes.q: Biochemical disturbance of vitamin D deficiency
vignettes.a: low Ca, low PO4, normal/high PTH, normal/high ALP

vignettes.q: Function of vitamin D
vignettes.a: increases Ca + PO4 absorption in the bowel (don’t worry about minimal role in bone)

vignettes.q: I don’t get it though; if in chronic renal failure there’s vitamin D deficiency due to less activation, why is there low Ca and high PO4? Isn’t vitamin D deficiency always low Ca and low PO4?
vignettes.a: chronic renal failure “wins” in terms of phosphate always → so although low vitamin D, there’s still high PO4.

vignettes.q: Any changes to the bones in a patient with chronic renal disease
vignettes.a: renal osteodystrophy

vignettes.q: Hip fracture in renal failure + x-ray shows “pseudofractures”
vignettes.a: vitamin D deficiency

vignettes.q: Osteitis fibrosa cystica
vignettes.a: high PTH can cause “brown tumors” of bone + cholesterol accumulation in bone

vignettes.q: Kid with bowing of tibias + chostochondritis + craniotabes
vignettes.a: rickets (vitamin D deficiency)

vignettes.q: Adult with pseudofractures
vignettes.a: osteomalacia (vitamin D deficiency)

vignettes.q: Where does vitamin D deficiency start
vignettes.a: stratum basale of skin (asked on USMLE)

vignettes.q: What is the sequence for production?
vignettes.a: 7-dehydrocholsterol in skin goes to cholecalciferol via UV-B → then cholecalciferol goes to liver where it takes on a hydroxylation to make 25-hydroxy-D3 (calcidiol) → then this goes to the kidney where, via PTH activing 1-alpha-h

vignettes.q: If person doesn’t get sunlight, what can he/she not make
vignettes.a: cholecalciferol (7-dehydro is wrong answer; this is on NBME)

vignettes.q: What about 7-dehydrocholesterol in relation to sunlight
vignettes.a: we make this on our own, then UV-B converts it into cholecalciferol

vignettes.q: Alcoholic who eats plenty of dairy + gets sunlight + has vitamin D deficiency
vignettes.a: decreased hepatic hydroxylation

vignettes.q: Inject person with Ca; what happens to their vitamin D notably
vignettes.a: increased 24,25-(OH)2- D3.
25-OH-D3 is immediately converted to 24,25 as a storage form (think of them as the same)

vignettes.q: Inject with Ca
vignettes.a: Ca binds to Ca-sensing receptor at parathyroid gland → negative feedback → causes reduction in PTH release → decreased 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity at kidney → buildup of 25 form → shunted to 24,25 form.

vignettes.q: Low calcium or potassium in a patient + he/she not responsive to supplementation
vignettes.a: hypomagnesemia → Mg needed for basal levels of PTH release (so low PTH → low Ca) + renal retention of K

vignettes.q: Alcoholic + low Ca or low K not responsive to supplementation
vignettes.a: check serum magnesium

vignettes.q: Why low Mg in alcoholic
vignettes.a: dietary deficiency

vignettes.q: Who gets high vitamin D (hypervitaminosis D)
vignettes.a: granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis) → don’t be the fool who says “girl tried to commit suicide by ODing on vitamin D pills?”

vignettes.q: Why high vitamin D in sarcoidosis
vignettes.a: epithelioid (activated) macrophages secrete 1-alpha hydroxylase → activate vitamin D → increased small bowel absorption

vignettes.q: Ca and PTH levels in sarcoidosis
vignettes.a: high Ca, low PTH (negative feedback)

vignettes.q: Sarcoidosis, any weird fact they ask about Ca?
vignettes.a: “decreased Ca in feces” (makes sense)

vignettes.q: Biochemical disturbance in high vit D
vignettes.a: high Ca, normal or high PO4, normal or low PTH, normal or low ALP (USMLE will only give you one correct answer, don’t worry, but I write the possibilities here so you don’t get a Q where you see normal PTH or PO4 and are wondering

vignettes.q: Sarcoidosis other weird info
vignettes.a: increased serum ACE (correct, angiotensin-converting enzyme; weird)

vignettes.q: Sarcoidosis, what happens first, high urinary Ca or high serum Ca
vignettes.a: high urinary Ca (kidney will compensate before serum levels go up)

vignettes.q: 20s-30s African American woman with dry cough; CXR shows nodularity; Dx?
vignettes.a: sarcoidosis; nodularity just means “bihilar lymphadenopathy”

vignettes.q: 20s-30s African American woman with dry cough; CXR shows nodularity; Dx?
vignettes.a: “noncaseating granulomas” (sarcoidosis)

vignettes.q: 20s-30s African American woman with dry cough; CXR is normal Dx?
vignettes.a: asthma (1/3 of asthma patients only have dry cough; this is called cough-variant asthma)

vignettes.q: 20s-30s African American woman with dry cough; CXR is normal Dx?
vignettes.a: “increased activation of mast cells” (asthma)

vignettes.q: Mutation in calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid gland
vignettes.a: loss of negative feedback → PTH goes up, serum Ca up

vignettes.q: Mutation in calcium-sensing receptor on parathyroid gland
vignettes.a: cause of familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH)

vignettes.q: High PTH + high serum Ca + low urinary Ca
vignettes.a: FHH

vignettes.q: High PTH + high serum Ca + high urinary Ca
vignettes.a: primary PTH

vignettes.q: Mechanism for low urinary Ca in FHH?
vignettes.a: not fully elucidated, but literature suggests increased tubular reabsorption, possibly paracellular, as serum Mg in FHH elevated relative to primaryPTH

vignettes.q: What is cinacalcet
vignettes.a: calcimimetic → activates Ca-sensing receptor at PTH gland

vignettes.q: When to use cinacalcet
vignettes.a: tertiary hyperPTH

vignettes.q: What is tertiary hyperparathyroidism?
vignettes.a: classically seen in renal transplant patients; autonomous four-gland hypersecretion of PTH following long-term secondary hyperparathyroidism and hypocalcemia → parathyroid chief cell hyperplasia that does not resolve with renal tr

vignettes.q: What is pseudohypoparathyroidism?
vignettes.a: insensitivity to PTH → high PTH but low Ca + high PO4

vignettes.q: Anything special about pseudohypoparathyroidism?
vignettes.a: Yes. This is one of the highest yield yet underemphasized conditions on the USMLE Step 1. In other words, my students get these Qs on the exam regularly but the resources don’t emphasize the different types of this condition

vignettes.q: What is presentation of pseudohypoparathyroidism?
vignettes.a: need to know Types 1a, 1b, 2

vignettes.q: Type 1a = Albright Hereditary Osteodystrophy = is simply the name of the phenotype
vignettes.a: AHO has shortened 4th + 5th metacarpals, short stature + intellectual disability + urinary cAMP does not increase with exogenous PTH administration (normally should go up in response to PTH)

vignettes.q: Type 1b
vignettes.a: high PTH + low Ca + high PO4 + no AHO phenotype (just biochemical disturbance)

vignettes.q: Type 2
vignettes.a: same as Type 1b but urinary cAMP increases in response to exogenous PTH

vignettes.q: Mike, this sounds pedantic though. The USMLE really asks about pseudohypoparathyroidism like that?
vignettes.a: Yeah. They ask it as arrow questions. And I personally had two pseudohypoPTH Qs on my Step 1 + my students do.

vignettes.q: What is pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism?
vignettes.a: AHO phenotype but no biochemical disturbance

vignettes.q: Graves disease parameters
vignettes.a: low TSH, high T3, high T4, increased iodine uptake

vignettes.q: Mechanism of Graves
vignettes.a: activating TSH-receptor antibody, called TSI – thyroid stimulating immunoglobulin)

vignettes.q: Tx for Graves
vignettes.a: propylthiouracil (PTU) or methimazole to address thyroid derangement

vignettes.q: PTU and methimazole MOAs
vignettes.a: both inhibit thyroperoxidase, but PTU also inhibits peripheral conversion by inhibiting 5-deiodinase → propylthiouracil is a longer word than methimazole, so it’s the one that does both

vignettes.q: Tx for tachycardia in Graves
vignettes.a: propranolol (because beta-blockade also decreases peripheral conversion of T4 to T3)

vignettes.q: Important point about Graves?
vignettes.a: proptosis/exophthalmos + pretibial myxedema are specific; in other words, there are numerous causes of hyperthyroidism (e.g., toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, etc.), but only Graves will cause the eye findings

vignettes.q: Tx for ophthalmopathy in Graves
vignettes.a: steroids

vignettes.q: Why do the eye findings occur in Graves?
vignettes.a: glycosaminoglycan deposition in/around extra-ocular muscles

vignettes.q: High BP + fever + increased CK
vignettes.a: thyroid storm (Tx with PTU + propranolol)

vignettes.q: What is the role of potassium iodide (KI) in hyperthyroid Tx?
vignettes.a: shuts off gland production (Wolff- Chaikoff effect) → answer in person exposed to nuclear fallout or radioiodine vapors in laboratory

vignettes.q: Hashimoto parameters
vignettes.a: high TSH, low T3, low T4, decreased iodine uptake

vignettes.q: Mechanism for Hashimoto
vignettes.a: antibodies against thyroperoxidase + thyroglobulin; anti-microsomal

vignettes.q: Histo of Hashimoto
vignettes.a: lymphocytic infiltrate (easy to remember bc the non-eponymous name for Hashimoto is chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis)

vignettes.q: 50M + low mood + BMI 26
vignettes.a: Hashimoto

vignettes.q: Proximal muscle weakness in Hashimoto + increased serum CK
vignettes.a: hypothyroid myopathy

vignettes.q: 45M + decreased ability to get up from chair unassisted + HR of 60
vignettes.a: Hashimoto

vignettes.q: 45M + high cholesterol + high hepatic AST + HR of 55
vignettes.a: Hashimoto (hypothyroidism can cause bradycardia, high cholesterol, and high AST [the latter is weird, correct])

vignettes.q: Thyroid cancer in Hashimoto
vignettes.a: thyroid lymphoma (autoimmune diseases → increased risk of lymphoma)

vignettes.q: 22M + viral infection + very tender thyroid
vignettes.a: subacute granulomatous thyroiditis (de Quervain)

vignettes.q: De Quervain parameters
vignettes.a: triphasic → causes hyper-, then hypo-, then rebounds to euthyroid state → most important point is that iodine uptake is DECREASED in de Quervain + drug-induced thyroiditis, even if patient is in a hyper-phase.

vignettes.q: Tx for de Quervain thyroiditis?
vignettes.a: NSAIDs

vignettes.q: 22M + very tender thyroid + HR of 88 + tremulousness + heat intolerance
vignettes.a: low TSH, high T3, high T4, decreased iodine uptake (in contrast to Graves, which is painless and uptake is high)

vignettes.q: 27F + gave birth to healthy boy 6 months ago following uncomplicated labor + no weight change or mood disturbance + on no meds + vitals WNL + dry skin + thyroid gland enlarged and non-tender + TSH high + T4 low
vignettes.a: “thyroiditis” → Dx = postpartum thyroiditis (a type of silent thyroiditis) → characterized by thyrotoxicosis followed by hypothyroidism (1/3 of women experience both phases; 1/3 experience just hyperthyroid phase; 1/3 only hypothy

vignettes.q: Tx for subacute thyroiditis
vignettes.a: aspirin first, not steroids; steroids may be used later

vignettes.q: Drugs causing thyroiditis
vignettes.a: lithium + amiodarone

vignettes.q: Surreptitious thyrotoxicosis
vignettes.a: self- injection of thyroxine → low TSH, high T3, high T4, small thyroid gland with decreased uptake

vignettes.q: Injection of triiodothyroinine (T3)
vignettes.a: TSH will go down, T3 goes up (clearly), T4 does not go up because T3 isn’t converted to T4; only T4 is converted to T3

vignettes.q: Injection of thyroxine
vignettes.a: TSH will go down (negative feedback), T4 goes up (clearly), T3 goes up (due to peripheral conversion), reverse T3 also goes up

vignettes.q: What is reverse T3?
vignettes.a: an inactive form of T3; T4 is converted peripherally into T3 (active) and reverse T3 (inactive)

vignettes.q: Anything else I need to know about reverse T3?
vignettes.a: it’s increased in euthyroid sick syndrome → times of stress/surgery/illness → cortisol increases → cortisol decreases conversion of T4 to active T3, so more T4 is converted to reverse T3 → parameters in euthyroid sick syndrome: no

vignettes.q: What is sublinical hypothyroidism
vignettes.a: high TSH but normal T3 + T4 (don’t confuse with ESS)

vignettes.q: Want to check thyroid function, what’s the first thing to order
vignettes.a: TSH

vignettes.q: Want to check thyroid function in pregnancy, what’s the first thing to order
vignettes.a: free-T4

vignettes.q: What is free-T4
vignettes.a: most thyroid hormone is protein-bound and inactive; free-T4 tells you definitively whether the patient has thyroid derangement or not

vignettes.q: Pregnancy and thyroid
vignettes.a: estrogen causes increased thyroid-binding globulin production by the liver → mops of T4 → less free-T4 → less negative feedback at hypothalamus + anterior pituitary → TSH goes up transiently to compensate → more T4 made → free-T4

vignettes.q: Hyperthyroidism in pregnancy
vignettes.a: LH, FSH, TSH, hCG all share same alpha-subunit; their beta-subunits differ; some women have increases sensitivity of TSH receptor to alpha-subunit, so high hCG in early pregnancy can stimulate thyroid gland and cause transient hyp

vignettes.q: Hashimoto in pregnancy
vignettes.a: increase pregnant woman’s dose of levothyroxine by 50%

vignettes.q: Graves in pregnancy
vignettes.a: avoid methimazole in first trimester (teratogenic; causes aplasia cutis congenita) → give PTU in first-trimester → in second + third trimesters, switch from PTU to methimazole (methimazole no longer teratogenic later in pregnancy

vignettes.q: Pt being treated for Graves + mouth ulcers
vignettes.a: agranulocytosis (neutropenia) caused by methimazole or PTU.

vignettes.q: Young child with normal free-T4 and low total T4
vignettes.a: thyroid-binding globulin deficiency (opposite of pregnancy)

vignettes.q: Young child + large belly + large tongue + hypotonia
vignettes.a: cretinism (congenital hypothyroidism)

vignettes.q: Most common cause of cretinism
vignettes.a: iodine deficiency

vignettes.q: Most common cause of hyperthyroidism in elderly
vignettes.a: toxic multinodular goiter

vignettes.q: Evaluation of thyroid cancer, first step?
vignettes.a: palpation of thyroid gland

vignettes.q: If thyroid nodule present, then check TSH; if TSH normal or high
vignettes.a: ultrasound first, then FNA; if TSH low, do radioiodine uptake scan; thyroid cancer is cold, not hot, which is why no ultimate FNA with low TSH

vignettes.q: Struma ovarii
vignettes.a: thyroid hormone secreting ovarian germ cell tumor

vignettes.q: Diabetic ketoacidosis parameters
vignettes.a: low serum Na, high serum K (hyperkalemia), low total body K, low bicarb, low pH, low CO2 (all exceedingly HY)

vignettes.q: Why low serum Na in DKA
vignettes.a: osmotic effect of high glucose in blood → dilutional hyponatremia; in addition, there’s believed to be a contributory renal mechanism related to increased absorption of water in the PCT due to increased SGLT2 reabsorption of gluco

vignettes.q: Then what does low total body potassium mean
vignettes.a: just to be clear, the patient is hyperkalemic (high K in the blood) yet has low K overall in the body → kidney senses high K in urine and therefore increases excretion of it (kaliuresis) → body is now losing K → but three above me

vignettes.q: Why does the potassium stuff matter so much with DKA
vignettes.a: because when you Tx DKA and start giving insulin (fluids first btw; giving insulin immediately is the wrong answer; give insulin after first administering a bolus of normal saline), K will now be driven into the cells, which will

vignettes.q: Overweight, middle-age patient with polydipsia + polyuria
vignettes.a: type II DM

vignettes.q: High in serum in type II DM
vignettes.a: insulin is high initially; ketones absent (only ketones in DKA; DKA is type I only)

vignettes.q: Type II diabetic crisis?
vignettes.a: hyperosmolar hyperglycemic non-ketotic syndrome (HHNS) → still give fluids first

vignettes.q: Glucose numbers in DKA vs HHNS
vignettes.a: low-hundreds for DKA (i.e., 2-300s); can be 600-1000 for HHNS

vignettes.q: Acid-base disturbance in aspirin toxicity first 20 mins
vignettes.a: resp. alkalosis (low CO2, high pH, normal O2, normal bicarb [too acute to change])

vignettes.q: Acid-base disturbance in aspirin toxicity after 20 mins
vignettes.a: mixed metabolic acidosis-respiratory alkalosis (low CO2, low pH, normal O2, low bicarb)

vignettes.q: Tx for aspirin toxicity
vignettes.a: bicarb (increased excretion through urinary alkalinization)

vignettes.q: Acid-base disturbance in PE
vignettes.a: resp. alkalosis (low CO2, high pH, low O2, normal bicarb [too acute to change])

vignettes.q: Acid-base disturbance in asthma
vignettes.a: resp. alkalosis (low CO2, high pH, low O2, normal bicarb [too acute to change])

vignettes.q: Electrolyte abnormality in anorexia
vignettes.a: hypokalemia

vignettes.q: Most common cause of death in anorexia
vignettes.a: arrhythmia from hypokalemia

vignettes.q: Refeeding syndrome (even if normal BMI)
vignettes.a: hypophosphatemia

vignettes.q: Amenorrhea in anorexia
vignettes.a: low FSH + low estrogen (hypogonadotropic)

vignettes.q: Premature ovarian failure + Turner syndrome + menopause
vignettes.a: high FSH (low inhibin) + low estrogen

vignettes.q: High BMI female + irregular menstrual cycles
vignettes.a: anovulation

vignettes.q: Anovulation + hirsutism
vignettes.a: PCOS

vignettes.q: Anovulation. Cause USMLE wants?
vignettes.a: insulin resistance → causes abnormal GnRH pulsation

vignettes.q: Why hirsutism in anovulation
vignettes.a: abnormal GnRH pulsation causes high LH/FSH ratio

vignettes.q: Why high LH/FSH ratio important in anovulation/PCOS
vignettes.a: ovulation stimulated when follicle not ready → no ovulation (anovulation) → follicle retained as cyst

vignettes.q: What’s LH do?
vignettes.a: Stimulates theca interna cells (females) and Leydig cells (males) to make androgens

vignettes.q: What’s FSH do?
vignettes.a: Stimulates granulosa cells (females) and Sertoli cells (males) to make aromatase; also primes follicles

vignettes.q: Tx for PCOS
vignettes.a: if high BMI, weight loss first always on USMLE

vignettes.q: Tx for PCOS if they ask for meds and/or weight loss already tried
vignettes.a: OCPs (if not wanting pregnancy); clomiphene (if wanting pregnancy)

vignettes.q: PCOS increases risk of what
vignettes.a: endometrial cancer (unopposed estrogen)

vignettes.q: Where does ADH (vasopressin) act
vignettes.a: medullary collecting duct → causes aquaporin insertion on apical membrane → enables free H2O reabsorption

vignettes.q: Where is ADH made?
vignettes.a: supraoptic nucleus of hypothalamus → merely stored in posterior pituitary

vignettes.q: Where is oxytocin made
vignettes.a: paraventricular nucleus of hypothalamus → merely stored in p. pituitary.

vignettes.q: Neurophysins I’ve heard about. What are those
vignettes.a: Showed up in UWorld → carrier proteins needed to transport oxytocin + ADH from hypothalamus to posterior pituitary

vignettes.q: When does ADH go up
vignettes.a: when serum sodium too high → brings sodium back down; ADH will also be secreted in response to lower blood volume, although aldosterone is major volume regulator; ADH is main tonicity regulator

vignettes.q: When considering SIADH vs diabetes insipidus (DI) vs psychogenic polydipsia (PP)
vignettes.a: what’s the next best step in evaluation/management → fluid restriction

vignettes.q: SIADH important causes
vignettes.a: small cell bronchogenic carcinoma ectopic ACTH, or head trauma (can actually cause SIADH or DI)

vignettes.q: SIADH parameters
vignettes.a: high urine osmolality (concentrated) + low serum sodium (normal is 135-145)

vignettes.q: Tx for SIADH
vignettes.a: if small cell lung cancer, chemotherapy (HY to know you can’t do surgery for small cell); if insufficient, give -vaptans (conivaptan, tolvaptan), which are ADH receptor antagonists, or demeclocycline (a tetracycline antibiotic tha

vignettes.q: Central diabetes insipidus
vignettes.a: lack of production by hypothalamus or storage problem of posterior pituitary → low ADH + low urine osmolality (dilute urine) + high serum sodium (concentrated serum)

vignettes.q: Cause of CDI
vignettes.a: idiopathic, local malignancy, or head trauma

vignettes.q: Nephrogenic DI
vignettes.a: lack of sensitivity of kidney V2 receptors to ADH → high ADH, low urine osmolality (dilute urine) + high serum sodium (concentrated serum)

vignettes.q: Cause of NDI
vignettes.a: lithium, demeclocycline

vignettes.q: Patient with bipolar disorder + tremors + polyuria + polydipsia
vignettes.a: NDI

vignettes.q: Dude jumps into cold lake; what happens to central blood volume + atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) + ADH levels?
vignettes.a: CBV up (cold → sympathetic activation → alpha-1 agonism peripherally to decrease surface area of blood vessels to conserve heat → blood forced to core) + ANP up (if CBV up, then right atrial stretch up; ANP is body’s natural diure

vignettes.q: Psychogenic polydipsia (PP)?
vignettes.a: person drinks too much → low serum sodium + low urine osmolality

vignettes.q: Prolactin does what
vignettes.a: milk production → acts through JAK/STAT tyrosine kinase

vignettes.q: Oxytocin does what
vignettes.a: milk letdown/secretion

vignettes.q: Growth hormone in young
vignettes.a: giantism; in adults → acromegaly

vignettes.q: Important points about acromegaly
vignettes.a: causes diabetes mellitus (GH causes insulin resistance), hypertension, carpal tunnel syndrome, arthritis, cardiomyopathy; and yes, prognathism (lantern jaw)

vignettes.q: Growth hormone acts directly at tissues?
vignettes.a: USMLE wants you to know it causes liver to increase insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1), which acts peripherally

vignettes.q: Which hormone counteracts GH
vignettes.a: somatostatin → generally acts to shut off other hormone secretions, and antagonizes the effects of GH (can be Tx for acromegaly)

vignettes.q: What is pegvisomant?
vignettes.a: GH receptor antagonist

vignettes.q: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH)
vignettes.a: caused by 21, 11, or 17 hydroxylase deficiency in adrenal cortex (21 is 90-95% of cases) → autosomal recessive conditions

vignettes.q: 21 hydroxylase deficiency
vignettes.a: severe lack of mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid production by adrenal → low BP + high K + high DHEA-S (adrenal androgen)

vignettes.q: 11 hydroxylase deficiency
vignettes.a: adrenal can still make 11-deoxycorticosterone in zona glomerulosa + 11- deoxycortisol in zona fasciculata → BP not low (sometimes high) + K not high; DHEA-S still high

vignettes.q: 17 hydroxylase deficiency
vignettes.a: can’t convert pregnenolone + progesterone to 17-OH forms → adrenal gland makes aldosterone in excess but not cortisol or DHEA-S

vignettes.q: What does ACTH do at adrenal gland
vignettes.a: upregulates desmolase, which converts cholesterol into pregnenolone to start adrenal hormone synthesis

vignettes.q: What does angiotensin II do at the adrenal gland
vignettes.a: upregulates aldosterone synthase, converting 11- deoxycorticosterone into aldosterone

vignettes.q: What is metyrapone testing?
vignettes.a: 11-beta hydroxylase inhibitor → can be used in the diagnosis of adrenal insufficiency or Cushing → re the former, if you give metyrapone, cortisol should go down normally and ACTH + 11-deoxycorticosterone should go up; if ACTH goe

vignettes.q: Normal calcium
Tx of hypercalcemia
vignettes.a: 10.2-12 → normal saline (0.9% NaCl)

vignettes.q: Tx of hypercalcemia
vignettes.a: 12-14 → normal saline (0.9% NaCl) only if asymptomatic; add bisphosphonate (e.g., pamidronate) if symptomatic

vignettes.q: Tx of hypercalcemia
vignettes.a: 14+ → normal saline (0.9% NaCl) + bisphosphonate

vignettes.q: Low calcium or potassium in alcoholic
vignettes.a: hypomagnesemia is cause

vignettes.q: Back pain in elderly patient with hypercalcemia
vignettes.a: multiple myeloma or metastases

vignettes.q: Polycythemia + hypercalcemia + smoker + red urine
vignettes.a: RCC (paraneoplasic EPO + PTH-rp)

vignettes.q: Electrolyte disturbance in sarcoid
vignettes.a: hypercalcemia → LOW PTH + high calcium

vignettes.q: Hypercalcemia in sarcoid, why?
vignettes.a: epithelioid (activated) macrophages produce 1-alpha hydroxylase, thereby activating vitamin D3

vignettes.q: Two main causes of pseudogout
vignettes.a: primary hyperparathyroidism + hemochromatosis

vignettes.q: Two ways pseudogout presents
vignettes.a: monoarthritis of large joint (i.e., knee) or osteoarthritis-like presentation in someone with primary hyperparathyroidism or hemochromatosis

vignettes.q: PTU and methimazole are used for what?
vignettes.a: Tx of Graves

vignettes.q: 17F + 1-year Hx of autoimmune thyroiditis + 2-year Hx of type I DM + Candidal infections since childhood; Dx?
vignettes.a: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis → two points: 1) clearly the Candidal infections can’t be due to the diabetes if she’s had them since childhood and only DM for two years; 2) USMLE likes “autoimmune conditions go together,” the s

vignettes.q: Thyroid dysfunction on ventilator
vignettes.a: euthyroid sick syndrome → normal TSH, normal T4, low T3, high reverse T3 (cortisol decreases peripheral conversion of T4 to T3, allowing more to go to reverse T3)

vignettes.q: is reverse T3?
vignettes.a: an inactive form of T3; all you need to know is that if T4 goes up (e.g., in Graves), reverse T3 should be up because T4 will convert to both T3 and reverse T3; it is also elevated in euthyroid sick syndrome (and T3 down!)

vignettes.q: Familial thyroid cancer
vignettes.a: medullary (even if they mention nothing else related to MEN 2A/2B); apple- green birefringence on Congo red stain due to amyloid deposition; serum calcitonin high

vignettes.q: Calcitonin mechanism of action
vignettes.a: inhibits osteoclast activity (not the opposite of PTH; in other words, doesn’t put calcium back into bone; it merely caps the Ca that can resorb out of the bone)

vignettes.q: Most common thyroid cancer
vignettes.a: papillary; extends lymphatogenously; has papillary structure and psammoma bodies on LM; don’t worry about buzzywordy things like Orphan Annie nuclei

vignettes.q: Follicular carcinoma
vignettes.a: literally just thyroid follicles on biopsy; will be a cold nodule, like any other type of thyroid cancer (for instance, if you see follicles but it’s a hot nodule w/ increased uptake, that’s a toxic adenoma, rather than follicular

vignettes.q: Hashimoto + thyroid cancer + no other histo description
vignettes.a: thyroid lymphoma → autoimmune diseases increase the risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma

vignettes.q: MEN1
vignettes.a: pituitary, pancreas, parathyroid (MEN1 gene; chromosome 11)

vignettes.q: MEN2A
vignettes.a: parathyroid, medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma

vignettes.q: MEN2B
vignettes.a: medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, Marfanoid body habitus (“oid” means looks like but ain’t)

vignettes.q: Riedel thyroiditis
vignettes.a: fibrosis of thyroid → can extend into adjacent structures, e.g., the esophagus, and resemble anaplastic carcinoma

vignettes.q: First drug to start in T2DM
vignettes.a: metformin

vignettes.q: Side-effect of metformin
vignettes.a: lactic acidosis

vignettes.q: Black widow spider bite
vignettes.a: causes hypocalcemia → give IV calcium gluconate

vignettes.q: Adult male is 4 feet tall + head and trunk proportional to limbs; Dx?
vignettes.a: Laron dwarfism (growth hormone receptor defect → insensitivity to GH).

vignettes.q: Biochemical disturbance in Addison?
vignettes.a: Low Na, high K, low pH, low bicarb

vignettes.q: Biochemical disturbance in Conn syndrome?
vignettes.a: High Na, low K, high pH, high bicarb

vignettes.q: 2-year-old boy has cardiac myxoma (correct, not rhabdomyoma) + perioral melanosis (sophisticated way of saying hyperpigmentation around the mouth/lips) + hyperthyroidism; Dx?

vignettes.q: Refusal of vaccination A 4-month-old boy is brought to the pediatrician by his parents. The physician recommends a number of vaccinations but the parents decline and are firm believers that vaccines cause autis
vignettes.a: A) “I am going to document this in the chart. If you change your mind, vaccines will be available.”. The parents have firmly stated that they do not wish to discuss this further. They have their beliefs and these must be respected

vignettes.a: C. The physician should simply communicate to the patient that he or she is attempting to help make things easier at home. The physician should be sensitive to patients in cognitive decline who are sometimes aware of their evanesc

vignettes.a: E. In order to establish healthy sleep hygiene, patients should be told to try to get up at the same time every day, even if it is difficult to do so and they feel tired. The result is they may be more inclined to go to bed earlie

vignettes.q: Sensitive examinations A 34-year-old woman at 34 weeks’ gestation presents to emergency with copious vaginal bleeding and severe pelvic pain. She has not noticed any fetal movements during the past 24 hours. Bl

vignettes.q: Medical students disclosing information A medical student is caring for a 68-year-old man who has been admitted to hospital for biopsy of a pancreatic mass. The resident physician asks the student not to discus
vignettes.a: D. The student was given instructions by a senior to not disclose the results. Professional conduct must be upheld and the results not disclosed. Choice A ignores the patient’s question. Even if the implication is, “I’m just a stu

vignettes.q: 500 factory workers are surveyed to determine whether they smoke or not and whether they have COPD or not; what kind of study design is this?
