vignettes.a: ↓ Hematocrit, ↑ indirect bilirubin, ↔ direct bilirubin, ↑ total bilirubin. — Diagnosis is G6PD deficiency. Hemolysis can be precipitated by drugs such as dapsone and primaquine, as well as by fava beans. • In G6PD deficiency, ther

vignettes.q: 43M + treated with cimetidine for gastric ulcers. As a result of this medication, what are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for intracellular inositol triphosphate (IP3), diacylglycerol (DAG), and cAMP?
vignettes.a: ↔ IP3, ↔ DAG, ↓ cAMP. — Cimetidine is a histamine-2 receptor blocker (H2 blocker). • The H2 receptor is a G-a-s G-protein. Agonism increases cAMP. However, since cimetidine is an H2 antagonist, cAMP will decrease. • Cimetidine can

vignettes.q: Virchow node (Troisier sign)
vignettes.a: palpable supraclavicular lymph node that can reflect visceral malignancy, especially gastric cancer. Hyperbilirubinemia

vignettes.q: USMLE likes acute exacerbations of hyperammonemia caused by GI bleeds
vignettes.a: ↑ ammonia absorption.

vignettes.q: Both are associated with HLA-B27
vignettes.a: PAIR → Psoriasis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD, Reactive arthritis.

vignettes.q: Pain starts at epigastrium (visceral pain) and migrates toward RLQ (parietal pain). USMLE will ask why there is movement of the pain
vignettes.a: “inflammation of the parietal peritoneum.” In other words, organ pain (visceral pain) is felt somewhat non-specifically around the epigastrium. But once it becomes more superficial and involves the parietal peritoneum, it is felt

vignettes.q: USMLE wants you to know appendicitis pain can be RUQ in pregnancy due to displacement of bowel and a shift in appendiceal location. What they will do is tell you pregnant woman in 3rd trimester has RUQ pain, fe
vignettes.a: “appendicitis.”

vignettes.q: USMLE will give ethics/consent Q, where they say patient has operation performed for ovarian procedure but it is seen that she has an acutely inflamed appendix
vignettes.a: “remove due to necessity of medical emergency.”

vignettes.q: ECG
vignettes.a: Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium parvum, and Giardia lamblia are all GI protozoa that are acquired via cysts in water (i.e., they are water-borne). If “water-borne” and “fecal-oral” are both listed as answers, USMLE wants “w

vignettes.q: 44M + fasting glucose of 112 mg/dL + dark skin on forearms + arthritis; Dx?
vignettes.a: hereditary hemochromatosis → AR, chromosome 6, HFE gene, C282Y or H63D missense mutations account for 90% → “Bronze diabetes” → hyperpigmentation (from hemosiderin deposition) + diabetes due to iron deposition in tail of pancreas

vignettes.q: 44M + fasting glucose of 130 mg/dL + hands are sore + x-ray of hands shows DIP involvement; what’s the Dx for the type of arthritis?
vignettes.a: pseudogout, not osteoarthritis. Student says ? The two most common etiologies for pseudogout are hemochromatosis and primary hyperparathyroidism (pseudogout is calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, and will present as either a

vignettes.q: Tx of hereditary hemochromatosis
vignettes.a: serial phlebotomy, not chelation therapy.

vignettes.q: 44M patient above + USMLE asks what’s the mechanism for his disease
vignettes.a: “increased intestinal absorption of iron.”

vignettes.q: 44M above + next best step in Dx?
vignettes.a: check serum ferritin (>300 ug/L in men + post-menopausal women; or >200 in premenopausal women; USMLE will always say >300 so don’t worry).

vignettes.q: Why do men get hemochromatosis younger + with worse Sx than women?
vignettes.a: menstruation slows progression of disease.

vignettes.q: What is secondary hemochromatosis?
vignettes.a: aka transfusional siderosis (amazing to remember if you want to sound sophisticated) → due to chronic blood transfusions → each transfusion of RBCs contains iron → seen classically in beta-thalassemia major or any other patients r

vignettes.q: Tx for secondary hemochromatosis (transfusional siderosis)
vignettes.a: chelation therapy (e.g., deferoxamine), not serial phlebotomy.

vignettes.q: Three main conditions causing hepatocellular carcinoma?
vignettes.a: HepB, HepC, hemochromatosis.

vignettes.q: Tumor marker of HCC?
vignettes.a: AFP (same as yolk sac tumor, aka endodermal sinus tumor).

vignettes.q: Parkinsonism in young patient; Dx?
vignettes.a: Wilson disease (AR, chromosome 13)

vignettes.q: Parkinsonism in older patient; Dx?
vignettes.a: Parkinson disease

vignettes.q: Parkinsonism + axial dystonia; Dx?
vignettes.a: progressive supranuclear palsy (this is on the USMLE!!)

vignettes.q: Parkinsonism + visual hallucinations + cognitive decline; Dx?
vignettes.a: Lewy body dementia

vignettes.q: Parkinsonism + urinary incontinence + gait instability + cognitive dysfunction; Dx?
vignettes.a: normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) = “wet, wobbly, wacky” + Parkinsonism.

vignettes.q: 23F + unilateral resting tremor + increased LFTs + hemolytic anemia; Dx?
vignettes.a: Wilson disease

vignettes.q: 23F + unilateral resting tremor + increased LFTs + hemolytic anemia; next best step?
vignettes.a: do a slit-lamp exam.

vignettes.q: How is most copper normally excreted by the body?
vignettes.a: through bile (hepatocyte transport pump).

vignettes.q: Important serum/blood findings in Wilson?
vignettes.a: decreased ceruloplasmin; increased urinary copper.

vignettes.q: How do we normally excrete iron?
vignettes.a: humans have poor elimination mechanism; losses are natural through skin (or menstruation in women).

vignettes.q: Where do we absorb iron and copper?
vignettes.a: duodenum mainly.

vignettes.q: Where do we absorb bile acids and B12?
vignettes.a: terminal ileum.

vignettes.q: Tx for Wilson disease?
vignettes.a: penicillamine (copper chelator).

vignettes.q: “Opposite” of Wilson disease?
vignettes.a: Menkes disease (can’t absorb intestinal copper).

vignettes.q: What vitamin helps absorb iron?
vignettes.a: vitamin C ferrireductase converts small bowel Fe3+ to Fe2+; only Fe2+ can be absorbed out of the lumen.

vignettes.q: What does cholecystokinin (CCK) do?
vignettes.a: increases contraction of gall bladder, relaxes sphincter of Oddi, and increases exocrine pancreas secretion of lipases, proteases, and amylase.

vignettes.q: Which cells make CCK
vignettes.a: “enteroendocrine cells of the small intestine” → HY.

vignettes.q: Macronutrients entering the duodenum (i.e., fats, proteins, carbs); what hormone is notably secreted in response?
vignettes.a: USMLE wants CCK for this one.

vignettes.q: Acid entering the duodenum; what hormone is notably secreted in response?
vignettes.a: USMLE wants secretin → causes bicarb secretion from pancreas.

vignettes.q: What do gastric chief cells do?
vignettes.a: secrete pepsinogen (inactive zymogen) → acid activates to pepsin.

vignettes.q: What do parietal cells secrete
vignettes.a: acid + intrinsic factor.

vignettes.q: 22M + vitiligo + macrocytic anemia; Dx?
vignettes.a: pernicious anemia causing B12 deficiency → “autoimmune diseases go together.”

vignettes.q: Mechanism for pernicious anemia?
vignettes.a: autoantibodies against parietal cells or intrinsic factor.

vignettes.q: Blood smear in pernicious anemia?
vignettes.a: hypersegmented neutrophils + high MCV RBCs.

vignettes.q: Pt has B12 deficiency + atrophic gastritis; what is most likely to be increased in this pt?
vignettes.a: gastrin → need to assume pernicious anemia → atrophy of parietal cells due to Abs → decreased acid production → increased gastrin → USMLE likes this question!

vignettes.q: Which nerve must be severed to remove cancer at gastroesophageal junction
vignettes.a: vagus (just memorize it; it’s on a retired NBME).

vignettes.q: HY structures passing through diaphragm?
vignettes.a: “I Ate 10 Eggs At 12.” → IVC T8; T10 Esophagus + thoracic duct; Aortic hiatus (aorta, azygous vein, thoracic duct) at T12.

vignettes.q: Drug-/pill-induced esophagitis
vignettes.a: USMLE wants bisphosphonates (i.e., alendronate) + tetracyclines + clindamycin as causes.

vignettes.q: What part of the brain is damaged in Wilson?
vignettes.a: USMLE wants putamen (they will show you a transverse head CT and expect you to pick out the letter labeling the putamen).

vignettes.q: Most active part of the bowel in terms of cell division?
vignettes.a: “base of the crypt.” Memorize it. “Top of the villi” is the wrong answer.

vignettes.q: Where are Brunner glands
vignettes.a: duodenum, proximal to the sphincter of Oddi.

vignettes.q: What do Brunner glands secrete?
vignettes.a: alkaline mucous.

vignettes.q: What do Paneth cells secrete?
vignettes.a: Defensins in the small intestine.

vignettes.q: Person who’s vomiting; what’s the biochemical disturbance?
vignettes.a: hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis → low K, low Cl, high pH, high bicarb, low H, anion gap normal (even though it’s alkalosis, not acidosis, the USMLE will still ask an arrow for the anion gap here).

vignettes.q: 2-week-old male + forceful non-bilious vomiting; Dx?
vignettes.a: hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.

vignettes.q: Dx of pyloric stenosis?
vignettes.a: abdominal ultrasound to show olive-shaped hypertrophied pylorus.

vignettes.q: Tx of pyloric stenosis?
vignettes.a: myomectomy

vignettes.q: Who gets pyloric stenosis?
vignettes.a: first-born males (weird, but it’s on an old NBME) + neonates taking oral erythromycin for chlamydial ophthalmia neonatorum (erythromycin is a motilin-receptor agonist).

vignettes.q: 2-week-old male + bilious vomiting; Dx?
vignettes.a: duodenal atresia, annular pancreas, congenital midgut volvulus, or Hirschsprung (correct, Hirschsprung can present with bilious vomiting).

vignettes.q: 2-week-old + Down syndrome + bilious vomiting + passed meconium ok; Dx?
vignettes.a: duodenal atresia

vignettes.q: 2-week-old + Down syndrome + bilious vomiting + slow to pass meconium; Dx?
vignettes.a: Hirschsprung

vignettes.q: How do you Dx duodenal atresia?
vignettes.a: abdominal x-ray (AXR) showing double-bubble sign (very HY).

vignettes.q: How do you Dx Hirschsprung?
vignettes.a: rectal manometry, followed by confirmatory rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells.

vignettes.q: Mechanism for Hirschsprung?
vignettes.a: failure of migration of neural crest cells distally to the rectum.

vignettes.q: Failure to pass meconium at birth. Most likely cause overall?
vignettes.a: cystic fibrosis.

vignettes.q: 18-month-old + intermittent abdominal pain + crying + blood in stool; Dx?
vignettes.a: intussusception.

vignettes.q: 18-month-old + intermittent squatting + crying + FOBT positive; Dx?
vignettes.a: intussusception.

vignettes.q: 18-month-old + occasionally brings legs to chest + vomits + abdo mass; Dx?
vignettes.a: intussusception.

vignettes.q: 18-month-old + occasionally brings legs to chest + vomits + no abdo mass Dx?
vignettes.a: volvulus → this is congenital midgut volvulus.

vignettes.q: Presentation sounds like intussusception but no mass
vignettes.a: congenital midgut volvulus.

vignettes.q: Cause of intussusception?
vignettes.a: >99% are in kids under age 2; caused by lymphoid hyperplasia due to viral infection (e.g., rotavirus) or recent vaccination; if in adult (usually elderly), it is caused by colorectal cancer.

vignettes.q: Dx and Tx of intussusception?
vignettes.a: USMLE wants enema as the answer. Even though ultrasound can be done which shows a target sign, the USMLE always wants enema. And it can be any type. I’ve seen “air contrast enema”, “air enema,” “contrast enema” all as answers. I a

vignettes.q: For contrast swallows, when to do barium vs water-soluble (gastrografin)?
vignettes.a: barium most of the time; if at risk of aspiration, must do barium because aspiration of gastrografin will cause pneumonitis. If patient has suspected esophageal perforation, do not do barium, as that will cause mediastinitis; must

vignettes.q: Level of celiac trunk and main branches + what’s it supply?
vignettes.a: T12; splenic artery, common hepatic artery, left gastric artery; supplies foregut (mouth to duodenum at ampulla of Vater).

vignettes.q: Level of SMA + what’s it supply?
vignettes.a: L1; supplies midgut (duodenum at ampulla of Vater until 2/3 distal transverse colon); so for instance, the right colic and middle colic arteries come off SMA.

vignettes.q: Level of IMA + what’s it supply?
vignettes.a: L3; supplies hindgut (2/3 distal transverse colon until the pectinate line 2/3 distal on the anal canal); left colic artery comes off IMA.

vignettes.q: Abdominal aortic aneurysm occurs in males over 55 who are ever-smokers
vignettes.a: a one-off abdo ultrasound is done in this patient group.

vignettes.q: Most common locations for atherosclerosis (in descending order)
vignettes.a: abdominal aorta, coronary arteries, popliteal arteries, carotid arteries.

vignettes.q: USMLE favorite question
vignettes.a: “Which of the following is supplied by an artery of the foregut but is not itself derived from the foregut?” → answer = spleen.

vignettes.q: Short gastric arteries come off which artery?
vignettes.a: splenic.

vignettes.q: What’s the main arterial supply to the pancreas?
vignettes.a: Arteria pancreatica magna (greater pancreatic artery) → a branch of the splenic.

vignettes.q: 79M + Hx of atrial fibrillation + severe, acute, diffuse abdo pain; Dx?
vignettes.a: acute mesenteric ischemia caused by mural thrombus embolizing to SMA or IMA.

vignettes.q: 55F diabetic + Hx of intermittent claudication + Hx of abdo pain 1-2 hours after eating meals; Dx?
vignettes.a: chronic mesenteric ischemia (CMI) caused by severe atherosclerosis of SMA or IMA (essentially angina of the bowel).

vignettes.q: 55F diabetic + Hx of CABG + Hx of abdo pain 1-2 hours after eating meals; next best step in Dx?
vignettes.a: mesenteric arteriography (CMI).

vignettes.q: 55F diabetic + Hx renal artery stenosis + Hx of abdo pain 1-2 hours after eating meals; Tx?
vignettes.a: angioplasty + stenting (CMI) to restore blood flow.

vignettes.q: What is pectinate line?
vignettes.a: separates upper 2/3 of the anal canal (part of hindgut; endoderm-derived) from the lower 1/3 of anal canal (aka proctodeum, which is ectodermal).

vignettes.q: Lymphatic drainage above/below pectinate line?
vignettes.a: above: internal iliac; below: superficial inguinal.

vignettes.q: Arterial supply above/below pectinate line?
vignettes.a: above: superior rectal artery; below: middle/inferior rectal arteries.

vignettes.q: Venous drainage above/below pectinate line?
vignettes.a: above: superior rectal vein; below: middle/inferior rectal veins.

vignettes.q: How does pectinate line relate to hemorrhoids?
vignettes.a: above: internal hemorrhoids (painless); below: external hemorrhoids (painful).

vignettes.q: Tx for hemorrhoids?
vignettes.a: conservative first, i.e., fiber + exercise; if they want intervention, banding (rubber band ligation) is the answer.

vignettes.q: How do you Dx congenital midgut volvulus?
vignettes.a: upper-GI series (AXR + contrast follow-through of esophagus, stomach, and duodenum with barium or gastrografin).

vignettes.q: What does upper vs lower GI mean?
vignettes.a: upper is above ligament of Treitz (suspensory ligament of duodenum; separates duodenum from jejunum; this ligament connects end of duodenum to the diaphragm) → below this ligament (jejunum and lower) is lower GI.

vignettes.q: Any significance to upper vs lower GI meaning?
vignettes.a: upper-GI bleeds tend to cause melena (black, tar- like stools caused by blood exposed to acid); lower-GI bleeds tend to cause hematochezia (frank blood); large upper-GI bleeds can sometimes cause hematochezia.

vignettes.q: What are the mucous-producing cells in the stomach?
vignettes.a: foveolar cells (aka surface mucous cells) secrete alkaline mucous; these are distinct from mucous neck cells, which secrete an acidic fluid containing mucin proteins.

vignettes.q: “Wait, so there aren’t goblet cells in the stomach?”
vignettes.a: correct.

vignettes.q: Barrett esophagus; what are the changes in mucosa (from what to what)?
vignettes.a: metaplasia of non- keratinized stratified squamous → intestinal simple columnar epithelium (intestinal means “has goblet cells”).

vignettes.q: What does Barrett look like on endoscopy?
vignettes.a: bright red mucosa (UWorld has a Q where they show the endoscopy).

vignettes.q: Barrett will go to what kind of cancer?
vignettes.a: adenocarcinoma of distal third of esophagus

vignettes.q: Biggest risk factor for Barrett?
vignettes.a: GERD (often in obese patients due to lower LES tone)

vignettes.q: Tx of Barrett?
vignettes.a: PPIs are standard to decrease GERD; they’re more efficacious than H2-blockers.

vignettes.q: Acute gastritis (inflammation of lining) main causes?
vignettes.a: NSAIDs, glucocorticoids, H. pylori.

vignettes.q: What is atrophic gastritis?
vignettes.a: a type of chronic gastritis in which ongoing inflammation of glandular cells causes them to be replaced with fibrotic tissue.

vignettes.q: What is type A vs B atrophic gastritis?
vignettes.a: Type A = non-antral (mainly fundus); caused by autoimmune attack against parietal cells (pernicious anemia), resulting in B12 deficiency due to insufficient intrinsic factor production. Type B = antral; caused by H. pylori.

vignettes.q: How do you Dx H. pylori?
vignettes.a: urea breath test or stool antigen test.

vignettes.q: How do you Tx H. pylori?
vignettes.a: CAP = Clarithromycin, Amoxicillin, Proton pump inhibitor. If patient has positive urea breath test four weeks after Tx, assume resistance of Abx, so switch out the clarithromycin and amoxicillin and give metronidazole + tetracycli

vignettes.q: Urease, oxidase, catalase; H. pylori is positive for which ones?
vignettes.a: all three (asked in a USMLE Q, where they had different + and – combos, and the answer was all three +).

vignettes.q: What is peptic ulcer?
vignettes.a: gastric ulcer and/or duodenal ulcer.

vignettes.q: Most common cause of gastric ulcers
vignettes.a: H. pylori, then NSAIDs, then smoking.

vignettes.q: What about alcohol?
vignettes.a: EtOH doesn’t cause ulcers; it just prevents their healing.

vignettes.q: Weird causes of gastric ulcers?
vignettes.a: Cushing ulcers (head trauma → increased ACh outflow → increased M3 receptor agonism on parietal cells → increased acid secretion); Curling ulcers (sloughing of intestinal mucosa due to acute fluid losses typically seen with burns;

vignettes.q: Most common cause of duodenal ulcers
vignettes.a: caused almost exclusively by H. pylori.

vignettes.q: What does USMLE care about relating to sucralfate?
vignettes.a: can coat the base of ulcers + protect them; activated by acidic pH, so can be inactivated in patients on antacids.

vignettes.q: Mechanism via which H. pylori causes ulcers?
vignettes.a: secretion of proteinaceous products that damage intestinal mucosa (on USMLE Free 120 I believe).

vignettes.q: Gastrin levels in H. pylori?
vignettes.a: elevated; H. pylori causes increased acid secretion

vignettes.q: Cancer caused by H. pylori?
vignettes.a: MALT lymphoma (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma); H. pylori is considered a pre-MALT lymphoma condition, where eradication causes remission of 80% of low-grade stage 1E MALT lymphomas (confined to mucosa + submucosa).

vignettes.q: Key points about Whipple disease?
vignettes.a: caused by bacterium Tropheryma Whipplei → causes PAS- positive macrophages in the lamina propria of the small bowel (USMLE is obsessed with this detail); can cause arthritis and diarrhea. Tx = Abx (e.g., doxycycline).

vignettes.q: What is Tropical sprue?
vignettes.a: malabsorptive disease characterized by flattening of intestinal villi (similar to Celiac histo); etiology obscure/manifold but bacterial infection is accepted as one cause; Tx = Abx (e.g., doxycycline).

vignettes.q: Celiac disease important points?
vignettes.a: gluten intolerance; fluten found in wheat, oats, rye, and barley, so therefore will get Sx after eating, e.g., pasta (too easy for the vignette to mention though); causes flattening of intestinal villi on biopsy (image HY); patien

vignettes.q: “I’ve heard IgA deficiency relates somehow to Celiac. Can you explain.”
vignettes.a: Remember that “autoimmune diseases go together,” so increased risk of one means increased risk of another; the HLA associations are not super-strict → if patient has Celiac, he or she is 10-15x more likely to have IgA deficiency (

vignettes.q: Weird factoid about Celiac?
vignettes.a: increased risk of T cell lymphoma; HLA-DQ2/8 positive.

vignettes.q: What immunoglobulin is produced at Peyer patches (GALT; gut-associated lymphoid tissue)?
vignettes.a: IgA. Peyer patches contain large number of IgA-secreting B cells. IgA is a dimer connected by a J-chain.

vignettes.q: USMLE wants you to know colipase deficiency is a reason why a patient with chronic pancreatitis might not be able to digest triglycerides
vignettes.a: yes, weird and random, but I don’t know what to tell you. It’s on the NBME.

vignettes.q: What’s Zollinger-Ellison syndrome?
vignettes.a: gastrin-secreting tumor → USMLE likes “recurrent” duodenal ulcers, or the presence of any single jejunal or ileal ulcer → frequently seen as part of MEN1 (pancreas, pituitary, parathyroid).

vignettes.q: Dx of ZES?
vignettes.a: check serum gastrin levels; if USMLE mentions secretin-stimulation test, it’s only because they’ll say in the vignette that “gastrin is not suppressed with secretin stimulation” as a way to tell you the Dx is ZES → secretin should

vignettes.q: Tx of ZES?
vignettes.a: PPIs, but definitive is surgical resection of tumor.

vignettes.q: What is Menetrier disease?
vignettes.a: don’t confuse with Meniere disease; Menetrier is atrophy of parietal cells (causing achlorhydria) and hypertrophy of foveolar cells (surface mucous cells) to the extent that the inner lining of stomach resembles brain gyri; can be

vignettes.q: Types of stomach cancer (apart from MALT lymphoma)
vignettes.a: intestinal vs diffuse type; USMLE doesn’t ask about intestinal (it’s characterized by irregular tubular histology); diffuse = linitis plastica, which is “leather bottle” appearance of the stomach → cells contain mucin and are call

vignettes.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + high amylase or lipase
vignettes.a: gallstone pancreatitis = choledocholithiasis.

vignettes.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + high amylase or lipase + remote Hx of cholecystectomy
vignettes.a: sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (can’t be a stone cuz the gallbladder was removed ages ago).

vignettes.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase in someone with recent cholecystectomy
vignettes.a: choledocholithiasis (retained stone in cystic duct that descended, but not distal to pancreatic duct entry point).

vignettes.q: Dx and Tx of choledocholithiasis
vignettes.a: ERCP.

vignettes.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase in someone with remote cholecystectomy
vignettes.a: pancreatic cancer.

vignettes.q: Dx of pancreatic cancer
vignettes.a: CT abdo with contrast.

vignettes.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase in someone with remote cholecystectomy + CT is negative
vignettes.a: cholangiocarcinoma.

vignettes.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase + diffuse pruritis + high cholesterol
vignettes.a: primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC).

vignettes.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase + autoimmune disease (in pt or family)
vignettes.a: PBC.

vignettes.q: Dx of PBC
vignettes.a: anti-mitochondrial Abx next best step; liver biopsy is confirmatory.

vignettes.q: Recent cholecystectomy + fever + abdo pain
vignettes.a: post-op bile leak.

vignettes.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase + CT shows cystic lesion in bile duct
vignettes.a: choledochal cyst → do simple excision of cyst (cholangiocarcinoma not cystic + CT can be negative).

vignettes.q: Imaging to view liver or pancreas
vignettes.a: CT with contrast.

vignettes.q: Imaging to view gallbladder
vignettes.a: abdominal ultrasound.

vignettes.q: Imaging to view gallbladder in suspected cholecystitis only if USS negative
vignettes.a: HIDA scan.

vignettes.q: Imaging to view bile ducts
vignettes.a: ERCP or MRCP (choose ERCP > MRCP if both listed).

vignettes.q: 22M + stressed studying for exams + yellow eyes + has had a few similar episodes in the past + is otherwise healthy; Dx?
vignettes.a: Gilbert syndrome (proncouned jeel-BEAR).

vignettes.q: Mechanism for Gilbert?
vignettes.a: decreased expression of glucuronosyltransferase (bilirubin conjugating enzyme) in the liver → decreased ability to take up unconjugated bilirubin at the liver → jaundice.

vignettes.q: Tx for Gilbert?
vignettes.a: reassurance; benign condition.

vignettes.q: How do those pathologic jaundice guidelines relate to actual USMLE Qs though?
vignettes.a: if pathologic, USMLE wants phototherapy as the Tx; if that’s insufficient, do exchange transfusion → in addition, even in adults, if you see a Q where someone’s direct bilirubin is >10% of total, that’ll be a huge clue to you that

vignettes.q: What are normal bilirubin levels?
vignettes.a: 0.1 mg/dL direct; 1.0 mg/dL total.

vignettes.q: 8-day-old neonate + jaundice + direct bilirubin 14 mg/dL + total bilirubin 15 mg/dL; Dx?
vignettes.a: biliary atresia → super HY Dx.

vignettes.q: 8-day-old neonate + jaundice + direct bilirubin 14 mg/dL + total bilirubin 15 mg/dL; next best step in diagnosis?
vignettes.a: straight-up liver biopsy → if positive, must do liver transplant.

vignettes.q: 8-day old neonate + jaundice + direct bilirubin 1 mg/dL + total bilirubin 20 mg/dL; Dx?
vignettes.a: Crigler- Najjar syndrome.

vignettes.q: Mechanism of Crigler-Najjar?
vignettes.a: absence (type I) or deficiency (type II) of glucuronyosltransferase.

vignettes.q: Tx of Crigler-Najjar?
vignettes.a: phenobarbital is helpful in type II (why the USMLE occasionally asks this I don’t know why); Type I does not respond to phenobarbital; plasmapheresis + phototherapy are temporizing measures; liver transplant is curative.

vignettes.q: What are Dubin-Johnson vs Rotor syndrome?
vignettes.a: never asked on the USMLE but I mention them here otherwise some students would probably spasm out → high direct bilirubin due to decreased ability to secrete it into bile → DJ has black liver; Rotor does not.

vignettes.q: Over-arching HY point about hepatitis infections for USMLE
vignettes.a: they want you to know that hepatocellular damage is due to “cytotoxic T lymphocytes,” not “viral cytopathic effects.”

vignettes.q: Hepatitis B HY points
vignettes.a: parenteral transmission; in all body fluids and can be transmitted through breastmilk, sex, and IV drug use → most common transmission is vertical at birth (through birth canal); vignettes associate HepB with China; 30% of patient

vignettes.q: Tx for HepB?
vignettes.a: a variety of meds; the USMLE isn’t really fussed and won’t ask you; this is more Qbank where they may show up; but some drugs are interferon-alpha, entecavir, tenofovir, telbivudine, and lamivudine.

vignettes.q: HepC important info
vignettes.a: longest incubation period (2-26 weeks); can become chronic; parenteral transmission; transmitted by blood only; not sexually transmitted (if you spend an hour and do a comprehensive literature review yourself, you’ll learn that th

vignettes.q: Appearance of liver in HepC?
vignettes.a: nodular; in contrast, HepB → ground-glass.

vignettes.q: Dx of HepC
vignettes.a: ELISA + serum HCV RNA levels.

vignettes.q: Tx of HepC
vignettes.a: USMLE likely won’t ask you; but pegylated-interferon-alpha has the greatest chance of showing up on the exam; other drugs are daclatasvir and sofosbuvir.

vignettes.q: HepD important points
vignettes.a: called a “subviral satellite” because it depends on HepB to cause infection (i.e., without HepB, HepD exposure won’t cause infection) → what’s the best way to prevent it? → answer = simply vaccinate against HepB → three types of H

vignettes.q: HepE important points
vignettes.a: fecal-oral transmission (enteral); acute disease only; classically when someone travels to India or Tibet → high mortality in pregnant women is highest yield point.

vignettes.q: Patient takes Abx for several days + has watery diarrhea; Dx?
vignettes.a: C. difficile (pseudomembranous colitis).

vignettes.q: Which Abx cause C. diff overgrowth?
vignettes.a: clindamycin, cephalosporins, ampicillin are highest yield.

vignettes.q: Mechanism for C. diff infection
vignettes.a: “Ingestion of spores” is correct over “bacterial overgrowth” on the USMLE → yes, disruption of normal flora leads to C. diff overgrowth, but ingestion of spores is correct answer on NBME exam.

vignettes.q: Dx of C. difficile?
vignettes.a: stool AB toxin test, not stool culture (exceedingly HY).

vignettes.q: Tx of C. difficile?
vignettes.a: guidelines as of Feb 2018 say oral vancomycin first-line, not metronidazole → apparently UW is updated on this too now → note that vanc is given orally → apart from C. diff, it’s always given IV because it has terrible oral bioava

vignettes.q: Mechanism of colonic necrosis in C. diff colonic necrosis?
vignettes.a: “cytoskeletal disruption.”

vignettes.q: Patient is treated with vanc for C. diff but gets recurrence weeks later; why?
vignettes.a: “regermination of spores.”

vignettes.q: Damage to which nerves can cause constipation?
vignettes.a: pelvic splanchnic (because these are parasympathetic, which drive bowel function) → in contrast, hypogastric nerves = sympathetic (internal anal sphincter); pudendal nerve = somatic (external anal sphincter).

vignettes.q: Hepatocellular carcinoma + peanut farmer from China; cause?
vignettes.a: aflatoxin → you don’t have to like this factoid, but it’s on the NBME.

vignettes.q: Vinyl chloride exposure + liver pathology; what’s the Dx?
vignettes.a: hepatic angiosarcoma.

vignettes.q: 17M + fever + tonsillar exudates + cervical lymphadenopathy + cough + hepatomegaly; Dx?
vignettes.a: EBV mononucleosis.

vignettes.q: Alcoholic + liver biopsy shows what?
vignettes.a: Mallory hyaline → damaged intermediate filaments.

vignettes.q: 45M + pan-acinar emphysema + increased LFTs; Dx?
vignettes.a: alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency → inability to break down elastase in the lungs, but enzyme is synthesized in liver; also causes cirrhosis.

vignettes.q: 45M + cirrhosis + fluid wave + fever + abdo pain; Dx?
vignettes.a: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)

vignettes.q: 69F diabetic + undergoing peritoneal dialysis + fever + abdo pain; Dx?
vignettes.a: SBP

vignettes.q: 8M + viral infection + pedal/periorbital edema + fluid wave + fever + abdo pain; Dx?
vignettes.a: SBP → minimal change disease (nephrotic syndrome) causing ascites.

vignettes.q: SBP Dx
vignettes.a: paracentesis (peritoneal aspiration; don’t confuse with periocardiocentesis) + do gram- stain + look for >250 WBCs per HPF.

vignettes.q: Tx for SBP
vignettes.a: ceftriaxone.

vignettes.q: Cause of spider angiomata, palmar erythema, and gynecomastia?
vignettes.a: failure of the liver to process estrogen → answer also = hyperestrogenism.

vignettes.q: Clubbing causes?
vignettes.a: pulmonary disease like CF and COBD; cardiac R→L shunts; GI disease; familial, etc. Bottom line is → just be aware GI disease can cause clubbing (i.e., IBD, Celiac, primary biliary cirrhosis).

vignettes.q: Woman 20s-50s + high cholesterol + diffuse pruritis + sister has rheumatoid arthritis; Dx?
vignettes.a: primary biliary cirrhosis → USMLE likes “autoimmune diseases go together” in patient (or family).

vignettes.q: How to Dx PBC?
vignettes.a: anti-mitochondrial Abs first; if positive, liver biopsy is confirmatory.

vignettes.q: Neonate born 32 weeks gestation + fever + abdominal distension + feeding intolerance + hematochezia; Dx?
vignettes.a: necrotizing enterocolitis → bowel infection in premature neonates usually <32 weeks gestation.

vignettes.q: Dx of NE?
vignettes.a: abdominal x-ray (AXR) visualizing pneumatosis intestinalis (air in the bowel wall), air in the portal vein, or free air under the diaphragm.

vignettes.q: Tx of NE?
vignettes.a: NPO (nil per os; nothing by mouth), NG decompression, broad-spectrum Abx; if necrotic bowel, must do surgery.

vignettes.q: 49M + Hx of abdo pain after meal; now presents with sepsis + diffuse, acute abdo pain; Dx?
vignettes.a: ruptured viscus (duodenum).

vignettes.q: 28F + pregnant + severe, acute abdo pain + jaundice + hepatomegaly + ascites + encephalopathy; Dx?
vignettes.a: Budd-Chiari syndrome → hepatic vein thrombosis → rare, but associated with pregnancy and malignancy.

vignettes.q: Bad type of colonic polyp/adenoma?
vignettes.a: villous + sessile characteristics are more sinister than tubular + pedunculated.

vignettes.q: Colon cancer progression?
vignettes.a: step-wise → APC → KRAS → PTEN → p53. That is highly simplified, but the point is that USMLE wants you to be aware CRC occurs as a result of many mutations in sequence.

vignettes.q: 18F + CRC in family + has hundreds or thousands of polyps on colonoscopy; Dx?
vignettes.a: FAP (familial adenomatous polyposis) → AD, chromosome 5, APC gene.

vignettes.q: FAP + soft tissue or bone tumors; Dx?
vignettes.a: Gardner syndrome

vignettes.q: FAP + CNS tumors; Dx?
vignettes.a: Turcot syndrome

vignettes.q: 18F + FAP; Tx?
vignettes.a: total proctocolectomy → 100% chance of colon cancer.

vignettes.q: 20M + FAP + skull tumor; Dx?
vignettes.a: Gardner, not Turcot → skull is bone, not CNS. Oh wow, craziness.

vignettes.q: 20M + FHx of CRC + has ten polyps seen on colonoscopy; Dx?
vignettes.a: HNPCC (Lynch syndrome), not FAP → FAP has hundreds or thousands of polyps on colonoscopy; HNPCC has “some polyps.”

vignettes.q: Mechanism of HNPCC?
vignettes.a: “microsatellite instability,” or “defect in mismatch repair genes” → mutations in MLH1, MSH2, PMS1.

vignettes.q: 22F + has 30 polyps on colonoscopy + mom died of endometrial cancer; Dx?
vignettes.a: HNPCC → Lynch syndrome associated with gyn tumors such as ovarian + endometrial, as well as other organ system tumors such as pancreas, stomach, and small bowel. Testicular + prostate very rare, but gyn common.

vignettes.q: 26F + they show you pic of spoon-shaped nail + tell you her lips have been cracked + they ask you what other symptom she might have; answer = dysphagia. Dx = Plummer-Vinson syndrome
vignettes.a: triad of iron deficiency anemia (causes koilonychia; spoon-shaped nails) + angular cheilosis (cracked corners of mouth) + esophageal webs (dysphagia).

vignettes.q: What does CREST stand for?
vignettes.a: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias

vignettes.q: 42M + dysphagia to solids + liquids + no other Hx; Dx?
vignettes.a: achalasia → inability to swallow solids + liquids together implies neurogenic etiology.

vignettes.q: 42M + EtOH Hx + dysphagia to solids that progresses to include liquids; Dx?
vignettes.a: esophageal cancer (SCC) → dysphagia to solids that progresses to solids + liquids = cancer until proven otherwise.

vignettes.q: HY points about esophageal cancer?
vignettes.a: adenocarcinoma is distal 1/3 and is caused by GERD (obesity → low LES tone → GERD → Barrett → adenocarcinoma); SCC is upper 2/3 of esophagus and is caused by smoking + alcohol; can also be caused by webs, burns, chemicals, and ach

vignettes.q: Mechanism for achalasia?
vignettes.a: loss of NO-secreting neurons in myenteric plexus of LES → increased LES tone → bird’s beak appearance on contrast swallow + increased tone on esophageal manometry; cause is often idiopathic, but Chagas disease (Trypansoma cruzi) i

vignettes.q: So when is manometry the answer for achalasia?
vignettes.a: when they show you a pic of the bird’s beak from the barium swallow already performed, so clearly the next best step is manometry. The USMLE will sometimes show a graph of a manometry that’s been performed, and you’ll simply see t

vignettes.q: Tx for achalasia
vignettes.a: surgery first-line (endoscopic myotomy is superior to pneumatic dilatation); if patient has high surgical risk, can use botulinum toxin as first-line therapy → if fails, dCCB or nitrates.

vignettes.q: Above 42M + Hx of GERD
vignettes.a: go straight to endoscopy as the answer (cancer, not Zenker).

vignettes.q: Location + mechanism of Zenker?
vignettes.a: false diverticulum just superior to the cricopharyngeus on the posterior pharyngeal wall → USMLE answers are “increased oropharyngeal pressure” and “cricopharyngeal muscle spasm.” They want you to know it is not a congenital weakn

vignettes.q: What is Whipple triad?
vignettes.a: means insulinoma → 1) hypoglycemia, 2) Sx of hypoglycemia (diaphoresis, tachycardia, tremulousness), 3) relief of Sx with meals (or they’ll say it gets worse between meals).

vignettes.q: 32M + high glucose levels + body rash; Dx?
vignettes.a: glucagonoma → rash is called necrolytic migratory erythema and is seen in glucagonoma.

vignettes.q: 32M + watery diarrhea + hypokalemia + achlorhydria; Dx?
vignettes.a: VIPoma, aka WDHA syndrome (Watery Diarrhea, Achlorhydria, Hypokalemia).

vignettes.q: 32M + increased bowel motions + facial flushing; Dx?
vignettes.a: VIPoma (another presentation I saw that was harder to Dx).

vignettes.q: 32M + steatorrhea + pancreatic tumor; Dx?
vignettes.a: somatostatinoma.

vignettes.q: Biggest risk factor pancreatic cancer?
vignettes.a: smoking

vignettes.q: Biggest risk factor for gall bladder cancer
vignettes.a: smoking

vignettes.q: 52F + 2 kids + BMI 28 + recurrent colicky epigastric pain; next best step in Dx?
vignettes.a: ultrasound (cholelithiasis).

vignettes.q: Why increased risk of cholesterol stones in pregnancy?
vignettes.a: estrogen upregulates HMG-CoA reductase + progesterone slows biliary peristalsis → both of these hormonal effects are exceedingly HY.

vignettes.q: Brown pigment stones
vignettes.a: bacterial infection → bacteria deconjugate bilirubin, making it less water soluble → stone precipitation.

vignettes.q: Black pigment stones
vignettes.a: hemolytic anemia / increased RBC turnover syndromes (e.g., sickle cell).

vignettes.q: What are pigment stones composed of?
vignettes.a: calcium bilirubinate.

vignettes.q: Random vignette of sickle cell anemia; Q asks you which of the following is the patient at increased risk of + all answers seem obscure
vignettes.a: cholelithiasis → black pigment stones.

vignettes.q: USMLE Q will ask you whether high vs low cholesterol, bile acids, and phosphatidylcholine = good or bad for cholesterol stone formation?
vignettes.a: high cholesterol = bad; high bile acids = good; high phosphatidylcholine = good.

vignettes.q: Travel + watery (or brown-green) diarrhea; Dx?
vignettes.a: Travelers diarrhea → ETEC HL/HS toxins.

vignettes.q: MOA of ETEC HL toxin?
vignettes.a: HL toxin ADP ribosylates adenylyl cyclase → increases cAMP → increases Cl secretion into small bowel lumen → Na follows Cl → water follows Na → secretory diarrhea.

vignettes.q: Which organism has same MOA as ETEC HL toxin?
vignettes.a: Cholera toxin → difference is cholera is described as “liters and liters” of high-volume stool (“rice-water stool” is buzzwordy and rarely seen); if vignette wants to describe rice-water, they’ll say “specks of mucous” in high-vol

vignettes.q: MOA of ETEC HS toxin?
vignettes.a: ADP ribosylates guanylyl cyclase → increases cGMP → decreases Cl reabsorption from lumen → more Na stays in lumen → more water stays with Na → watery diarrhea.

vignettes.q: Which organism has same MOA as ETEC HS toxin?
vignettes.a: Yersinia enterocolitica toxin → difference is Y. enterocolitica causes bloody, not watery, diarrhea, and Y. enterocolitica also causes pseudoappendicitis in children (due to terminal ileitis / mesenteric adenitis) and arthritis in

vignettes.q: Reheated fried rice + watery diarrhea; organism + mechanism?
vignettes.a: Bacillus cereus → activation of spores.

vignettes.q: Kid + bloody diarrhea + petechiae + red urine; Dx?
vignettes.a: hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) caused by EHEC O157:H7 or Shigella → HUS = triad of thrombocytopenia + schistocytosis (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia) + renal insufficiency; toxin will inhibit ADAMTS13 in afferent arterioles +

vignettes.q: How does HUS contrast with TTP?
vignettes.a: TTP is caused by a mutation that results in defective ADAMTS13, or antibodies against ADAMTS13, resulting in the inability to cleave vWF multimers → platelet clumping → similar progression as HUS. One of the points of contrast is

vignettes.q: Bloody diarrhea + chicken / turtles
vignettes.a: Salmonella enteritidis / typhimurium.

vignettes.q: Chicken + bloody diarrhea + most common cause overall in the US
vignettes.a: Campylobacter jejuni

vignettes.q: Bloody diarrhea + ascending paralysis
vignettes.a: Guillain-Barre syndrome caused by Campylobacter jejuni (many vignettes for GBS will not mention recent infection; GBS can also be caused by Shigella, Salmonella, and Yersinia).

vignettes.q: Homeless shelter + diarrhea or constipation + rose spots on abdomen + prostrated (lying down in pain); Dx?
vignettes.a: typhoid fever → Salmonella typhi → don’t confuse with food poisoning Salmonella strains (enteritidis + typhimurium) → the reservoir for typhoid is humans; it is not spread by chickens or turtles.

vignettes.q: Shigella vs Salmonella points
vignettes.a: Salmonella produces H2S gas, is motile, and requires many organisms to cause infection; Shigella does not produce H2S gas, is non-motile, and very few organisms cause infection; they are both oxidase-negative.

vignettes.q: Incubation period for infective diarrhea?
vignettes.a: gram-negative rods are 1-3 days (E.coli, Salmonella, Shigella, Yersinia).

vignettes.q: Tx for food poisoning diarrhea
vignettes.a: don’t treat majority of time → answer = “Abx increase duration of fecal excretion of organism.”

vignettes.q: Creams + custards + mayo + potato salad + vomiting 1-6 hours after meal; Dx?
vignettes.a: S. aureus heat- stable preformed toxin.

vignettes.q: Immunocompromised + watery diarrhea; Dx?
vignettes.a: Cryptosporidum parvum.

vignettes.q: Tx for C. parvum?
vignettes.a: supportive is correct over nitazoxanide.

vignettes.q: Fresh water lake / scuba diving + floaty stools; Dx?
vignettes.a: Giardia causing steatorrhea.

vignettes.q: Who notably gets Giardia on USMLE?
vignettes.a: IgA deficiency.

vignettes.q: Tx for Giardia
vignettes.a: metronidazole.

vignettes.q: Travel + bloody diarrhea + epigastric/RUQ pain; Dx?
vignettes.a: Entamoeba histolytica + liver abscess.

vignettes.q: Tx for the liver abscess
vignettes.a: drain.

vignettes.q: Intestinal obstruction + rough-surfaced eggs in stool; Dx?
vignettes.a: Ascariasis (Ascaris lumbricoides)

vignettes.q: Tx for most nematodes (roundworms)
vignettes.a: mebendazole or pyrantel pamoate.

vignettes.q: Kid + perianal itching; Dx?
vignettes.a: Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm).

vignettes.q: Walking on soil / beach + microcytic anemia
vignettes.a: hookworm (Ancylostoma duodenale / Necator Americanus) → USMLE will ask how you acquired hookworm, and the answer is “through your feet.”

vignettes.q: Strongyloides stercoralis; how do you acquire?
vignettes.a: through skin (“through your feet”).

vignettes.q: Pregnant woman + ring-enhancing lesions on CT + cats is not an answer; how did she acquire?
vignettes.a: pork → can also get Toxo from pork.

vignettes.q: Travel to Mexico + cystic lesion seen in lateral ventricle on CT and/or “swiss cheese” appearance of brain; Dx?
vignettes.a: cysticercosis Taenia solium → pork tapeworm (cestode).

vignettes.q: Travel to Mexico + muscle cysts
vignettes.a: taenia solium.

vignettes.q: Pork or bear meat + fever + myalgia + periorbital edema; Dx?
vignettes.a: Trichinella spiralis (trichinosis) → pork nematode (in contrast pork cestode [tapeworm] is Taenia solium).

vignettes.q: Fish + high MCV; Dx?
vignettes.a: Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) causing B12 deficiency.

vignettes.q: Beef + tapeworm; Dx?
vignettes.a: Taenia saginata.

vignettes.q: Worm + portal hypertension; Dx?
vignettes.a: Schistosoma mansoni / japonicum

vignettes.q: Worm + cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer); Dx?
vignettes.a: Clonorchis sinensis.

vignettes.q: Dogs or travel + liver cysts + diarrhea; Dx?
vignettes.a: Hydatid cyst disease → Echinococcus granulosis.

vignettes.q: Rupture of gastric ulcer
vignettes.a: left shoulder pain; which structure is irritated? → answer = diaphragm.

vignettes.q: Alcoholic liver disease
vignettes.a: AST/ALT classically ~2/1 and in the low-hundreds (e.g., 250/125), but I’ve seen plenty of Qs where this is not the case (e.g., ALT is normal and AST slightly elevated); in chronic disease, enzymes can be completely normal; in cont

vignettes.q: Acetaminophen toxicity
vignettes.a: metabolite called NAPQI causes necrosis; give activated charcoal acutely (apparently there’s a UW Q where this is the answer); give N-acetylcysteine otherwise to “regenerate reduced glutathione” → reduced-G has a thiol group (-SH)

vignettes.q: Other notable hepatotoxic drugs?
vignettes.a: RIP from the TB RIPE drugs (i.e., rifampin, INH, and pyrazinamide are hepatotoxic); statins + fibrates; antifungal -azoles + terbinafine; methotrexate; halothane; acetaminophen; those are highest yield probably.

vignettes.q: 45F + BMI 29 + BP 140/90 + high TGAs + low HDL + elevated fasting glucose + slightly elevated AST and ALT; Dx?
vignettes.a: NASH (non-alcoholic steatohepatitis) → caused by metabolic syndrome → Tx is lifestyle modification to eradicate the metabolic syndrome.

vignettes.q: Above 45F + completely normal liver enzymes; Dx?
vignettes.a: NASH → I’ve seen plenty of Qs where all labs values they show you are completely normal + the only thing you’re left with is, “well she’s fat / has metabolic syndrome,” and you eliminate the others to just say, “well, this is NASH

vignettes.q: Histo of liver showing you large-ish circular lesion + tiny circles immediately next to it; Dx?
vignettes.a: primary hepatocellular carcinoma → smaller lesions are satellite lesions, not mets.

vignettes.q: Histo of liver showing you cancer everywhere; Dx?
vignettes.a: colon cancer; bc cancer is everywhere it’s mets.

vignettes.q: Leptin causes satiety (feeling of fullness); greatest just after a meal has started
vignettes.a: sounds obvious, but they show this in graph form, and the wrong answer is immediately when you start eating.

vignettes.q: Liver disease + ascites; why the ascites?
vignettes.a: increased hydrostatic pressure (portal HTN).

vignettes.q: Liver disease + peripheral edema; why the edema?
vignettes.a: decreased oncotic pressure (decreased albumin production by the liver).

vignettes.q: Tx for chronic pancreatitis
vignettes.a: give patient pancreatic enzymes → “pancrelipase” is an answer on another NBME Q, which is a mixture of pancreatic lipases, proteases, and amylases.

vignettes.q: Cause of chronic pancreatitis
vignettes.a: multiple bouts of acute pancreatitis.

vignettes.q: Major causes of pancreatitis
vignettes.a: alcohol + gallstones are major causes; hypertriglyceridemia + hypercalcemia are other known causes; may also be caused by ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography), mumps, drugs (e.g., sulfa). Absolutely do not say “sc

vignettes.q: Gallstone pancreatitis = choledocholithiasis = stone in ampulla of Vater = high ALP + high direct bilirubin + high lipase or amylase
vignettes.a: Dx + Tx = ERCP.

vignettes.q: First Tx for pancreatitis in general
vignettes.a: USMLE wants triad of NPO (nil per os; nothing by mouth) + fluids + NG tube → if USMLE asks for imaging, do CT with contrast to look for fluid collections + degree of necrosis → drain fluid collections percutaneously; if pseudoabsc

vignettes.q: 72M + fatigue + low Hct
vignettes.a: do colonoscopy; most common cause of per rectum blood loss in elderly → diverticular bleed + colorectal cancer + angiodysplasia

vignettes.q: What is angiodysplasia
vignettes.a: tortuous, superficial vessels on colonic wall that rupture + bleed → painless bleeding in elderly.

vignettes.q: Difference between diverticulosis vs diverticulitis
vignettes.a: diverticulosis is simply the presence of diverticula → 50% of the US population over age 60 has them → most commonly in sigmoid colon due to law of Laplace (decreased diameter of sigmoid means greater pressure on the wall → greate

vignettes.q: 69M + LLQ pain + fever = diverticulitis
vignettes.a: Dx with CT with contrast of abdomen → Tx w/ Abx (metronidazole, PLUS fluoroquinolone or Augmentin; USMLE won’t ask you the exact Abx, but you should be aware that metro covers anaerobes below the diaphragm) → never do a colonoscop

vignettes.q: 12M + pic showing you perioral melanosis (sophisticated way of saying hyperpigmentation around the lips); Dx?
vignettes.a: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome → they’ll sometimes just show you the pic and then ask what kind of colonic polyps you’ll see → answer = hamartomatous polyps

vignettes.q: They show you pic of PJS hamartomatous polyp; high cancer risk from this lesion?
vignettes.a: non- cancerous.

vignettes.q: What is IBS?
vignettes.a: Irritable bowel syndrome → classically constipation +/- diarrhea +/- other GI Sx like cramping pain or GERD-like Sx that are relieved with defecation → there are many ways to Tx IBS, such as starting with psych screen, but if the

vignettes.q: What is IBD?
vignettes.a: IBD = inflammatory bowel disease = Crohn and ulcerative colitis (UC) collectively.

vignettes.q: HLA association with IBD?
vignettes.a: HLA-B27 → “PAIR” → Psoriasis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD, Reactive arthritis.

vignettes.q: Crohn GI findings?
vignettes.a: mouth to anus; classically terminal ileum; frequently intermittent bloody diarrhea if colonic involvement; skip lesions causing “string sign” on contrast studies; “cobblestone mucosa”; transmural inflammation with non-caseating gr

vignettes.q: 25M + oral ulcer + bloody diarrhea; Dx?
vignettes.a: Crohn

vignettes.q: Extra-intestinal manifestations of Crohn?
vignettes.a: classically erythema nodosum (red shins; not a rash; this is panniculitis, which is inflammation of subcutaneous fat); anterior uveitis (red eyes); oxalate nephro- / ureterolithiasis (decreased fat absorption → more binding of fat

vignettes.q: Any weird factoid about Crohn?
vignettes.a: sometimes patients (+) for anti-Saccharomyces cerevisiae Abs

vignettes.q: How to Dx Crohn?
vignettes.a: USMLE wants colonoscopy

vignettes.q: Tx for Crohn?
vignettes.a: USMLE wants NSAIDs (either sulfasalazine or mesalamine [5-ASA] will be listed) before steroids → use immunosuppressants late (i.e., infliximab, azathioprine, etc.).

vignettes.q: Does Crohn share anything with UC?
vignettes.a: Yes, bear in mind in real life, there is overlap between the two diseases, so don’t pigeonhole things; think of these disease-associations as propensities rather than as intransigent rules.

vignettes.q: 28M + lower back pain worse in morning and gets better throughout the day + mouth ulcer; Dx?
vignettes.a: Crohn disease (oral involvement only) + sacroiliitis (back pain Sx of ankylosing spondylitis).

vignettes.q: 20F + bloody diarrhea + sore joints + eczematoid plaque on forehead
vignettes.a: IBD + psoriatic arthritis

vignettes.q: UC GI findings?
vignettes.a: rectum-ascending (meaning, starts at rectum and ascends; does not involve anus; Crohn of course is mouth to anus); bloody diarrhea; not transmural (mucosa + submucosa involved only; unlike Crohn); no granulomas (unlike Crohn); lea

vignettes.q: Extra-intestinal manifestations of UC?
vignettes.a: primary sclerosing cholangitis (beaded appearance of common bile duct; can be p-ANCA positive); pyoderma gangrenosum (crater on the forearm with necrotic debris); like Crohn, is associated with anterior uveitis + HLA-B27 associati

vignettes.q: How to Dx UC?
vignettes.a: USMLE wants colonoscopy.

vignettes.q: Tx for UC?
vignettes.a: same as Crohn for USMLE purposes, but just be aware in severe cases colectomy is performed.

vignettes.q: 65M + intermittent bloody diarrhea + now has fever of 104F + abdominal pain + high leukocytes; Dx?
vignettes.a: toxic megacolon → Dx with AXR, not colonoscopy! → if you scope, patient will perforate and die → AXR will show dilated bowel (e.g., one NBME Q says “12-cm cecum”); in general, know that AXR is done when you’re looking for gas.

vignettes.q: Where do most colonic ischemic ulcers occur?
vignettes.a: watershed areas → splenic flexure (watershed of SMA and IMA) + sigmoidal-rectal junction (watershed of IMA and hypogastric artery).

vignettes.q: Ondansetron
vignettes.a: 5HT3 (serotonin) receptor antagonist → anti-emetic classically for those with malignancy / undergoing chemotherapy → for Step 1, USMLE is content with you knowing MOA for ondansetron + that it acts at the chemoreceptor trigger zon

vignettes.q: Metoclopramide
vignettes.a: D2 receptor antagonist used as a prokinetic agent / anti-emetic → don’t up this MOA; students all the time remember that it acts at D2 receptors, but not whether it’s an antagonist or agonist → easy way to remember is based on kno

vignettes.q: 55M + BMI of 33 + vignette doesn’t mention diabetes + 3 months burning in throat
vignettes.a: Dx = GERD → Tx? = trial of PPIs (i.e., trial of omeprazole) for two weeks → relief of Sx is consistent with GERD as the correct Dx.

vignettes.q: 55M + BMI of 33 + poorly controlled diabetes (type I or II) + 3 months of burning in throat
vignettes.a: Dx = diabetic gastroparesis, NOT GERD (woahhh crazy) → first pharm Tx = metoclopramide, not PPIs. If metoclopramide not listed, choose erythromycin (motilin receptor agonist).

vignettes.q: Ursodeoxycholic acid (Ursodiol)
vignettes.a: naturally occurring bile acid given to patients with cholesterol cholelithiasis as an alternative to cholecystectomy. On USMLE, Dx of cholelithiasis = abdominal ultrasound, followed by Tx = cholecystectomy. Ursodiol can be given t

vignettes.q: Octreotide
vignettes.a: somatostatin analogue → in general, think of somatostain as a hormone that shuts of secretion of other hormones (e.g., GH, VIP); it also decreases portal blood flow → used for Tx of esophageal varices AFTER banding (endoscopic lig

vignettes.q: Octreotide also can be used for carcinoid tumors by causing decreased serotonin release from tumor
vignettes.a: carcinoid tumors are usually small-bowel or appendiceal (can also be bronchial) → small blue cells + S-100 positive + neuroendocrine origin → Dx with urinary 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindole acetic acid) → symptomatic only if metastasizes

vignettes.q: Cyproheptadine (serotonin receptor antagonist) can also be used for carcinoid, but is classically used for serotonin syndrome instead
vignettes.a: classically drug interactions like switching to an MOAi from an SSRI without not enough time passing; can also be caused by taking St John Wort if on SSRI, or by tramadol alone → serotonin syndrome does not cause tricuspid valve l

vignettes.q: Aluminum (antacid)
vignettes.a: causes constipation → “Aluminimum amount of feces.”

vignettes.q: Magnesium (antacid)
vignettes.a: causes diarrhea → this actually showed up as a case on 2CS (correct, CS).

vignettes.q: Calcium carbonate (antacid)
vignettes.a: can cause rebound gastric acid hypersecretion + milk alkali syndrome → hypercalcemia + metabolic alkalosis.

vignettes.q: Orlistat
vignettes.a: pancreatic lipase inhibitor used in some patients for weight loss → could theoretically cause fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption due to decreased intestinal fat absorption → for USMLE simply know the MOA and that the drug exists.

vignettes.q: Loperamide
vignettes.a: mu-opiod receptor agonist used in the Tx of diarrhea → NBME exam asks this drug as an arrow question → addictive potential LOW (DOWN arrow) → because it can be used in the Tx of diarrhea, it can also therefore theoretically cause

vignettes.q: Lactulose
vignettes.a: used to Tx hepatic encephalopathy by decreasing serum NH3 → undigestible carbohydrate that gut bacteria convert to acidic end-product → intraluminal NH3 (absorbable) produced by bacteria is converted to NH4+ (not absorbable) → USM

vignettes.q: Neomycin
vignettes.a: used to Tx hepatic encephalopathy by killing NH3-producing bacteria in the gut; USMLE will give you a big, rambling paragraph on hepatic encephalopathy and simply tell you this drug is given then ask for MOA → answer = “kills intr

vignettes.q: Three mechanisms for stomach acid secretion are 1, ACh binding directly to M3 receptors on parietal cells (Vagus activity), 2, gastrin binding directly to gastrin receptors on parietal cells, and 3, gastrin cau
vignettes.a: these three effects are synergistic → USMLE, in contrast, wants “permissive” for the effects of cortisol on catecholamines (cortisol upregulates alpha-1 receptors so NE + E can bind and do their job), and “additive” for the effect

vignettes.q: What is Dumping syndrome?
vignettes.a: caused by gastric bypass surgery, diabetes, or malfunctioning pyloric sphincter, in which stomach contents following a meal enter the duodenum too quickly; there are two types: early vs late → both show up in vignettes (without pe

vignettes.q: Early Dumping syndrome
vignettes.a: 10-30 minutes after a meal → rapid entry of hyperosmolar gastric contents into duodenum → osmotic expansion of small bowel lumen → diarrhea + bloating → on USMLE, answer = “rapid emptying of hyperosomlar chyme into small bowel.”

vignettes.q: Late Dumping syndrome
vignettes.a: 1-2 hours after meal → rapid absorption of carbohydrates through small bowel wall → hyperglycemia → pancreas secretes lots of insulin → rebound hypoglycemia → USMLE merely wants you to identify this in a vignette as Dumping syndro

vignettes.q: What is Blind loop syndrome?
vignettes.a: disturbance of normal floral balance in the small bowel due to disruption of peristalsis (i.e., surgery / post-surgical ileus), but may also be caused by conditions like IBD and scleroderma → leads to steatorrhea + B12 def + fat-s

vignettes.q: Important points about intestinal transporters?
vignettes.a: apical = side of intestinal lumen; basolateral = side of blood; SGLT-1 are GLUT5 are apical transporters that take in monosaccharides from small bowel lumen; GLUT5 takes in fructose; SGLT1 takes in glucose + galactose (think 5 for

vignettes.q: 32M + exquisitely painful anal verge + refuses rectal exam; Dx?
vignettes.a: anal fissure.

vignettes.q: Where do anal fissures occurs?
vignettes.a: posterior in the midline, below the pectinate line.

vignettes.q: Tx for anal fissure?
vignettes.a: Sitz bath

vignettes.q: Acanthocytes on blood smear; Dx?
vignettes.a: abetalipoproteinemia or liver disease → USMLE loves heat stroke as cause of acanthocytes → 82F found unconscious on summer day + body temperature of 107F + blood smear shows acanthocytes; Dx = liver failure (heat stroke) → heat st

vignettes.q: 8M + bloody stool + perfectly healthy otherwise; Dx?
vignettes.a: Meckel diverticulum; student says, “huh, I thought that was age 2.” I agree with you. But there’s an NBME Q where the kid was 8, and the answer was Meckel → bleeding due to “heterotopic gastric / pancreatic tissue.”

vignettes.q: How to Dx Meckel diverticulum?
vignettes.a: Meckel scan (Tc99 uptake scan that localizes to diverticulum).

vignettes.q: Tx for Meckel
vignettes.a: if asymptomatic, can leave alone; if symptomatic, surgical removal.

vignettes.q: Meckel diverticulum (true or false diverticulum?)
vignettes.a: true → contains all layers of bowel → mucosa + submucosa + muscularis propria + adventitia; in contrast, false (Zenker) is just mucosa + submucosa.

vignettes.q: 16F + fever + high leukocytes + RLQ pain that migrated from epigastrium; Dx?
vignettes.a: appendicitis (easy, but so HY how can I not at least mention it classically) → USMLE wants you to know that migration is because, initially, epigastric pain = visceral pain; RLQ pain = inflammation of parietal peritoneum. Must do

vignettes.q: Mallory-Weiss tear vs esophageal varices HY point
vignettes.a: MWT usually caused by vomiting/retching in alcoholic + presents with a little bit of blood in the vomitus; varices present with LOTS of blood → about half of patients with ruptured varix die.

vignettes.q: Mallory-Weiss tear vs Boerhaave
vignettes.a: MWT is not transmural; Boerhaave is transmural → causes subcutaneous emphysema (crepitus due to air under the skin).

vignettes.q: Tx of varix?
vignettes.a: banding + octreotide.

vignettes.q: Prophylaxis for varix?
vignettes.a: propranolol. HY GASTRO

vignettes.q: Bloody diarrhea + appendicitis-like pain (pseudoappendicitis) in a child
vignettes.a: Yersinia enterocolitica

vignettes.q: Parkinsonism in young patient
vignettes.a: Wilson disease till proven otherwise

vignettes.q: Tx for hereditary hemochromatosis
vignettes.a: serial phlebotomy

vignettes.q: Tx for secondary hemochromatosis (transfusional siderosis)
vignettes.a: chelation therapy (deferoxamine)

vignettes.q: Colon cancer in first-degree relative (sibling or parent)
vignettes.a: start at age 40 or ten years before diagnosis in relative, whichever is earlier, and do every 5 years.

vignettes.q: Dysphagia to solids and liquids at the same time to start
vignettes.a: says neurogenic cause → achalasia

vignettes.q: Dysphagia to solids that progresses to solids and liquids
vignettes.a: esophageal cancer

vignettes.q: Halitosis +/- gurgling sound when swallowing +/- regurgitation of undigested food
vignettes.a: Zenker

vignettes.q: Zenker + achalasia initial Dx modality
vignettes.a: barium swallow

vignettes.q: After barium swallow is done and shows bird’s beak appearance
vignettes.a: monometry to confirm Dx of achalasia

vignettes.q: Pt with Hx of GERD + dysphagia
vignettes.a: straight to endoscopy to rule out cancer

vignettes.q: Diabetic pt with new-onset GERD
vignettes.a: diabetic gastroparesis

vignettes.q: Diabetic pt with new-onset GERD
vignettes.a: give metoclopramide, not PPI

vignettes.q: Cholelithiasis
vignettes.a: Dx with abdo ultrasound; fat, forties, female, fertile

vignettes.q: Biliary colic + fever
vignettes.a: cholecystitis

vignettes.q: Tx of cholelithiasis + cholecytitis
vignettes.a: cholecystectomy

vignettes.q: Abdo USS negative in suspected cholecystitis
vignettes.a: HIDA scan

vignettes.q: Gall bladder doesn’t light up on HIDA scan
vignettes.a: confirms cholecystitis

vignettes.q: Cholelithiasis in pregnancy
vignettes.a: estrogen upregulates HMG-CoA reductase + progesterone slows biliary peristalsis

vignettes.q: Dx of pancreatic cancer
vignettes.a: CT abdo with contrast High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase in someone with remote cholecystectomy + CT is

vignettes.q: High ALP + high direct bilirubin + normal amylase or lipase + CT shows cystic lesion in bile duct
vignettes.a: choledochal

vignettes.q: Odynophagia (painful swallowing) in immunocompromised pt
vignettes.a: esophageal candidiasis till proven otherwise

vignettes.q: Circular lesion in pancreas seen in pancreatitis
vignettes.a: pseudoabscess → answer = ERCP to drain internally

vignettes.q: 32M + dark skin on forearms + increased fasting glucose; Dx?
vignettes.a: hemochromatosis (bronze diabetes)

vignettes.q: 25F + intermittent bloody diarrhea for 3 months + intermittent fever + weight loss
vignettes.a: answer IBD (Crohn or UC)

vignettes.q: Tx for Crohn + UC
vignettes.a: USMLE wants oral sulfasalazine (or mesalamine) first before oral steroids; for perianal disease in Crohn, topical agents / enemas can be used; NBME won’t make you pick between oral and topical distinguish (that’s more Qbank being

vignettes.q: UC + high bilirubin + high ALP
vignettes.a: primary sclerosing cholangitis

vignettes.q: Biopsy of small bowel in Celiac
vignettes.a: flattening of intestinal villi

vignettes.q: Dx of Celiac
vignettes.a: IgA anti-tissue transglutaminase, anti-gliadin (aka anti-endomysial)

vignettes.q: After Celiac Ab positivity, what’s the next best step (no further intervention necessary or duodenal biopsy)
vignettes.a: duodenal biopsy (sounds wrong, but it’s what USMLE wants)

vignettes.q: Vague vignette where it sounds like either Celiac or lactose intolerance but it’s in a young adult who’s had zero symptoms until now
vignettes.a: lactose intolerance (can be adult-onset)

vignettes.q: PAS-positive macrophages in the lamina propria + arthritis
vignettes.a: Whipple disease

vignettes.q: Tx for Wilson disease
vignettes.a: penicillamine

vignettes.a: left gastric vein; ↑ portal venous pressure causes backup to left gastric vein, which backs up to esophageal veins.

vignettes.q: 49M + long history of alcoholism + presents with smelly stools + pancreatic enzymes are normal; Dx?
vignettes.a: chronic pancreatitis → exocrine pancreas insufficiency due to repeated bouts of acute pancreatitis; pancreatic enzymes low or low-normal; steatorrhea from lack of lipases in pancreatic secretions; Tx with pancrelipase.

vignettes.a: pseudocyst; this is a common complication of acute pancreatitis; called a pseudocyst because it doesn’t have actual walls; the pancreatic parenchyma encases the fluid collection; can be drained internally via ERCP.

vignettes.q: 55M + obese + gurgling sounds when swallowing + sometimes regurgitates undigested food + halitosis; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: Zenker; risk factor is obesity; can also be seen in setting of dysphagia (e.g., from stroke Hx) due to increased oropharyngeal pressure → increased risk of outpouching.

vignettes.q: 28F + spoon-shaped nails + chapped lips + trouble swallowing; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: Plummer-Vinson syndrome; risk factor is iron deficiency anemia. PV syndrome is triad of 1) iron deficiency anemia (can present as koilonychia), 2) angular cheilitis, and 3) esophageal webs (dysphagia).

vignettes.q: 40M + Hx of GERD + new-onset dysphagia; Dx + risk factor? → adenocarcinoma of esophagus; GERD / Barrett is major risk factor; do immediate endoscopy.
vignettes.a: In short, do immediate endoscopy on USMLE to look for esophageal cancer in any patient with new-onset dysphagia who has Hx of GERD or heavy smoking/alcohol. Progression of dysphagia from solids only to solids + liquids is HY for c

vignettes.q: 65M + long-standing diabetes + new-onset GERD; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: diabetic gastroparesis; do endoscopy first to rule out physical obstruction, followed by gastric-emptying scintigraphy to diagnose; can give metoclopramide and/or erythromycin (motilin receptor agonist) to Tx.

vignettes.q: 30F + pregnant + severe epigastric pain after meals starting during third-trimester; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: cholelithiasis; progesterone slows biliary peristalsis (causing biliary sludge) + estrogen upregulates HMG-CoA reductase (increasing cholesterol concentration within bile).

vignettes.q: 2M + recent viral infection + now has intermittent vomiting and crying with blood in the stool; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: intussusception; risk factor is recent viral infection; can cause adenitis of bowel leading to telescoping; almost all intussusceptions occur under age 2; if elderly, can be colorectal cancer.

vignettes.q: Neonate + duodenal atresia and/or Hirschsprung; risk factor?
vignettes.a: –> Down syndrome is HY cause of these two findings.

vignettes.q: “Can you explain T cell migration through the thymus? What do I need to know?”
vignettes.a: T cells migrate into the thymic cortex first as CD4 and CD8 negative. They then differentiate, still in the thymic cortex, into T cells that are both CD4+ and CD8+ (i.e., each T cell has both CD4 and 8 on its surface). Positive se

vignettes.q: Identify the diagnosis & key pearl (Immunology Vignette):
vignettes.a: Humoral immunity means antibodies are involved in the killing of the organism. If antibodies are not involved, then the process does not relate to humoral immunity. § Plasma B cells produce antibody and hence are the main cell of

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about the different antibody types and their structure?
vignettes.a: ” Antibody types + HY points Ab type Binds complement? Crosses placenta? In breastmilk? Function / HY points IgM Yes No No

vignettes.q: Hyper-IgM syndrome
vignettes.a: caused by deficiency of CD40L on Th2 CD4+ T cells, leading to ↓ binding of CD40 on B cells → differentiation into plasma B cells + ↓ isotype class-switching (i.e., plasma B cell is “stuck” at IgM and cannot make other types of Ig)

vignettes.q: Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome
vignettes.a: FATED → abnormal Facies, Staphylococcal “cold” Abscesses, retained deciduous Teeth, hyper-IgE, Dermatologic findings (i.e., eczematoid skin lesions). IgD No No No

vignettes.q: “Can you quickly explain passive vs active immunity?
vignettes.a: ” Passive vs active immunity

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about the complement cascade/pathways? I hear about complement a lot but I’m not really sure what it does. Can you explain that.”
vignettes.a: No, you do not need to memorize / draw out the complement pathways for Step 1. Waste of time. You just need to have a broad sense of the role complement plays in the innate immune system + some factoids about the different complem

vignettes.q: “Can you explain thymus-independent vs thymus-dependent antigens?”
vignettes.a: Thymus-independent means an antigen is not displayed on MHC molecules. Therefore there is no resultant T cell response. Thymus-dependent means an antigen is displayed on MHC molecules. Therefore there is a resultant T cell respons

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about the various cytokines?”
vignettes.a: Memorize macrophages as secreting, most importantly: TNF-a, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, and IL-12. Memorize IL-2 as a T cell stimulator. Memorize TNF-a and IL-1 as the two associated with sepsis: TNF-a causes low BP; IL-1 causes fever. Memo

vignettes.q: “What should I know about various cell surface markers?
vignettes.a: ” Cell surface marker HY points for USMLE

vignettes.q: “What autoantibodies do I need to know for USMLE?
vignettes.a: ” HY autoantibodies for USMLE

vignettes.q: “What about vaccine types? Are those important?” Yeah.
vignettes.a: Killed vaccines: § RIPP Always → Rabies, Influenza (IM), Polio (Salk; IM), Pertussis, Hep A. § A TRIPP could Kill you → Hep A, Typhoid (IM), Rabies, Influenza (IM), Polio (Salk; IM), Pertussis, Killed vaccines. § Generate a humora

vignettes.q: “What are the highest yield points about the immunodeficiencies?
vignettes.a: ” Immunodeficiencies HY points

vignettes.q: 4F + has her MHC class I molecules investigated; which of the following processes is most likely to be seen?
vignettes.a: “degradation by proteasome”; MHC I has antigen peptides loaded in the RER before being transported to cell surface with b2-microglobulin; wrong answers are “association with invariant chain,” “antigen loaded following release of i

vignettes.q: Researcher investigating an immune structure that naturally concentrates within endosomes, lysosomes, and phagolysosomes + directly kills organisms (e.g., TB) + increasing pH within phagolysosomes decreases eff
vignettes.a: “MHC II molecule peptide loading.” If you think about it, since MHC II is expressing phagocytosed extracellular antigen, it makes sense that that’s the MHC where endosomes play a role.

vignettes.q: Transgenic rats + incapable of expressing b2-microglobulin; which of the following host defenses is most likely to be altered?
vignettes.a: cytotoxic T cells; b2-microglobulin is associated with MHC I, which interacts with T cell receptor on CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes.

vignettes.q: 4F + thymus is investigated using laser scanning microscopy; what is most likely to be seen?
vignettes.a: T lymphocyte antigen receptor selection.

vignettes.q: 3M + bacterial infections since 6 months of age + scanty lymph nodes/tonsils; what mechanism best explains this patient’s condition?
vignettes.a: “deficiency of humoral immunity”; diagnosis is X-linked agammaglobulinemia → mutation in Bruton tyrosine kinase → decreased B cell function → decreased immunoglobulins.

vignettes.q: 19F + Hx of recurrent sinopulmonary infections since elementary school + asthma + Hx of Giardia infection; what mechanism best explains this patient’s condition?
vignettes.a: “deficiency of humoral immunity,” OR “deficiency of mucosal immunoglobulin”; diagnosis is IgA deficiency.

vignettes.q: 17F + Hx of cutaneous candida infections since childhood + 2-year Hx of type I diabetes mellitus + Hx of autoimmune thyroiditis; Dx?
vignettes.a: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis → answer = “T cell dysfunction” = “impaired cell-mediated immunity” (both answers); although candida infections can be seen in diabetes, the durations don’t match up here, so you know the Dx is CM

vignettes.q: 2F + numerous infections of skin + oral mucosa since birth + P/E shows numerous superficially ulcerated skin lesions + WBC 20,000 (75% neutrophils) + biopsy of skin lesion shows no neutrophils within the dermis
vignettes.a: integrin; diagnosis is leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD), caused by deficient CD18/LFA-1 integrin. LFA-1 is a type of integrin; CD18 is a common subunit of integrins. LAD Qs need not mention delayed separation of umbilical cord

vignettes.q: 3M + severe skin infections caused by S. aureus since birth + no pus at infection sites + previous laboratory studies showed leukocytosis even in the absence of infection; which mechanism is impaired in this pa
vignettes.a: “leukocyte adhesion and migration”; diagnosis is LAD.

vignettes.q: 23F + one week of difficulty walking + blurry vision in left eye + MRI shows white matter lesions in cerebellum; which of the following immune mechanisms best describes the pathogenesis in this patient?
vignettes.a: “CD4+ T cells are activated by myelin basic protein” (MBP); diagnosis is multiple sclerosis (MS); MBP is a component of myelin. As one proposed mechanism for MS, T cells will attack MBP, via molecular mimicry, following HHV-6 infe

vignettes.q: 45M + bilateral crackles + fever of 102F + Legionella grown from sputum culture; Q asks, which mechanism is most integral to clearing the organism from his alveoli?
vignettes.a: “T cell-mediated immunity”; Legionella is facultative intracellular; CD8+ cell-mediated immunity is helpful in clearing Legionella for this reason; very HY detail for Step 1.

vignettes.q: 29M + splenectomy following motor vehicle accident + now has target cells; this is due to loss of what?
vignettes.a: red pulp → part of spleen (~75%) that normally clears out senescent RBCs; asplenia is rare cause of target cells for USMLE, although this shows up on one NBME Q (target cells almost always thalassemia). White pulp of the spleen (~

vignettes.q: 29M + splenectomy + must now receive which three vaccines?
vignettes.a: S. pneumo, Haemophilus influenzae type B, Neisseria meningitides → encapsulated organisms → increased risk because normally encapsulated organisms are removed via opsonization + phagocytosis, and the spleens plays a major role in

vignettes.q: What will be seen on blood smear post-splenectomy (or with auto-splenectomy)?
vignettes.a: Howell-Jolly bodies (RBC nuclear remnants) + target cells (although the latter usually thalassemia).

vignettes.q: How does the spleen relate to platelets?
vignettes.a: splenomegaly can sequester platelets and cause thrombocytopenia; splenectomy can cause transient thrombocytosis.

vignettes.q: 16F + has fever and confusion + CSF culture shows gram (-) diplococci + younger brother had similar infection last year; which of the following immune disorders does this patient have?
vignettes.a: “late component of complement deficiency” → terminal complement deficiency (C6-C9) leads to recurrent Neisseria infections (both meningococcus and gonococcus) → defective membrane attack complex (MAC); sometimes the answer will si

vignettes.q: 7M + three infections with Neisseria meningitides the past year; which of the following is most likely to be abnormal in this patient?
vignettes.a: “total hemolytic complement activation.”

vignettes.q: 40F + receives new chemotherapeutic drug that causes myelosuppression; Q asks, in order to follow for risk of infectious complications, what should be monitored?
vignettes.a: neutrophil counts → agranulocytosis (neutropenia) is often seen with chemotherapy; also seen with various drugs such as the thionamides (propylthiocuracil + methimazole, for hyperthyroidism), ganciclovir (for CMV), methotrexate (f

vignettes.q: 35M + red spots on shins, joint pain, and fatigue + HepC + urine protein and blood; which hypersensitivity type is responsible for the renal damage?
vignettes.a: type III; diagnosis is cryoglobulinemia (immunoglobulins / Ag-Ab complexes that precipitate below 37C), causing skin lesions/ulcers, Raynaud phenomenon, muscle pain, and glomerulonephritis.

vignettes.q: 4F + leukocytes fail to express CD40 ligand; the immunoglobulin that predominates in this patient’s serum has which biologic property?
vignettes.a: “complement activation” → diagnosis is hyper-IgM syndrome → caused by failure of expression of CD40 ligand on T cells → therefore B cells cannot be activated for immunoglobulin isotype class-switching (i.e., cannot switch from IgM

vignettes.q: 42M + inflammatory bowel disease + trial of monoclonal antibody is begun; what does it most likely target?
vignettes.a: tumor necrosis factor; anti-TNF-a agents such as infliximab, adalimumab, and etanercept can be used for IBD non-responsive to NSAIDs and steroids.

vignettes.q: 38F + rheumatoid arthritis + treatment with NSAIDs, prednisone, and methotrexate not effective; the most appropriate next step in pharmacology blocks which cytokine?
vignettes.a: TNF-a; sounds similar to above IBD Q, but these are distinct immuno NBME Qs (let that emphasize yieldness).

vignettes.q: 35F + SLE + has diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis; what is the most likely immunological mechanism associated with this patient’s disease?
vignettes.a: anti-DNA/DNA immune complex deposition in the glomeruli.”

vignettes.q: 41M + infection of dorsolateral foot that ascends lymphatically; Q asks, what is the most likely source of drainage? → answer = popliteal lymph nodes (HY). Other HY lymph node drainage points:
vignettes.a: Testes + ovaries → para-aortic. Foregut, midgut, hindgut → celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric, respectively. Cervix + body of uterus → external iliac. Anal canal above pectinate line + bladder → internal iliac. Anal

vignettes.q: 29M + HIV + receives drug that blocks viral entry into the cell; which of the following is the molecular target of this drug?
vignettes.a: chemokine receptor → refers to CCR5 as the target of maraviroc, which is an HIV entry inhibitor. Don’t confuse this with enfuvirtide, which targets Gp41 and functions as an HIV fusion inhibitor.

vignettes.q: An investigator is comparing the live-attenuated (Sabin) vs killed (Salk) Polio vaccines; what is a common feature of these vaccines that accounts for their efficacy?
vignettes.a: “neutralizing antibodies in the circulation.” The live-attenuated is given oral; it enters cells and is expressed on MHC I for interaction with CD8+ T cells for cell-mediated immunity; there is production of neutralizing secretory

vignettes.q: 20F + healthy + painful swelling on the chest wall inferior to right breast + physician identifies it as a nipple; biopsy of the specimen is most likely to show what?
vignettes.a: “epithelial cells” (i.e., normal finding) → supernumerary nipples are common in women; yes, this is on the NBME for Step 1.

vignettes.q: 33F + shortness of breath + fever + sputum shows gram (+) diplococci; which of the following enzymes is most likely to initiate intracellular killing of the organism?
vignettes.a: “NADPH oxidase.”

vignettes.q: 5-month-old girl + recurrent sinopulmonary infections since birth + hypopigmentation of skin, eyes, and hair + peripheral smear shows giant granules in neutrophils and eosinophils; what’s the most likely diagno
