vignettes.a: Chediak-Higashi syndrome; phagolysosomal fusion disorder with disruption of microtubule function; melanosome function also impaired.

vignettes.q: 4F + immunodeficiency + fairer skin than siblings + giant granules seen in phagocytes; Dx?
vignettes.a: Chediak-Higashi syndrome; phagolysosomal fusion disorder with disruption of microtubule function; melanosome function also impaired.

vignettes.q: 2M + immunodeficiency + delayed separation of umbilical cord; Dx?
vignettes.a: leukocyte adhesion deficiency → deficiency of LFA-1/CD18 integrin.

vignettes.q: 2M + viral, fungal, bacterial, protozoal infections since birth + absent thymic shadow + scanty/absent lymph nodes/tonsils; Dx?
vignettes.a: severe-combined immunodeficiency (SCID) → XR type is most common and due to common gamma-chain mutation or IL-2 receptor deficiency; AR is due to adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency; Tx is bone marrow transplant; absent thymic sh

vignettes.q: 2M + bacterial infections from ~6 months of life + scanty/absent lymph nodes/tonsils; Dx?
vignettes.a: “deficiency of humoral immunity” (Bruton X-linked agammaglobulinemia); it must be pointed out that a Q on one of the newer Peds forms has Bruton as the answer for a kid who has bacterial infections since birth (which throws a dagg

vignettes.q: 5-month-old boy + severe diarrhea and pneumonia + thymus decreased in size + Pneumocystis jiroveci is isolated + decreased serum immunoglobulin concentrations + karyotype normal; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID); wrong answer is DiGeorge; hypogammaglobulinemia has not been reported in DiGeorge; also, DiGeorge would have 22q11 deletion identified on karyotype analysis.

vignettes.q: 3M + sore throat + grey membrane at back of throat; immunization with which of the following would have prevented this?
vignettes.a: toxoid vaccine; Corynebacterium diphtheriae is a toxoid vaccine; presents classically with grey pseudomembrane in oropharynx and myocarditis, although vignette need not mention these.

vignettes.q: 34F + septic shock caused by gram (-) rod; which of the following is responsible for her low BP?
vignettes.a: “lipopolysaccharide stimulating production of tumor necrosis factor” → lipid A of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) will stimulate macrophages to release cytokines → IL-1 causes fever; TNF- alpha causes vascular permeability and low BP. Im

vignettes.q: 16M + nose bleeding in car accident + has nasal packing + now gets low BP; what are the immunological receptor(s) bound?
vignettes.a: MHC II and TCR → toxic shock syndrome from the cotton packing; CD14 (toll-like receptor 4 is co-receptor) is wrong answer, since that is endotoxic shock from gram (-) sepsis.

vignettes.q: 2M + mental retardation + fairer skin than siblings + deficiency of hydroxylase enzyme; how could this patient’s presentation have been prevented?
vignettes.a: “routine newborn screening” via heel-prick test at birth for phenylketonuria (PKU; autosomal recessive; deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase) → tyrosine becomes essential; phenylalanine must be avoided in diet; malignant PKU =

vignettes.q: 8-month-old girl + oropharyngeal candidiasis + Hx of parainfluenza infection + 3/6 harsh systolic murmur at left sternal border; what does she have a deficiency of?
vignettes.a: T lymphocytes → possibly DiGeorge syndrome in this case (tetralogy of Fallot with murmur being a mix of VSD and pulmonary stenosis); T lymphocyte deficiency will cause viral, fungal and protozoal infections; if the USMLE wants B c

vignettes.q: 8-day-old newborn + truncus arteriosus + serum calcium of 7mg/dL + no thymic shadow; Dx?
vignettes.a: hypoparathyroidism (DiGeorge; 3rd and 4th pouch agenesis → 3rd = thymus and inferior parathyroids; 4th = superior parathyroids).

vignettes.q: An 8-month-old boy has recurrent respiratory tract infections since birth + hypocalcemia + broad nasal bridge; deficiency of which of the following is responsible for this patient’s condition?
vignettes.a: T cell; diagnosis is DiGeorge → 22q11 deletion.

vignettes.q: 3M + recurrent OM + recently underwent placement of tympanostomy tube + mom HIV negative; Dx?
vignettes.a: “antibody deficiency” → IgA deficiency.

vignettes.q: 8F + fever + purpuric lesions over trunk and extremities + brother died of fulminant meningococcemia four years ago; Dx?
vignettes.a: answer “complement system immunodeficiency” → terminal complement deficiency (C5-9) is associated with recurrent Neisseria infections (gonococcal and meningococcal).

vignettes.q: 18M + African American + Neisseria meningitides infection + had similar infection two years ago + vignette gives no other info; Q asks, this patient should be examined for which of the following conditions?
vignettes.a: “complement deficiency”; wrong answer = sickle cell disease; no reason to suspect asplenia from sickle cell.

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about the respiratory burst and chronic granulomatous disease (CGD; aka NADPH oxidase deficiency)?”
vignettes.a: Respiratory burst is a process by which phagocytes such as neutrophils and macrophages can produce hydrogen peroxidase and hydroxy-halide radicals (bleach) to kill microbes. CGD is caused by NADPH oxidase deficiency → decreased H2

vignettes.q: 5F + life-threatening Staph infections since age 3 months + WBCs normal + serum immunoglobulins normal; which of the following will best help establish the Dx?
vignettes.a: NBME answer = “NADPH oxidase test”; if the Q gets specific, dihydrorhodamine test is now correct over tetrazolium blue assay; this is on either retired NBME 15 or 16 for Step 1, where the latter is wrong; the former is correct.

vignettes.q: 19M + type I diabetes + recurrent yeast infections + analysis shows deficiency of myeloperoxidase; Q asks most likely cause of infection susceptibility in this patient; answer = “decreased ability to produce hy
vignettes.a: Dx is myeloperoxidase deficiency; enzyme normally converts hydrogen peroxide into bleach (hydroxy-halide radicals).

vignettes.q: 32F + has PPD test performed + large area of induration; which cell type is predominant in this area of induration?
vignettes.a: macrophages; wrong answer = cytotoxic T lymphocytes; macrophages phagocytose the TB antigen and express it on MHC II to CD4+ T cells (humoral immunity); cytotoxic T cells are CD8+ and will interact with virus expressed on MHC I (c

vignettes.q: 60M + undergoes chemotherapy + has fever of 102F + neutrophil count is low + antibiotics are administered; which of the following should be given to this patient to improve his neutrophil count?
vignettes.a: granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF; molgramostim), or G-CSF (filgrastim).

vignettes.q: 3-week-old boy born at term + experienced two weeks of respiratory distress following birth + mom has myasthenia gravis; this patient’s transient respiratory distress was due to transplacental transfer of which
vignettes.a: IgG (only one that crosses the placenta).

vignettes.q: 14M + fever + stiff neck + non-blanching purpura on abdomen + BP of 60/35 + IV fluids and norepinephrine have limited effect; Tx?
vignettes.a: hydrocortisone; Dx = Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome; hemorrhagic necrosis of adrenal cortices secondary to meningococcal septicemia; non- blanching rash in the setting of meningitis = meningococcus; hydrocortisone is the answer

vignettes.q: 1-month-old male + diffuse white plaques in oral cavity that bleed when scraped + papular erythematous rash with satellite lesions over the diaper area; mechanism?
vignettes.a: “decreased T lymphocyte activity” → chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis.

vignettes.q: 8M + super high IgM on lab report; what’s the mechanism?
vignettes.a: deficiency of CD40 ligand on T cells (can’t activate CD40 on B cells to induce isotype class switching) → Dx = Hyper IgM syndrome.

vignettes.q: 6F + recurrent Staph abscesses + eczematoid skin lesions + abnormal dentition; Dx?
vignettes.a: hyper IgE syndrome (Job syndrome) → FATED → abnormal Facies, staphylococcal cold Abscesses, retained primary Teeth, hyper IgE, Dermatologic findings (e.g., eczematoid lesions).

vignettes.q: 12M + eczematoid skin lesion on forehead + nosebleeds + Hx of infections; Q asks which cell is dysfunctional
vignettes.a: T cell; Dx = Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (XR) → classic triad of eczematoid skin lesions + thrombocytopenia + immunodeficiency.

vignettes.q: 3F + dilated superficial blood vessels on face + wobbly gait; mechanism?
vignettes.a: failure of double-stranded DNA break repair” → Dx = ataxia-telangiectasia.

vignettes.q: 17M + 3-wk Hx of lymphadenopathy, fever, and loose stools + hepatosplenomegaly + low RBCs and WBCs + high IgM and IgG; Dx?
vignettes.a: HIV infection; wrong answers are CVID, IgA deficiency, SCID, DiGeorge, Bruton (so you can eliminate to get there); CVID is can rarely occur as young as adolescence but Dx is with IgG and IgA >2SD less than the mean (IgG high in th

vignettes.q: 47M + farmer + nodule on nose + biopsy shows invasive melanoma with features of regression; which of the following best explains the mechanism of regression?
vignettes.a: “T lymphocyte-mediated cytotoxicity” → T cells can recognize and destroy cancer cells; aldesleukin is a recombinant IL-2 used for melanoma that stimulates T cells.

vignettes.q: 20M + Crohn disease + treated with prednisone + recovers; the mechanism of this pharmacologic therapy is suppression of which of the following?
vignettes.a: T lymphocytes; steroids lead to suppressed T cell responses; wrong answers are antibody binding, complement activity, mast cell degranulation, neutrophil function.

vignettes.q: 28F + squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix + biopsy of tumor cells shows HPV-18; which of the following cell types is most important for killing these virally infected cells?
vignettes.a: T cells; CD8+ T cells kill virus-infected cells; wrong answers are dendritic cells, macrophages, and plasma cells.

vignettes.q: 45M + has tuberculosis + which cytokine concentration is most likely to be increased in this patient?
vignettes.a: interferon-gamma (IFN-γ); IFN-γ from CD4+ T cells stimulates macrophages in order to form granulomas.

vignettes.q: 25M + receives bone marrow transplant + one week later develops rash, diarrhea, and increased LFTs; what’s the most likely mechanism for this patient’s condition?
vignettes.a: “Donor T cells reacting against host cells”; diagnosis is graft vs host disease → usually seen in bone marrow transplants, but sometimes in liver transplants; donor (graft) T cells recognize the host (recipient) antigens as foreig

vignettes.q: 45M + bone marrow transplant 7 weeks ago + now has increased LFTs; Q asks, which of the following hypersensitivity types is most responsible?
vignettes.a: cell-mediated; graft-vs-host disease is considered to be cell-mediated hypersensitivity; wrong answers are antibody-mediated, immediate, and immune complex.

vignettes.q: 46F + receives liver transplant + the vessels supporting the graft appear to necrose within 15 minutes of transplantation; what’s the mechanism?
vignettes.a: preformed antibodies; hyperacute rejection (graft rejection on the operating table). Acute rejection on USMLE will be up to several months; chronic rejection will be >6 months; for both acute and chronic, USMLE wants T cell respon

vignettes.q: 52M + infiltrating parietal lobe mass identified as astrocytoma; impaired activity of which of the following is most likely responsible?
vignettes.a: p53; this is often the answer if the USMLE asks about what needs to be mutated for there to be cancer invasion; effect of p53 mutation is “defective DNA repair”; p53 normally facilitates DNA repair by halting the cell cycle to all

vignettes.q: 31M + cellulitis + goes on to develop fever, confusion, tachycardia, and low BP + WBC 18,000/uL; which two cytokines are responsible for his condition?
vignettes.a: IL-1 and TNF-a. Really HY Q for USMLE → IL-1 causes fever associated with sepsis; TNF-a causes low BP (increased vascular permeability). If the Q gives you a vignette of sepsis and forces you to choose one molecule, the answer is

vignettes.q: 52F + breast cancer + lost 20 lbs past month + no appetite; what is responsible for this patient’s loss of appetite?
vignettes.a: “effect of cytokine” → TNF-a causes cachexia.

vignettes.q: Researcher compares two cell lines; one cell line has an IL-2 gene transfected; the other does not; the transfected group generates a stronger immune response; what kind of cell is responsible for this differen
vignettes.a: T lymphocyte; IL-2 stimulates T cells.

vignettes.q: 40M + has a wound surgically repaired; Q asks, which of the following inflammatory mediators is most likely released from aggregated platelets in this patient during wound repair?
vignettes.a: thromboxane A2 (I guess more of a heme/onc Q, but life moves on doesn’t it).

vignettes.q: 65F + fever of 102F + muscle pain + non-productive cough + shortness of breath; which vaccine would have prevented these findings?
vignettes.a: influenza virus.

vignettes.q: 20M + fever of 100.8F + non-productive cough + pale conjunctivae + blood sample agglutinates while waiting for transport to laboratory; which of the following antibody isotypes most likely caused the agglutinat
vignettes.a: IgM; Mycoplasma pneumoniae can cause atypical pneumonia, as well as cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia (pale conjunctivae); cold AIHA is associated with IgM targeting RBCs (cold = “Mmm ice cream” = IgM); agglutination of RBCs occurs

vignettes.q: 61M + goes hiking + has linear vesicles on his leg; this finding is most likely caused by activation of which of the following cell types?
vignettes.a: T cells → contact dermatitis (type IV hypersensitivity) caused by poison ivy/sumac; “linear vesicles” is HY for brushing up / walking past weeds; if Q asks how to avoid this condition, answer = “avoidance of contact with weeds.”

vignettes.q: Researcher makes a cell line that produces an inactive form of caspase. What’s most likely to be the result of this?
vignettes.a: continued proliferation of cells; caspases enable apoptosis.

vignettes.q: 50F + has flow cytometry performed showing CD3 50%; CD4 40%; CD8 10%; CD20 50%; surface kappa 48%; surface lambda 3%; what is most predictive of clonal lymphoid proliferation in this patient?
vignettes.a: “surface kappa/lambda ratio”; CD3 = T cell marker; CD20 = B cell marker (so we know the analysis is showing us 50% T cells and 50% B cells); CD4 and CD8 are T cell markers (so 80% of the patient’s T cells are CD4, and 20% are CD8)

vignettes.q: 4F + bloody diarrhea caused by Salmonella; which of the following factors is most responsible for neutrophil recruitment to intestinal cells?
vignettes.a: IL-8; neutrophilic chemotactic molecules include IL-8, kallikrein, platelet-activating factor, C5a, LTB-4, and bacterial products.

vignettes.q: 72M + fever 101 + WBCs 15,000 + CXR shows patchy infiltrate; which endogenous chemoattractant primarily causes leukocytic recruitment to his site of acute inflammation?
vignettes.a: C5a. Don’t get pulled into weird distractors like filamin or N-formyl methionine terminal amino acid peptides.

vignettes.q: 2-month-old girl + feeding and developing well + pregnancy uncomplicated + temperature of 99.8F + hematocrit, platelets, and WBC count normal, but neutrophils 5%; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: congenital neutropenia”; neutrophils should be 50-55%; asked on the NBME.

vignettes.q: 22F + vesicular lesions on lower lip + recurrences most likely caused by viral latency where?
vignettes.a: sensory neurons.

vignettes.q: 4F + fever 102F + crackles and rhonchi heard in the lungs + CXR shows dextrocardia and right-sided gastric bubble; deficiency of which of the following is responsible for this patient’s disorder?
vignettes.a: dynein; Dx is primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome); patients present with situs inversus, sinopulmonary infections, and immotile sperm / ectopic pregnancy. Sometimes the answer can be “dynein arm” or “cilium.”

vignettes.q: 4M + lymphadenopathy + absent granulomata seen on lymph node biopsy + acid-fast bacilli identified as Mycobacterium avium intracellulare + normal serum immunoglobulin concentrations and B and T cells; the patie
vignettes.a: interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) receptor → IFN-γ needed for granulomas.

vignettes.q: 60F + fever + night sweats + PPD test positive; sputum culture is most likely to show organisms inside which of the following cells?
vignettes.a: macrophages; T cells are wrong answer because they help facilitate granulomas, but the TB are phagocytosed by alveolar macrophages.

vignettes.q: 28F + AIDS + develops tuberculosis + which cell types is most likely to have deficient function in the tuberculous areas of lung?
vignettes.a: macrophages; CD4+ T cells normally activate macrophages via IFN-gamma, and macrophages stimulate CD4+ T cells via IL-12; wrong answers = eosinophils, neutrophils, fibroblasts, Langerhan cells.

vignettes.q: 29M + PPD test positive + IFN-γ administered improves his condition; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: IL-12 receptor deficiency → causes increased susceptibility to TB infections; macrophages and CD4+ T cells have an IL-12-IFN-γ stimulatory loop → macrophages secrete IL-12, which stimulates CD4+ T cells to make IFN-γ, which in tur

vignettes.q: 2-month-old girl + given vaccine that converts T cell-independent antigens into T cell-dependent antigens; which vaccine was given?
vignettes.a: Haemophilus influenzae type B (HiB). Only proteins can be expressed on MHC molecules in order to induce T cell response; HiB has polysaccharide capsule that will alone will not get expressed on MHC, so it is conjugated to a protei

vignettes.q: 2M + scaly, seborrheic eruption over scalp, palms, and diaper region + hepatosplenomegaly + generalized lymphadenopathy + x-ray of skull shows osteolytic legions + biopsy of skin lesion shows a tennis racquet-s
vignettes.a: dendritic cells; Dx = Langerhan cell histiocytosis; tennis racquet-shaped granules are called Birbeck granules. Langerhan cells are a type of dendritic cell found in the skin. Dendritic cells are antigen-presenting cells found thr

vignettes.q: 34M + chronic HepC; what mechanism best describes any hepatic damage in this patient?
vignettes.a: “Cytotoxic T cell response”; wrong answer is “direct viral cytopathic effects.” Hepatitis viruses (except HepD) primarily cause hepatic damage by inducing a T cell-mediated immune response to hepatocytes; direct viral cytopathic e

vignettes.q: 26M + lower back pain worse in the morning + gets better throughout the day + eczematoid lesion on his forehead; what is most likely to be seen in this patient?
vignettes.a: HLA-B27 positivity; HLA-B27 → PAIR → Psoriasis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD, Reactive arthritis; never choose HLA-B27 for diagnostic purposes; USMLE just wants you to know the immunologic link for these PAIR conditions.

vignettes.q: 47M + cystic fibrosis + receives bilateral lung transplant + on immunosuppressive agents for several months + now has higher fasting glucose levels; Q asks why; answer = adverse effect of medication (tacrolimus
vignettes.a: HY drug that causes diabetes; tacrolimus binds to to FK506 → decreases intracellular calcineurin → decreases IL-2 transcription (cyclosporin also decreases IL-2 transcription; in contrast, sirolimus decreases responsiveness to IL-

vignettes.q: 42M + receives intramuscular antibiotic + three days later has rash in his arm where the drug was administered; Q asks, what kind of hypersensitivity is this?
vignettes.a: type III → diagnosis is Arthus reaction → localized skin reaction due to immune complex deposition; can be distinguished from type I hypersensitivities because type III require 3-5 days after exposure to be seen. Arthus reaction i

vignettes.q: 16F + starts taking TMP/SMX for UTI + three days later has polyarthritis; Q asks, what kind of hypersensitivity is this?
vignettes.a: type III; diagnosis is serum sickness due to sulfa drug. Serum sickness can also occur as result of infections, notably HepB/C, Rubella, Yersinia, and Chlamydia (reactive arthritis).

vignettes.q: 17M + leukemia + neoplastic cells do not express CD4 and CD8, however they do express T lymphocyte receptor b-chain D and J segments; Q asks, which of the following best refers to these malignant cells?
vignettes.a: “T cell thymocytes localized to thymic cortex.” Recall that T cell precursors first migrate into the thymic cortex as CD4 and CD8 negative, before differentiating into CD4 and CD8 positive cells. Pedantic, but asked on NBME.

vignettes.q: “I always get confused about the immunosuppressants. Can you consolidate some of what I need to know?
vignettes.a: ” Cyclosporine vs tacrolimus vs sirolimus

vignettes.q: “What about monoclonal antibodies?
vignettes.a: What are some worthy of memorizing for USMLE?” Highest yield monoclonal antibodies for USMLE (i.e., sans the superfluousness)

vignettes.q: Travel + self-limiting watery or brown/green diarrhea
vignettes.a: Traveler diarrhea = ETEC HL or HS toxin

vignettes.q: Bloody diarrhea + poultry consumption
vignettes.a: Campylobacter jejuni or Salmonella spp.

vignettes.q: Abx (clindamycin, beta-lactam, cephalosporin) + diarrhea
vignettes.a: C. difficile

vignettes.q: Dx of C. diff
vignettes.a: stool AB toxin test, not stool culture

vignettes.q: Tx of C. diff
vignettes.a: vancomycin, not metronidazole (updated guidelines as of Feb 2018)

vignettes.q: Bloody diarrhea + travel
vignettes.a: Entamoeba histolytica

vignettes.q: Tx of E. histolytica
vignettes.a: metronidazole + iodoquinol; can give paromomycin

vignettes.q: Close quarters or military barracks or cruise ship + watery diarrhea
vignettes.a: Norwalk virus

vignettes.q: Child <5 years + watery diarrhea
vignettes.a: rotavirus

vignettes.q: Few organisms causing bloody diarrhea
vignettes.a: Shigella

vignettes.q: Bloody diarrhea + reactive arthritis in an adult
vignettes.a: Y. enterocolitica, Campylobacter, Shigella, Salmonella

vignettes.q: CPP + lobar pattern, but they say “interstitial” in the vignette description
vignettes.a: Mycoplasma, not S. pneumo

vignettes.q: Empiric Tx for CPP
vignettes.a: azithromycin

vignettes.q: Tx for CPP is pt on Abx past three months
vignettes.a: fluoroquinolone over azithro

vignettes.q: Prostatitis Tx
vignettes.a: ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolone → DNA gyrase / topoisomerase II inhibitor)

vignettes.q: Dx of PBC
vignettes.a: anti-mitochondrial Abx next best step; liver biopsy is confirmatory

vignettes.q: Teenage girl with Hx of cutaneous candida infections since childhood
vignettes.a: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis

vignettes.q: Bacterial + fungal + protozoal + viral infections since birth
vignettes.a: SCID

vignettes.q: Bacterial infections since age 6 months
vignettes.a: Bruton

vignettes.q: Bacterial infections only since birth
vignettes.a: Bruton

vignettes.q: SCID XR variant
vignettes.a: common gamma-chain mutation (IL-2 receptor deficiency)

vignettes.q: SCID AR variant
vignettes.a: adenosine deaminase deficiency

vignettes.q: Bruton mechanism
vignettes.a: tyrosine kinase mutation

vignettes.q: Tx of cutaneous candida
vignettes.a: oral azole

vignettes.q: Sporothrix schenckii (rose thorn + finger papule)
vignettes.a: itraconazole

vignettes.q: Give killed IM influenza vaccine when?
vignettes.a: Every year in fall/winter only; start from 6 months of age

vignettes.q: Killed IM Influenza vaccine safe in pregnancy?
vignettes.a: Yes, give anytime to pregnant women

vignettes.q: Live-attenuated intranasal influenza vaccine guidelines?
vignettes.a: Only give age 2-49 to non-pregnant, non- immunocompromised persons Vaccines at age 2, 4, 6 months: HepB, Polio Salk, Pneumo PCV13, DPT, HiB, rotavirus (also give HepB at birth)

vignettes.q: Most common cause of otitis externa
vignettes.a: Pseudomonas

vignettes.q: Platelet problem?
vignettes.a: epistaxis, bruising, petechiae → generally mild and cutaneous

vignettes.q: Broad-spectrum Abx example?
vignettes.a: Pipericillin/tazobactam; cefepime + vancomycin

vignettes.q: What is ganciclovir used for?
vignettes.a: Tx of CMV (DNA polymerase inhibitor)

vignettes.q: Vomiting (or any unusual Sx like bloody diarrhea) + eating custards, creams, potato salad
vignettes.a: S. aureus preformed HS toxin → the type of food in this scenario “wins” over the weird bloody diarrhea finding → bear in mind typical bloody-diarrhea-inducing gram (-) rods like EHEC, Yersinia enterocolitica, Campylobacter, Shigel

vignettes.q: Tx for Strep pharyngitis?
vignettes.a: Amoxicillin or penicillin only (not Augmentin)

vignettes.q: Empiric Abx therapy for meningitis
vignettes.a: ceftriaxone + vancomycin (+/- steroids)

vignettes.q: Lumbar puncture or Abx first in suspected meningitis?
vignettes.a: new guidelines say LP first

vignettes.q: 36M + long-bone fractures + petechiae on the chest
vignettes.a: fat embolism

vignettes.q: Red shins + Crohn
vignettes.a: erythema nodosum (type III hypersensitivity; panniculitis → inflammation of subcutaneous fat, not a rash)

vignettes.q: AIDS patient with CD4 count of 47 + confluent ulcers seen on colonoscopy
vignettes.a: CMV colitis → confluent means “linear” → CMV = linear ulcers; HSV = punched-out ulcers

vignettes.q: Tx for CMV
vignettes.a: ganciclovir (DNA polymerase inhibitor)

vignettes.q: Tx of herpes
vignettes.a: acyclovir

vignettes.q: Hereditary angioedema
vignettes.a: due to C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency

vignettes.q: 16M goes snowboarding all day + takes pain reliever for sore muscles afterward + next day develops wheezing out on the slopes again; what’s going on?
vignettes.a: took aspirin + this is Samter triad (now cumbersomely known as aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease [AERD]) → triad of aspirin-induced asthma + aspirin hypersensitivity + nasal polyps). Just to be clear, other NSAIDs can precip

vignettes.q: Dude moves into new apartment building and uses the hot tub a lot + has low oxygen sats + dyspnea + crackles at lung bases + no wheezing + low-grade fever
vignettes.a: hot tub lung (outrageous, but an answer on an NBME exam) → caused by hot tube fumes; not related to Pseudomonas (hot tub folliculitis) (weird factoid to end this pdf but we’ll run with it) HY USMLE REVIEW PART II

vignettes.q: Dx of malaria
vignettes.a: thick + thin blood smears, not antibody titer for Plasmodium species

vignettes.q: Girl goes to Africa + is taking chloroquine prophylaxis
vignettes.a: gets malaria anyway; why? Is the answer non-adherence or resistance to chloroquine? → answer = resistance to chloroquine

vignettes.q: What is the MOA of chloroquine?
vignettes.a: inhibits Plasmodium heme polymerase.

vignettes.q: Which malaria type is the worst and why?
vignettes.a: P. falciparum because it causes cerebral malaria.

vignettes.q: Which drug is often given to people for malaria prophylaxis who go to chloroquine-resistant areas?
vignettes.a: mefloquine

vignettes.q: Girl goes to Africa + gets malaria + she is then treated after the fact with atovoquine + proguanil and the presentation subsides; then one month later she has malaria again; why?
vignettes.a: reactivation of non-erythrocytic form of organism” → she has P. vivax or P. ovale → cause hypnozoites which are an intra-hepatic form of the disease.

vignettes.q: Travel + bloody diarrhea + RUQ pain; Dx?
vignettes.a: liver abscess due to Entamoeba histolytica

vignettes.q: Abx for E. histolytica?
vignettes.a: metronidazole + iodoquinol (latter kills intraluminal parasite); paromomycin may also be given.

vignettes.q: Watery diarrhea in immunocompromised patient
vignettes.a: Cryptosporidium parvum

vignettes.q: How is Giardia transmitted (is the answer “water-borne” or “fecal-oral”?
vignettes.a: ); answer = water-borne

vignettes.q: Steatorrhea in guy who went swimming or scuba diving
vignettes.a: Giardia

vignettes.q: Tx for Giardia
vignettes.a: metronidazole

vignettes.q: Cestode (tapeworm) from pork
vignettes.a: Taenia solium

vignettes.q: Tx for nec fasc
vignettes.a: surgical debridement + IV broad-specrum Abx with anaerobic coverage.

vignettes.q: 17M comes to emergency with cellulitis + getting worse + holding amoxicillin canister he got from GP; Dx?
vignettes.a: improper Abx treatment; should have received oral dicloxacillin or oral cephalexin outpatient → cellulitis must have been caused by Staph not Strep.

vignettes.q: 27M + from Pennsylvania + Hx of splenectomy + RBCs show intraerythrocytic rings; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Babesia; causes Malaria-like hemolytic disorder in patients who’ve never left the United States; ring forms and Maltese crosses can be seen within RBCs; if the Q tells you the patient went to Africa, choose malaria, not Babesia. B

vignettes.q: 21F + vesicular, painful rash across left flank + pic shows you multinucleated giant cells; what’s the most likely pathogen this patient should be screened for?
vignettes.a: HIV; only answer listed that makes sense, as VZV not listed; young patient with shingles (herpes zoster; VZV); immunosuppression in young patient resulting in shingles could reflect HIV infection.

vignettes.q: 25M + rash on palms and soles + receives antibiotic Tx with drug he has received in the past; following current Tx, now has fever, tachycardia, and tachypnea; what’s the most likely diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction; answer can also be written as “reaction to lysis of spirochetes”; patient has secondary syphilis (Treponema pallidum), as indicated by the palms/soles rash; Tx is with penicillin G; lysis of spirochete

vignettes.q: 19F + alkaline urine + renal tract calculi; which organism is most likely responsible?
vignettes.a: Proteus; other correct answers could be Klebsiella or Serratia; struvite (ammonium magnesium phosphate) stones form in alkaline urine secondary to UTIs caused by urease-positive organisms.

vignettes.q: Newborn + chorioretinitis + cataracts + microcephaly + no other info; Dx in the neonate?
vignettes.a: CMV; congenital Toxo always = triad of chorioretinitis + hydrocephalus + intracranial calcifications; so if you do not get this exact latter triad, you can eliminate congenital Toxo. Congenital CMV tends to have a mix of non-speci

vignettes.q: 35F + Hx of recurrent miscarriages + positive VDRL test; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: SLE causing antiphospholipid syndrome, resulting in recurrent miscarriages due to uteroplacental microthromboses; antiphospholipid syndrome can cause a false (+) VDRL syphilis test.

vignettes.q: 40M + comes back from Africa with hemolytic condition + image shows schizonts of malaria; Q asks what patient is at greatest risk for
vignettes.a: hypoglycemia; you need to know malaria (particularly P. falciparum) can lead to hypoglycemia. If you think it’s weird, don’t take it up with me. It’s on one of the Step 1 NBME exams.

vignettes.q: 6F + 10th percentile for weight and height + bowing of the tibias + family recently immigrated to the US from Ireland. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for serum Ca2+ , serum PO43- , and PTH?
vignettes.a: ↓ Serum Ca2+ , ↓ serum PO43- , ↑ PTH. — Diagnosis is rickets (vitamin D deficiency in children). In adults, the condition is called osteomalacia. • Calcium and phosphate are both low because vitamin D is needed for intestinal abso

vignettes.q: 77F + bone densitometry shows bone density of hips and vertebrae >2.5 standard deviations below the mean for 20-yr-old women. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for serum Ca2+ , serum PO43-, PTH, and 1,25-(
vignettes.a: ↔ Serum Ca2+ , ↔ serum PO43- , ↔ PTH, ↔ 1,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3. — Diagnosis is osteoporosis. All laboratory findings will be normal. • Students often get this question wrong, assuming, e.g., calcium must be low, but serum findings

vignettes.q: 15F + asymptomatic + cardiac auscultation reveals fixed splitting of the S2 heart sound. Compared to normal values, what are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for superior vena cava pO2, right atrial pO2, right ven
vignettes.a: ↔ Superior vena cava pO2, ↑ right atrial pO2, ↑ right ventricular pO2, ↑ pulmonary artery pO2. — Diagnosis is atrial septal defect (ASD). • Since the defect is between the atria, and pressures are greater on the left side of the h

vignettes.q: Student Q showed electron micrograph (EM) pic of sarcomere + they asked what does not change length during muscle contraction + had letters at different locations. Answer = A-band.
vignettes.a: Before you instantly freak out, relax. First look at above EM of sarcomere. Then compare with bottom images here: All you need to know is: as the myosin and actin overlap during muscle contraction, the H- zone, I-band, and sarcome

vignettes.q: 24M + partakes in research study of muscle contraction; Q asks, on the following electron micrograph of a sarcomere, which segment will not change length? (choose the number):
vignettes.a: #2 (A-band). In contrast, the I-band (#6), H-zone (#7), and length of sarcomere (#1; Z-Z) all shorten during contraction.

vignettes.q: 31M + in wilderness for 3 weeks without food; Q asks what allows him to maintain normal serum glucose levels during this time; answer = “skeletal muscle protein”
vignettes.a: you must know that skeletal muscle does not contain glucose-6-phosphatase and therefore does not directly carry out gluconeogenesis; glucogenic amino acids can be liberated in the fasting state from skeletal muscle, with the liver

vignettes.q: Q on offline Step 1 NBME form asks why ATP does not fall appreciably during a series of muscle twitches
vignettes.a: “ATP is quickly regenerating from creatine phosphate.”

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about shoulder anatomy for USMLE?”
vignettes.a: USMLE is known to occasionally give images of shoulder, clavicular, and humeral fractures. Spending a few moments to gain an idea of normal shoulder anatomy is not “nitpicky.”

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about the rotator cuff? It’s high-yield right?”
vignettes.a: Yes. Same as with the above x-rays, you need to know the rotator cuff muscles. Just deal with it.

vignettes.q: Empty-can (thumb-down) / full-can (thumb-up) tests for diagnosis
vignettes.a: patient abducts arm to 90 degrees with thumbs up or down → downward pressure applied to arm → if elicits pain, answer = supraspinatus injury.

vignettes.q: Gerber lift-off test = patient places dorsal aspect of hand on lower back, with palm facing posteriorly
vignettes.a: examiner applies pressure into the patient’s palm against his/her lower back → patient is then asked to move hand away under the pressure → if elicits pain / difficult to do, answer = subscapularis injury.

vignettes.q: “Are there other shoulder conditions sometimes confused with rotator cuff injury?”
vignettes.a: Yes. USMLE likes subacromial bursitis and biceps tendonitis as well. Frequently confused shoulder conditions for USMLE

vignettes.q: “I know upper limb nerves are HY. What do I need to know for USMLE without all of the .”
vignettes.a: You need to know the injuries associated with the nerves, and then just basic motor/sensory issues. Upper limb nerve HY Points for USMLE

vignettes.q: 45M + construction worker + sensation to pinprick is reduced on the thumb and a portion of the forearm; physician suspects compression of C5/C6; Q asks, which movement is most likely impaired in this patient
vignettes.a: “abduction of upper extremity”; deltoid is innervated by axillary nerve from C5/C6.

vignettes.q: 32F + office worker + paresthesias of lateral three fingers; wrist pad when using computer and wrist splint have not worked; next best step?
vignettes.a: triamcinolone injection into carpal tunnel; NSAIDs are wrong answer.

vignettes.q: 49F + skiing accident + decreased sensation over lateral forearm + weakened flexion at elbow; Q asks nerve that’s impaired
vignettes.a: musculocutaneous.

vignettes.q: 35M + in car accident and wasn’t wearing seatbelt + x-ray of arm is shown below; Q wants to know the most likely deficit in this patient:
vignettes.a: inability to extend the wrist; answer can also be inability to supinate the forearm; x-ray shows midshaft fracture of humerus → radial nerve injury resulting in pronated arm with wrist drop.

vignettes.q: 29F + motorcycle accident + has x-ray of arm shown below; Q asks most likely deficit to be seen in this patient:
vignettes.a: impaired abduction of arm, or loss of sensation over deltoid; x-ray shows surgical neck of humerus fracture → axillary nerve injury.

vignettes.q: 45M + has arm slashed in street fight + now is unable to supinate and extend wrist; which letter on the following brachial plexus image corresponds to this patient’s deficit?
vignettes.a: radial nerve (choice C). A = musculocutaneous nerve; B = axillary nerve; D = median nerve; E = ulnar nerve. USMLE will ask you relatively easy presentation for a neurologic deficit but require you to identify where on the brachial

vignettes.q: 24M + in motorcycle accident + has loss of sensation over deltoid + diminished ability to abduct shoulder; question asked which nerve on the following diagram is impaired.
vignettes.a: E (axillary nerve); A = musculocutaneous nerve; B = median nerve; C = ulnar nerve; D = radial nerve; F = long thoracic nerve; the black lines on the left side of the above image, from top to bottom, are the C5-T1 nerve roots.

vignettes.q: “Does USMLE care about upper limb reflexes?”
vignettes.a: They do show up on NBME, yes. You could be aware that if biceps reflex is weakened, they want C5 as the nerve root that’s impaired. And if triceps reflex is weakened, it’s C6-7 that’s impaired.

vignettes.q: 14-month-old boy + arm has been adducted, pronated, and wrist flexed since birth but has gradually been improving with physiotherapy; Q asks location of injury
vignettes.a: upper brachial plexus (C5- C6); Erb-Duchenne palsy presents with “waiter’s tip” deformity; most commonly seen in neonates during traumatic birth, but can also occur in older patients due to trauma.

vignettes.q: 22M + grabbed onto tree branch while falling from tree + presents with claw-like appearance of hand; Q wants to know location of injury
vignettes.a: lower brachial plexus (C8-T1); you just need to know Klumpke palsy = lower brachial plexus injury and presents with claw-hand.

vignettes.q: 49F + underwent mastectomy one year ago + physical examination demonstrates winged scapula; Q asks nerve injury; answer = long thoracic nerve
vignettes.a: innervates serratus anterior; nerve can be damaged during mastectomy.

vignettes.q: 21F + paresthesias of the hand and forearm + sometimes exacerbated by wearing backpack for long periods; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: thoracic outlet syndrome; common cause is “first cervical rib.” USMLE just wants you to know there’s some strange anatomic variant of the cervical ribs where a “first cervical rib” can cause miscellaneous paresthesias and/or muscl

vignettes.q: 31F + was painting fence + pain in anterior/lateral shoulder that is worse when lying on side in bed + no weakness in shoulder; Q asks diagnosis
vignettes.a: subacromial bursitis (impingement syndrome).

vignettes.q: 31F + was painting fence + pain in anterior/lateral shoulder that is worse when lying on side in bed + weakness on external rotation of shoulder; Q asks diagnosis
vignettes.a: rotator cuff tendonitis.

vignettes.q: 26M + pain in anterior shoulder + palpation of anterior shoulder elicits pain; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: biceps tendonitis.

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about bones of hand / wrist?” → USMLE likes carpal bones.
vignettes.a: The two rows of carpal bones (i.e., proximal and distal), from lateral to medial, are: “She Looks Too Pretty. Try To Catch Her.” § First row: Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform; § Second row: Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Ha

vignettes.q: 16M + skateboarding + falls on outstretched hand + no pain over anatomic snuffbox + pain in central palm; Q asks which bone is fractured (choose a letter):
vignettes.a: D (lunate); this is on Step 1 NBME; as described, they’ll give pain in central palm + no pain over anatomic snuffbox.

vignettes.q: 17M + skateboarding + falls on outstretched hand + pain over anatomic snuffbox + x-ray shows no abnormalities; Q asks which bone is fractured:
vignettes.a: C (scaphoid); next best step is thumb-spica cast; x-ray is often negative initially; patient needs thumb-spica cast to prevent avascular necrosis, followed by re-x-ray in 2-3 weeks.

vignettes.q: 17F + injured index finger at softball game + can’t flex distal interphalangeal joint of right index finger; Q wants to know which tendon is most likely damaged → answer = flexor digitorum profundus; USMLE want
vignettes.a: “Wait, are you saying we need to know all about hand/forearm muscles and tendons, etc. then?” → No. USMLE really doesn’t tests hyper-nitpicky details, but I’ve seen this one asked on an offline Step 1 NBME.

vignettes.q: 24M + hunting accident in which he sustains gunshot wound and severs flexor digitorum profundus tendon; Q asks which forearm tendon can be used as a graft to repair the damaged tendon
vignettes.a: palmaris longus; classically used as graft tendon; not present in about 1/7 people in the population.

vignettes.q: 59M + alcoholic + smoker + worked in construction + image of hand shown below; Q wants to know biggest risk factor in this patient:
vignettes.a: alcoholism; diagnosis is Dupuytren contracture, which is abnormal proliferation of palmar connective tissue and fascia; risk factors are Norwegian descent, alcoholism, diabetes, and epilepsy. Constellation of risk factors makes no

vignettes.q: 33F + breastfeeding + severe pain in lateral wrist; pain is worsened with maneuver shown below; Q asks for the next step in management
vignettes.a: steroid injection; diagnosis is deQuervain tenosynovitis; tenosynovitis means inflammation of tendon sheaths; deQuervain is classic in breastfeeding women and is worsened with Finkelstein test (shown above) → 1) thumb is placed in

vignettes.q: 35F + painless 2-cm bump on dorsal aspect of hand/wrist + image shown below; Q wants diagnosis:
vignettes.a: ganglion cyst, which is gelatinous collection of joint fluid; Tx is observation. Needle drainage is only done if causing functional/cosmetic issues for the patient. Recurrence common; can occur on ankles and flexor areas as well,

vignettes.q: 16F + history of easy bruising + hyperextensible skin + image shown below; Q wants to know mechanism:
vignettes.a: “defect in synthesis of fibrillar collagen”; diagnosis is Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (usually caused by collagen III defect); wrong answer = “abnormal synthesis of extracellular glycoprotein” (refers to fibrillin, which is a glycoprot

vignettes.q: 54F + smoker past 40 years + bilateral hand pain with clubbing; Q wants next best step in diagnosis
vignettes.a: chest x-ray; Dx is hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (osteoarthropathia hypertrophicans); presents as arthritis + clubbing as a result of lung cancer.

vignettes.q: “Do I need to know hip dislocation stuff? I’ve seen an occasional question like that but don’t really get it?”
vignettes.a: Not super-high-yield, but you just need to know that posterior hip dislocation causes a shortened and internally rotated leg; anterior hip dislocation causes a shortened and externally rotated leg.

vignettes.q: “What are some HY things I need to know about MSK spinal stuff?”
vignettes.a: I talk about neuro-related stuff a lot more in my HY Neuroanatomy PDF, but below is a table of some HY MSK spinal stuff. HY MSK spinal conditions for USMLE

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know for cauda equina syndrome versus conus medullaris syndrome?”
vignettes.a: The spinal cord ends at L1-L2. The terminal cone of the spinal cord is the conus medullaris. The nerve fibers that branch from the spinal cord and run inferior to it are the cauda equina. Resources make these conditions way more c

vignettes.q: 65M + painful neck + no neurologic findings + elective MRI shows degenerative changes of cervical spine; Q asks most likely diagnosis
vignettes.a: cervical spondylosis; this is merely osteoarthritic degenerative changes to the cervical vertebrae; it is idiopathic, but often has familial association.

vignettes.q: 63M + pain in buttocks and thighs when walking + no cardiovascular disease + peripheral pulses normal; Q wants to know diagnosis
vignettes.a: lumbar spinal stenosis; this presentation is “neurogenic claudication,” where the vignette sounds like intermittent claudication due to aortoiliac atherosclerosis, but the patient will have no cardiovascular disease history and th

vignettes.q: 67M + lower back pain worse when standing or walking for 30 minutes + relieved when leaning forward; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: lumbar spinal stenosis; classically pain in lower back that is worse when standing or walking for extended periods of time; it is worse when leaning back + better when leaning forward.

vignettes.q: 79F + difficulty fastening buttons + weakness of hand muscles + numbness in 5th finger; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: “C7-T1 foraminal stenosis” (cervical spinal stenosis).

vignettes.q: 61F + vignette is big rambling paragraph of nonsense + they tell you there’s a “step-off” of one vertebra relative to another on palpation; Q wants to know diagnosis
vignettes.a: spondylolisthesis.

vignettes.q: 48F + gardening + sudden-onset severe pain down right leg + straight-leg test elicits radiating pain; Q asks what is most likely to confirm diagnosis
vignettes.a: MRI.

vignettes.q: 48F + gardening + sudden-onset severe pain down right leg + straight-leg test elicits radiating pain; Q asks most appropriate treatment
vignettes.a: “analgesics + exercise as tolerated”; analgesics = NSAIDs; bed-rest is wrong answer on USMLE for both lumbosacral strain and disc herniations.

vignettes.q: 50M + high BMI + 24-hour history of pain starting in lower back and shooting down left leg; Q wants treatment
vignettes.a: NSAIDs; Dx is sciatica; 90% of the time due to disc herniation.

vignettes.q: 55F + pain + paresthesias in lateral thigh + no history of trauma; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: meralgia paresthetica.

vignettes.q: 74M + lifted heavy suitcases around the house + sudden-onset pain and tingling in lower back + suprapubic mass + has not urinated for past 24 hours + perianal anesthesia; Q asks diagnosis
vignettes.a: conus medullaris syndrome; findings tend to be sudden-onset (cone is “sharp”/sudden); perianal anesthesia is characteristic; both conus medullaris and cauda equina syndromes can present with urinary retention and pain in the lower

vignettes.q: “Do I need to know dermatomes for USMLE?”
vignettes.a: USMLE doesn’t crazy-obsess, but you need to have an idea of the basics → C6 is thumb; C7 is middle finger; C8 is pinky; nipples are T4; umbilicus is T10; groin and lower back are L1; anteromedial leg is L4; sole of foot is S1.

vignettes.q: 57F + burning/itching pain along lower back close to the hip on the left; Q asks which dermatome this represents (answers are T10, L1, S1)
vignettes.a: L1; diagnosis is shingles (herpes zoster; VZV).

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about lower limb reflexes / radiculopathies?
vignettes.a: ” Lower limb reflexes / radiculopathies

vignettes.q: 41F + pain radiating down distal anterior thigh, knee, medial leg, and medial foot; compression of nerve root in which intervertebral foramina is most likely the cause of her symptoms?
41F + random leg sensory issues + knee jerk is impaired; Q asks nerve root
41F + random leg sensory issues + ankle jerk is impaired; Q asks nerve root
41F + big paragraph of nonsense + loss of sensation of sole of foot; Q asks nerve root
65F + gradual-onset inability to stand on the tippytoes + diminished sensation on sole of the foot + MRI is shown below; Q wants most likely diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Disc herniation of L5-S1; USMLE doesn’t expect you to be a radiology expert; the diagnosis is inferable based on the vignette alone; MRI shows herniation of nucleus pulposus of L5-S1 disc with impingement on the spinal cord.

vignettes.q: “Do I need to know ankle sprain stuff for USMLE?” → For both USMLE Step 1 Family Medicine, yes.
vignettes.a: Anterior talofibular ligament is on the lateral side of the ankle and will be injured if the foot inverts (rolls inward). This is the most commonly injured ankle ligament. The deltoid ligament is stronger and on the medial side of

vignettes.q: 23M + playing basketball + lands on right ankle where it forcibly everts; x-ray is shown below; left side of x-ray shows prior to ligamental repair; right side is after repair; Q asks which ligament is injured:
vignettes.a: deltoid ligament; notice the large joint space on the medial aspect of the ankle in the left x-ray.

vignettes.q: 26F + went running and rolled her ankle + pain in lateral ankle + tenderness posterior to malleolus + can bear weight; Q wants next best step
vignettes.a: x-ray of ankle; patient fulfills Ottawa criteria for x-ray → she has pain in malleolar region + tenderness posterior to the malleolus; although she can bear weight, the former two findings satisfy the Ottawa criteria.

vignettes.q: “Does USMLE care about knowing all of the muscles and their insertions/origins, etc.?” → USMLE does have random Qs where they show MRI cross-sections of the thigh:
vignettes.a: 1 = rectus femoris; 2 = vastus lateralis; 3 = vastus intermedius; 4 = vastus medialis; 5 = sartorius; 6 = biceps femoris short head; 7 = biceps femoris long head; 8 = semimembranosus; 9 = semitendinosis; 10 = adductor magnus; 11 =

vignettes.q: 34M + plays soccer + pain in the leg + MRI cross-section shows muscle that’s injured; Q asks which muscle it is:
vignettes.a: rectus femoris.

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about the arthritis conditions for USMLE?
vignettes.a: ” HY Arthritides / joint pathologies for USMLE

vignettes.q: 49F + left knee pain + BMI 40 + Q asks what would most likely have prevented this patient’s condition
vignettes.a: weight loss; diagnosis is osteoarthritis (OA). As easy as it gets, but this Q is rampant on USMLE.

vignettes.q: 32F + 6’2” + right knee pain + BMI 30; Q asks, in addition to weight loss, what is the most appropriate treatment for this patient
vignettes.a: acetaminophen; diagnosis is OA; patient here is young, but big and tall; NSAID as first answer is wrong. As I mentioned above, OA is non-inflammatory, so NSAIDs don’t help more than acetaminophen + they kill the kidney.

vignettes.q: 29F + history of intermittent wrist and knee pain + presents today with fever 101 F and a hot, red, painful knee; Q wants next best step in diagnosis?
vignettes.a: arthrocentesis; diagnosis is septic arthritis in patient with underlying RA.

vignettes.q: 59M + pain in his hands + x-ray is shown below; Q asks the mechanism for this patient’s condition:
vignettes.a: “degenerative joint disease”; diagnosis is OA; image is showing Heberden nodes. If you look at x-ray, the DIPs “look a little swollen”; if you get a hand x-ray like this on USMLE and have no idea what you’re looking at, just ask y

vignettes.q: 34M + walks in bent over at the waist with chest pain + painful wrists and knee + hemoglobin of 10 g/dL; Q asks how to treat the patient’s hematologic findings
vignettes.a: “no specific therapy indicated”; patient has RA; autoimmune diseases can present with serous pericarditis (patient bends / leans forward to relieve chest pain) and anemia of chronic disease; even though we treat the underlying con

vignettes.q: 51M + advanced rheumatoid arthritis + paresthesias of upper limbs; Q asks next step in diagnosis
vignettes.a: MRI of cervical spine; Q has nothing to do with surgery, but upper limb neurologic findings in RA patient suggest atlantoaxial subluxation.

vignettes.q: 42F + sore wrists and knee + diffuse pruritis + high serum cholesterol, direct bilirubin, and ALP; Q asks for treatment of jaundice
vignettes.a: ursodeoxycholic acid (ursodiol); patient has rheumatoid arthritis and primary biliary cirrhosis; remember that “autoimmune diseases go together”; USMLE also wants you to know MOA of ursodiol is “decreased secretion of cholesterol

vignettes.q: 22M + low back pain worse in the morning and gets better throughout the day + occasional hand pain; Q wants to know next step in diagnosis
vignettes.a: x-ray of sacroiliac joints; diagnosis is ankylosing spondylitis and psoriatic arthritis; both are linked via HLA-B27 (PAIR → Psoriasis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD, Reactive arthritis).

vignettes.q: 29M + back pain worse in morning and gets better throughout the day + x-ray of spine shown below; Q wants to know next step in management?
vignettes.a: slit-lamp examination; diagnosis is ankylosing spondylitis with x-ray showing bamboo spine; USMLE wants you to know annual slit-lamp examination for anterior uveitis is part of workup.

vignettes.q: 28M + silvery, scaly plaque on elbow + scraping of the plaque causes bleeding; Q asks for the most appropriate treatment
vignettes.a: topical calcipotriene (vitamin D derivative); Tx of psoriasis is topicals first → topical calcipotriene, or topical steroids (triamcinolone or hydrocortisone), or coal tar, usually in that order.

vignettes.q: 44M + long history of plaque psoriasis that responds well to topicals + has increasing hand pain over past year + x-ray shown below; Q wants to know the most appropriate treatment:
vignettes.a: methotrexate; x-ray shows pencil-in-cup deformity of DIP of 2nd digit; methotrexate is first-line oral agent for systemic psoriasis (psoriatic arthritis), or if patient has unremitting plaque psoriasis that fails topicals.

vignettes.q: 39M + long history of psoriasis that does not respond to topicals; Q asks for oral treatment + methotrexate is not listed
vignettes.a: acitretin (oral vitamin A derivative used for psoriasis).

vignettes.q: 9F + painful knee + has had a few episodes similar to this before + hemoglobin 10 g/dL + MCV 72; Q asks most likely hematologic diagnosis
vignettes.a: anemia of chronic disease due to JRA; you need to know that MCV can absolutely be low in AoCD; this is

vignettes.q: 6M + runny nose for 3 days + now has left hip pain + temperature is 100.5 F + hip is not erythematous or warm; patient can bear weight on the hip; Q asks for next step in management
vignettes.a: ibuprofen; diagnosis is toxic (transient) synovitis; this is viral infection that, for whatever magical reason, can cause inflammation of the hip that can be misdiagnosed as septic arthritis; recognize that this is a common condit

vignettes.q: 10M + painful left hip for 2 days + fever of 101 F + leukocytes elevated + cannot bear weight on the hip + question says nothing about warmth or redness of hip; Q asks next best step
vignettes.a: arthrocentesis; septic arthritis must be ruled out here; for these types of Qs, you have to use your intuition; remember that for toxic synovitis, they’ll usually say viral infection precedes the hip pain + no leukocytosis + patie

vignettes.q: 8F + intermittent knee pain and salmon-pink body rash + presents today with hot, red, painful knee with limited mobility; Q wants to know most likely diagnosis (JRA not listed)
vignettes.a: septic arthritis; as discussed earlier, JRA is a risk factor for septic arthritis, so although patient has JRA above, the acute diagnosis is SA; USMLE will often give this type of Q where they have “toxic synovitis” as a wrong ans

vignettes.q: 30F + arthritis of hands + low platelets + no other information; Q asks most likely diagnosis
vignettes.a: SLE; you need to know lupus can present with low platelets due to antibodies causing peripheral destruction; arthritis is most common presenting feature of lupus.

vignettes.q: 31F + arthritis of hands + low platelets + low WBCs + low hemoglobin; Q asks mechanism for this patient’s hematologic findings
vignettes.a: “increased peripheral destruction”; wrong answer = “defective bone marrow production”; in SLE, patients can have antibodies against their hematologic cell lines; isolated thrombocytopenia is most common, but antibodies resulting i

vignettes.q: 34M + sore hands and knee + malar rash + question asks what’s most likely to be deficient in this patient
vignettes.a: C1q; for whatever reason, complement protein C1q deficiency is a cause of lupus. Also remember that in acute flares, C3 decreases and dsDNA Abs increase.

vignettes.q: 36F + arthritis + thrombocytopenia + positive syphilis test; Q asks what’s most likely to be seen in this patient
vignettes.a: antibodies against phospholipid; patients with SLE who have anti-phospholipid syndrome can have false-positive VDRL syphilis screening.

vignettes.q: 45M + sore knee + drinks alcohol + takes daily aspirin for ischemic heart disease; Q wants to know treatment for this patient’s condition
vignettes.a: indomethacin; steroids are wrong answer; diagnosis is acute gout; student says, “But why do we give NSAID as Tx if patient is taking daily aspirin, which is an NSAID?” → it’s what the NBME exam wants; daily low-dose aspirin is act

vignettes.q: 45M + sore knee + joint aspirate shows needle-shaped crystals + patient has history of NSAID allergy; Q asks most appropriate treatment (steroids not listed)
vignettes.a: colchicine; used for acute gout in patients who can’t take NSAIDs (e.g., peptic ulcers or allergy).

vignettes.q: 45M + presents with swollen and painful big toe; Q asks which of the following will decrease recurrence of this patient’s condition
vignettes.a: allopurinol; xanthine oxidase inhibitors (i.e., allopurinol or febuxostat) are first-line for chronic gout to decrease recurrence.

vignettes.q: 45M + being treated in hospital with IV nafcillin for MSSA endocarditis + is administered probenecid; Q asks reason for this management
vignettes.a: decreases renal clearance of beta-lactam; probenecid inhibits organic anion transporter (OAT), which both prevents reabsorption of uric acid and secretion of beta-lactams; uricosurics not used first-line for chronic gout because t

vignettes.q: 39M + left knee pain + hyperpigmentation of forearms + increased serum glucose; Q asks what is most likely to be seen on joint aspirate
vignettes.a: calcium pyrophosphate; diagnosis is pseudogout; biggest risk factors are hereditary hemochromatosis and primary hyperparathyroidism; patient here has “bronze diabetes,” which is buzzy presentation for hemochromatosis; hyperpigment

vignettes.q: 50F + painful hands with soreness of DIPs + overweight + serum calcium 11 mg/dL (NR 8.4-10.2); Q asks most likely diagnosis
vignettes.a: pseudogout, not OA; pseudogout can present as an OA-like presentation in patients with primary hyperparathyroidism or hereditary hemochromatosis.

vignettes.q: 40M + painful knee + joint aspirate shows rhomboid positively birefringent crystals; Q asks most appropriate treatment
vignettes.a: indomethacin; treat acute pseudogout exactly the same as “regular” gout. However, for chronic pseudogout, treat the underlying condition.

vignettes.q: 40M + sore shoulder + ESR not elevated; Q asks what’s most likely to be seen on joint aspiration
vignettes.a: basic calcium phosphate → BCP crystals cause “Milwaukee shoulder,” which is a cold (non- inflammatory) shoulder effusion.

vignettes.q: 28M + painful red knee + fever 102 F + went hiking for 12 hours two days ago; Q asks for the most likely organism
vignettes.a: Staph aureus; USMLE wants you to know that otherwise young, healthy patients who’ve had recent microtrauma (e.g., hiking, soccer/kickboxing tournament) or overt trauma (i.e., car accident where knee hit the dashboard) can get sept

vignettes.q: 24M + med student + knocked up however many chicks the past year + presents with sore knee + joint aspiration shows no organisms; Q asks the most likely diagnosis
vignettes.a: Gonococcal arthritis; if Q is overt about sexual activity in younger patient, they want Gonococcus.

vignettes.q: 26F + history of rheumatoid arthritis + presents with hot, red, painful knee and fever of 102 F; Q asks most likely organism
vignettes.a: Staph aureus; if Q doesn’t emphasize unprotected sexual activity + patient has clear risk factor for SA, then S. aureus is more likely than Gonococcus.

vignettes.q: 14F + sickle cell + painful, red, hot knee; Q asks most likely organism
vignettes.a: Staph aureus; Salmonella, although a common cause of osteomyelitis in sickle cell, there is not increased risk of it causing septic arthritis.

vignettes.q: 27M + painful knee and wrist + cutaneous papules along the wrist; Q asks for the most appropriate treatment
vignettes.a: ceftriaxone + azithromycin; diagnosis is Gonococcal arthritis; HY to know it can present with cutaneous papules; must co-treat for chlamydia with azithromycin or doxycycline.

vignettes.q: 23M + sore hands and knees + urethral discharge + red eyes; Q asks most likely organism
vignettes.a: Chlamydia; wrong answer is Gonorrhea; reactive arthritis is classically Chlamydia; Gonococcus does not cause reactive arthritis.

vignettes.q: 17M + pain, redness, and swelling of shaft of left forearm + fever of 103 F + WBCs 14,000/µL; Q wants most likely organism
vignettes.a: Staph aureus; Dx is osteomyelitis; S. aureus is most common organism overall, especially when etiology is idiopathic.

vignettes.q: 8M + sickle cell disease + pain in foot for 3 weeks + fever 102 F + WBCs 14,000/µL; Q wants most likely organism
vignettes.a: Salmonella spp.; if Q gives you sickle cell with osteomyelitis, the organism they want is Salmonella. You still need to use your head though. If they say “gram-positive coccus” in patient with sickle cell, that would be Staph aure

vignettes.q: 47M + immigrant to USA from Albania + history of tuberculosis + pain over T9/T10 vertebrae; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: vertebral osteomyelitis (Pott disease).

vignettes.q: 28M + migrant worker + rigid abdomen + fever + holds right lower extremity in extension + PPD shows 16 mm induration; Q asks which muscle is most likely to be affected in this patient
vignettes.a: psoas major; you don’t have to worry about the anatomy here; just know that TB can cause psoas abscess.

vignettes.q: 56M + IV drug user + diabetes mellitus type II + left-sided back pain radiating to flank + fever 102 F + pyelonephritis not listed as answer; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: psoas abscess; just be aware of it as a DDx; most likely organism is Staph aureus; Tx = surgical drainage + IV antibiotics. Other random joint/MSK disorders

vignettes.q: 34M + left knee pain that is worse when sitting for long periods of time, or when going up or down stairs; Q asks for treatment
vignettes.a: “quadriceps strengthening exercises”; diagnosis is chrondromalacia patellae (aka patellofemoral pain syndrome).

vignettes.q: 50M + started playing recreational basketball two years ago + knee pain initially worse with activity but now is present even when not playing; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: patella tendonitis (“Jumper’s knee”).

vignettes.q: 16F + plays volleyball + pain in knee past 6 weeks worse when running or jumping + exam shows crepitus; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: “patellofemoral instability” (patellar tendonitis / “jumper’s knee” not listed as answer); shows up on NBME.

vignettes.q: 65M + Q gives big paragraph of unnecessary info + they tell you guy has lateral hip pain that is worse when palpated and while lying on his side in bed; Q just asks diagnosis
vignettes.a: trochanteric bursitis.

vignettes.q: 50M + started playing recreational basketball two years ago + knee pain worse with activity but now is present even when not playing; patient had fracture to proximal tibia 30 years ago that was treated with op
vignettes.a: post-traumatic arthritis, not patella tendonitis.

vignettes.q: 28M + playing football + injures knee + increased anterior displacement of tibia on examination; Q wants to know what is injured on the following MRI:
vignettes.a: anterior cruciate ligament (choice B). A = femur; C = PCL; D = tibia.

vignettes.q: 34F + painful, red, warm knee + joint aspiration shows no effusion; Q asks most likely diagnosis
vignettes.a: septic bursitis; vignette will sound like septic arthritis, but there will be no effusion.

vignettes.q: 15M + plays a lot of soccer + 5’11” + painful knee; Q wants mechanism of pathology
vignettes.a: inflammation of patellar ligament at tibial tuberosity; diagnosis is Osgood-Schlatter.

vignettes.q: 22M + plays basketball + right heel pain for 5-10 minutes after getting out of bed in the morning; Q asks mechanism of pathology
vignettes.a: inflammation of planta fascia.

vignettes.q: 16F + in car accident + hits her left knee on the dashboard + physical exam shows excessive posterior displacement of the tibia; Q asks for diagnosis
vignettes.a: PCL injury (dashboard injury).

vignettes.q: 19M + hurt his knee wakeboarding + physical exam shows excessive motion of lateral aspect of knee when pressure applied to medial knee; Q asks diagnosis
vignettes.a: lateral collateral ligament injury; test described is the varus test.

vignettes.q: 24M + hurt his knee wakeboarding + medial knee pain + vignette mentions “catching” or “locking” of the knee; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: medial meniscal tear.

vignettes.q: 65M + BMI 30 + pain on the inner side of the left knee a few centimeters below the kneecap; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: pes anserine bursitis; the answer on USMLE if they give inferomedial knee pain.

vignettes.q: Neonate born at term + perfectly healthy + feet bent inward; Q wants to know treatment
vignettes.a: serial casting; observation is wrong answer; diagnosis is talipes equinovarus (clubbed feet).

vignettes.q: Neonate born at term + clubbed feet + multiple joint contractures; Q asks for diagnosis
vignettes.a: arthrogryposis.

vignettes.q: 44F + wears high-heels + has severe pain under foot along the 2nd and 3rd metatarsals; Q asks for treatment
vignettes.a: orthotics first, then steroid injection second; Dx is Morton neuroma.

vignettes.q: 4-month-old boy + clicking and clunking on physical examination; Q wants next best step in imaging
vignettes.a: ultrasound; diagnosis is primary hip dysplasia; do ultrasound under 6 months; x-ray over 6 months.

vignettes.q: 4-month-old girl + clicking and clunking on physical exam; Q asks for mechanism of patient’s condition
vignettes.a: “poorly developed acetabulum.”

vignettes.q: 5M + right hip pain + walks with limp + x-ray shows contracted capital femoral epiphysis; Q asks straight-up for diagnosis
vignettes.a: Legg-Calve-Perthes, not SCFE. Once again, it’s on the NBME exam, so if you think it’s weird or disagree, don’t take it up with me;

vignettes.q: 8M + sickle cell disease + painful hip pain and limp; Q asks diagnosis
vignettes.a: “avascular necrosis”; Legg-Calve-Perthes is wrong answer; remember that LCP is idiopathic avascular necrosis; if the cause is known (i.e., sickle cell, Gaucher, corticosteroids), LCP is wrong.

vignettes.q: 8M + hepatomegaly + hip pain + macrophages with wrinkled tissue appearance; Q asks mechanism for disorder
vignettes.a: deficiency of glucocerebrosidase; diagnosis is Gaucher disease; for Gaucher, you just need to know it’s the answer if you get a glycogen storage disease + a bone problem.

vignettes.q: 9F + painful left hip + x-ray shows no abnormalities + diagnosis is made using bone-scan; Q just asks the most likely diagnosis
vignettes.a: Legg-Calve-Perthes; x-ray can be negative initially; in this case, the next best step is bone-scan or MRI.

vignettes.q: 7F + hip pain + x-ray is shown below; Q asks for diagnosis:
vignettes.a: Legg-Calve-Perthes; student says, “No idea what I’m looking at.” Relax. If we try to imagine, the right femoral head (left side of image) looks “contracted” or “flattened.” Once again, this is HY and buzzy for avascular necrosis.

vignettes.q: 59F + advanced rheumatoid arthritis managed with multiple medications + MRI of pelvis is shown; Q wants diagnosis:
vignettes.a: avascular necrosis; etiology is chronic corticosteroids in the setting of advanced autoimmune disease; the right femoral head (left side of image) appears hypointense (more black). The necrotic / lack of bone in the black superior

vignettes.q: 13M + left hip pain + walks with antalgic gait + 95%tile for weight; Q asks mechanism for patient’s condition
vignettes.a: “displacement of the epiphysis of the femoral head”; diagnosis is SCFE; classic vignette is overweight pre-adolescent boy with a painful limp; “antalgic gait” just means walking with a painful limp; it is non-specific and I’ve see

vignettes.q: 12M + left hip pain + BMI 20 + 6’0” + x-ray is shown below; Q asks diagnosis:
vignettes.a: slipped capital femoral epiphysis; x-ray shows the “ice cream slipping off its cone”; student is confused because the Q says BMI is normal; as I said earlier, although the kid being overweight is HY and buzzy, plenty of NBME Qs ei

vignettes.q: “Do I need to know the mechanism of PTH on bone?” → Yes, it’s HY.
vignettes.a: PTH binds to osteoblasts, not -clasts. This sounds paradoxical, since osteoblasts build bone and PTH has the role of causing bone resorption in order to increase serum calcium. After PTH binds to the osteoblast, it will express RA

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about OPG in relation to RANK-L. Can you quickly clarify.”
vignettes.a: Osteoprotegerin (OPG) is protective of bone loss. It is a RANK receptor decoy (i.e., it looks like RANK receptor), and therefore acts as an endogenous competitive inhibitor of RANK-L. In other words, if more OPG is present, then R

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and bone?”
vignettes.a: USMLE wants you to know that increased osteoblast activity causes high ALP. This is why ALP levels go up when PTH is high, or why ALP is elevated in Paget disease of bone. There is Q on one of the Step 1 NBMEs where they give weir

vignettes.q: 62F + shows graph with lines of bone density for two different women without family history of osteoporosis; Q asks what is the reason why one woman has higher bone density than the other
vignettes.a: ethnicity; black race is protective against osteoporosis.

vignettes.q: 64F + image of vertebral column shown below; Q asks what is responsible for this patient’s condition:
vignettes.a: Interleukin-1; IL-1 is aka osteoclast-activating factor; post-menopausal state → ↓ estrogen → ↓ suppression of cytokines (namely IL-1) on bone → ↓ OPG/RANK-L ratio → bone resorption → osteoporosis.

vignettes.q: 22F + runs a lot + BMI 20 + no other issues; Q asks what patient is at increased risk for
vignettes.a: osteoporosis; makes no sense, as BMI isn’t low, but

vignettes.q: 34M + bitemporal hemianopsia + 20-lb weight gain past 6 months + compression fracture of a vertebra; Q asks what the tumor is secreting
vignettes.a: ACTH; patient has Cushing disease; cortisol can cause osteoporosis; compression fractures = osteoporosis on USMLE; student asks, “But why can’t TSH be the answer? Can’t hyperthyroidism cause osteoporosis?” → Two points: 1) Patient

vignettes.q: 72F + fractures femur + no mention of osteoporosis; Q asks, during the rehabilitation process, what is the most important predictor of success in this patient
vignettes.a: “activity level before the fracture” → protective of bone density / osteoporosis.

vignettes.q: 4M + came to USA from Ireland with parents one year ago + has bowed tibias; Q asks serum calcium, phosphate, and PTH
vignettes.a: low calcium, low phosphate, high PTH; diagnosis is rickets with genu varum.

vignettes.q: 70F + type II diabetes + renal failure + left hip pain; Q asks most likely MSK diagnosis
vignettes.a: osteomalacia; renal failure causes low vitamin D, resulting in osteomalacia; renal osteodystrophy = osteomalacia cause by renal failure.

vignettes.q: 70F + renal failure + left hip pain + x-ray shows pseudofracture; Q asks what’s most likely responsible for this patient’s condition
vignettes.a: “decreased intestinal absorption of calcium”; we have osteomalacia due to low 1,25-D3, causing reduced intestinal absorption. “Pseudofracture” is buzzy for osteomalacia.

vignettes.q: 70F + left hip pain + x-ray shows pseudofracture; Q asks arrows for calcium, phosphate, PTH, and calcitriol
vignettes.a: low calcium, high phosphate, high PTH, low calcitriol (aka 1,25-D3); even though vitamin D is low, phosphate is always high in renal failure; so even though, yes, vitamin D deficiency causes low calcium and low phosphate in the se

vignettes.q: 3M + recurrent fractures + increased bone density; Q asks which type of molecular signaling is up
vignettes.a: GM-CSF; diagnosis is osteopetrosis, which is caused by either deficiency of carbonic anhydrase II, or a problem with GM-CSF signaling; osteoclasts are defective.

vignettes.q: 6M + recurrent fractures + engages well with the parents + mom has history of recurrent miscarriages; Q asks mechanism for patient’s condition
vignettes.a: “defect of procollagen synthesis”; diagnosis is osteogenesis imperfecta (collagen I gene mutation); USMLE doesn’t actually care about the exact collagen step that is defective; the answer will be the only one that refers to collag

vignettes.q: 16M + falls off bike while BMX dirt jumping + broken radius + cast applied + now has acutely increased severe pain in arm; Q asks for most likely diagnosis
vignettes.a: compartment syndrome; although circumferential burns are fixated on as hyper-HY for compartment syndrome on USMLE, it’s to my observation NBME cares less about this and more about acute casting as the highest yield cause. If a lim

vignettes.q: 20M + housefire + 3rd -degree burns all over legs + severe pain in left leg; Q asks for next best step
vignettes.a: “measure compartment pressures”; treatment is then “fasciotomy.”

vignettes.q: 34F + central chest pain + worsens when reaches behind her back and over her head + pain on palpation; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: costochondritis; any chest pain on USMLE that worsens with change in positioning (except pericarditis, which worsens when leaning back), think MSK etiology – i.e., costochondritis.

vignettes.q: 34F + pain in chest + worse when reaching behind her back and over her head + there is no pain on palpation; Q wants treatment
vignettes.a: NSAIDs; diagnosis is costochondritis. I’ve seen NBME Qs where they mention pain that changes with position and/or with palpation – i.e., it need not be both.

vignettes.q: 25M + recently recovered from viral infection + severe right lateral chest pain + no friction rub + increased serum creatine kinase; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: pleurodynia. Despite the name, this has nothing to do with the lungs/pleura. It is intercostal muscle spasm following viral infection (i.e., viral myalgia) that presents as lateral chest pain; CK can be elevated due to increased m

vignettes.q: 47M + alcoholic + found on bench in park + urine dipstick shows 2+ blood + urine RBCs negative; Q wants most likely diagnosis
vignettes.a: rhabdomyolysis; alcoholism is huge risk factor; urinalysis classically shows false-positive blood on dipstick, where the dipstick can’t differentiate between free myoglobin and RBC hemoglobin, but light microscopy will be negative

vignettes.q: 47M + alcoholic + found on bench in park + serum potassium elevated + urine shows brown pigmented casts; Q wants most likely diagnosis
vignettes.a: rhabdomyolysis; urine can be either false- positive blood on dipstick or characteristic of acute tubular necrosis (i.e., brown pigmented casts, or dirty/muddy brown granular casts).

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about bone tumors?
vignettes.a: ” HY bone tumor points for USMLE

vignettes.q: 1-year-old boy + leukocoria (white pupil) + Q wants to know what he is most likely to develop later in life
vignettes.a: osteosarcoma; diagnosis is congenital retinoblastoma; Rb mutations cause both retinoblastoma as well as osteosarcoma.

vignettes.q: 20M + pain in left distal femur + x-ray shows elevation of periosteum and spiculated new bone formation; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: osteosarcoma; elevation of periosteum = Codman triangle; spiculated new bone formation = sunburst appearance.

vignettes.q: 61M + pain in left hip + histo image below; Q just asks for diagnosis straight-up:
vignettes.a: chondrosarcoma; easy if you know this HY image.

vignettes.q: 54M + pain in right hip + x-ray shows tumor + biopsy shows glistening / shiny lesion; Q wants to know what is most likely to be characteristic of this lesion
vignettes.a: “chondrocytes embedded in lacunae”; diagnosis is chondrosacoma.

vignettes.q: 25F + pain in proximal tibia + x-ray shows a lesion + pain is relieved with ibuprofen; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: osteoid osteoma; this is the answer on USMLE if they give a bone tumor where the pain is relieved with NSAIDs.

vignettes.q: 18F + 1-cm hard mass growing from skull + father died of colon cancer at age 32; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: Gardner syndrome presenting with osteoma. Gardner syndrome = familial adenomatous polyposis + either osteoma or lipoma.

vignettes.q: 12M + fever 101 F + pain in left forearm + bone scan shows uptake in the diaphysis; Q asks diagnosis
vignettes.a: Ewing sarcoma; can present similarly to osteomyelitis, except bone scan is more likely to show uptake in the diaphysis; in osteomyelitis, the uptake is in the metaphysis.

vignettes.q: 12M + fever 101 F + pain in left forearm + biopsy with histo image of lesion shown below; Q asks for the genetics:
vignettes.a: t(11;22) translocation; diagnosis is Ewing sarcoma; image shows the small blue cells of neuroendocrine origin.

vignettes.q: 17M + pain in upper left humerus + x-ray shown below; Q wants diagnosis:
vignettes.a: unicameral bone cyst. This is an underrated diagnosis for USMLE but shows up on the real deal.

vignettes.q: 37M + pain in right elbow + x-ray is shown below; Q asks diagnosis (answers are all bone tumors):
vignettes.a: giant cell tumor of bone (osteoclastoma); x-ray shows soap-bubble appearance. In contrast to unicameral bone cyst, which occurs usually from birth to age 20, osteoclastoma usually occurs age 20-40.

vignettes.q: 55M + diffuse bone pain + high serum calcium; bone scan is shown below; Q wants diagnosis:
vignettes.a: metastatic malignancy (most likely prostate cancer if no past medical history); wrong answer is primary hyperparathyroidism; metastases are important cause of high Ca2+ .

vignettes.q: 32M + large, yellow, soft infiltrating mass in gluteus maximus + biopsy shows irregular vacuolated cells + clear cells with many mitoses; Q asks diagnosis
vignettes.a: liposarcoma; lipoma is wrong answer (presumably would sound less sinister / not invasive, clearly); lipoma = benign tumor of fat (Gardner syndrome); liposarcoma = malignant tumor of fat; rhabdomyoma = benign tumor of striated (ske

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about fracture types for USMLE?”
vignettes.a: I’ll give summary here: HY bone fracture points for USMLE

vignettes.q: 24M + car accident + linear skull fracture; Q asks what type of bleed is most likely in this patient?
vignettes.a: epidural hematoma.

vignettes.q: 20M + car accident + high blood pressure + bradycardia + bruising around the eyes and behind the ears + low GCS score; Q asks for most likely reason for the patient’s high blood pressure
vignettes.a: increased intracranial pressure; Cushing reflex = triad of HTN + bradycardia + bradypnea due to increased ICP; patient here has base of skull fracture (Battle sign + raccoon eyes); Q need not mention all four findings (i.e., rhino

vignettes.q: 37M + cyclist + mild weakness of finger abduction/adduction + has positive Froment sign; Q asks which structure is most likely compressed
vignettes.a: “deep branch of ulnar nerve at the hook of hamate.”

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about myopathy / muscular dystrophies for USMLE?
