vignettes.a: ” HY myopathies / muscular dystrophies for USMLE

vignettes.q: 52F + 6-month history of pain and stiffness of shoulders + elevated ESR; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR); presents as pain and stiffness of proximal muscles, usually in patient over 50; Q will not mention anything about elevated CK or weakness on physical exam.

vignettes.q: 52F + 6-month history of pain and stiffness of shoulders + elevated ESR and CK; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: polymyositis, not PMR, because Q mentions CK elevation. Pain and stiffness are not unique to PMR. They can absolutely be seen in polymyositis. The notion that they are unique to PMR is complete nonsense for USMLE purposes.

vignettes.q: 52F + 6-month history of pain and stiffness of shoulders + elevated ESR + normal CK + physical exam shows 3/5 strength in shoulders; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: polymyositis; even though CK is normal, patient has weakness on physical exam.

vignettes.q: 64F + 6-month history of pain and stiffness of shoulders + elevated ESR + weakness on physical exam; Q wants next best step in diagnosis?
vignettes.a: “electromyography and nerve conduction studies”; diagnosis is polymyositis; Q will not force you to choose between anti-Jo1 antibodies and EMG/NCS, but the latter is correct on NBME forms; biopsy is confirmatory.

vignettes.q: 64F + 6-month history of pain and stiffness of shoulders + physical exam shows weakness + anti-Jo1 antibodies are positive; Q asks the most likely pathophysiology for this patient’s condition?
vignettes.a: “CD8 + T cells and macrophages surrounding muscle fibers.”

vignettes.q: 64F + bilateral temporal headache + slightly blurry vision on left + high ESR + bilateral hip pain; Q wants next best step
vignettes.a: “IV methylprednisolone”; temporal (giant cell) arteritis can show up bilaterally on NBME forms; do steroids first to prevent blindness, then do biopsy of temporal artery; the patient’s hip pain is polymyalgia rheumatica, which is

vignettes.q: 64F + right-sided temporal pain + high ESR + low-grade fever + pain in the jaw + low hemoglobin; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: giant cell arteritis; can present with jaw claudication; low hemoglobin is due to anemia of chronic disease.

vignettes.q: 64F + right-sided temporal and facial pain + worsens with eating + proximal muscles a little stiff; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: temporomandibular joint dysfunction, not temporal arteritis; if it worsens with eating, then they want TMJ dysfunction, not jaw claudication.

vignettes.q: 45F + 6-month history of muscle pain; physical exam shows 12 symmetric tender points; ESR not elevated; Q wants treatment
vignettes.a: “anti-depressant therapy”; diagnosis is fibromyalgia; this is a psych condition treated with SSRIs; as mentioned earlier, students get confused here because the patient is not depressed, but SSRIs are still anti-depressant medicat

vignettes.q: 61F + 20-pound weight loss past one month despite no change in diet + fatigue + anemia + proximal muscle weakness + increased serum CK + pulling sensation in groin + Q shows image below; Q wants to know diagnos
vignettes.a: ovarian adenocarcinoma; for whatever magical reason, dermatomyositis can be a paraneoplastic syndrome of ovarian cancer. Around 10-20% of women with dermatomyositis have ovarian cancer.

vignettes.q: 44F + 6-month history of low energy and fatigue + gradually lengthening periods + HR 60 + hepatic AST, total cholesterol, and serum creatine kinase are elevated; Q asks most likely diagnosis
vignettes.a: hypothyroidism (Hashimoto); elevated CK is due to hypothyroid myopathy, which may or may not present with proximal muscle weakness in the vignette; transaminases can be elevated in thyroid dysfunction; USMLE likes menstrual irregu

vignettes.q: 66M + started taking a statin and fibrate simultaneously + develops myopathy; Q wants mechanism
vignettes.a: “P-450-mediated interaction.”

vignettes.q: 3M + hypotonia + lactic acidosis + no mention of eye/ear problems + biopsy of muscle shows ragged red fibers; Q wants most likely inheritance
vignettes.a: mitochondrial.

vignettes.q: 3M + large calves + uses arms to walk up off the floor; Q wants organelle / cellular structure that is disrupted in patient’s condition
vignettes.a: cytoskeleton; a-/b-dystroglycan are encoded by the DMD (dystrophin) gene and are required for proper anchoring of the muscle cell cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix.

vignettes.q: 3M + large calves + uses arms to walk up off the floor + Q wants to know what will be seen on muscle biopsy
vignettes.a: “connective tissue stromal cells” or “fibroadipose tissue”; patient will have pseudohypertrophy, which is replacement of muscle cells with connective tissue.

vignettes.q: 3M + large calves + uses arms to walk up off the floor; Q wants molecular mechanism for patient’s condition
vignettes.a: frameshift mutation; this results in truncated, non-functional protein due to early formation of stop codon.

vignettes.q: 18M + increasing muscle weakness and muscular enlargement + maternal uncle died of cardiomyopathy in his 20s; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: Becker muscular dystrophy; less severe form of Duchenne; usually due to non-frameshift mutations in the DMD gene. Becker usually presents in adolescence or young adulthood; Duchenne will be a kid.

vignettes.q: 4M + short arms and legs; trunk and head are normal size; parents are normal; Q wants mechanism for patient’s condition
vignettes.a: gonadal (germline) mosaicism; diagnosis is achondroplasia; disease is constitutive activation of FGFR3 gene; results in failed cartilage conversion into bone; presents as shortened limbs but normal head size and postural height (t

vignettes.q: “How HY is hernia stuff for USMLE?”
vignettes.a: Unfortunately decently HY. But good news: I’ll tell you exactly what you need to know for them for USMLE without all of the absolute nonsense. HY MSK hernia points for USMLE

vignettes.q: 1-year-old boy + enlarged testis + scrotal mass that is reducible with pressure over deep inguinal ring; Q asks mechanism for patient’s condition
vignettes.a: patent processus vaginalis; diagnosis is indirect inguinal hernia; mechanism is same as formation of hydrocele; since the hernia passes through deep inguinal ring (which is lateral to inferior epigastric artery), pressure applied

vignettes.q: 12-year-old boy + testicular mass that enlarges with cough and reduces when lying down; pressure applied over deep inguinal ring hides hernia; Q wants to know whether the hernia is lateral vs medial to inferior
vignettes.a: lateral to inferior epigastric artery + superior to inguinal ligament; diagnosis is indirect inguinal hernia.

vignettes.q: 64M + bulging mass in groin + not painful; worsens with cough and improves when supine; Q wants location of hernia relative to inferior epigastric artery
vignettes.a: medial to inferior epigastric artery; diagnosis is direct inguinal hernia; usually occurs in older men.

vignettes.q: 40F + pain and palpable mass in groin inferior to inguinal ligament; Q wants to know which structure is lateral to the mass
vignettes.a: femoral vein; diagnosis is femoral hernia.

vignettes.q: 60M + Q shows CT scan of an abnormality with arrow pointing to it; asks for what the medial border of the hernia is (in other words, what is medial to the arrow)?
vignettes.a: lateral border of rectus abdominus; diagnosis is Spigelian hernia; hernia protrudes just lateral to the linea semilunaris. Students get hysterical and worried when they see CT scans like this. Recognize that the USMLE doesn’t care

vignettes.q: 55M + pelvic hernia + physical exam causes worsening of pain when ipsilateral leg is extended, medially rotated, and abducted; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: obturator hernia; the Howship- Romberg sign is used to diagnose. The USMLE can be vague with this question, where they just tell you “patient has hernia that’s worsened with this exam maneuver” and you have to know it’s obturator

vignettes.q: 8-month-old boy + large tongue + hypotonia + umbilical hernia; Q asks what would have most likely prevented this patient’s condition
vignettes.a: routine newborn screening; diagnosis is congenital hypothyroidism (cretinism); heel-prick test at birth tests for hypothyroidism, PKU, and galactose disorders, among others.

vignettes.q: Neonatal male + enlarged occiput + clenched fingers + rocker-bottom feet + protrusion of abdominal contents through umbilicus that are covered in thin membrane; Q wants diagnosis
vignettes.a: trisomy 18 (Edward syndrome); omphalocele is described; in contrast, gastroschisis protrudes to the right of the umbilicus and is not covered in a layer of peritoneal membrane.

vignettes.q: “Is there any chest wall MSK I should know?”
vignettes.a: For a thoracentesis (removing fluid from the pleural space when treating a pleural effusion) or needle decompression (for pneumothorax), the needle should be inserted just above the rib. This is in order to avoid injury to the neu

vignettes.q: “Is there any high-yield neck anatomy I should know?
vignettes.a: ” HY neck MSK masses for USMLE

vignettes.q: “Do I need to know nasal sinus/concha anatomy for USMLE?
vignettes.a: There are rare Qs that show up asking sinus anatomy, but now that Step 1 is P/F, I’d say studying this is largely venturing into left-field territory. There is a question on one of the offline Step 1 NBMEs, however, where they say

vignettes.q: “Are there any random HY points for pediatrics I should know?”
vignettes.a: USMLE likes bone age in some vignettes. If an x-ray is done of the hand, the approximate age of the child can be ascertained; if the child is short and “bone age equals chronologic age,” that is genuine short stature (e.g., famili

vignettes.q: “Anything I should know about random infections and muscle?”
vignettes.a: USMLE likes myalgias = influenza virus when patient has head cold. Vignette will be big paragraph + they mention muscle pain in there + answers are all different viruses; answer is simply influenza. Taenia solium (pork tapeworm; p

vignettes.q: “Anything I should know about random immuno and MSK?”
vignettes.a: Muscle pain at the site of injection of a drug or vaccine 3-7 days post-injection = Arthus reaction = type III hypersensitivity (immune complexes); was seen with Moderna Covid vaccine (“Moderna arm”). Polyarthritis 3-7 days follow

vignettes.q: “Anything random I should know about genetics and MSK?”
vignettes.a: USMLE wants you to know the Hox genes, or homeobox genes, are necessary for proper body/limb patterning (i.e., body parts developing at correct locations). They will say if Hox genes 9-12 are turned on, phalanges are produced; whe

vignettes.q: “Is there any HY Pharm I should know in relation to MSK?
vignettes.a: ” Highest yield “MSK pharm” for USMLE

vignettes.q: Identify the diagnosis & key pearl (MSK & Anatomy Vignette):
vignettes.a: 32F + history of multiple sclerosis with muscular spasticity; Q asks the mechanism of action of the drug used to treat her spasticity → answer = GABAB receptor agonist; drug is baclofen. 45M + started on aripiprazole for schizophr

vignettes.q: Waiter tip position in kid
vignettes.a: upper brachial plexus injury → C5/6 → Erb-Duchenne palsy

vignettes.q: Claw hand
vignettes.a: lower brachial plexus → C8/T1 → Klumpke palsy

vignettes.q: Pronated arm + wrist-drop
vignettes.a: radial nerve injury

vignettes.q: Midshaft fracture of humerus
vignettes.a: Radial nerve injury

vignettes.q: Supracondylar fracture of humerus
vignettes.a: median nerve injury

vignettes.q: Surgical neck of humerus fracture
vignettes.a: axillary nerve injury

vignettes.q: Medial epicondylar injury
vignettes.a: ulnar nerve injury

vignettes.q: Point tenderness over a vertebra in older woman
vignettes.a: osteoporosis (compression fracture)

vignettes.q: Point tenderness over a vertebra in younger patient on steroids
vignettes.a: osteoporosis (compression fracture)

vignettes.q: Point tenderness over a vertebra in patient with autoimmune disease
vignettes.a: recognize patient is on steroids → osteoporosis (compression fracture)

vignettes.q: Back pain worse in the morning and gets better throughout day in male 20s-40s
vignettes.a: ankylosing spondylitis

vignettes.q: Bamboo spine
vignettes.a: ankylosing spondylitis

vignettes.q: Bilateral paresthesias in the arms in rheumatoid arthritis patient
vignettes.a: atlantoaxial subluxation

vignettes.q: Bilateral paresthesias in the arms in rheumatoid arthritis patient
vignettes.a: MR of spine to Dx atlantoaxial subluxation

vignettes.q: Prior to surgery in rheumatoid arthritis patient
vignettes.a: cervical CT or flexion/extension x-rays of cervical spine to check for atlantoaxial subluxation

vignettes.q: Heart problem in neonate of mom with SLE
vignettes.a: congenital third-degree heartblock

vignettes.q: Infective causes of third-degree
vignettes.a: Lyme disease, congenital lupus, diphtheria

vignettes.q: Tx of anemia of chronic disease if renal failure not cause (IBD, RA, SLE, etc.)
vignettes.a: CANNOT give EPO; Tx underlying condition.

vignettes.q: Tx of acute gout
vignettes.a: indomethacin (NSAID) first on USMLE; then steroids, then colchicine

vignettes.q: Tx of acute gout if indomethacin + steroids not listed
vignettes.a: colchicine

vignettes.q: Tx of acute gout in pt with renal insufficiency or Hx of renal transplant
vignettes.a: steroids

vignettes.q: Tx of chronic gout (decrease recurrence)
vignettes.a: allopurinol or febuxostat (xanthine oxidase inhibitors)

vignettes.q: Crystal type in pseudogout
vignettes.a: calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease

vignettes.q: Same male + painful hands + x-ray shows DIP involvement. Joint pain Dx?
vignettes.a: pseudogout

vignettes.q: Tx of pseudogout
vignettes.a: same as gout acutely; Tx underlying condition for chronic

vignettes.q: Biggest risk factor for osteoarthritis
vignettes.a: obesity

vignettes.q: Tx of osteoarthritis
vignettes.a: weight loss; if normal BMI → acetaminophen before NSAIDs

vignettes.q: Patient with OA taking naproxen (NSAID) + peripheral edema
vignettes.a: increased renal retention of sodium

vignettes.q: Tx of rheumatoid arthritis
vignettes.a: Two-armed: symptom-relief + disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs)

vignettes.q: Symptom-relief for RA
vignettes.a: NSAID first, then steroids (these do symptoms only; do not slow disease progression)

vignettes.q: DMARDs for early RA
vignettes.a: always methotrexate first; if insufficient, add another DMARD (sulfasalazine or leflunomide); if insufficient add anti-TNF-alpha agent

vignettes.q: Sulfasalazine MOA
vignettes.a: metabolized into sulfapyridine + mesalamine in the gut by bacteria Mesalamine is 5-ASA absorbed as the Tx for RA; only NSAID considered to be DMARD

vignettes.q: Most specific Abs in RA
vignettes.a: anti-CCP (cyclic citrullinated peptide), not RF (rheumatoid factor)

vignettes.q: X-ray of hands in RA vs OA
vignettes.a: Only OA has DIPs involved; RA is PIPs + MCPs

vignettes.q: Symmetry in RA vs OA
vignettes.a: RA is symmetrical; OA is not

vignettes.q: Pt groups most likely to get SA
vignettes.a: prosthetic joints, RA/OA, recent intense exercise/joint trauma; peds (JRA)

vignettes.q: Pt with OA or RA has red, warm, tender knee
vignettes.a: do arthrocentesis (septic arthritis)

vignettes.q: Kid + recurrent knee redness, warmth, pain + fever
vignettes.a: Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (JRA; Still disease)

vignettes.q: Most common presentation finding in SLE
vignettes.a: arthritis (>90%)

vignettes.q: Woman 20s-40s + arthritis + thrombocytopenia
vignettes.a: SLE

vignettes.q: Woman 20s-40s + arthritis + mouth ulcer + circular skin lesions
vignettes.a: SLE

vignettes.q: Malar rash + low RBCs + low WBCs + low platelets; mechanism for low cell lines?
vignettes.a: increased peripheral destruction (antibodies against hematologic cells lines seen in SLE; isolated thrombocytopenia most common)

vignettes.q: Tx of SLE flare
vignettes.a: steroids

vignettes.q: Tx of lupus nephritis
vignettes.a: mycophenolate mofetil

vignettes.q: Tx of discoid lupus
vignettes.a: hydroxychloroquine

vignettes.q: Most specific Abs for SLE
vignettes.a: anti-Smith (RNP), not anti-dsDNA

vignettes.q: Which Abs go up in acute SLE flares
vignettes.a: anti-dsDNA (and C3 goes down)

vignettes.q: Drug-induced lupus Abs
vignettes.a: anti-histone

vignettes.q: Viral-induced aplastic anemia; mechanism?
vignettes.a: defective bone marrow production (contrast with SLE)

vignettes.q: IBD + eczematoid plaque on forehead + sore joints
vignettes.a: psoriatic arthritis (HLA-B27 → PAIR → Psoriasis, Ankylosing spondylitis, IBD, Reactive arthritis)

vignettes.q: IBD + back pain
vignettes.a: sacroiliitis (or ankylosing spondylitis)

vignettes.q: What kind of vignette is a patient classically on naproxen?
vignettes.a: osteoarthritis (OA).

vignettes.q: How do we treat OA?
vignettes.a: weight loss (biggest risk factor is obesity), then acetaminophen, then NSAIDs → sometimes USMLE will mention naproxen being taken by OA patient to illustrate this common scenario of poor self-management → acetaminophen recommended

vignettes.q: 65F + unilateral temporal headache + blurry vision; Dx?
vignettes.a: temporal arteritis

vignettes.q: What other condition is TA associated with?
vignettes.a: polymyalgia rheumatica (in fact, they’re considered to be on the same disease spectrum, rather than as two inherently distinct conditions)

vignettes.q: 65F + unilateral temporal headache + muscle pain/stiffness
vignettes.a: temporal arteritis + polymyalgia rheumatica

vignettes.q: Tx for PR if patient doesn’t also have temporal arteritis
vignettes.a: oral steroids are okay bc not an emergency.

vignettes.q: Polymyalgia rheumatica vs polymyositis
vignettes.a: PR presents with stiffness/pain generally without weakness; polymyositis can present with pain, but it also has proximal muscle weakness. Both conditions can present with elevations of ESR and CRP, so these aren’t reliable for Dx.

vignettes.q: Dx of polymyositis
vignettes.a: same as with dermatomyositis, do anti-Jo1 and -Mi2 antibodies, then do confirmatory muscle biopsy.

vignettes.q: Violaceous rash around the eyelids
vignettes.a: heliotrope rash → Dx = dermatomyositis (don’t confuse that with malar rash of SLE).

vignettes.q: Rash around back of neck + top of back + adult with proximal muscle weakness (difficulty standing from chair unassisted)
vignettes.a: shawl rash → dermatomyositis.

vignettes.q: Dx of dermatomyositis
vignettes.a: anti-Jo1 or -Mi2 antibodies first → muscle biopsy confirmatory.

vignettes.q: USMLE wants you to know that in dermatomyositis, there’s specifically an increased risk of what?
vignettes.a: malignancy (non-Hodgkin lymphoma) → that being said, autoimmune diseases in general increase the risk of NHL → so if you have, e.g., patient with SLE with irregular ring-enhancing lesion on head CT, answer = primary CNS lymphoma,

vignettes.q: Tx for flare of polymyositis/dermatomyositis
vignettes.a: oral corticosteroids.

vignettes.q: 32F + arthritis + mouth ulcer + low platelets; Dx?
vignettes.a: SLE

vignettes.q: First Tx for carpal tunnel syndrome in patient who can’t stop offending activity (e.g., office worker)
vignettes.a: wrist splint first; then triamcinolone (steroid) injection into the carpal tunnel; do not select anything surgical as it’s always wrong on the USMLE; NSAIDs are a wrong answer and not proven to help

vignettes.q: What is cubital tunnel syndrome
vignettes.a: ulnar nerve entrapment at elbow → presents similarly to carpal tunnel syndrome but just in an ulnar distribution and involves the forearm.

vignettes.q: What is Guyon canal syndrome
vignettes.a: ulnar nerve entrapment at the wrist → hook of hamate fracture or chronic handle bar impaction in avid cyclists.

vignettes.q: 43M + elevated fasting glucose + arthritis + cardiomegaly; what’s the mechanism for this patient’s condition?
vignettes.a: increased intestinal absorption of iron; Dx = hemochromatosis; AR; chromosome 6; Fe can deposit in tail of pancreas, leading to diabetes; hemochromatosis and primary hyperparathyroidism are two HY causes of pseudogout (calcium pyr

vignettes.q: 30F + rheumatoid arthritis + currently being managed with infliximab but has not improved; Q asks for which immune mediator is most likely contributing to symptoms; answer = IL-1. Infliximab is a monoclonal ant
vignettes.a: Normal Tx for RA is two-armed: symptoms and DMARDs (disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs). For Sx: USMLE wants NSAIDs followed by steroids; these do not slow disease progression. For slowing disease progression, the first-line D

vignettes.q: 37F + rheumatoid arthritis + PR-depressions and ST-elevations seen in many leads on ECG; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: pericarditis; common in autoimmune diseases such as RA; PR-depressions are highly specific for pericarditis but not common; diffuse ST-elevations seen in all cases on USMLE if they mention ECG findings.

vignettes.q: Patient has autoimmune disease (i.e., SLE, RA, etc.); question wants to know how to decrease recurrence of flares
vignettes.a: smoking cessation.

vignettes.q: 42F + long-standing history of rheumatoid arthritis managed with prednisone + undergoes appendectomy + experiences drop of BP to 80/40 during surgery; risk factor for this precipitous drop in BP?
vignettes.a: chronic prednisone use causing adrenal suppression → can’t mount stress response in setting of stressor (i.e., surgery, trauma, infection) → can cause BP to fall precipitously → after IV fluids, give hydrocortisone. Normally, cort

vignettes.q: 42F + long-standing rheumatoid arthritis managed with multiple medications + 6-month Hx of dry cough + CXR shows reticular pattern; what’s the risk factor for this condition?
vignettes.a: methotrexate-induced pulmonary fibrosis + rheumatoid lung (the autoimmune disease itself, independent of methotrexate, can cause pulmonary fibrosis, so patients will have restrictive lung disease due to both methotrexate and the R

vignettes.q: 39F + rheumatoid arthritis + low RBCs, WBCs and platelets + splenomegaly; Q wants risk factor for this condition
vignettes.a: rheumatoid arthritis; diagnosis is Felty syndrome (RA + neutropenia + splenomegaly); sometimes RBCs and platelets can be down as well.

vignettes.q: 50F + BMI 40 + smoker + HTN; Q asks #1 way to decrease risk of osteoarthritis in this patient
vignettes.a: weight loss (exceedingly HY).

vignettes.q: 62F + has peripheral edema + using high doses of naproxen for past 6 weeks to manage her osteoarthritis; Q wants to know #1 way to minimize risk for this patient’s condition
vignettes.a: avoidance of NSAIDs; patient has fluid retention due to NSAIDs (decreased renal blood flow causes kidney to reabsorb fluid to compensate).

vignettes.q: 35F + pregnant + fetus shows intrauterine growth restriction; risk factor?
vignettes.a: often uteroplacental insufficiency, e.g., from smoking, cocaine use, HTN, SLE.

vignettes.q: 35F + ovarian mass + purple discoloration of knuckles + violaceous eyelids + proximal muscle weakness; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: dermatomyositis due to ovarian cancer. Dermatomyositis usually idiopathic, but a risk factor for it that’s assessed is ovarian cancer.

vignettes.q: 2M + enucleation of eye for retinoblastoma; Q asks about this being risk factor for which of the following in the future?
vignettes.a: osteosarcoma; hereditary retinoblastoma can also lead to osteosarcoma. HY RISK FACTORS

vignettes.q: 50M + Cushingoid appearance + proximal muscle weakness + successful ability to maintain upward gaze for 60 seconds + serum ACTH levels high + serum cortisol high; if high-dose dexamethasone is administered, wha
vignettes.a: ↔ ACTH, ↔ cortisol. — The patient has both Lambert-Eaton and Cushing syndromes secondary to small cell bronchogenic carcinoma. • Since the etiology for his Cushing syndrome is not Cushing disease, ACTH and cortisol will not suppre

vignettes.a: ↓ Glucose, ↑ protein, ↑ PMNs, ↔ lymphocytes. — Bacterial meningitis: low glucose, high protein, high PMNs (neutrophils), no change lymphocytes. • Fungal meningitis: low glucose, high protein, no change PMNs (neutrophils), high lym

vignettes.q: A = CN III (oculomotor) lesion
vignettes.a: presents as down and out.

vignettes.q: B = CN IV (trochlear) lesion
vignettes.a: presents as upward gaze + patient will tilt head toward unaffected side.

vignettes.q: C = CN VI (abducens) lesion
vignettes.a: medially directed eye. Glaucoma

vignettes.a: answer on NBME is Brown-Sequard syndrome secondary to viral infection.

vignettes.q: Patient with restless leg syndrome is at increased risk for what disease later in life?
vignettes.a: answer on USMLE = Parkinson disease (if D2 agonist can Tx, then lack of dopamine transmission may be etiology in some patients).

vignettes.q: 58M + loses consciousness while shaving + tilt-table test shows no abnormalities; Dx?
vignettes.a: NBME wants “carotid sinus hypersensitivity” as answer. If tilt-table test (+), answer = vasovagal syncope.

vignettes.q: 45F + fundoscopy shows hard exudates + cotton wool spots + scattered hemorrhages; Dx?
vignettes.a: diabetic retinopathy.

vignettes.q: Medication that can cause tardive dyskinesia that is not an antipsychotic?
vignettes.a: metoclopramide (D2 antagonist); can also prolong QT interval and cause hyperprolactinemia.

vignettes.q: Anti-depressant med causing seizures?
vignettes.a: bupropion.

vignettes.q: 56M + 3-day Hx of cutting from 12 beers a day down to 4; develops tremulousness; Tx?
vignettes.a: chlordiazepoxide (delirium tremens); classic vignette is guy has surgery + two days later has tachycardia, tremulousness, and hallucinations (alcoholic hallucinosis).

vignettes.q: 50F + high ESR and creatine kinase (CK) + proximal muscle weakness +/- muscle pain; Dx?
vignettes.a: polymyositis.

vignettes.q: 50F + high ESR + no mention of high CK or weakness in the vignette + muscle pain + muscle stiffness; Dx?
vignettes.a: polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR).

vignettes.q: 59F + temporal headache + muscle pain and stiffness + high ESR; Dx?
vignettes.a: temporal arteritis + polymyalgia rheumatica → next best step? = IV methylprednisolone first, followed by temporal artery biopsy.

vignettes.q: 68M + Hx of prostate cancer + now has neurologic findings; next best step in Dx?
vignettes.a: MRI of spine to look for mets → however if corticosteroids are listed, choose these before MRI → for spinal cord compression on NBME (from cancer or trauma), choose steroids first if listed.

vignettes.q: 65F + breast cancer + neurologic findings; next best step?
vignettes.a: answer on Neuro NBME is “intravenous high-dose dexamethasone.”

vignettes.q: 72M + prostate cancer + neurologic findings; Dx?
vignettes.a: “epidural spinal cord compression” due to spinal mets → do steroids first (if listed), then MRI.

vignettes.q: Patient has brain cancer; next best step?
vignettes.a: steroids.

vignettes.q: How to Dx brain cancer?
vignettes.a: contrast head CT (done for cancer and abscess).

vignettes.q: How to Dx brain bleed?
vignettes.a: non-contrast CT (always done for intracranial bleeds).

vignettes.q: Epidural hematoma; next best step after CT confirms?
vignettes.a: intubation and hyperventilation on Neuro NBME. After this is done, craniotomy is the answer.

vignettes.q: Subdural hematoma; next best step after CT?
vignettes.a: craniotomy on NBME, not observation.

vignettes.q: What do you see on non-contrast CT with epidural vs subdural?
vignettes.a: epidural hematoma = lens-shaped bleed; subdural = crescent-shaped.

vignettes.q: BP of 220/120 + sodium nitroprusside administered; now patient has confusion; Dx?
vignettes.a: cyanide toxicity caused by nitroprusside.

vignettes.q: Drug that can be given to prevent vasospasm after a subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)?
vignettes.a: nimodipine (dihydropyridine CCB).

vignettes.q: Severe headache + stiff neck; Dx?
vignettes.a: SAH (can cause meningism, similar to meningitis).

vignettes.q: Brain bleed in patient with Alzheimer; Dx?
vignettes.a: amyloid angiopathy (intracerebral hemorrhage).

vignettes.q: 87F + Alzheimer + low-grade fever + delirium; next best step?
vignettes.a: do urinalysis to look for UTI as cause of delirium.

vignettes.q: Viral infection + tinnitus + vertigo +/- neurosensory hearing loss
vignettes.a: labyrinthitis.

vignettes.q: Viral infection + vertigo
vignettes.a: vestibular neuritis.

vignettes.q: Tx for acute flare of MS
vignettes.a: IV steroids (oral is wrong and can make flares worse).

vignettes.q: Tx between flares of MS (the patient must by asymptomatic)
vignettes.a: IFN-beta (interferon beta).

vignettes.q: Tx for spasticity in MS
vignettes.a: baclofen (GABA-B receptor agonist).

vignettes.q: Incontinence in MS
vignettes.a: urge (hyperactive detrusor; detrusor instability).

vignettes.q: Mechanism for MS?
vignettes.a: T cell-mediated attack against oligodendrocytes.

vignettes.q: How to Dx MS?
vignettes.a: MRI is gold standard; choose MRI over CSF IgG oligoclonal bands.

vignettes.q: 27F + intermittent headaches + blurry vision; Dx?

vignettes.q: How to differentiate CN III lesion from INO?
vignettes.a: INO patients can converge normally.

vignettes.q: 20F + stiffness of hands + frontal balding + impaired relaxation of hypothenar muscles; Dx?
vignettes.a: myotonic dystrophy (CTG TNR disorder).

vignettes.q: Cancer patient on cisplatin or vincristine + develops neuropathy; Dx?
vignettes.a: toxic neuropathy (chemotherapy-induced neuropathy); these drugs are neurotoxic.

vignettes.q: Confusion and/or seizure due to electrolyte disturbance; Dx?
vignettes.a: hypo-/hypernatremia and hypercalcemia all cause CNS dysfunction.

vignettes.q: Confusion in the setting of high BUN and creatinine; Dx?
vignettes.a: uremic encephalopathy.

vignettes.q: Floppy baby syndrome; Dx and location of CNS/PNS affected?
vignettes.a: Werdnig-Hoffmann syndrome (spinal muscular atrophy); anterior horns affected.

vignettes.q: Antipsychotic medication started + muscle rigidity + no fever; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: acute dystonia, not neuroleptic malignant syndrome (because no fever); Tx with benztropine (muscarinic receptor antagonist) or diphenhydramine (1st gen H1 blocker, which has strong anti-muscarinic side-effects).

vignettes.q: Antipsychotic medication started + abnormal eye movements + stiff neck; Dx?
vignettes.a: acute dystonia (oculogyric crisis + torticollis).

vignettes.q: Antipsychotic medication started + muscle rigidity + fever; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: neuroleptic malignant syndrome; give dantrolene (inhibits ryanodine channel).

vignettes.q: Antipsychotic med + restlessness; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: akathisia; Tx with propranolol.

vignettes.q: Antipsychotic med + bradykinesia; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: drug-induced Parkinsonism; Tx with amantadine or propranolol.

vignettes.q: Antipsychotic med + abnormal tongue movements; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: tardive dyskinesia; stop antipsychotic + switch to atypical.

vignettes.q: Tx for diabetic neuropathic pain?
vignettes.a: TCA (i.e., amitriptyline). Second-line is gabapentin

vignettes.q: Tx for herpetic / post-herpetic neuralgia (i.e., from shingles)?
vignettes.a: gabapentin

vignettes.a: switch the meds to nortriptyline (a TCA) → student then asks, “Wait, I thought you said TCAs are first-line. Why does this Q have the guy on those two meds then?” → two points: 1) we don’t like giving TCAs to elderly because of th

vignettes.q: How to differentiate cluster headache from trigeminal neuralgia?
vignettes.a: cluster will be a male 20s-40s with 11/10 lancinating pain behind the eye waking him up at night (he may pace around the room until it goes away); details such as lacrimation and rhinorrhea are too easy and will likely not show up

vignettes.q: Tx and prophylaxis for cluster headache?
vignettes.a: Tx = 100% oxygen; prophylaxis = verapamil.

vignettes.q: Tx and prophylaxis for trigeminal neuralgia?
vignettes.a: Tx = goes away on its own because it lasts only seconds; prophylaxis = carbamazepine.

vignettes.q: Tx and prophylaxis for migraine?
vignettes.a: Tx = NSAID, followed by triptan (triptans are NOT prophylaxis; they are for abortive therapy only after NSAIDs); prophylaxis = propranolol.

vignettes.q: 32M + diffuse headache relieved by acetaminophen + sleep; Dx?
vignettes.a: tension-type headache; Tx = rest + taper caffeine (if taking it).

vignettes.q: Other HY uses for propranolol?
vignettes.a: Migraine prophylaxis Akathisia (with antipsychotic use) Thyroid storm (decreases peripheral conversion of T4 to T3) Essential tremor (bilateral resting tremor in young adult; autosomal dominant; patient will self-medicate with EtO

vignettes.q: 47M + bitemporal hemianopsia; most likely tumor?
vignettes.a: prolactinoma (most common pituitary tumor in adults).

vignettes.q: 8M + bitemporal hemianopsia; most likely tumor?
vignettes.a: craniopharyngioma (most common pituitary tumor in children; some sources argue not true pituitary tumor because it’s derived from Rathke pouch, which is the roof of the primitive pharynx).

vignettes.q: Most common primary brain cancer in children?
vignettes.a: pilocytic astrocytoma → solid + cystic on MRI; has Rosenthal fibers → not aggressive.

vignettes.q: 3F + morning vomiting + truncal ataxia; Dx?
vignettes.a: medulloblastoma of cerebellar vermis.

vignettes.q: Most common primary brain cancer in adults?
vignettes.a: glioblastoma multiforme (butterfly glioma) → areas of necrosis + hemorrhage (large, irregular mass on head CT); often presents with seizure.

vignettes.q: 44F + SLE + irregular ring-enhancing lesion seen on head CT; Dx?
vignettes.a: primary CNS lymphoma, not Toxo.

vignettes.q: Neonate + intracranial calcifications + chorioretinitis + hydrocephalus; Dx?
vignettes.a: Congenital Toxo.

vignettes.q: Neonate + intracranial calcifications + deafness + hepatomegaly + rash; Dx?
vignettes.a: CMV.

vignettes.q: Neonate with bilateral deafness due to maternal infection + no other info given; Dx?
vignettes.a: congenital CMV.

vignettes.q: CNS tumors seen in neurofibromatosis?
vignettes.a: oligodendroglioma + ependymoma + optic nerve glioma in NF1; in NF2, meningioma. These may overlap, but be aware that these tumors can merely occur in either NF, period.

vignettes.q: 50F + jaw pain + headaches + normal ESR; Dx?
vignettes.a: temporal mandibular joint syndrome; if ESR is high, answer is jaw claudication caused by temporal arteritis.

vignettes.q: 40F being treated for TB + has neurologic findings in extremities +/- seizure; Dx?
vignettes.a: B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency caused by isoniazid.

vignettes.q: 65F + metastatic breast cancer + suprapubic mass + decreased sphincter tone + pain over lumbar vertebrae on fist percussion; Dx?
vignettes.a: metastases to cauda equina.

vignettes.q: 44M + saddle anesthesia + late urinary incontinence; Dx?
vignettes.a: cauda equina syndrome → bundle of spinal nerves and rootlets arising from the conus medullaris).

vignettes.q: 44M + perianal anesthesia + early urinary + fecal incontinence; Dx?
vignettes.a: conus medullaris syndrome → bulbous end of the spinal cord = conus medullaris.

vignettes.q: 48M + burns his thumb; pain sensed via which dermatome?
vignettes.a: C6; lateral digits primarily C6; middle finger C7; medial digits primarily C8.

vignettes.q: What does CSF show in GBS?
vignettes.a: albuminocytologic dissociation (high protein but normal cells).

vignettes.q: 24M + weakness proximally and distally in lower limbs + weakness distally in upper limbs; rest of the vignette is vague; Dx?
vignettes.a: GBS → this descriptor means paralysis/paresis has ascending in lower limbs but not yet in upper limbs.

vignettes.q: Mechanism of GBS?
vignettes.a: T cell attack against Schwann cells of PNS.

vignettes.q: Tx of GBS?
vignettes.a: IVIG + plasmapheresis; steroids are the wrong answer.

vignettes.q: 32F + paresthesias in thenar region of hand +/- hand weakness + sensation intact over dorsum of hand; next best step in Dx?
vignettes.a: Neuro NBME exam wants “Electrophysiological testing.” it’s what they want. Examination findings such as Tinel sign, Phalen maneuver, Flick test are insufficient for diagnosis.

vignettes.q: First Tx for carpal tunnel syndrome in patient who can’t stop offending activity (e.g., office worker)
vignettes.a: wrist splint first; then triamcinolone (steroid) injection into the carpal tunnel; do not select anything surgical as it’s always wrong on the USMLE; NSAIDs are a wrong answer and not proven to help

vignettes.q: Tx for cubital tunnel syndrome
vignettes.a: elbow splint.

vignettes.q: What is cubital tunnel syndrome
vignettes.a: ulnar nerve entrapment at elbow → presents similarly to carpal tunnel syndrome but just in an ulnar distribution and involves the forearm.

vignettes.q: What is Guyon canal syndrome
vignettes.a: ulnar nerve entrapment at the wrist → hook of hamate fracture or chronic handle bar impaction in avid cyclists.

vignettes.q: Midshaft fracture of humerus; which nerve is injured?
vignettes.a: radial → wrist-drop + pronated forearm.

vignettes.q: Supracondylar fracture of humerus; which nerve is injured?
vignettes.a: median.

vignettes.q: Medial epicondylar fracture; nerve injury?
vignettes.a: ulnar.

vignettes.q: Surgical neck of humerus fracture; nerve injury?
vignettes.a: axillary.

vignettes.q: Mastectomy + post-operative winged scapula; nerve injury?
vignettes.a: long thoracic nerve.

vignettes.q: Which muscle is innervated by long thoracic nerve?
vignettes.a: serratus anterior.

vignettes.q: 6M + ECG shows miscellaneous arrhythmia + seizure-like episode; Dx?
vignettes.a: Adam-Stokes attack → not true seizure disorder as per EEG; arrythmia leads to hypoxia of brainstem → seizure-like fits ensue.

vignettes.q: 75M + episodes of loss of consciousness (LoC) for 2 years + tonic-clonic-like episodes + becomes pale and sweaty + Hx of MI; Dx?
vignettes.a: “syncope” on the NBME (convulsive syncope).

vignettes.q: Mechanism of narcolepsy?
vignettes.a: deficiency of orexin (hypocretin).

vignettes.q: What is cataplexy?
vignettes.a: loss of muscle tone usually in response to emotional stimulus (e.g., laughter) → seen in narcolepsy.

vignettes.q: What is simple vs complex seizure?
vignettes.a: simple = no LoC; complex = LoC; patient staring off into space not aware of surroundings = LoC.

vignettes.q: What is partial vs generalized seizure?
vignettes.a: partial = affecting one part of the brain; generalized = involves the wholes of both cerebral hemispheres.

vignettes.q: What is myoclonic seizure?
vignettes.a: jerks in muscle or group of muscles; no LoC.

vignettes.q: Empiric Abx therapy for meningitis
vignettes.a: ceftriaxone + vancomycin (+/- steroids).

vignettes.q: Lumbar puncture or Abx first in suspected meningitis?
vignettes.a: new guidelines say LP first.

vignettes.q: When do you do CT head before LP in suspected meningitis?
vignettes.a: Confusion that interferes with neurologic exam / decreased GCS score. Seizure. Focal neurologic signs (motor or sensory). Papilledema or if the optic fundi cannot be visualized. Above reasons indicate potential mass lesion, where

vignettes.q: Herpes encephalitis: lots of RBCs in CSF due to temporal lobe hemorrhage
vignettes.a: CT is often negative, but sometimes Q will mention wave slowing or temporal complexes on EEG. Tx = IV acyclovir.

vignettes.q: Difference between meningitis and encephalitis
vignettes.a: meningitis is nuchal rigidity (neck stiffness) + photophobia + ophthalmoplegia; encephalitis presents with confusion.

vignettes.q: Dx of Cryptococcal meningitis?
vignettes.a: latex agglutination if it’s listed over India ink; mucicarmine staining (red stain) can also be done.

vignettes.q: Tx for Cryptococcal meningitis
vignettes.a: amphotericin B + flucytosine, followed by fluconazole taper.

vignettes.q: Nodular density in upper lobe in immunocompromised pt
vignettes.a: aspergilloma → next best step = open lung biopsy (sounds radical, but it’s the answer on one of the NBME forms) → Tx with -azole → invasive aspergillosis can be treated with caspofungin or voriconazole.

vignettes.q: 44F + diplopia + dysphagia + eyelid ptosis; all worsen throughout the day; Dx?
vignettes.a: myasthenia gravis (MG).

vignettes.q: 44F + proximal muscle weakness + able to perform upward gaze without a problem for 60 seconds; Dx?
vignettes.a: Lambert-Eaton (LE) syndrome (if cannot perform, answer = MG).

vignettes.q: Vignette where Dx is either MG or LE but it’s not listed; answer?
vignettes.a: “neuromuscular junction.”

vignettes.q: 44F + difficulty getting up from chair but is able to after several attempts; Dx?
vignettes.a: LE.

vignettes.q: Mechanism of MG vs LE?
vignettes.a: MG = antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors; LE = antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels.

vignettes.q: MG can sometimes be paraneoplastic syndromes of which cancer?
vignettes.a: MG from thymoma (do chest imaging to check for thymoma after Dx of MG; if thymoma present + removed, this cures the MG). Up to 80% of patients with thymoma + MG have anti-MUSK Abs (muscle-specific kinase).

vignettes.q: LE can sometimes be a paraneoplastic syndrome of which cancer?
vignettes.a: small cell lung cancer.

vignettes.q: How to Dx MG vs LE?
vignettes.a: If both are listed, choose antibodies over Tensilon (edrophonium) test.

vignettes.q: What is edrophonium
vignettes.a: short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.

vignettes.q: How do MG vs LE perform with edrophonium?
vignettes.a: MG improves drastically; LE less change.

vignettes.q: Tx of MG?
vignettes.a: give an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (i.e., pyridostigmine).

vignettes.q: 6M + dancing eyes + HTN + lesion visualized in posterior mediastinum on CXR; Dx?
vignettes.a: neuroblastoma; students says ? → can occur anywhere in the median sympathetic chain, although classically intra- abdominal. Dancing eyes = opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome.

vignettes.q: Neuroblastoma; how to Dx?
vignettes.a: answer on NBME is “urinary homovanillic acid (HVA) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA); mIBG scan may also be used; n-myc gene.

vignettes.q: 25M + impaired plantar flexion + inversion; Dx?
vignettes.a: tibial nerve injury.

vignettes.q: 25M + impaired dorsiflexion + eversion; Dx?
vignettes.a: common peroneal nerve injury.

vignettes.q: 22F returns from Central America + has tonic-clonic seizure + CT of head shows “swiss cheese” appearance of brain, or cystic structures in ventricles, or white specs somewhat diffusely (I’ve seen all three imag
vignettes.a: neurocysticercosis (Taenia solium); Tx = albendazole (or praziquantel).

vignettes.q: AIDS patient with CD4 count of 47/uL + cognitive degeneration + miscellaneous peripheral neurologic findings; Dx?
vignettes.a: progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) caused by JC polyoma virus; USMLE wants “reactivation of latent infection”; “acute infection in immunocompromised patient” is the wrong answer. T2-weighted MRI shows multiple hyperi

vignettes.q: 55F + few-month Hx of spinning sensation + no vomiting + when head hangs off examination table she develops coarse, rotary nystagmus beating to one side; Dx?
vignettes.a: answer on NBME is benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BBPV); need not be associated with vomiting; Dx with Dix-Hallpike maneuver; Tx with Epley maneuver.

vignettes.q: Cause of BPPV?
vignettes.a: posterior semicircular canal otolith.

vignettes.q: What is cholesteatoma?
vignettes.a: non-cancerous squamous proliferation of middle ear.

vignettes.q: Most common cause of carotid plaques?
vignettes.a: HTN → the strong systolic impulse from the heart pounds the carotids --> endothelial damage --> atherosclerosis.

vignettes.q: What % of people over age 80 have AF?
vignettes.a: 8% of people over age 80 have AF, which is why age is a huge risk factor. In other words, if the vignette says the guy is 58, AF is probably less likely just based on shear probability, regardless of hypertensive status." And, onc

vignettes.q: Age 50s-60s + high BP + TIA/stroke/retinal artery occlusion; next best step in Dx?
vignettes.a: carotid duplex ultrasound to look for carotid plaques.

vignettes.q: Age >75 + good BP + TIA/stroke/retinal artery occlusion; answer = ECG to look for AF
vignettes.a: if normal, do Holter monitor to pick up paroxysmal AF.

vignettes.q: How to Mx carotid plaques?
vignettes.a: first we have to ask whether the patient is symptomatic or asymptomatic. A bruit does not count as symptoms (that's a sign). Symptomatic means stroke, TIA, or retinal artery occlusion. According to recent guidelines: carotid occlu

vignettes.q: 6F + rheumatic fever + has Sydenham chorea; Q asks mechanism
vignettes.a: autoimmune disorder to the basal ganglia.

vignettes.q: 38F + hoarseness of voice + various stress factors; Dx?
vignettes.a: conversion disorder; merely be aware that hoarseness of voice is assessed for this.

vignettes.q: Back pain worse when standing or walking for long periods of time
vignettes.a: lumbar spinal stenosis.

vignettes.q: Radiculopathy down an arm
vignettes.a: cervical disc herniation.

vignettes.q: Bilateral paresthesias in the arms in rheumatoid arthritis patient
vignettes.a: atlantoaxial subluxation.

vignettes.q: Bilateral paresthesias in the arms in rheumatoid arthritis patient
vignettes.a: MRI of spine to Dx atlantoaxial subluxation.

vignettes.q: Prior to surgery in rheumatoid arthritis patient
vignettes.a: cervical CT or flexion/extension x-rays of cervical spine to check for atlantoaxial subluxation.

vignettes.q: 40M + combination of LMN and UMN findings + no sensory abnormalities; Dx?
vignettes.a: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis; make sure you memorize that there are NO sensory findings, as this is the detail most students forget. Sometimes the answer won’t be “ALS,” but will instead be “motor neuron” (i.e., they’ll ask for s

vignettes.q: 1-year-old boy + hypotonia + honey consumption; Dx?
vignettes.a: ingestion of spores (honey); botulism (Clostridium botulinum).

vignettes.q: 13M + camping trip + Bell palsy + constipation + hypotonia; Dx?
vignettes.a: ingestion of preformed toxin from compromised canned goods. Tx = anti-toxin.

vignettes.q: 32M + waxing and waning tinnitus and hearing loss + difficulty hearing conversations at dinner and in groups + has family Hx of similar Sx; Dx?
vignettes.a: Meniere disease → low-frequency hearing loss.

vignettes.q: Mechanism for Meniere?
vignettes.a: defective endolymphatic drainage; may attempt antihistamines and diuretics.

vignettes.q: Viral infection + tinnitus +/- vertigo + no hearing loss; self-resolves over weeks to months; Dx?
vignettes.a: vestibular neuritis.

vignettes.q: Viral infection + tinnitus + hearing loss +/- vertigo self-resolves over weeks to months; Dx?
vignettes.a: labyrinthitis. One Q on the neuro forms has presentation similar to vestibular neuritis but answer is labyrinthitis; vestibular neuritis isn’t listed as alternative answer.

vignettes.q: 3M + pinna displaced upward and outward + fever; Dx?
vignettes.a: mastoiditis (malignant otitis externa).

vignettes.q: 25M IV drug user + Tx for endocarditis + now the room is spinning; Dx?
vignettes.a: CN VIII toxicity caused by aminoglycoside (can be hearing loss, tinnitus, or vertigo); empiric endocarditis Tx is usually gentamicin + either vancomycin or ampicillin/sulbactam.

vignettes.q: Endocarditis patient + has stroke-like episode + fever; next best step?
vignettes.a: IV antibiotics → septic embolus to the brain; can lead to brain abscess.

vignettes.q: MCA stroke on dominant hemisphere (usually left-sided); HY findings?
vignettes.a: contralateral limb + face sensory and/or motor deficits; also classically associated with Broca and Wernicke aphasias.

vignettes.q: ACA stroke; HY findings?
vignettes.a: contralateral lower leg sensory and/or motor dysfunction.

vignettes.q: PCA stroke; HY findings?
vignettes.a: contralateral hemianopsia with macular sparing.

vignettes.q: Broca aphasia; HY findings?
vignettes.a: non-fluent aphasia; telegraphic speech; comprehends normally but cannot communicate easily, leading to frustration; repetition impaired.

vignettes.q: Where is Broca area?
vignettes.a: posterior, lateral, inferior frontal lobe.

vignettes.q: Wernicke aphasia; HY findings?
vignettes.a: fluent aphasia; word salad; non-sensical speech + does not comprehend; repetition impaired.

vignettes.q: Where is Wernicke area?
vignettes.a: superior temporal gyrus (temporal lobe).

vignettes.q: What is conduction aphasia?
vignettes.a: patient has only impaired repetition (arcuate fasciculus connecting Broca and Wernicke areas).

vignettes.q: What is global aphasia?
vignettes.a: patient has presentation of Broca and Wernicke aphasias at the same time.

vignettes.q: What is transcortical motor aphasia?
vignettes.a: patient sounds like he/she has Broca aphasia but repetition is intact.

vignettes.q: What is transcortical sensory aphasia?
vignettes.a: patient sounds like he/she has Wernicke aphasia but repetition is intact.

vignettes.q: What is mixed transcortical aphasia?
vignettes.a: patient sounds like he/she has Broca and Wernicke at the same time but repetition is intact.

vignettes.q: 42M + acalculia + left-right agnosia + finger agnosia + agraphia; Dx?
vignettes.a: Gerstmann syndrome (angular gyrus syndrome; junction of parietal and temporal lobes).

vignettes.q: Stroke causing Horner syndrome + dysphagia + loss of pain/temp from contralateral body and ipsilateral face; Dx?
vignettes.a: lateral medullary syndrome (PICA infarct) → “Pikachu” = PICA-chew = dysphagia with PICA infarct.

vignettes.q: Stroke causing ipsilateral Bell palsy; Dx?
vignettes.a: lateral pontine syndrome (AICA infarct) → FACIAL spelled backwards has AICA in it → face is affected.

vignettes.q: Stroke causing ipsilateral tongue deviation + contralateral paralysis and loss of propioception; Dx?
vignettes.a: medial medullary syndrome (paramedian branch of anterior spinal artery).

vignettes.q: Lacunar infarct HY points?
vignettes.a: caused by HTN leading to lipohyalinosis of lenticulostriate vessels → if affecting posterior limb of internal capsule, deficits are pure motor (contralateral); if thalamic, deficits are pure sensory (contralateral).

vignettes.q: Stroke causing locked-in syndrome; Dx?
vignettes.a: Basilar artery stroke.

vignettes.q: Correct hyponatremia too quickly?
vignettes.a: locked-in syndrome due to central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination).

vignettes.q: Correct hypernatremia too quickly?
vignettes.a: cerebral edema.

vignettes.q: Pain in contralateral limb months after stroke resolves; Dx?
vignettes.a: thalamic pain syndrome.

vignettes.q: Coma or persistent vegetative state following deceleration injury (i.e., MVA or fall); Dx?
vignettes.a: diffuse axonal injury.

vignettes.q: 10-month old boy + jerking movements of the limbs + EEG shows chaotic high-amplitude spikes with no recognizable pattern; Dx?
vignettes.a: West syndrome (infantile spasms) → triad of spasms + hypsarrhythmia on EEG (no recognizable pattern with high amplitude spikes) + developmental regression; international definition of the diagnosis requires two out of three; start

vignettes.q: 13M + tonic-clonic seizure + 4-month Hx of hypnagogic/hypnopompic jerking of left arm + uncle has epilepsy; Dx?
vignettes.a: juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; genetic with unclear inheritance pattern; characterized by myoclonic jerks (usually hypnagogic and/or hypnopompic) that progress to tonic- clonic seizures after several months; age of onset is usually

vignettes.q: 4F + few-month Hx of near-daily seizures + seizures typically occur while she’s sleeping + has started putting objects in her mouth and making less eye contact + seizures not responding to anti-epileptic meds;
vignettes.a: Lennox-Gastaut syndrome → severe childhood-onset epilepsy characterized by near-daily seizures and cognitive decline (hyperoralism is a sign of cognitive regression [babies put things in their mouths]); poor prognosis, with 5% mor

vignettes.q: 27F + long-standing Hx of seizures + the following picture represents her condition; Dx?
vignettes.a: arteriovenous malformation (AVM) → looks almost like swiss cheese. This is a HY image for Step 1.

vignettes.q: 82M + long-standing HTN + weakness of right arm and right side of face; occlusion of which vessel is responsible for patient’s presentation?
vignettes.a: left middle cerebral artery (MCA) → MCA strokes will cause deficits of contralateral upper limb and face; Hx of HTN suggests carotid atherosclerosis with a plaque launching off to the circle of Willis.

vignettes.q: 74F + atrial fibrillation + weakness of left leg; occlusion of which vessel is responsible for patient’s presentation?
vignettes.a: right anterior cerebral artery (ACA) → ACA strokes will cause deficits of contralateral lower limb; Hx of AF suggests left atrial mural thrombus launched off to circle of Willis.

vignettes.q: 66M + HTN + weakness of left arm; where is the stroke lesion? (answer the following three Qs)
vignettes.a: 1) left or right side of the brain? → answer = right (contralateral). 2) medial or lateral cerebral hemisphere? → answer = lateral (homunculus for upper limb and face is lateral; leg is medial). 3) anterior or posterior to the cen

vignettes.q: 92F + atrial fibrillation + numbness/tingling of her right leg; where is the stroke lesion?
vignettes.a: 1) left or right side of the brain? → answer = left (contralateral). 2) medial or lateral cerebral hemisphere? → answer = medial (homunculus for lower limb is medial; upper limb and face are lateral). 3) anterior or posterior to t

vignettes.q: 66M + chronic HTN managed with lisinopril + paresthesias of left leg; using the following diagram, which letter corresponds to the part of the brain that is affected?
vignettes.a: F → stroke affects left side of body, is sensory, and is lower limb, so we know that the lesion must be contralateral (i.e., we can eliminate A-D, which are the left side of the brain; i.e., the stroke must be on the right side of

vignettes.q: Using the above image, describe how each letter corresponds to a stroke in terms of 1) side of the body affected, 2) sensory vs motor, and 3) upper limb/face vs lower limb:
vignettes.a: A → Motor disturbance (i.e., paresis/paralysis) of right arm + face. B → Sensory disturbance (i.e., numbness, paresthesias, pain) of right arm + face. C → Motor; right leg. D → Sensory; right leg. E → Motor; left leg. F → Sensory;

vignettes.q: 91M + Hx of atrial fibrillation + new-onset difficulty articulating speech (i.e., words come out “telegraphic”); repetition is impaired; comprehension is intact; where on the following diagram is affected? Also
vignettes.a: A (Broca area; inferior frontal gyrus; frontal lobe) → Broca aphasia → non-fluent aphasia with repetition impaired; patient comprehends without a problem and appears frustrated with inability to articulate fluently. Choice B (prim

vignettes.q: 72M + Broca aphasia; which vessel is affected?
vignettes.a: left MCA (always assume left brain is dominant, unless Q specifically explicates the patient is left-handed).

vignettes.q: 72M + Wernicke aphasia; which vessel is affected?
vignettes.a: left MCA (same).

vignettes.q: 72M + Broca aphasia; where in the brain is affected?
vignettes.a: inferior frontal gyrus of frontal lobe (reiterating this because of yieldness for Step 1).

vignettes.q: 72M + Wernicke aphasia; where in the brain is affected?
vignettes.a: superior temporal gyrus of temporal lobe (reiterating this because of yieldness for Step 1).

vignettes.q: 72M + cannot draw clockface properly; Dx + where is the stroke?
vignettes.a: hemineglect syndrome caused by stroke in non-dominant parietal lobe (i.e., right MCA in most people) → leads to neglect of left visual field, although the patient can still see perfectly fine; hemineglect usually affects left visu

vignettes.q: Identify:
vignettes.a: A = Broca area; B = premotor cortex; C = primary motor cortex; D = primary sensory cortex; E = primary auditory cortex; F = Wernicke area; G = occipital pole of occipital lobe.

vignettes.q: Identify:
vignettes.a: A = frontal lobe; B = medial premotor cortex; the answer if the vignette mentions the patient planning on making a movement of his left leg. C = medial primary motor cortex (pre-central gyrus); the answer if post-stroke patient ha

vignettes.q: Identify:
vignettes.a: L = somatosensory association area; integrates information received from the primary sensory cortex (lies just posterior to primary sensory cortex). M = lateral primary sensory cortex (post-central gyrus); the answer if the post-s

vignettes.q: Now identify:
vignettes.a: Frontal lobe shown in blue because of its high yieldness. In other words, the USMLE will show you a gross specimen without the cerebellum, where it can be difficult to tell which side is the frontal lobe. Therefore, recognizing th

vignettes.q: 72M + progressive personality change + apathy + pulls pants down when guests come over to the house; where on the following specimen is most likely the location of the pathology in this patient?
vignettes.a: L (frontal lobe); Dx = frontotemporal dementia (classically apathy, disinhibition, personality change).

vignettes.q: 69F + Hx of HTN + stroke + tongue deviated to left side; which of the following letters corresponds on the stroke lesion?
vignettes.a: Most students: “ am I looking at?” Yeah I get, but stick with me here. Answer = A → medial medullary syndrome. The NBMEs for Step 1 are littered with these types of cross- sections. You do not need to know every structure labeled

vignettes.q: How the medulla cross-sections tend to appear on the Step 1 NBME/USMLE:
vignettes.a: If you get these types of slices on your exam and are deer in the headlights (i.e., you have no idea what you’re looking at), just remember: pay attention to whether they give you tongue deviation versus hoarseness/dysphagia +/- H

vignettes.q: 70M + Hx of HTN + left-sided Bell’s palsy + left-sided hearing loss + loss of temperature/pain to left side of face and right side of body; which of the following letters corresponds to the stroke lesion?
vignettes.a: B → lateral pontine syndrome → classically causes ipsilateral Bell’s palsy +/- hearing loss; the Bells palsy is literally the key detail you need to know. Caused by lesion of anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) → mnemonic i

vignettes.q: Looking at the following CT of the pons, what’s the diagnosis; and what was the most likely cause?
vignettes.a: Diagnosis is central pontine myelinolysis secondary to correction of hyponatremia too rapidly with hypertonic saline; the patient will present with locked-in syndrome (inability to move entire body except for eye muscles; describe

vignettes.q: Identify:
vignettes.a: A = crus cerebri; B = CN III (oculomotor) nucleus; C = cerebral aqueduct; D = substantia nigra. HY point: crus cerebri lesions cause contralateral spastic paralysis.

vignettes.q: 78M + Hx of HTN + left eye is directed laterally and inferiorly + weakness of right side of the body; Dx? → NBME answer = Weber syndrome → midbrain lesion resulting in ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (CNIII) palsy
vignettes.a: Bottom line is: if the vignette gives you a stroke syndrome of some kind where there’s oculomotor nerve palsy, choose Weber syndrome (midbrain lesion).

vignettes.q: 75F + many years ago had cerebral infarction + brain on autopsy appears as follows; what would her main deficit have been?
vignettes.a: spastic paralysis on the left side of the body (right crus cerebri infarcted).

vignettes.q: Identify:
vignettes.a: A = right inferior colliculus; B = right pyramidal tract; C = right medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF); D = left MLF; E = left pyramidal tract; F = left inferior colliculus. The inferior colliculi are part of the auditory system

vignettes.q: 32F + one-week Hx of urge to run to the bathroom at inopportune moments + physical exam shows inability to adduct left eye when gazing to the right + convergence of gaze not affected; where on the following dia
vignettes.a: D; diagnosis is medial longitudinal fasciculus syndrome (MLF syndrome; aka internuclear ophthalmoplegia; INO) in a patient with multiple sclerosis (vignette also describes urge incontinence); normal convergence tells us that CN II

vignettes.q: 74M + unilateral resting tremor + shuffling gait; where on the following MRI be represents the location of his pathology?
vignettes.a: D (midbrain); the substantia nigra pars compacta (blue) are located bilaterally within the midbrain:

vignettes.q: “Do I need to know the cranial nerves coming off the brainstem?”
vignettes.a: Yeah. NBME/USMLE will show you a brainstem specimen or drawing, and you need to be able to identify the nerve(s) they’re referring to:

vignettes.q: 32F + hiking in Connecticut + circular rash on forearm + Bell’s palsy; which nerve on the following diagram explains her findings?
vignettes.a: facial nerve (choice H) → Bell’s palsy secondary to Lyme disease.

vignettes.q: 76M + stroke + uvula deviates to the left when he says “Ahh”; which letter on the following image is the most likely location of this patient’s pathology?
vignettes.a: right vagus nerve (choice E); uvula deviates to contralateral side; Choice A = right trochlear nerve; B = right facial nerve; C = right vestibulocochlear nerve; D = right glossopharyngeal nerve; F = left trigeminal nerve; G = left

vignettes.q: 35F + complete loss of hearing in left ear; which CN is damaged?
vignettes.a: left vestibulocochlear.

vignettes.q: Which nerves enable the gag reflex?
vignettes.a: CN IX (afferent); CN X (efferent).

vignettes.q: 47M + touching the face just lateral to the nose produces pain; the nerve supplying this area of the face exits the skull through where?
vignettes.a: foramen rotundum (maxillary branch of trigeminal nerve).

vignettes.q: 19M + viral infection + Bell palsy; Q asks what other finding might be seen in this patient as a result of the nerve lesion
vignettes.a: right sided hyperacusis (loud sounds) → CN VII (facial) innervates stapedius muscle, which controls the stapes bone and functions to dampen sounds; lesion of CN VII can lead to hyperacusis in some patients.

vignettes.q: 48F + Hx of cystic kidneys + right pupil enlarged; an aneurysm of which of the following vessels might explain this presentation?
vignettes.a: posterior communicating artery (choice B); PCoM aneurysms can cause ipsilateral mydriasis (blown pupil); ↑ risk of ACoM and PCoM aneurysms in ADPKD; A = right internal carotid artery; C = posterior cerebral artery (PCA); D = front

vignettes.q: 82F + Hx of atrial fibrillation + inability to move all muscles of body except for eyes; which of the letters on the following angiogram best reflects the location of the patient’s stroke?
vignettes.a: Angiogram is of the circle of Willis; answer = basilar artery stroke (choice F), resulting in locked-in syndrome; A = anterior cerebral artery (ACA); B = anterior communicating artery (ACoM); C = middle cerebral artery (MCA); D =

vignettes.q: 68M + Hx of HTN + acute-onset painless loss of vision in the right eye; which letter on the following circle of Willis illustration best reflects the path of the patient’s embolus?
vignettes.a: D (ophthalmic artery); patient has central retinal artery occlusion from carotid plaque that launched off secondary to HTN; the retinal artery (aka central retinal artery) is a branch of the ophthalmic artery; A = anterior communi

vignettes.q: 32M + Hx of fainting episodes + blood pressure lower in right arm than left arm; retrograde flow through which vessel in the following angiogram might be expected in this patient?
vignettes.a: right vertebral artery (choice D); diagnosis is subclavian steal syndrome (proximal stenosis of subclavian artery results in retrograde flow through the vertebral artery, which is the first branch of the subclavian). Choice A = ri

vignettes.q: 34F + boating accident + dysmetria of right side of body + normal strength; which letter on the following sagittal brain cross-section most likely corresponds to the site of her injury?
vignettes.a: cerebellar hemisphere (choice F; posterior lobe is labeled); cerebellar injuries cause ipsilateral dysmetria; choice E, in contrast, which is the cerebellar vermis, would cause truncal ataxia. Choice A = thalamus; B = midbrain; C

vignettes.q: 26M + has arm slashed in bar fight + presents with arm pronated and unable to extend wrist; which letter on the following image corresponds to this patient’s deficit? -
vignettes.a: radial nerve (choice C). A = musculocutaneous nerve; B = axillary nerve; D = median nerve; E = ulnar nerve. USMLE will ask you relatively easy presentation for a neurologic deficit but require you to identify where on the brachial

vignettes.q: “Okay, but what do those tracts actually do?”
vignettes.a: Spinothalamic → pain and temperature. (HIGH YIELD) Dorsal columns → vibration + proprioception. (HIGH YIELD) Anterior + lateral corticospinal tracts → motor function. (HIGH YIELD)

vignettes.q: Choice A = dorsal horn; B = dorsal root; C = dorsal root ganglion; D = lateral horn; E = ventral horn; F = anterior white commissure; G = ventral root; H = spinal nerve.
vignettes.a: A = right corticospinal tract; B = right spinothalamic tract; C = right fasciculus cuneatus; D = right fasciculus gracilis; E = left fasciculus gracilis; F = left fasciculus cuneatus; G = left corticospinal tract; H = left spinoth

vignettes.q: 45M + boating accident years prior to death + autopsy is performed in which a myelin stain is used; what was the most likely deficit in this patient?
vignettes.a: loss of vibration/proprioception of the lower limbs → there are bilateral lesions of the fasciculus gracilis of the dorsal columns (only white matter part of the spinal cord not stained black with the myelin stain, meaning it was

vignettes.q: 24M + viral infection + loss of left leg motor function + loss of left leg vibration/proprioception + loss of right leg pain/temperature sensation; Dx?
vignettes.a: Brown-Sequard syndrome → hemisection of the spinal cord; classically stab wound, but can also be autoimmune (i.e., secondary to lupus myelitis or viral infection).

vignettes.q: 67M + long history of cervical spondylosis + whiplash injury after being rear-ended in MVA + weakness in upper limbs > weakness in lower limbs; Dx? → answer = central cord syndrome.
vignettes.a: Central cord syndrome is the answer when weakness in the upper limbs is greater than weakness in the lower limbs; typically follows hyperextension injury of the neck during whiplash in a rear-end MVA.

vignettes.q: 69M + long Hx of T2DM + bilateral loss of motor function and pain/temperature below level of nipples + intact vibration/proprioception; Dx? → answer = anterior cord syndrome (dorsal columns spared); often due t
vignettes.a: Anterior cord syndrome is the answer when there’s preservation of vibration/proprioception but loss of motor + pain/temperature, classically in patient with arterial disease.

vignettes.q: Answer = tabes dorsalis
vignettes.a: neurosyphilis → loss of dorsal columns → dorsal columns are the only part not stained, reflective of demyelination → isolated loss of vibration/proprioception; motor function and pain/temperature sensation intact.

vignettes.q: 31M + motorcycle accident + presents with spinal lesion affecting the following area on the cross- section; what type of neurologic dysfunction is most likely in this patient?
vignettes.a: bilateral loss of pain and temperature; diagnosis is syringomyelia (lesion of anterior white commissure); can be due to trauma, infections, and classically Chiari I.

vignettes.q: 23F + unilateral restring tremor + increased hepatic ALT and AST + low hematocrit; which letter on the following MRI correctly labels this patient’s putamen?
vignettes.a: A = caudate nucleus; B = putamen; C = globus pallidus. Parkinsonism in a young patient is Wilson disease until proven otherwise; copper deposition can occur anywhere in the basal ganglia; the putamen is described as a classic loca

vignettes.q: 41M + one-year Hx of jerking movements of extremities + 6-month Hx of worsening dementia + father had similar presentation and died at age 56; where on the following MRI is the location of this patient’s pathol
vignettes.a: The answer is the caudate nucleus, which is choice B. Choice A = anterior horn of lateral ventricle; C = internal capsule; D = putamen; E = third ventricle; F = thalamus.

vignettes.q: Identify:
vignettes.a: A = frontal lobe (medial frontal gyrus); B = frontal lobe (middle frontal gyrus); C = caudate nucleus; D = internal capsule; E = thalamus; F = occipital lobe (occipital pole).

vignettes.q: 78M + long Hx of HTN + sudden paresis of left side of his body; which letter on the following specimen is the most likely location of his stroke?
vignettes.a: The answer is C (posterior limb of internal capsule). A = anterior limb of internal capsule; B = genu of internal capsule. USMLE wants you to know that the lenticulostriate vessels supply the internal capsule. Chronic hypertension

vignettes.q: 63M + longstanding Hx of HTN + acute-onset flailing movements of left arm; where on the following cross-section of the corpus striatum is the most likely location of the patient’s pathology? Answer = subthalami
vignettes.a: hippocampus; B = crus cerebri; C = ventral medial nucleus of thalamus; D = substantia nigra; E = subthalamic nucleus; F = ventral lateral nucleus of thalamus.

vignettes.q: Identify:
vignettes.a: A = corpus collosum; B = thalamus; C = pituitary gland; D = medulla; E = clivus; F = cerebellum; G = pineal gland; H = superior sagittal sinus; I = torcular herophili.

vignettes.q: 32M + presents with hydrocephalus + MRI shows colloid cyst most likely located where on the following illustration?
vignettes.a: choice C (foramen of Monro); colloid cysts are almost always found originating from the roof of the anterior third ventricle, just posterior the foramen of Monro. Weirdly specific, but just be aware. A = frontal horn; B = third ve

vignettes.q: Identify:
vignettes.a: A = lateral ventricles; B = colloid cyst of roof of the third ventricle; C = third ventricle. “How would the brain development stuff like diencephalon, mesencephalon, etc., be asked?” → First learn the following diagram:

vignettes.q: 72M + unsteady gait + personality change + urinary incontinence + Parkinsonism; the enlarged structures labeled on the following CT are derived from which component of brain development (i.e., prosencephalon, d
vignettes.a: telencephalon of the prosencephalon → dilated lateral ventricles are seen in normal pressure hydrocephalus (wet, wobbly, wacky +/- Parkinsonism).

vignettes.q: 84M + one-year Hx of progressive cognitive decline + no Hx of HTN, CVD, or atrial fibrillation + experiences a stroke and dies; which of the following head CTs might best reflect this patient?
vignettes.a: intracerebral (intraparenchymal) hemorrhage (choice D); Dx is amyloid angiopathy resulting in hemorrhagic stroke in Alzheimer disease; A = subdural hematoma; B = epidural hematoma; C = subarachnoid hemorrhage. Subdural hematoma (c

vignettes.q: 17M + motorcycle accident + severe cognitive impairment two years following accident; based on the following MRI, what is the most likely diagnosis?
vignettes.a: diffuse axonal injury; caused by shearing forces from rapid-deceleration injury. Note the irregular areas of hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted MRI.

vignettes.q: 44F + SLE + the following CT of head shows ring-enhancing lesion; what’s the diagnosis?
vignettes.a: primary CNS lymphoma; the wrong answer is Toxoplasmosis. Ring-enhancing lesions can refer to abscesses, malignancy, Toxo, and neurocysticerosis. Autoimmune diseases (e.g., Hashimoto, SLE, etc.) and immunosuppression (i.e., AIDS) c

vignettes.q: 3M + failure to thrive + seizure; based on the following MRI, what’s the most likely diagnosis?
vignettes.a: pilocytic astrocytoma. Notice the large solid and cystic lesion. The solid component is white (hyperintense) on the MRI; the cystic component is black (hypointense). This is a HY image for Step 1.

vignettes.q: 54M + 3-month Hx of cognitive disturbance + presents today with seizure; based on the following head CT, what’s the most likely diagnosis?
vignettes.a: glioblastoma multiforme (butterfly glioma); notice the heterogeneity due to areas of necrosis and hemorrhage; it need not cross the midline, but when it does it is sometimes referred to as “butterfly glioma.”

vignettes.q: 16M + developed cataracts at young age + six-month history of left-sided tinnitus and hearing loss; if his diagnosis is the same as that seen in the following gross specimen, what is his most likely underlying
vignettes.a: Dx is acoustic schwannoma occurring at the cerebellopontine junction; in a young patient, neurofibromatosis type II (NF2) is likely etiology; can progress to be bilateral; if elderly patient, usually sporadic and unilateral.

vignettes.q: 56M + nine-year Hx of progressive right-sided hearing loss; MRI shows large mass at the cerebellopontine junction; the mass most likely arises from which nerve and cell type?
vignettes.a: vestibulocochlear nerve and neural crest cells.

vignettes.q: Looking at the following MRI, what’s the diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Chiari malformation, characterized by inferior herniation of the cerebellar tonsils. Note the inferior herniation of the cerebellar tonsils; Chiari type I is characterized by mere herniation and is the answer if the vignette gives

vignettes.q: Learn the following herniation types:
vignettes.a: HY point is that neural tube defects (spina bifida) occur between 3-4 weeks gestation. The pregnant woman needs adequate folic acid (vitamin B9) prior to and during early pregnancy for prevention. Antiepileptics (i.e., particularl

vignettes.q: Newborn + myelomeningocele; what is the affected developmental process?
vignettes.a: “closure of caudal neuropore.”

vignettes.q: 23F at 20 weeks gestation + ultrasound shows fetus with anencephaly; what is the mechanism for this condition?
vignettes.a: “failure of closure of rostral neuropore.”

vignettes.q: Neonate + tuft of hair on midline in lumbar region + palpation of region shows absence of spinous process; what is the mechanism for this condition?
vignettes.a: “failure of fusion of the sclerotomes.”

vignettes.q: Looking at the following MRI, what’s the diagnosis?
vignettes.a: Dandy-Walker malformation; all you need to know: this is the answer if the vignette describes absent cerebellar vermis + cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle.

vignettes.q: Identify the following brain herniation types:
vignettes.a: A = cingulate (subfalcine) herniation; B = transcalvarial herniation; C = central transtentorial herniation; D = uncal herniation; E = upward transtentorial hernation; F = tonsillar herniation.

vignettes.q: The area labeled X on the following diagram notably contains a high density of which kind of channel(s) (i.e., Na, Ca, K, etc.)?
vignettes.a: Area labeled X = node of Ranvier; answer = contains high concentrations of sodium channels.

vignettes.q: Identify the following cranial nerve lesions:
vignettes.a: A = lesion of CN III (oculomotor) → presents as down and out; B = CN IV lesion (trochlear) → presents as upward gaze + patient will tilt head toward unaffected side; C = CN VI (abducens) → medially directed eye. PCoM aneurysmal co

vignettes.q: 31F + Hx of multiple sclerosis + presents with the following visual problem; where is the location of her pathology?
vignettes.a: right parietal lobe (contralateral inferior quadrantanopsia).

vignettes.q: 45F + lung cancer + 2-week Hx of progressive loss of vision of the left visual field of both eyes; if MRI of the brain is performed, metastases might be seen where?
vignettes.a: right occipital Lobe; Dx is homonymous hemianopia.

vignettes.q: “Can you explain that Marcus-Gunn pupil and optic neuritis stuff?”
vignettes.a: MG pupil caused by CN II (optic nerve) lesion, classically as a result of optic neuritis in flare of multiple sclerosis; because of the CN II lesion, the intensity of the light is under-sensed by that eye (afferent signal), so the

vignettes.q: 45M + presents with the left pupil larger than the right pupil after undergoing cranial surgery; which letter on the following image best reflects the location of his pathology?
vignettes.a: D (CN III; oculomotor nerve), lesion can cause down and out pupil and/or mydriasis; this illustration of the cavernous sinus is exceedingly HY for Step 1. A = cavernous sinus; B = sphenoid sinus; C = internal carotid artery; E = t

vignettes.q: 34M + sinus infection one week ago treated with amoxicillin/clavulanate + now presents with diplopia, ophthalmoplegia, and headache + has fever of 103F; Dx?
vignettes.a: cavernous sinus thrombosis; sinus infections can ascend to cavernous sinus via the valveless facial veins; the sequence of sinus infection followed by fever, diplopia, and ophthalmoplegia is classic for cavernous sinus thrombosis;

vignettes.q: 41F + new-onset neurologic dysfunction following surgery of her sphenoid sinus; what additional finding is likely present on the examination?
vignettes.a: inability to abduct eye (abducens nerve injury); CN VI is most medial / closest to the sphenoid sinus and is susceptible to injury.

vignettes.q: 22M + needs to undergo laminectomy; where on the following illustration of a vertebra is the most appropriate location for surgical entrance to the neural canal?
vignettes.a: E (lamina); A = transverse process; B = pedicle; C = vertebral body; D = facet joints; F = spinous process. Should be noted as a tangential factoid that the vertebral arteries (first branch of subclavians) ascend bilaterally throu

vignettes.q: 17M + undergoing spinal surgery + if needle is inserted posteriorly between L3 and L4 vertebral arches, what ligament must be traversed to reach the spinal canal?
vignettes.a: Answer = ligamentum Flavum.

vignettes.q: 24M + lumbar disc herniation; which spinal ligament is pushed into the spinal root nerves?
vignettes.a: posterior longitudinal ligament.

vignettes.q: 63M + pain radiating down distal anterior thigh, knee, medial leg, and medial foot; compression of nerve root in which intervertebral foramina is most likely the cause of her symptoms? → answer = L3-L4.
vignettes.a: HY dermatomes and reflexes: C5 = biceps jerk; C7 = triceps reflex; T4 = nipples; T10 = umbilicus; L1 = groin; L3/4 = knee jerk; S1 = ankle jerk + sole of foot.

vignettes.q: 32F + gestational pemphigoid with itchy vesicles around the umbilicus; her pain is sensed by which dermatome?

52M + sudden loss of vision in right eye + no pain + central scotoma of visual field + fundoscopy shows pale opaque fundus and bright red fovea centralis; 8 months later, if right eye is illuminated, what react
vignettes.a: “no constriction because retinal ganglion cells in right eye have been destroyed”; normal loop should be CN II of right eye signaling (afferent) to midbrain, with CN III relaying efferent parasympathetic activity back to both eyes

vignettes.q: 42F + complains of diplopia + can read books normally + decreased adduction in left eye when gazing to the right; what is the likely location of the demyelinating plaque causing these symptoms?
vignettes.a: left MLF (internuclear ophthalmoplegia).

vignettes.q: 68M + transient ischemic attack + new-onset anterograde Amnesia; what is the most likely affected location?
vignettes.a: hippocampus, which is known to be very sensitive to ischemic insult; it is also an answer sometimes for Alzheimer (progressive shrinking of hippocampus and nucleus Basalis of Maynert).
