vignettes.q: 35F + chronic pain in arm since MVA last year + says to physician “I’m realizing I’ll be like this forever.” Question wants most appropriate response; answer = “have you been feeling like just giving up?”
vignettes.a: must assess suicide risk.

vignettes.q: Patient with restless leg syndrome is at increased risk for what disease later in life?
vignettes.a: answer on USMLE = Parkinson disease (if D2 agonist can Tx, then lack of dopamine transmission may be etiology in some patients).

vignettes.q: 58M + loses consciousness while shaving + tilt-table test shows no abnormalities; Dx?
vignettes.a: NBME wants “carotid sinus hypersensitivity” as answer. If tilt-table test (+), answer = vasovagal syncope.

vignettes.q: 45F + fundoscopy shows hard exudates + cotton wool spots + scattered hemorrhages; Dx?
vignettes.a: diabetic retinopathy.

vignettes.q: Medication that can cause tardive dyskinesia that is not an antipsychotic?
vignettes.a: metoclopramide (D2 antagonist); can also prolong QT interval and cause hyperprolactinemia.

vignettes.q: Anti-depressant med causing seizures?
vignettes.a: bupropion.

vignettes.q: 18M + enters emergency department; which blood parameter would indicate recent alcohol intoxication?
vignettes.a: elevation of serum GGT.

vignettes.q: 56M + 3-day Hx of cutting from 12 beers a day down to 4; develops tremulousness; Tx?
vignettes.a: chlordiazepoxide (delirium tremens); classic vignette is guy has surgery + two days later has tachycardia, tremulousness, and hallucinations (alcoholic hallucinosis).

vignettes.q: 32M + fear of flying; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: specific phobia; Tx with benzo.

vignettes.q: 32M + fear of public speaking (glossophobia); Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: social phobia, not specific phobia; Tx = atenolol (propranolol also OK).

vignettes.q: 25F + fear of flying + must fly soon; Tx?
vignettes.a: lorazepam → specific phobia.

vignettes.q: Psych NBME form has both vignettes, practically identical, with the same answer choices:
vignettes.a: 27M + asthma + very anxious about speech he needs to make soon; Tx? → Psych NBME wants lorazepam, not propranolol (because asthma patient). 27M + very anxious about speech he needs to make soon; Tx? → Psych NBME wants propranolol,

vignettes.q: Antipsychotic medication started + muscle rigidity + no fever; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: acute dystonia, not neuroleptic malignant syndrome (because no fever); Tx with benztropine (muscarinic receptor antagonist) or diphenhydramine (1st gen H1 blocker, which has strong anti-muscarinic side-effects).

vignettes.q: Antipsychotic medication started + abnormal eye movements + stiff neck; Dx?
vignettes.a: acute dystonia (oculogyric crisis + torticollis).

vignettes.q: Antipsychotic medication started + muscle rigidity + fever; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: neuroleptic malignant syndrome; give dantrolene (inhibits ryanodine channel).

vignettes.q: Antipsychotic med + bradykinesia; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: drug-induced Parkinsonism; Tx with amantadine or propranolol.

vignettes.q: Mechanism for tardive dyskinesia?
vignettes.a: answer on Psych NBME = “increased sensitivity of dopamine receptors.”

vignettes.q: 8-month-old boy + 3rd -centile for weight + slanted palpebral fissures + epicanthal folds + single palmar crease + thin upper lip with a “fish mouth” appearance + indistinct nasal philtrum; Dx?
vignettes.a: answer on Psych NBME = fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), not Down syndrome; everyone says about this question, so what I tell my students is: if Q sounds like Down syndrome but they mention anything about the philtrum (i.e., long, smo

vignettes.q: 6M + IQ of 60 + small for age + born to female age 41 + no other information given; Q asks: most likely cause of mental retardation?
vignettes.a: Down syndrome, not FAS; although FAS is most common cause of MR overall, two points: 1) if they want FAS, they’ll mention the philtrum as per above, and 2) most common cause of MR over the age of 40 is Down, not FAS.

vignettes.q: 8M + prominent jaw + protruding ears + IQ of 65; most likely explanation?
vignettes.a: “Fragile site on the X chromosome” → Fragile X (CGG TNR disorder).

vignettes.q: 7M + prominent ears + flattened nasal bridge + long philtrum + low IQ; Dx?
vignettes.a: FAS, not Fragile X; the Q mentions the philtrum.

vignettes.q: 4F + wringing of the hands + putting objects in her mouth + less eye contact; Dx?
vignettes.a: Rett syndrome; only seen in girls; hyperoralism may reflect cognitive regression (babies put everything in their mouths).

vignettes.q: 5M + talks to imaginary friends; Dx?
vignettes.a: age-appropriate behavior.

vignettes.q: 7F + preoccupation with death + fear of dying + constantly asking parents about dying; Dx?
vignettes.a: age- appropriate behavior. Weird, but the NBME will do what it wants.

vignettes.q: 40F + headaches + abdo pain + mild weight loss + fatigue + 5/9 SIGECAPS not met + no mention of low mood; Dx?
vignettes.a: NBME wants somatization disorder, not MDD; this Q is a little challenging, as mere weight loss/gain + low mood will often be MDD, particularly in elderly; somatization disorder Dx is recurring, multiple, current somatic complaints

vignettes.q: 59M + wife says he has bizarre behavior at night where he jumps out of bed and runs back and forth across the room punching the air + says he does not recall such behavior but remembers bad dreams; Dx?
vignettes.a: REM sleep behavior disorder → incomplete or absent REM muscle atonia; tends to occur in older adult men; if recurrent, may indicate onset of neurodegenerative disorder like Parkinson disease.

vignettes.q: 8M + gets out of bed at night and tries to leave the house; when his mom tries to stop him, he violently tries to pull away from her; once he got out of the house and woke up outside while in the middle of an e
vignettes.a: sleep terror disorder; tends to occur in pre-adolescent boys.

vignettes.q: 23M + used synthetic heroin + diffuse stiffness + drooling; Dx?
vignettes.a: MPTP-induced Parkinsonian syndrome → affects substantia nigra; MPTP-containing powder is sometimes sold as “synthetic heroin.”

vignettes.q: 42M prisoner + can’t feel his foot + pulses and reflexes normal; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: malingering (secondary gain – i.e., money, drugs, time away from prison; not willing to undergo invasive procedures) → “no treatment indicated.”

vignettes.q: Serum abnormalities seen in bulimic patient?
vignettes.a: increased serum amylase + hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.

vignettes.q: 18F + repeated purging + BMI 17; Dx?
vignettes.a: anorexia, not bulimia → if BMI low, answer is anorexia.

vignettes.q: 18F + anorexia; what electrolyte disturbance is most likely?
vignettes.a: hypokalemia.

vignettes.q: 18F + anorexia + BMI of 14 + reintroduced to foods; what electrolyte must we notably look out for?
vignettes.a: hypophosphatemia (refeeding syndrome).

vignettes.q: 26M + lost in the woods for three weeks + BMI 27 + reintroduced to foods; what electrolyte must we notably look out for?
vignettes.a: hypophosphatemia (refeeding syndrome).

vignettes.q: Amenorrhea in patient with anorexia; why?
vignettes.a: decreased GnRH pulsation → decreased LH + FSH; Q wants “↓ FHS, ↓ estrogen” as the answer; in contrast, premature ovarian failure, Turner syndrome, and menopause have “↑ FHS, ↓ estrogen” as the answer.

vignettes.q: Anorexia in patient with edema; mechanism for edema?
vignettes.a: decreased serum albumin (yes, this is straight from the Psych NBME, no idea why).

vignettes.q: 45M + has repeated thoughts of harming his son + finds the thoughts absolutely outrageous and disturbing + says he would never do such a thing; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) → obsessions are the thoughts; compulsions are the actions; OCD can be just obsessions without actions; Tx is CBT and/or SSRI.

vignettes.q: 33M + witnessed construction accident at work where many people were injured + found by police in bowling alley parking lot talking to himself + unable to respond to questions about his identity; Dx?
vignettes.a: dissociative fugue (dissociative disorder); fugue = amnesia for personal identity + travel.

vignettes.q: Tx of panic attack vs panic disorder?
vignettes.a: benzo on USMLE. For panic disorder, Tx = SSRI.

vignettes.q: Fainting in panic disorder; why?
vignettes.a: “decreased cerebral perfusion,” or “cerebral hypoperfusion”; hyperventilation → decreased CO2 → causes decreased cerebral blood flow.

vignettes.q: 56M + depressed mood + sleep apnea; Dx?
vignettes.a: mood disorder due to a general medical condition.

vignettes.q: 22F + hyperphagia + hypersomnolence + improved mood with pleasurable events; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: atypical depression; Tx = SSRI, not MAOi; MAOi (e.g., phenelzine) are considered highly efficacious but carry dangerous side-effects, so SSRIs remain first-line.

vignettes.q: 22M + schizophrenia + poor adherence to medications; best med to give to Tx?
vignettes.a: haloperidol decanoate.

vignettes.q: 26F in Australia picking peaches + pinpoint pupils; Q is “how could this have been prevented?”
vignettes.a: “wearing gloves,” not “use of facemask.” Apparently organophosphate poisoning is acquired through skin, not droplets.

vignettes.q: Tx for organophosphate poisoning?
vignettes.a: atropine before pralidoxime. Retired NBME 15 or 16 for Step 1 has both as answers, and atropine is correct.

vignettes.q: 57M + trouble with intercourse with his wife + has nocturnal erections; Dx?
vignettes.a: secondary erectile dysfunction (psychological) → if nocturnal tumescence is intact, he’s physiologically fine.

vignettes.q: 57M + recently divorced + now sleeping with new women + cannot ejaculate during sex + achieves erection during sex with no problem; Dx?
vignettes.a: performance anxiety.

vignettes.q: Tx for premature ejaculation?
vignettes.a: SSRI.

vignettes.q: 44M + comes in dressed all in yellow + high energy; Dx?
vignettes.a: histrionic personality disorder.

vignettes.q: 44F + sexual toward doctor + high energy; Dx?
vignettes.a: histrionic personality disorder

vignettes.q: 16F + slice marks on wrists and thighs + Hx of two prior broken engagements; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: borderline personality disorder; parasuicidal behavior common (suicidal gestures, but not true attempts at suicide); Tx = dialectal behavioral therapy (DBT).

vignettes.q: Defense mechanism in borderline personality disorder?
vignettes.a: splitting: “all doctors are bad; all nurses are good.”

vignettes.q: 26M + works at plastics factory + quiet/loner; Dx?
vignettes.a: schizoid personality disorder (ego-syntonic).

vignettes.q: 47F + highly sensitive to rejection + poor self-esteem; Dx?
vignettes.a: avoidant personality disorder (ego- dystonic).

vignettes.q: 26M + “wild thinking” + no auditory hallucinations; Dx?
vignettes.a: schizotypal personality disorder.

vignettes.q: 8M + causes frequent disruption at school and at home; Dx?
vignettes.a: ADHD; Tx = methylphenidate.

vignettes.q: 16M + disruptive in class + numerous suspensions from school + caught stealing at the mall; Dx?
vignettes.a: conduct disorder → pattern of law-breaking + must be under age 18; in contrast, a patient with oppositional defiant disorder does not break the law.

vignettes.q: 27M + cheated on the Bar Exam + fired from job at 23 for stealing + arrested for drunk driving in high school; Dx?
vignettes.a: antisocial personality disorder; key detail is: must break the law; must be older than age 18 and must have had conduct disorder prior to age 15 → in other words, just because an adult breaks the law does not mean he or she has AS

vignettes.q: 60M + recovering from a recent MI; he is at high risk of which of the following?
vignettes.a: MDD → common following major adverse events (e.g., trauma, serious Dx); give sertraline for post-MI MDD.

vignettes.q: Is abuse reportable?
vignettes.a: child + elderly abuse: yes. Domestic abuse: no. Answer for latter is to provide supportive care + as much information as possible about what she can do if she feels unsafe.

vignettes.q: 72M + wife passed away 5 months ago + sometimes hears her voice at night; Dx?
vignettes.a: normal bereavement.

vignettes.q: 72M + wife passed away 7 months ago + still grieves; Dx?
vignettes.a: pathological grief (normal grief is <6 months).

vignettes.q: 72M + wife passed away 3 months ago + 5kg weight loss + cries + guilt; Dx?
vignettes.a: MDD (weight loss/gain is huge indicator MDD in elderly).

vignettes.q: 22M + 1mm pupils + RR of 8 + stuporous; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Dx = Opioid/heroin overdose; Tx = naloxone.

vignettes.q: Different between obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD)?
vignettes.a: OCD is ego-dystonic (patient doesn’t want/like the thoughts/actions); OCPD is ego-syntonic (patient is content / not looking to modify behavior).

vignettes.q: Tx for diabetic neuropathic pain?
vignettes.a: TCA (i.e., amitriptyline). Second-line is gabapentin

vignettes.q: Tx for herpetic / post-herpetic neuralgia (i.e., from shingles)?
vignettes.a: gabapentin

vignettes.q: 82M diabetic + neuropathic pain + already taking carbamazepine + gabapentin to no avail; next best step?
vignettes.a: switch the meds to nortriptyline (a TCA) → student then asks, “Wait, I thought you said TCAs are first-line. Why does this Q have the guy on those two meds then?” → two points: 1) we don’t like giving TCAs to elderly because of th

vignettes.q: How to differentiate cluster headache from trigeminal neuralgia?
vignettes.a: cluster will be a male 20s-40s with 11/10 lancinating pain behind the eye waking him up at night (he may pace around the room until it goes away); details such as lacrimation and rhinorrhea are too easy and will likely not show up

vignettes.q: Tx and prophylaxis for cluster headache?
vignettes.a: Tx = 100% oxygen; prophylaxis = verapamil.

vignettes.q: Tx and prophylaxis for trigeminal neuralgia?
vignettes.a: Tx = goes away on its own because it lasts only seconds; prophylaxis = carbamazepine.

vignettes.q: Tx and prophylaxis for migraine?
vignettes.a: Tx = NSAID, followed by triptan (triptans are NOT prophylaxis; they are for abortive therapy only after NSAIDs); prophylaxis = propranolol.

vignettes.q: 32M + diffuse headache relieved by acetaminophen + sleep; Dx?
vignettes.a: tension-type headache.

vignettes.q: 44F + diplopia + dysphagia + eyelid ptosis; all worsen throughout the day; Dx?
vignettes.a: myasthenia gravis (MG).

vignettes.q: 44F + proximal muscle weakness + able to perform upward gaze without a problem for 60 seconds; Dx?
vignettes.a: Lambert-Eaton (LE) syndrome (if cannot perform, answer = MG).

vignettes.q: Vignette where Dx is either MG or LE but it’s not listed; answer?
vignettes.a: “neuromuscular junction.”

vignettes.q: 44F + difficulty getting up from chair but is able to after several attempts; Dx?
vignettes.a: LE.

vignettes.q: Mechanism of MG vs LE?
vignettes.a: MG = antibodies against postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors; LE = antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels.

vignettes.q: MG can sometimes be paraneoplastic syndromes of which cancer?
vignettes.a: MG from thymoma (do chest imaging to check for thymoma after Dx of MG; if thymoma present + removed, this cures the MG). Up to 80% of patients with thymoma + MG have anti-MUSK Abs (muscle-specific kinase).

vignettes.q: LE can sometimes be a paraneoplastic syndrome of which cancer?
vignettes.a: small cell lung cancer.

vignettes.q: How to Dx MG vs LE?
vignettes.a: If both are listed, choose antibodies over Tensilon (edrophonium) test.

vignettes.q: What is edrophonium
vignettes.a: short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.

vignettes.q: How do MG vs LE perform with edrophonium?
vignettes.a: MG improves drastically; LE less change.

vignettes.q: Tx of MG?
vignettes.a: give an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (i.e., pyridostigmine).

vignettes.q: 6M + ECG shows miscellaneous arrhythmia + seizure-like episode; Dx?
vignettes.a: Adam-Stokes attack → not true seizure disorder as per EEG; arrythmia leads to hypoxia of brainstem → seizure-like fits ensue.

vignettes.q: 75M + episodes of loss of consciousness (LoC) for 2 years + tonic-clonic-like episodes + becomes pale and sweaty + Hx of MI; Dx?
vignettes.a: “syncope” on the NBME (convulsive syncope).

vignettes.q: Mechanism of narcolepsy?
vignettes.a: deficiency of orexin (hypocretin).

vignettes.q: What is cataplexy?
vignettes.a: loss of muscle tone usually in response to emotional stimulus (e.g., laughter) → seen in narcolepsy.

vignettes.q: Polysomnography findings in narcolepsy?
vignettes.a: REM latency: ↓; sleep latency: ↓.

vignettes.q: What is simple vs complex seizure?
vignettes.a: simple = no LoC; complex = LoC; patient staring off into space not aware of surroundings = LoC.

vignettes.q: What is partial vs generalized seizure?
vignettes.a: partial = affecting one part of the brain; generalized = involves the wholes of both cerebral hemispheres.

vignettes.q: Tx of serotonin syndrome?
vignettes.a: cyproheptadine (serotonin receptor antagonist).

vignettes.q: Difference between serotonin syndrome and carcinoid syndrome?
vignettes.a: serotonin syndrome is from drug-drug interactions and notably causes hyperpyrexia (high fever), tachycardia, and tachypnea; carcinoid syndrome is a result of carcinoid tumors (usually small bowel, appendiceal, or bronchial) secret

vignettes.q: How to Dx + Tx carcinoid syndrome?
vignettes.a: Dx with urinary 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindole acetic acid); Tx with octreotide, among other agents.

vignettes.q: Patient witnesses terror attack + has felt emotionally numb for two years since + sometimes disturbed sleep; next best step?
vignettes.a: “provide information about the ranges of reactions to trauma.”

vignettes.q: 64M + Parkinson disease + 2-month Hx of paranoid behavior; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: Dx is Parkinson disease psychosis (PDP); Tx on shelf = quetiapine (can Tx with quetiapine or clonidine).

vignettes.q: 45M + survived plane crash two weeks ago + wakes up screaming in middle of night reliving the event; Dx?
vignettes.a: acute stress disorder, not post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD); acute stress disorder is < 1 month; PTSD is > 1 month. Treatment for both is CBT.

vignettes.q: Tx for TCA toxicity?
vignettes.a: sodium bicarb → causes dissociation of drug from myocardial sodium channels.

vignettes.q: 25M + schizophrenic non-responsive to many meds + started on new drug + mouth ulcers; Dx?
vignettes.a: agranulocytosis secondary to clozapine; stop drug immediately; must do granulocyte checks frequently when first commencing this agent.

vignettes.q: 16M + BMI 31 + snores loudly + morning headaches + 3-5 beats of jerk nystagmus with lateral gaze; Dx?
vignettes.a: “sleep-related hypoventilation”; nystagmus is weird finding, but it’s on the Psych NBME; morning headaches are common in sleep-related hypoventilation; can do polysomnography to diagnose. HY PSYCH

vignettes.q: High calcium + confusion
vignettes.a: delirium caused by high calcium

vignettes.q: Bulimia nervosa or anorexia
vignettes.a: never give buproprion (seizure risk)

vignettes.q: Electrolyte abnormality in anorexia
vignettes.a: hypokalemia

vignettes.q: Most common cause of death in anorexia
vignettes.a: arrhythmia from hypokalemia

vignettes.q: Tx of anorexia + depression
vignettes.a: mirtazapine (alpha-2 antagonist); stimulates appetite

vignettes.q: Amenorrhea in anorexia
vignettes.a: low FSH + low estrogen (hypogonadotropic)

vignettes.q: Trichotillomania (eating one’s hair) + GI symptoms
vignettes.a: gastric bezoar (hair ball)

vignettes.q: HY drugs that cause agranulocytosis
vignettes.a: clozapine, ganciclovir, propylthiouracil, methimazole, methotrexate, ticlopidine

vignettes.q: Difference between meningitis and encephalitis
vignettes.a: meningitis is nuchal rigidity (neck stiffness) + photophobia + ophthalmoplegia; encephalitis presents with confusion

vignettes.q: Pt has tachy + diaphoresis + diarrhea after drug
vignettes.a: serotonin syndrome (tramadol; MOA too soon after stopping SSRI)

vignettes.q: Tx of serotonin syndrome
vignettes.a: remove offending agents + administer cyproheptadine (serotonin receptor antagonist)

vignettes.q: 42M has surgery + two days later in hospital he has restlessness + tremulousness + tachycardia + diaphoresis; Dx?
vignettes.a: delirium tremens (alcohol withdrawal)

vignettes.q: When is buspirone the answer?
vignettes.a: second-line Tx for generalized anxiety disorder (first-line is SSRI).

vignettes.q: Kid is given over-the-counter med by his mom for a cold + gets mental status changes; Dx?
vignettes.a: anticholinergic delirium caused by first-generation antihistamine (e.g., diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine).

vignettes.q: 30F + last menstrual period 8 weeks ago + USS shows no obvious fetus or gestational sac + curettage shows trophoblastic proliferation; what will chromosomal analysis of this tissue show?
vignettes.a: 46XX; Dx = complete mole; empty egg fertilized by one sperm that then duplicates (i.e., genetic material is only of paternal origin); complete mole has no fetal parts; partial mole carries 67 chromosomal karyotype → one egg fertil

vignettes.q: 44M + recent surgery in hospital + tachycardia + fever + high BP; what drug should be administered?
vignettes.a: chlordiazepoxide; Dx is delirium tremens (alcohol withdrawal); Tx is benzo (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide). If the Q asks why tremulousness (tremor) present in delirium tremens, the answer is beta-2 agonism.

vignettes.q: 32F + one-year Hx of amenorrhea + had dilation & curettage performed to remove miscarriage last year; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: Asherman syndrome; uterine synechiae (scarring) due to instrumentation within the uterus; NBME likes amenorrhea as the major symptom.

vignettes.q: Neonate born with small right ventricle; risk factor?
vignettes.a: lithium during pregnancy is risk factor for Ebstein anomaly (atrialization of right ventricle).

vignettes.q: 54M + recovering in hospital from ARDS secondary to pancreatitis + currently being weaned from a ventilator. This is all the Q says and they want you to pick the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for TSH, T3, T4, and r
vignettes.a: ↔ TSH, ↔ T4, ↓ T3, ↑ rT3. — This is where a lot of students say ? Relax. • Diagnosis is euthyroid sick syndrome (or sick euthyroid syndrome). • Vignette will either be patient being weaned from a ventilator, or a patient who’s had

vignettes.q: 35F + long history of dry cough + fever + chest x-ray shows bihilar lymphadenopathy. What are the most likely arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for fecal calcium, 24,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3, and 1,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3?
vignettes.a: ↓ Fecal calcium, ↓ 24,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3, ↑ 1,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3. — Diagnosis is sarcoidosis. Fever can sometimes be seen in autoimmune flares even when there’s no infection of any kind. • The non-caseating granulomas are secret

vignettes.q: 38F + in hospital recovering from C-section 48 hours ago + sore left leg + acute-onset shortness of breath and tachycardia. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for pH, HCO3-, and CO2?
vignettes.a: ↑ pH, ↔ HCO3- , ↓ CO2. — Diagnosis is pulmonary embolism. • Patients have respiratory alkalosis because respiratory rate is increased (tachypnea). • CO2 diffuses quickly. O2 diffuses slowly. This means that even if lung pathology

vignettes.q: 12M + wheezing and difficulty breathing on the soccer field past 10 minutes; family Hx of eczema and seasonal allergies. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for pH, HCO3-, and CO2?
vignettes.a: ↑ pH, ↔ HCO3- , ↓ CO2. — Diagnosis is acute asthma attack. • Similar to pulmonary embolism, CO2 is low because the patient is hyperventilating, so we have an acute respiratory alkalosis. • Bicarbonate is unchanged because it takes

vignettes.q: 12M + wheezing on soccer field and in respiratory distress + given nebulized albuterol. After 40 minutes, O2 remains low. Respiratory rate is 6 per minute. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for pH, HCO3-,
vignettes.a: ↓ pH, ↔ HCO3- , ↑ CO2. — The patient has respiratory acidosis due to respiratory fatigue. • Initially in an asthma attack, we have respiratory alkalosis, not acidosis, because respiratory rate is high in order to try to get oxygen

vignettes.q: 16F + called to principal’s office + hyperventilates. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for pH, HCO3- , CO2, cerebral perfusion?
vignettes.a: ↑ pH, ↔ HCO3- , ↓ CO2. — This patient has a panic attack. Hyperventilation causes a respiratory alkalosis. • Bicarbonate is unchanged because it takes 12-24 hours for the kidney to significantly alter reabsorption/excretion. • Dec

vignettes.q: 68M + long history of COPD + not in acute distress. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑ or ↓) for pH, HCO3-, and CO2?
vignettes.a: ↓ pH, ↑ HCO3, ↑ CO2. — Patients with COPD are chronic CO2 retainers and will have chronic respiratory acidosis. • Since this is a chronic process, bicarbonate is elevated as compensation. Patients may have blood pH that is normal

vignettes.q: 60F + recovering in hospital following hip surgery + on morphine for pain; physical examination shows mild crackles at the lung bases bilaterally. Respiratory rate is 8 per minute. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑
vignettes.a: ↑ CO2, ↔ A-a gradient. — Opioids (such as morphine), barbiturates, and benzodiazepines can all cause respiratory depression and respiratory acidosis. CO2 is increased since respiratory rate is low (NR 12-16/minute). • A-a gradient

vignettes.q: 8M + Hx of recurrent lung infections + failure to pass meconium at birth + increased pulmonary vascular markings seen on chest x-ray + loud P2 heart sound + right bundle branch block + JVD. What are the arrows
vignettes.a: ↔ PCWP, ↓ 24,25-(OH)2-vitamin D3. — Diagnosis is cor pulmonale due to cystic fibrosis (CF). • Cor pulmonale is defined as right heart failure due to a pulmonary cause (i.e., COPD, CF, pulmonary fibrosis, etc.). • Recall that PCWP

vignettes.q: 47M + occasional color change of fingers with cold + Hx of gastroesophageal reflux + one-year Hx of worsening shortness of breath. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑ or ↓) for ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratio, anti-
vignettes.a: ↓ V/Q, ↑ anti-centromere antibodies, ↓ anti-mitochondrial antibodies. — Diagnosis is pulmonary fibrosis secondary to limited systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome). • Patients can develop pulmonary fibrosis in both limited and diffus

vignettes.q: 40F + heavy smoker past 20 years + taking combined oral contraceptive pills + develops acute-onset shortness of breath and tachycardia. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for pH, CO2, bicarb, and V/Q?
vignettes.a: ↑ pH, ↓ CO2, ↔ HCO3- , ↑ V/Q. — Diagnosis is pulmonary embolism. Combined oral contraceptive pills are contraindicated in women over 35 who are smokers because of increased risk for thromboembolic events. • As discussed earlier, i

vignettes.q: 55M + non-smoker + 6-month Hx of progressive shortness of breath and dry cough + CT of the chest shows reticulonodular pattern (“honeycombing”). What are the arrows (i.e., ↑ or ↓) for forced expiratory volume (
vignettes.a: ↓ FEV1, ↓ FVC, ↑ FEV1/FVC. — Diagnosis is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a type of restrictive lung disease. • FEV1/FVC can be normal or increased in restrictive lung disease. Sometimes Qs will only give one arrow direction and fo

vignettes.q: 70F + healthy + has pulmonary function tests performed as part of a study. In comparison to a healthy woman age 20, what are her arrows (i.e., ↑ or ↓) for FEV1, FVC, and FEV1/FVC?
vignettes.a: ↓ FEV1, ↓ FVC, ↓ FEV1/FVC. — USMLE wants you to know that people naturally develop obstructive lung disease throughout the course of their lives, likely as a result of lifetime inhalation of particulates. • These arrows are the sa

vignettes.q: 25M + non-smoker + progressively worsening shortness of breath + chest x-ray shows bullous changes; dad died of alcoholic liver disease at age 45. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for residual volume, art
vignettes.a: ↑ residual volume, ↓ arterial pO2, ↑ A-a gradient. — Diagnosis is a1-antitrypsin deficiency. • Classically causes pan-acinar emphysema and cirrhosis of the liver. • a1-antitrypsin is a protease produced in the liver that breaks do

vignettes.q: Neonate born at 26 weeks’ gestation + respiratory distress. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for pulmonary compliance, pulmonary elastic recoil, pulmonary sphingomyelin, and lamellar body activity?
vignettes.a: ↓ pulmonary compliance, ↑ elastic recoil, ↑ sphingomyelin, ↓ lamellar body activity. — Diagnosis is neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS), caused by surfactant deficiency. • Compliance = ability to expand. • Elastic recoil

vignettes.q: 50M + long history of smoking + COPD. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for mucous production, activity of airway cilia, and alveolar macrophage function?
vignettes.a: ↑ mucous production, ↓ activity of airway cilia, ↓ alveolar macrophage function. — In COPD, bronchiolar mucous production is increased (increased Reid index ratio). • Cilia function of pseudostratified columnar epithelial cells of

vignettes.q: 65M + orthopnea + paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, alveolar interstitial hydrostatic pressure, and alveolar interstitial oncotic
vignettes.a: ↑ pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure, ↑ alveolar interstitial hydrostatic pressure, ↓ alveolar interstitial oncotic pressure. — The patient has left heart failure. The backup of pressure from the left heart causes increased

vignettes.q: 55M + long history of systemic hypertension + chest x-ray shows pleural effusion and diffuse pulmonary infiltrates; ECG shows left bundle-branch block. If we are forced to pick high or low values, what are the
vignettes.a: ↓ Pleural fluid LDH, ↓ pleural fluid protein, ↑ glucose. — Patient has fluid in his lungs due to increased pressures in his left heart secondary to systemic hypertension. • LBBB = left ventricular hypertrophy on USMLE. • The fluid

vignettes.q: 22F + iron deficiency anemia. Compared to individuals without IDA, what are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for arterial pO2, hemoglobin saturation, and arterial O2 content?
vignettes.a: ↔ Arterial pO2, ↔ hemoglobin saturation, ↓ arterial O2 content. — NBME loves this Q. It’s repeated across forms. • Arterial O2 content = oxygen dissolved in the blood (pO2) + oxygen bound to hemoglobin (Hb-O2). • The pathway for o

vignettes.q: Shunt = ↓ V/Q
vignettes.a: refers to almost all lung conditions on USMLE.

vignettes.q: Dead space = ↑ V/Q
vignettes.a: refers to basically just pulmonary embolism on USMLE.

vignettes.q: ↓ V/Q can also refer to the physiologic (i.e., normal) shunt we see at the lung bases, where V/Q is 0.6. This is because despite both ventilation and perfusion ↑ apex
vignettes.a: base, gravity pulls blood down more greatly than air, so perfusion ↑↑ toward the bases, whereas ventilation only ↑. So V/Q is ↓ at the bases (shunt).

vignettes.q: But the above needs to be taken with a caveat. For example, the Q might say the patient is on a ventilator and has arterial pO2 of 40 mm Hg (normal is 80-100) + FiO2 is 100% + tidal volume is 1000 mL, and the a
vignettes.a: Sure, but we can’t do that here because pO2 is super-low, so that would only exacerbate it further.

vignettes.q: They also ask the inverse of this on NBME – i.e., they say an anesthesiologist wants to ↑ a patient’s cerebral perfusion, and the answer is “decrease respiratory rate”
vignettes.a: causes ↑ CO2 → ↑ cerebral perfusion.

vignettes.q: Patients should ideally be weaned from ventilators as quickly as possible. USMLE also likes patients who are sick on ventilators as sometimes having euthyroid sick syndrome – i.e., they will say patient cannot
vignettes.a: euthyroid sick syndrome. The full array of arrows are: ↓ T3, ↑ rT3, ↔ T4, ↔ TSH. If you have no idea what I’m talking about, then I recommend going through my HY Arrows PDF.

vignettes.q: 58F + 6-month Hx of shortness of breath and non-productive cough + 2-year Hx of worsening dysphagia + 20-yr Hx of hands turning white when exposed to cold; what lung condition is this patient most at risk of de
vignettes.a: pulmonary hypertension → pulmonary fibrosis common in CREST syndrome (scleroderma; limited systemic sclerosis) → pulmonary fibrosis seen in both diffuse and limited types of systemic sclerosis; the latter is sans the renal phenome

vignettes.q: What will the USMLE frequently say in the Q if they’re hinting at pulmonary hypertension?
vignettes.a: HY vignette descriptors are loud S2 or P2 (pulmonic valve slams shut when the distal pressure is high); dilation of proximal pulmonary arteries; increased pulmonary vascular markings (congestion + increased hydrostatic pressure).

vignettes.q: When is “pulmonary hypertension” important as the answer? → notably in Eisenmenger syndrome and cor pulmonale.
vignettes.a: Regarding Eisenmenger: the reversal of the L-to-R shunt across the VSD such that it’s R-to-L requires the tunica media of the pulmonary arterioles to hypertrophy secondary to chronic increased preload → proximal backup of hydrosta

vignettes.q: “Please explain PCWP. I’ve seen that before but no idea what that means or how it applies to questions.” → If you stick a catheter into the venous circulation and feed it all the way back up to the right heart
vignettes.a: Hypovolemic shock arrows → CO down, VR down, TPR up, PCWP down (or low-normal). Cardiogenic shock arrows → CO down, VR down, TPR up, PCWP up. Septic + anaphylactic shock arrows → CO up, VR up, TPR down, PCWP normal. Neurogenic sho

vignettes.q: 23F + non-smoker + gradually worsening shortness of breath + loud P2 + CXR shows increased pulmonary vascular markings; Dx?
vignettes.a: primary pulmonary hypertension → common cause is mutations in BMPR2.

vignettes.q: Treatment of pulmonary hypertension?
vignettes.a: USMLE will generally not make you pick and choose between agents, however it is generally accepted in the literature that dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, such as nifedipine, are effective in vasoreactive pulmonary hypert

vignettes.q: “Am I supposed to know something about endothelin-1?”
vignettes.a: Step 1 pulmonary material has an obsession with it. Be aware that endothelin-1 is a potent vasoconstrictor → so increased endothelin-1 activity is associated with pulmonary hypertension.

vignettes.q: 23F with primary pulmonary hypertension; Q asks which of the following might be seen in this patient; answer = “increased endothelin-1 activity”
vignettes.a: essentially, if bosentan is a HY antagonist of endothelin-1 as a Tx for pulmonary hypertension, then it makes sense that increased activity is correlated with pulmonary hypertension in patients.

vignettes.q: 68M + S3 + crackles in both lungs + JVD + peripheral edema; what would be seen in this patient?
vignettes.a: “increased endothelin-1 activity” → congestive heart failure is defined as right heart failure caused by left heart failure; because the lungs need to accommodate more fluid secondary to the backup from the decompensated left hear

vignettes.q: Which lung cancers are apical vs central?
vignettes.a: Central → sounds like Sentral → Squamous cell, Small cell; peripheral → adenocarcinoma, large cell.

vignettes.q: 45F + non-smoker + apical lung mass; no other information; most likely cancer?
vignettes.a: adenocarcinoma → classically female non-smokers with peripheral lesion, although I’ve seen it show up in a male as well on NBME.

vignettes.q: 45F + non-smoker + peripheral lung mass + proximal muscle weakness + increased serum CK + rash on shoulders; Dx?
vignettes.a: paraneoplastic dermatomyositis secondary to bronchogenic adenocarcinoma.

vignettes.q: 45F + non-smoker + lung mass + thrombosis; lung cancer Dx?
vignettes.a: adenocarcinoma. In general, cancer is associated with hypercoagulable state, but this is particularly the case for adenocarcinomas; in addition, Trousseau sign of malignancy (migratory thrombophlebitis) is characteristic of adenoc

vignettes.q: 45F + long smoking Hx + shooting groin pain; Dx?
vignettes.a: ureterolithiasis secondary to hypercalcemia from bronchogenic squamous cell carcinoma PTHrp (PTH related peptide) secretion.

vignettes.q: 45F + long smoking Hx + shooting groin pain + serum studies show high calcium; what is the patient’s PTH level?
vignettes.a: decreased (suppressed in the setting of high PTHrp).

vignettes.q: 45F + dies of lung cancer + Q shows you gross pathologic specimen of large, cavitating, central lesion; Dx?
vignettes.a: squamous cell carcinoma → cavitations are common.

vignettes.q: 45F + lung cancer + Hx of stabbing flank pain a couple months ago + today presents with confusion; Dx?
vignettes.a: hypercalcemic crisis → squamous cell carcinoma with PTHrp secretion with Hx of nephrolithiasis; high calcium can cause delirium.

vignettes.q: 45F + long smoking Hx + central coin lesion on CXR + violaceous abdominal striae + potassium level of 3.0 mEq/L; Dx?
vignettes.a: small cell carcinoma with ectopic ACTH secretion; student says, “Wait but why’s the potassium low?” → effect of chronically high cortisol (can act to secrete K at distal kidney similar to aldosterone; only seen in ongoing Cushing

vignettes.q: 45F + confirmed Dx of early-stage small cell lung cancer + wobbly gait; Q asks the mechanism for her presentation; answer = autoimmune
vignettes.a: paraneoplastic anti-Hu and anti-Yo antibodies causing cerebellar dysfunction; Dx is small cell cerebellar dysfunction (small cell is known to cause neuronal paraneoplastic syndromes beyond Lambert-Eaton).

vignettes.q: 45F + central lung lesion + confusion + increased urinary osmolality; Dx?
vignettes.a: SIADH secondary to small cell → low serum sodium + high urinary osmolality; should be noted that sodium derangement (high or low), as well as high calcium, can cause CNS disturbance / delirium.

vignettes.q: 45F + long smoking Hx + difficulty getting up from chair but is successful after multiple attempts; what is the location of her pathology?
vignettes.a: neuromuscular junction → small cell paraneoplastic Lambert-Eaton syndrome → antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels.

vignettes.q: 45F non-smoker + episodic flushing, wheezing, and dyspnea + coin lesion seen on CXR; Dx?
vignettes.a: bronchial carcinoid tumor.

vignettes.q: 33F + Hx of recent molar pregnancy + very high serum beta-hCG levels + new-onset non-productive cough; CXR shows multiple peripheral densities in right lobe; Dx?
vignettes.a: metastatic choriocarcinoma (loves to metastasize to the lungs; chorio can progress from hydatidiform mole).

vignettes.q: Do we do lung cancer screening? → Annual low-dose chest CT in patients who meet all of the following:
vignettes.a: Age 50-80. >20-pack-year Hx of smoking. Have smoked in past 15 years.

vignettes.q: What kind of acid-base disturbance do we have in COPD exacerbation?
vignettes.a: Acute on chronic respiratory acidosis. NBME can write this as "chronic respiratory acidosis with acute respiratory acidosis." Patients with COPD are chronic CO2 retainers so will have chronic respiratory acidosis (high CO2, high b

vignettes.q: Why is the FEV1/FVC ratio normal or increased in restrictive?

vignettes.a: “measurement of FEV1 of the right lung” → seemingly weird answer but HY for pulm component of surg shelves → minimum acceptable postoperative FEV1 for both lungs is 800mL.

vignettes.q: What is definition of chronic bronchitis?
vignettes.a: productive cough every day for >3 months in a year for at least two consecutive years; most common cause is smoking.

vignettes.q: 57M + 4-day Hx of productive cough + COPD managed with ipratropium inhaler + afebrile + HR 110 + RR 22 + BP 130/80 + O2 sats 90% + breath sounds decreased bilaterally + CXR shows hyperinflation of both lungs; D
vignettes.a: answer on NBME = “bronchitis” → i.e., acute bronchitis; usually viral.

vignettes.q: Classic way to differentiate COPD from asthma?
vignettes.a: in asthma, spirometry showing decreased respiratory function is largely reversible with albuterol; this is modestly effective at best in COPD; “flattened diaphragm” is classic CXR descriptor for hyperinflated lungs seen in COPD; t

vignettes.q: “What do I need to know about DLCO?”

vignettes.q: 72F + longitudinal study comparing her lung function to 20-yr-olds’ lungs; what changes would we expect in her versus young individuals?
vignettes.a: residual volume ↑; arterial pO2 ↓; A-a pO2 gradient ↑; essentially, people develop obstructive lung disease changes as they age (likely due to lifelong inhalation of particulates, akin to smoking).

vignettes.q: 38F smoker + study performed comparing her to healthy individuals; what changes would we expect in her compared to non-smokers
vignettes.a: mucous production and secretion ↑; activity of airway cilia ↓; alveolar macrophage function ↓; increased mucous production and secretion reflects changes tending toward bronchitis; activity of airway cilia decreases with exposure

vignettes.q: What is one of the most important descriptors in a Q for restrictive lung disease?
vignettes.a: reticulonodular or reticular pattern seen on CXR and CT → memorize these descriptors as = restrictive lung disease; they are also known as honeycombing colloquially.

vignettes.q: “When is centri-acinar vs pan-acinar emphysema important?”
vignettes.a: you just need to know that centri- acinar is the distribution seen in smoking; pan-acinar is seen in alpha-1 anti-trypsin deficiency.

vignettes.q: 32M non-smoker + reduced lung function + has a 40-year-old brother with COPD + father died of alcoholic liver disease; Dx?
vignettes.a: alpha-1 anti-trypsin deficiency → enzyme is produced in liver and travels to the lungs; functions to breakdown elastase; deficiency results in pan-acinar emphysema (Q will mention non-smoker with emphysema); can also result in hep

vignettes.q: “When is bronchiectasis the answer?”
vignettes.a: when the vignette tells you “cups and cups of foul-smelling sputum”; this is how bronchiectasis presents 8 out of 10 times; there is destruction of the musculature of the bronchioles resulting in ectatic (dilated) airways → “loss

vignettes.q: 34F + non-productive cough + CXR shows hilar nodularity; Dx?
vignettes.a: “non-caseating granulomas” → sarcoidosis; Tx = steroids; CXR will show bihilar lymphadenopathy; non-caseating granulomas produce 1-alpha hydroxylase, which converts inactive 25-OH-D3 into active 1,25-(OH)2- D3, leading to increase

vignettes.q: Any drug that can be used to help diagnose asthma?
vignettes.a: methacholine (muscarinic agonist); will reproduce asthma Sx; never use during acute attacks.

vignettes.q: 34F + non-productive cough + CXR normal; Dx?
vignettes.a: “activation of mast cell” → asthma.

vignettes.q: Asthma Tx (outpatient)? → albuterol (short-acting beta-2 agonist; SABA) inhaler for immediate Mx → if insufficient, start low-dose ICS (inhaled corticosteroid) preventer → if insufficient, maximize dose of ICS
vignettes.a: 1) SABA; then 2) low-dose ICS; then 3) maximize dose ICS; then 4) LABA. The above order is universal. After the LABA, any number of agents can be given in any order – i.e., nedocromil, cromolyn sodium, zileuton, montelukast, zafir

vignettes.q: 12M + ongoing wheezing episodes + is on albuterol inhaler; next best step?
vignettes.a: add low-dose ICS.

vignettes.q: 12M + ongoing wheezing episodes + is on albuterol inhaler; what’s most likely to decrease recurrence?
vignettes.a: oral corticosteroids (student says “? I thought you said ICS was what we do next and that oral steroids are last resort” Yeah, you’re right, but they’re still most effective at decreasing recurrence. This isn’t something I’m roman

vignettes.q: MOA of nedocromil and cromolyn sodium?
vignettes.a: mast cell stabilizers.

vignettes.q: MOA of zileuton?
vignettes.a: lipoxygenase inhibitor (enzyme that makes leukotrienes from arachidonic acid).

vignettes.q: MOA of the -lukasts?
vignettes.a: leukotriene LTC, D, and E4 inhibitors. LTB4 receptor agonism is unrelated and induces neutrophilic chemotaxis (LTB4, IL-8, kallikrein, platelet-activating factor, C5a, bacterial proteins).

vignettes.q: 16M goes snowboarding all day + takes pain reliever for sore muscles afterward + next day develops wheezing out on the slopes again; what’s going on?
vignettes.a: took aspirin + this is Samter triad (now cumbersomely known as aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease [AERD]) → triad of aspirin- induced asthma + aspirin hypersensitivity + nasal polyps). Just to be clear, other NSAIDs can preci

vignettes.q: 16M takes aspirin + gets wheezing; what are we likely to see on physical exam?
vignettes.a: answer on USMLE = nasal polyps.

vignettes.q: “Wait I don’t understand. Why would aspirin cause asthma?”
vignettes.a: arachidonic acid can be shunted down either the cyclooxygenase or lipoxygenase pathways; if you knock out COX irreversibly by giving aspirin (or reversibly with another NSAID), more arachidonic acid will be shunted down the lipoxy

vignettes.q: Kid has Hx of AERD; physician considers agent to decrease his recurrence of Sx
vignettes.a: zileuton, or -lukasts (both are correct; and only one will be listed).

vignettes.q: 10F + diffuse wheezes heard bilaterally + sputum sample shows numerous eosinophils and Charcot- Leyden crystals; which of the following is implicated in her disease pathogenesis?
vignettes.a: leukotriene C4 (LTC4); should be noted that LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4 all cause bronchoconstriction; LTB4 stimulates neutrophilic chemotaxis; Charcot-Leyden crystals are seen in asthma and are composed to eosinophil protein galectin-10

vignettes.q: Any weird asthma Txs?
vignettes.a: omalizumab → monoclonal antibody against IgE → used for intractable, severe asthma unresponsive to oral steroids + in patients who have eosinophilia + high IgE levels (I asked a pulmonologist about this drug years ago when I was i

vignettes.q: Acute asthma Mx (emergencies)
vignettes.a: most important piece of info straight-up is: USMLE wants you to know that inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) have no role in acute asthma management. First thing we do is give oxygen (any USMLE Q that shows depressed O2 sats, answer is

vignettes.q: 25F + runny nose and eyes in spring + cobblestoning of nasal mucosa; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: allergic rhinitis (“cobblestoning” is buzz term but used on the NBME); Tx = avoidance of precipitating allergen (if known, e.g., pollen); if meds used, first-line = intranasal corticosteroids; second-line is oral or intranasal ant

vignettes.q: 27M + inhalation injury from housefire + Q asks “destruction to which structure is most likely to preclude restoration of normal pulmonary architecture and lung function?”
vignettes.a: basement membranes → USMLE wants you to know intact basement membranes necessary for complete healing from lung injury or infection.

vignettes.q: 44M alcoholic + fever + air-fluid level seen on CXR; Dx + TX?
vignettes.a: pulmonary abscess; Tx = clindamycin; air-fluid level = circle on CXR, where bottom half is pus (radiopaque; white); top half is air (radiolucent; black); due to aspiration of “oropharyngeal anaerobes” (bacteroides, Mobiluncus, Pep

vignettes.q: 44M alcoholic + fever + CXR shows lobar consolidation + sputum is thick and red; Dx?
vignettes.a: Klebsiella pneumoniae (produces thick, mucoid colonies with “currant jelly sputum”); common cause of aspiration pneumonia (increased risk in alcoholics).

vignettes.q: 44M alcoholic + fever + CXR shows lobar consolidation + extremely foul-smelling sputum; Dx?
vignettes.a: Bacteroides pneumonia.

vignettes.q: 44M alcoholic + fever + air-fluid level seen on CXR + clindamycin is given and resolves his condition + months later he has residual lesion seen on CXR; why?
vignettes.a: failure of maintenance of basement membranes.

vignettes.q: Function of type I vs II pneumocytes?
vignettes.a: type I composes 95% of alveolar surface area (simple squamous) and is responsible for gas exchange; type II pneumocytes are interspersed and fewer; they produce surfactant (contain specialized surfactant-producing organelles calle

vignettes.q: What are Clara cells
vignettes.a: secrete glycosaminoglycans to protect the lining of bronchioles.

vignettes.q: Child born at 28 weeks gestation + dyspnea + Q asks which of the following is likely true in the patient
vignettes.a: “deficiency of lamellar bodies” → neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS); aka hyaline membrane disease → deficiency of surfactant → reduced lecithin (dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine) to sphingomyelin ratio; ratio should be

vignettes.q: Child born at 28 weeks gestation + dyspnea + Q asks which of the following is likely true in the patient
vignettes.a: deficiency of surfactant protein D → need to know this is decreased in NRDS.

vignettes.q: Neonate born at 38 weeks gestation via C-section + RR of 70 (normal 40-60) + CXR shows bilateral mild hyperinflation and prominent perihilar interstitial markings ; Dx?
vignettes.a: transient tachypnea of the newborn → TTN is the answer when the vignette “sounds like NRDS but the kid is term”; seen in C-sections and fast vaginal deliveries in term neonates; mechanism is delayed absorption of the fetal lung fl

vignettes.q: Neonate born at 26 weeks + required oxygen in ICU for several weeks + is now on home oxygen; child is at increased risk for what?
vignettes.a: answers = bronchopulmonary dysplasia, retinopathy of prematurity, germinal matrix bleed → all can be seen in neonates on oxygen therapy.

vignettes.q: Newborn + decreased bowel sounds in abdomen + tracheal shift to the right; Dx?
vignettes.a: congenital diaphragmatic hernia → incomplete formation of pleuroperitoneal membranes → occurs on the left side, with bowel herniating into the left hemithorax.

vignettes.q: Newborn + bowel sounds heard in the left chest; mechanism?
vignettes.a: incomplete formation of pleuroperitoneal membranes.

vignettes.q: 12-hour-old newborn + becomes blue when breastfeeding + becomes pink again when crying; Dx?
vignettes.a: atresia of the choanae (CHARGE syndrome → Coloboma of the eye, Heart defects, Atresia of the choanae, Retardation, Genitourinary abnormalities, Ear abnormalities/deafness).

vignettes.q: Can you comment on HY pneumoconioses? → lung disease secondary to occupational exposures.
vignettes.a: Asbestosis → workers in shipbuilding, plumbing, construction/insulation, roofing industries → causes supradiaphragmatic and pleural plaques; plaques can calcify; biopsy may show ferruginous bodies (due to deposition of hemosiderin

vignettes.q: 34M hay farmer + progressive dyspnea over many months + clubbing; Dx?
vignettes.a: hypersensitivity pneumonitis; can be acute, subacute, or chronic; occurs in response to various antigens, including thermophilic Actinomycetes (hay farmers; sugarcane); non-tuberculous mycobacterium (hot tub lung; on NBME); bird f

vignettes.q: 28M + asthma + recurrent lung infections + skin allergy testing shows hypersensitivity to aspergillus antigen; Dx?
vignettes.a: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA); usually seen in patients who have asthma or cystic fibrosis.

vignettes.q: 34M + HIV positive + nodular density seen in right upper lobe on CXR; next best step?
vignettes.a: “biopsy of the mass” → Aspergilloma (fungus ball); increased risk with Hx of TB (can occupy cavities).

vignettes.q: 57M + Hx of dermatomyositis + few weeks ago had fever and pneumonia + presentation hasn’t resolved with multiple antibiotics + multiple sputum cultures are negative; Dx?
vignettes.a: cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP; formerly known as bronchiolitis obliterans organizing pneumonia [BOOP]); → frequently presents as pneumonia-like presentation (i.e., fever, dyspnea) in patients with Hx of autoimmune disease

vignettes.q: 43F + lung transplant several months ago + declining lung function + CXR shows mild flattening of the diaphragm + CT shows air-trapping; Dx?
vignettes.a: bronchiolitis obliterans (constrictive bronchiolitis; “popcorn lung”); do not confuse with COP (BOOP); bronchiolitis obliterans is the answer for obstructive lung disease that progressively manifests post-lung transplant (75%) or

vignettes.q: 43F + rheumatoid arthritis + progressive shortness of breath over six months + CT of chest shows reticulonodular pattern; Dx?
vignettes.a: “usual interstitial pneumonia” (UIP); student says ? → on the NBME; this Dx refers to a patient with scarring and fibrosis of the lungs; if the cause is idiopathic, we call the UIP “idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis,” but IPF is still

vignettes.q: Drugs causing pulmonary fibrosis?
vignettes.a: methotrexate (patients with RA who have UIP → hard to know whether it’s from the methotrexate or rheumatoid lung, or both); amiodarone, bleomycin, busulfan, nitrofurantoin.

vignettes.q: 10-month-old + fever of 101F + wheezes bilaterally; DX + Tx?
vignettes.a: RSV bronchiolitis → Tx is supportive; answers such as ribavirin and palivizumab are almost always wrong on actual NBME assessment.

vignettes.q: 8M + leaning forward in tripod position + drooling; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: epiglottitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae type B; Tx = immediate intubation; neck x-ray shows thumbprint sign; even if kid is stable, still intubate (airway can inflame + obstruct at any moment); give ceftriaxone to patient; g

vignettes.q: 8M + hoarse cough + improves when father brings him out in the cold; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) caused by parainfluenza virus (paramyxovirus); classically “seal-like, barking cough”; neck x-ray shows steeple sign (subglottic narrowing); Tx = supportive; if you’re forced to pick an actual Tx h

vignettes.q: 8M + two weeks ago recovered from influenza infection + now has fever + inspiratory stridor + can open mouth fully; Dx?
vignettes.a: bacterial tracheitis caused by Staph aureus. Dx with bronchoscopy; Tx with antibiotics. Being able to open the mouth fully is important detail, since with peritonsillar abscess, one has difficulty opening the mouth fully. If a pat

vignettes.q: 40M + 6-month Hx of episodic sinusitis + cough with blood-tinged sputum + no improvement of Sx after several months of antibiotics, decongestants, and nasal corticosteroids + P/E shows two small ulcerations on
vignettes.a: eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly known as Churg-Strauss) → presents as asthma-like Sx and eosinophilia in a patient with positivity for p-ANCA (anti-myeloperoxidase; anti-MPO); overlap of features with granu

vignettes.q: 44M + hemoptysis + hematuria + ANCA screen is negative; next best step?
vignettes.a: anti- glomerular basement membrane antibody screen → Dx likely Goodpasture; if anti-GBM antibodies positive, do renal biopsy showing linear immunofluorescence; anti-GBM Abs = antibodies against type IV collagen (“2, 3, 4; 2, 3, 4;

vignettes.q: How to Dx TB?
vignettes.a: PPD skin test is performed first diagnostically. If history of BCG vaccine, do interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) instead. Do not do IGRA in addition to PPD. If PPD is negative, repeat after one week. If negative again, no furt

vignettes.q: How to manage a positive PPD test?
vignettes.a: Measure induration only. Erythema does not count.

vignettes.q: 5+ mm
vignettes.a: Recent contact with people with active TB HIV + status Organ transplant recipients Chronic prednisone use (>15mg/day for >1 month); anti-TNF-α agent use Findings consistent with TB on CXR

vignettes.q: 10+ mm
vignettes.a: Immigrant status (Western countries not included) IV drug users Healthcare workers; prison workers; homeless shelter personnel TB laboratory personnel Children under 4 years of age

vignettes.q: How to Tx latent TB?
vignettes.a: 9 months INH + pyridoxine (vitamin B6) - The USMLE USMLE Step 1 assess this as the answer. 4 months rifampin 3 months INH + rifapentine + pyridoxine Vitamin B6 must be given with INH to prevent vitamin B6 deficiency.

vignettes.q: Tx of active TB
vignettes.a: Rifampin, INH, pyrazinamide, ethambutol (RIPE) for 2 months, followed by RI alone for 4 more months (6 months total) And of course add pyridoxine (annoying that it sounds similar to pyrazinamide)

vignettes.q: 32M + fever of 101F + CXR shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates; Dx?
vignettes.a: Mycoplasma pneumoniae; most common cause of atypical pneumonia after viruses; classically bilateral.

vignettes.q: 32M + fever 101F + CXR shows lobar consolidation + dullness to percussion on P/E; Dx?
vignettes.a: Streptococcus pneumoniae → need to know is gram-positive diplococci (don’t confuse with Neisseria gonorrhea and meningitides, which are gram-negative diplococci).

vignettes.q: 32M + fever 101F + CXR shows lobar consolidation with interstitial markings; Dx?
vignettes.a: Mycoplasma → likely implication is that even though Strep pneumo is classically lobar and Mycoplasma bilateral, if the Q says the word “interstitial,” that wins over distribution/location.

vignettes.q: Pneumonia + diarrhea + hyponatremia; Dx?
vignettes.a: Legionella pneumophila.

vignettes.q: Pneumonia in a cattle farmer; Dx?
vignettes.a: Coxiella burnetti.

vignettes.q: Pneumonia in someone with a pet rabbit; Dx?
vignettes.a: Francisella tularensis.

vignettes.q: Pneumonia in bird owner; Dx?
vignettes.a: Chlamydia psittaci.

vignettes.q: Pneumonia in 2-week-old neonate who had ophthalmia neonatorum treated a week ago; Dx?
vignettes.a: Chlamydia trachomatis pneumonia → chlamydial neonatal conjunctivitis → drains through nasolacrimal duct into nasopharynx and into the lung.

vignettes.q: Pneumonia in someone who recently recovered from viral infection (usually flu); Dx?
vignettes.a: Staph aureus → similar to post-viral bacterial tracheitis caused by Staph.

vignettes.q: Lobar pneumonia in HIV patient; Dx?
vignettes.a: Strep pneumo, not Pneumocystis.

vignettes.q: HIV patient + CXR shows bilateral ground-glass pneumonia; next best step in Dx?
vignettes.a: bronchoalveolar lavage with silver-staining of the yeast; Dx? → Pneumocystis jirovecii → Tx = TMP/SMX.

vignettes.q: Empiric Tx for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP)?
vignettes.a: azithromycin (macrolide) → covers atypicals (i.e., Mycoplasma, etc.) and S. pneumo.

vignettes.q: Empiric Tx for CAP when patient’s had antibiotics in the past three months?
vignettes.a: respiratory fluoroquinolone (i.e., levofloxacin).

vignettes.q: When is pneumonia considered hospital-acquired (HAP)?
vignettes.a: if Sx start >48 hours after admission to hospital.

vignettes.q: How is HAP and ventilator-acquired pneumonia (VAP) Tx differently from CAP?
vignettes.a: need to cover MRSA and Pseudomonas just in case → Tx entails various broad-spectrum options; classics are vancomycin + third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin; ceftazidime (3rd gen ceph) and cefepime (4th gen ceph) are effective

vignettes.q: When to do home oxygen therapy in COPD?
vignettes.a: when patient’s arterial pO2 <55 mmHg (or <60 mmHg if patient has cor pulmonale).

vignettes.q: 55M with COPD; number-one way to decrease mortality?
vignettes.a: smoking cessation; if patient has already stopped smoking, answer = home oxygen therapy (decreases mortality, but only indicated as per criteria above).

vignettes.q: 48M + BMI 45 + snores loudly during sleep; what is most likely seen in this patient?
vignettes.a: increased serum bicarbonate → Dx = obesity hypoventilation syndrome → blood levels of CO2 are increased, with bicarb increased to compensate (chronic respiratory acidosis).

vignettes.q: 8-month-old girl + stridor that improves with neck extension; Dx?
vignettes.a: vascular ring → weird but HY diagnosis for peds → aberrant embryologic development where the aorta and/or surrounding vessels form a ring around the esophagus and/or trachea.

vignettes.q: 8-month-old girl + stridor that improves when prone or upright; Dx?
vignettes.a: laryngomalacia → most common cause of stridor in peds → soft cartilage of upper larynx collapses during inhalation.

vignettes.q: 2F + stridor + laryngoscopy shows small growths of larynx; Dx?
vignettes.a: HPV 6/11 → laryngeal papillomatosis.

vignettes.q: Highest yield points about cystic fibrosis?
vignettes.a: autosomal recessive; chromosome 7; CFTR gene; codes for chloride channel that functions to secrete chloride in the lungs and pancreas, and reabsorb chloride in the sweat glands; DF508 (deletion of phenylalanine at position 508) is

vignettes.q: 32M + Hx of recurrent lung infections + two years of inability to have children with wife + wife has two children from prior marriage + his sperm sample shows immotile sperm; Dx?
vignettes.a: Kartagener syndrome (primary ciliary dyskinesia) → dynein arm defect of cilia (a cilium on cross- section has a 9x2 arrangement of microtubules); associated with dextrocardia / situs inversus; sperm are immotile (require cilia fun

vignettes.q: What should I know about breath sounds, percussion, tracheal shift, etc.?
vignettes.a: Basically all of that annoying physical exam stuff.”

vignettes.q: Pleural effusion in someone who has pneumonia; Dx?
vignettes.a: parapneumonic effusion (exudative pleural effusion secondary to a lung infection).

vignettes.q: What is empyema?
vignettes.a: pus in a preexisting cavity (i.e., refers to pus in the pleural space); in contrast, an abscess is pus in a location where there was not a preexisting cavity (e.g., the forearm).

vignettes.q: Characteristic of parapneumonic effusion most predictive of progression to empyema?
vignettes.a: decreased pH of the pleural fluid (<7.1).

vignettes.q: Transudative vs exudative pleural effusion? → Light’s criteria for exudative:
vignettes.a: Pleural fluid to serum protein ratio >0.5, OR Pleural fluid to serum LDH ratio >0.6, OR Pleural fluid LDH > 2/3 upper limit of serum LDH.

vignettes.q: Any other characteristics notable for transudative vs exudative?
vignettes.a: qualitatively, in exudative, pleural fluid cell count will be higher than in transudative; glucose can also be reduced in infective causes (parapneumonic).

vignettes.q: 44M + long Hx of smoking + dullness to percussion 2/3 up the lung field; Dx?
vignettes.a: malignant pleural effusion → malignancy, congestive heart failure, and infection are very common causes of pleural effusion.

vignettes.q: 32F + ovarian fibroma + ascites + hydrothorax; Dx?
vignettes.a: Meig syndrome.

vignettes.q: Treatment for pulmonary embolism?
vignettes.a: heparin before spiral CT of the chest; if pregnant, do V/Q scan instead of CT (sufficient for USMLE).

vignettes.q: When is IVC filter the answer for pulmonary embolism? → if the patient gets a PE while already on anticoagulation (warfarin, dabigatran, etc.) and the spiral CT has already been performed. In other words:
vignettes.a: 58F on warfarin + gets PE; next best step? → answer = CT. 58F on warfarin + gets PE + CT confirms Dx; next best step? → answer = IVC filter.

vignettes.q: 32M + plays basketball + few hours of shortness of breath; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: spontaneous pneumothorax caused by ruptured subapical bleb; Tx = needle decompression followed by chest tube (some small pneumothoraces can be observed, but on USMLE always Tx).

vignettes.q: 32M + MVA + dyspnea + low BP + breath sounds decreased on left + tracheal shift to right; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: tension pneumothorax; Tx = needle decompression followed by chest tube.

vignettes.q: “Cephalization of pulmonary vasculature”; Dx?
vignettes.a: pulmonary edema → important description that shows up in NBME vignettes → due to increased hydrostatic pressure from left heart pathology.

vignettes.q: 36M + long-bone fractures + petechiae on the chest; Dx?
vignettes.a: fat embolism.

vignettes.q: Motor vehicle accident (MVA) + paradoxical breathing (chest moves outward with exhalation; inward with inhalation); Dx?
vignettes.a: flail chest.

vignettes.q: MVA + rib fractures + underlying infiltrates in lung + low O2 sats; Dx?
vignettes.a: pulmonary contusion.

vignettes.q: MVA + no rib fractures + non-central chest pain + pulmonary infiltrates underlying the painful area; Dx?
vignettes.a: pulmonary contusion (resources will say “white out of the lung” for pulmonary contusion, but this is buzzywordy and never shows up on actual NBME material).

vignettes.q: MVA + pulmonary infiltrates + low O2 sats + bolus of normal saline given, resulting in worsening of O2 sats; Dx?
vignettes.a: pulmonary contusion (contused lung is very sensitive to fluid overload).

vignettes.q: MVA + bruising/pain over the sternum +/- rib fractures; Dx?
vignettes.a: myocardial contusion.

vignettes.q: Important point about Mx of myocardial contusion?
vignettes.a: do troponins + must monitor for arrhythmia.

vignettes.q: Adult male + abdo pain + Hx of alcohol use + diffuse pulmonary infiltrates + low O2 sats; Dx?
vignettes.a: ARDS → must have pO2/FiO2 <300; if the Q asks about ventilator settings, know that low- tidal volume mechanical ventilation is often used (prevents barotrauma) + permissive hypercapnia + prone positioning.

vignettes.q: When you get a random ventilator Q and they want an answer?
vignettes.a: “increase PEEP” almost always right.

vignettes.q: Patient has improving O2 sats on ventilator; next best step?
vignettes.a: “wean from ventilator. ”

vignettes.a: ↑ temperature; ↑ 2,3-BPG; CO2; ↓ pH; ↑ H+ → right-shift means increased oxygen unloading at tissues; protons in the blood are buffered by deoxygenated hemoglobin (Step 1 NBME).

vignettes.q: Pneumonia in CF patient >10 years

vignettes.a: SABA, then low-dose ICS, then maximize dose of ICS, then LABA, then use any number of drugs (e.g., mast cell stabilizers, anti-leukotriene, etc.), then oral steroids last resort

vignettes.a: radial traction on outside of airways is sticky (keeps airways from closing)

vignettes.a: Never an answer on the USMLE because the indications are debated.

vignettes.a: TRALI (transfusion related acute lung injury)

vignettes.a: donor Abs against recipient MHCs → activated neutrophils cause alveolar damage → most common cause of transfusion-associated death
