vignettes.q: 15M + jumps into cold lake. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for change in central blood volume, atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) secretion, and ADH release?
vignettes.a: ↑ Central blood volume, ↑ ANP secretion, ↓ ADH release. — If the kid jumps into cold water, he will experience increased peripheral vasoconstriction in order to conserve heat. This will increase central blood volume (i.e., blood r

vignettes.q: 40M with chronic renal failure + high BUN + high creatinine + 2-week history of nosebleeds. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for platelet count, bleeding time, PT, and aPTT?
vignettes.a: ↔ Platelet count, ↑ bleeding time, ↔ PT, ↔ aPTT. — Diagnosis is uremic platelet dysfunction. USMLE may also write it as “acquired platelet dysfunction.” • For whatever reason, high BUN causes platelets to not work, leading to a qu

vignettes.q: There are four main points you should memorize as being part of each syndrome type. Nephritic syndromes: 1) Hematuria (blood in the urine). 2) Oliguria (↓ urinary output; the definition is <400 mL/day, but USML
vignettes.a: ↓ serum oncotic pressure → transudation of fluid into interstitial spaces; if severe can present with ascites; if the stem says “pre-sacral edema,” this is nephrotic syndrome till proven otherwise on USMLE). 4) Hyperlipidemia (liv

vignettes.q: Nephrotic syndromes can ↑ risk of DVT, renal vein thrombosis, and varicocele due to loss of antithrombin III in the urine
vignettes.a: hypercoagulable state. This is because nephrotic syndrome usually entails non-specific massive protein loss due to loss of size and charge barrier, and antithrombin is a protein. The NBME wants you to know left renal vein thrombus

vignettes.q: The stem need not say “eosinophils” either. They can just say patient is on b-lactam + now has WBCs in the urine + no mention of rash
vignettes.a: interstitial nephritis. If they say the rash, it’s even easier.

vignettes.q: NBME also can give you simple vignette of interstitial nephritis, and then ask for the location in the kidney that’s affected (e.g., efferent arterioles, etc.)
vignettes.a: “renal tubule.”

vignettes.q: For example, 40M + treated with nafcillin for 6 weeks for MSSA endocarditis + now has maculopapular rash and eosinophils in the urine; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: interstitial nephritis.

vignettes.q: 60F + using naproxen (an NSAID) for 6 weeks for her osteoarthritis + has peripheral edema
vignettes.a: interstitial nephropathy.

vignettes.q: 35F + just recently finished 10-day course of cephalexin + has mild proteinuria and hematuria
vignettes.a: interstitial nephropathy.

vignettes.q: 35F + taking ibuprofen + has maculopapular rash and eosinophils in the urine; Q asks where in the kidney is impaired
vignettes.a: “renal tubule.” Student says, “But don’t NSAIDs affect the afferent arteriole?” → Yes, but this particular presentation is clearly tubulointerstitial nephropathy. I haven’t seen them be ambiguous here with “NSAID + peripheral edem

vignettes.q: 27M + dilated renal pelvis and collecting system + ureters not dilated; Dx?
vignettes.a: USMLE wants “incomplete recanalization of proximal ureter.”

vignettes.q: Four classic findings you see in nephrotic syndrome?
vignettes.a: Proteinuria (usually high, i.e., >3g/24 hours) Hypoalbuminemia (because of the proteinuria) Peripheral edema (due to decreased intravascular oncotic pressure because of the hypoalbuminemia) Hyperlipidemia (liver exports more apoli

vignettes.q: Four classic findings you see in nephritic syndrome?
vignettes.a: Hematuria (due to glomerular inflammation allowing RBCs to escape into the urine) Oliguria (<400mL/24 hours in adults; due to defective glomerular filtration with diminished GFR) Azotemia (means high nitrogen compounds in the bloo

vignettes.q: Is there proteinuria in nephritic syndrome?
vignettes.a: almost always yes, but just typically not as much as in nephrotic syndrome. The key differentiator between nephritic and nephrotic is the former has blood in the urine.

vignettes.q: Important nephrotic syndromes for USMLE?
vignettes.a: membranous glomerulonephritis/nephropathy; minimal change disease (lipoid nephrosis); focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS); renal amyloidosis; diabetic glomerulonephropathy.

vignettes.q: Important nephritic syndromes for USMLE?
vignettes.a: IgA nephropathy (Berger disease); post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN);

vignettes.q: 12M + sore throat + blood in the urine 1-3 days later; Dx?
vignettes.a: IgA nephropathy, not post- streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN).

vignettes.q: 12M + sore throat + blood in the urine 1-2 weeks later; Dx?
vignettes.a: PSGN. This distinction between IgA nephropathy and PSGN is mega-HY.

vignettes.q: 12M + viral infection + red urine 2 days later; renal biopsy finding?
vignettes.a: IgA deposition in the mesangium (IgA nephropathy).

vignettes.q: 12M + GI infection (diarrhea) + red urine 2 days later; Dx?
vignettes.a: IgA nephropathy.

vignettes.q: 3F + violaceous lesions on her buttocks/thighs + arthralgias + abdominal pain + red urine; renal Dx?
vignettes.a: IgA nephropathy. The tetrad of findings here is classic for Henoch-Schonlein purpura (HSP). The renal component is IgA nephropathy.

vignettes.q: “Wait I’m confused. How does HSP relate to IgA nephropathy?”
vignettes.a: don’t think of IgA nephropathy and HSP as distinct / unrelated conditions; they’re on the same disease spectrum. While some patients might just get IgA nephropathy from a viral or GI infection, others might get the immune complex

vignettes.q: 12F + crusty yellow lesions around the mouth for past week + today has red urine; Dx?
vignettes.a: PSGN secondary to impetigo → give topical mupirocin to Tx the impetigo.

vignettes.q: Can you get PSGN from skin infections?
vignettes.a: as per above, clearly → impetigo, cellulitis, and erysipelas, if caused by Group A Strep, can cause PSGN, yes. This is HY for the USMLEs. However it should be noted that rheumatic heart disease does not occur from cutaneous Strep

vignettes.q: 28M + blurry vision and/or hearing issue + red urine; Dx?
vignettes.a: Alport syndrome.

vignettes.q: Inheritance pattern of Alport?
vignettes.a: X-linked recessive (according to retired NBME 19 for Step 1; I point this out because some sources say X-linked dominant, but the NBME says XR; the NBME always wins).

vignettes.q: Mechanism of Alport?
vignettes.a: mutation in type IV collagen (in contrast to Goodpasture, which is antibodies against type IV collagen) → important in the lens of the eye + stereocilia within the cochlea + basement membranes within the kidney → classically “ear

vignettes.q: 13M + PSGN; renal biopsy shows what?
vignettes.a: subepithelial deposits or “lumpy bumpy appearance.”

vignettes.q: When is membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) the answer?
vignettes.a: red urine in patient with hepatitis C or malignancy.

vignettes.q: “Splitting of glomerular basement membrane”; Dx?
vignettes.a: MPGN. “Tram-track appearance.”

vignettes.q: When is diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (DPGN) the answer?
vignettes.a: red urine in patient with SLE.

vignettes.q: When is rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) the answer?
vignettes.a: acute deterioration in renal function (high Cr, high BUN, oliguria) in someone who has a vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis [formerly Wegener], eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis [formerly Churg- Stauss], or m

vignettes.q: If the question is about Wegener, what will the renal biopsy often show?
vignettes.a: “necrotizing” glomerulonephritis.

vignettes.q: Antibodies in Wegener vs CS vs MP?
vignettes.a: Wegener = c-ANCA; CS + MP = p-ANCA. It should be noted that in real life, there is often overlap between the ANCAs, as well as times when patients may be ANCA-negative, but on the USMLE, the classic associations stand correct.

vignettes.q: Which antibodies are present in the ANCAs?
vignettes.a: c-ANCA = anti-proteinase 3 (anti-PR3); p-ANCA = anti- myeloperoxidase (anti-MPO).

vignettes.q: Mechanism for Goodpasture?
vignettes.a: antibodies against the alpha-3 chains of type IV collagen (anti- glomerular basement membrane antibodies; anti-GBM) → an NBME Q asks for mechanism, and answer is → “autoantibodies against host cell basement membranes.”

vignettes.q: Diagnosis of Goodpasture?
vignettes.a: biopsy shows linear immunofluorescence.

vignettes.q: How does Goodpasture present?
vignettes.a: 40s male with hemoptysis + hematuria.

vignettes.q: How does Wegener present?
vignettes.a: hematuria + hemoptysis + “head”-itis (i.e., any type of head finding, e.g., nasal septal perforation, mastoiditis, otitis, sinusitis).

vignettes.q: How does Churg-Strauss present?
vignettes.a: asthma + eosinophilia; head findings rare.

vignettes.q: How does microscopic polyangiitis present?
vignettes.a: basically just isolated hematuria in patient who’s p- ANCA positive.

vignettes.q: Wrist- or foot-drop in someone with W, C-S, or MP; Dx?
vignettes.a: Mononeuritis multiplex, which is palsy of one large nerve in multiple locations, such as the radial or peroneal, causing wrist or foot drop. Seen sometimes in vasculitides where you say, "Why is there neuropathy in this Wegener pa

vignettes.q: 38F + hematuria + hemoptysis + anti-PR3; Dx?
vignettes.a: Wegener.

vignettes.q: 38F + hematuria + nasal septal perforation + c-ANCA; Dx?
vignettes.a: Wegener.

vignettes.q: 38F + hematuria + p-ANCA; Dx?
vignettes.a: MP.

vignettes.q: 38F + hematuria + anti-MPO; Dx?
vignettes.a: MP.

vignettes.q: 38F + asthma + eosinophilia + nasal septal perforation; Dx?
vignettes.a: Churg-Strauss (yes, “head”-itis is more rare, but the asthma + eosinophilia are overwhelmingly CS over Wegener; saw one question like this).

vignettes.q: 44M + hematuria + hemoptysis + no other findings; Dx?
vignettes.a: Goodpasture most likely. If Wegener, they usually give you a "head-itis" finding, such as nasal septal perforation. If microscopic polyangiitis, usually just hematuria alone.

vignettes.q: 44M + hematuria + hemoptysis + renal biopsy shows necrotizing glomerulonephritis; Dx?
vignettes.a: Wegener.

vignettes.q: 44M + hematuria + hemoptysis + linear immunofluorescence on renal biopsy; Dx?
vignettes.a: Goodpasture.

vignettes.q: Alport syndrome vs Goodpasture key difference?
vignettes.a: Alport = mutation in type IV collagen gene (COL4A3/4/5); Goodpasture = antibodies against type IV collagen.

vignettes.q: 12M + periorbital edema + red urine + low C3; Dx?
vignettes.a: PSGN.

vignettes.q: 12M + periorbital edema + no blood in the urine + no other information; Dx?
vignettes.a: minimal change disease (MCD; lipoid nephrosis).

vignettes.q: 12M + recent viral infection + periorbital/pedal edema + ascites; Dx?
vignettes.a: MCD.

vignettes.q: 40M + Hodgkin lymphoma + renal condition (no blood in urine); Dx?
vignettes.a: MCD → student says ? → MCD is almost always children following viral infection, but it’s also seen in adults with Hodgkin. First time you hear this it’s super-weird, but it’s not a big deal.

vignettes.q: Tx for MCD?
vignettes.a: steroids (highly effective)

vignettes.q: Sickle-cell + nephrotic syndrome; Dx?
vignettes.a: FSGS.

vignettes.q: HIV / IV drug use + nephrotic syndrome; Dx?
vignettes.a: FSGS.

vignettes.q: Interferon use + nephrotic syndrome; Dx?
vignettes.a: FSGS.

vignettes.q: What does FSGS mean?
vignettes.a: focal vs global; segmental vs diffuse; focal means a part of the kidney; diffuse means the whole kidney; segmental means part of a single nephron; global means an entire single nephron. So in FSGS, parts of some nephrons are invol

vignettes.q: Tx for FSGS?
vignettes.a: steroids (not as effective as compared to MCD).

vignettes.q: Sulfa drug + kidney issue + no blood in urine; Dx?
vignettes.a: membranous glomerulonephropathy (MG).

vignettes.q: Biopsy finding in MG?
vignettes.a: subepithelial deposits; “spike and dome” appearance.

vignettes.q: HepB or C + nephrotic syndrome; Dx?
vignettes.a: MG → usually due to HepB.

vignettes.q: Autoantibodies in membranous glomerulonephropathy?
vignettes.a: Sometimes patients are positive for anti- phospholipase A2 receptor antibodies.

vignettes.q: HepC + nephritic syndrome; Dx?
vignettes.a: MPGN.

vignettes.q: Multiple myeloma + renal diagnosis?
vignettes.a: renal amyloidosis → immunoglobulin light chains at high levels moving through the kidney (Bence Jones proteinuria) leads to deposition in the renal parenchyma. You should memorize the sentence: “Multiple myeloma is the most common

vignettes.q: First change in the kidney with diabetes?
vignettes.a: hyperfiltration → increased filtered glucose pulls water with it. USMLE Q mentions guy with diabetes + polyuria; asks why he has increased urinary output → answer = “increased glomerular filtration rate.”

vignettes.q: First histologic change in the kidney with diabetes?
vignettes.a: thickening of the glomerular basement membrane → due to non-enzymatic glycosylation of basement membrane. If the question asks you for the first renal change seen overall in diabetes, select hyperfiltration.

vignettes.q: Amount of glucose reabsorbed in PCT?
vignettes.a: 100% physiologically; glycosuria not seen until serum levels exceed around 180 mg/dL.

vignettes.q: Late finding seen histologically in diabetic nephropathy?
vignettes.a: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules.

vignettes.q: What are KW nodules composed of?
vignettes.a: hyaline → HY on Step 1 for some reason; don’t confuse this fibrin, which is the answer for the crescents in RPGN.

vignettes.q: Example of type II diabetes drug that acts in the kidney?
vignettes.a: Dapagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor in PCT; prevents reabsorption of glucose).

vignettes.q: What is hyaline arteriolosclerosis?
vignettes.a: hyaline deposition in the arterioles of the kidney usually seen in diabetes → non-enzymatic glycosylation of vascular endothelium leads to leakage of plasma proteins into vessel walls.

vignettes.q: First drug given to diabetics with HTN or proteinuria?
vignettes.a: ACEi (e.g., enalapril) or ARB (e.g., valsartan).

vignettes.q: Most common cause of chronic renal failure?
vignettes.a: diabetes mellitus.

vignettes.q: Comment on which endogenous mediators affect diameter of the renal afferent vs efferent arterioles
vignettes.a: prostaglandins dilate the afferent; angiotensin-II constricts the efferent.

vignettes.q: What do NSAIDs do to renal vasculature?
vignettes.a: decrease dilation of the afferent arterioles (decreased prostaglandin synthesis doesn’t cause constriction; we simply see attenuated degree of dilation).

vignettes.q: What do ACEi/ARBs do to renal vasculature?
vignettes.a: decrease constriction of the efferent arterioles (decreased AT-II synthesis/binding doesn’t cause dilation; we simply see attenuated degree of constriction). USMLE will show you pic of glomerulus + ask where NSAID or ACEi acts, so

vignettes.q: Student asks, “Why does AT-II act on the efferent arteriole? What’s the physiologic reason for that?”
vignettes.a: physiologically, AT-II increases in the setting of low blood volume → constriction of efferent arteriole → increased filtration fraction (GFR/RBF) → GFR can be maintained in the setting of reduced renal blood flow

vignettes.q: What do ACEi/ARB do to filtration fraction?
vignettes.a: decrease it.

vignettes.q: Student asks, “If diabetes is most common cause of chronic renal failure, and renal failure is defined as low GFR, why would we give them ACEi or ARB then first-line if those drugs decrease filtration fraction?
vignettes.a: It’s paradoxical, yes. Although you’d be decreasing filtration fraction with one of these drugs, you’d also be decreasing the rate at which glucose is being filtered across the basement membrane, thereby slowing the non-enzymatic

vignettes.q: Fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa) in pre-/intra-/post-renal failure?
vignettes.a: need to know it’s <1% in pre-renal; >1% in intra-/post-renal → the low FeNa in pre-renal is due to the PCT’s attempt to reabsorb Na (water follows sodium) in low-volume state (or in FMD, RAS).

vignettes.q: Urine osmolality in pre-/intra-/post-renal failure?
vignettes.a: concentrated (high; >500 mOsm) in pre-; dilute (low; <350 mOsm) in intra-/-post.

vignettes.q: When is pre-renal failure the answer?
vignettes.a: Chronic heart failure, NSAID or diuretic use, dehydration from vomiting/diarrhea. Reduced perfusion over sub-acute to chronic time frame.

vignettes.q: Guy has MI + has low BP; NBME Q asks what is most likely to be seen (ask a bunch of reabsorption / secretion answers); answer = “increased potassium secretion”
vignettes.a: low-volume status leads to RAAS upregulation and distal renal K wasting.

vignettes.q: When is intra-renal failure the answer?
vignettes.a: ATN due to drugs (aminoglycosides, cisplatin), acute ischemia from acute blood loss (surgery, trauma), contrast nephropathy, rhabdomyolysis.

vignettes.q: Why does acute hypoxia cause acute tubular necrosis?
vignettes.a: PCT is most susceptible to anoxic injury. Proximal convoluted tubules have high concentrations of Na-K-ATPase transporters with high oxygen demand.

vignettes.q: Lab animal is given 100% nitrogen in dumb experiment; most likely part of the kidney to experience anoxic injury (they list everything)
vignettes.a: “proximal tubule.”

vignettes.q: Electrolyte disturbance in ATN?
vignettes.a: first week is oliguric phase (hyperkalemia due to decreased filtration); weeks 2-3 are polyuric phase (hypokalemia due to increased kaliuresis from PCT cells not being able to reabsorb K yet) → btw, kaliuresis means urination of K

vignettes.q: When is post-renal the answer?
vignettes.a: classically BPH or distal obstruction secondary to strictures or malignancy.

vignettes.q: How does USMLE like to assess post-renal?
vignettes.a: classically will give you BPH + show you a pic of hydronephrosis (massively dilated kidney), then they’ll ask the most likely cause of this patient’s condition; answer = “increased Bowman capsule hydrostatic pressure,” or “increas

vignettes.q: BPH Tx?
vignettes.a: alpha-1 blocker (e.g., tamsulosin, terazosin) and/or 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor (i.e., finasteride); patients may receive mono- or dual therapy.

vignettes.q: Tx for prostatic adenocarcinoma?
vignettes.a: flutamide + leuprolide administered together (if the USMLE forces you to choose a sequence, pick flutamide then leuprolide, but in practice they’re administered together) → flutamide blocks androgen receptors; leuprolide is a GnRH

vignettes.q: When are hyaline casts the answer?
vignettes.a: classically dehydration on USMLE.

vignettes.q: When are waxy casts the answer?
vignettes.a: end-stage renal disease (not HY, but student occasionally asks).

vignettes.q: When are RBC casts the answer?
vignettes.a: glomerulonephritis.

vignettes.q: When are WBC casts the answer?
vignettes.a: pyelonephritis classically.

vignettes.q: is Tamm-Horsfall protein?
vignettes.a: most common protein found in urine; not found in plasma; produced by tubular cells (classically thick ascending limb); no other real significance; more just the name pops up in Qbank rarely and student will ask about it.

vignettes.q: What is interstitial nephropathy?
vignettes.a: aka interstitial nephritis, or tubulointerstitial nephritis, where there are WBCs (eosinophils) in the urine; patient may or may not present with a fine maculopapular rash → almost always due to beta-lactams, cephalosporins, NSAID

vignettes.q: 62M + 6 weeks nafcillin for MSSA endocarditis + WBCs on U/A; Dx?
vignettes.a: interstitial nephropathy.

vignettes.q: 35F + uses ibuprofen daily for headaches + rash + eosinophils in urine; what do you see on biopsy?
vignettes.a: NBME answer = “inflammatory infiltrates in the interstitium” = interstitial nephropathy.

vignettes.q: What is analgesic nephropathy?
vignettes.a: renal damage due to NSAIDs → can be renal papillary necrosis, interstitial nephritis, or generalized edema from reduced renal blood flow. If renal papillary necrosis, will present with dark urine from ischemia. If interstitial nep

vignettes.q: 80F + taking high doses of naproxen for 6 weeks for osteoarthritis + peripheral edema; mechanism of the edema?
vignettes.a: Mechanism for edema in setting of NSAID use → USMLE answer = “increased renal retention of sodium,” or “decreased renal excretion of sodium.”

vignettes.q: Why would analgesic nephropathy cause increased renal retention of sodium?
vignettes.a: NSAID knocks out COX → decreased prostaglandin synthesis → decreased diameter of afferent arterioles → decreased renal blood flow → PCT attempts to increase water reabsorption to compensate for perceived low volume status → PCT ac

vignettes.q: When is renal papillary necrosis the answer?
vignettes.a: classically in sickle cell; can also from drugs like NSAIDs; urine will be dark → renal papillae in the medulla receive less blood flow, so small changes in the microvascular supply can lead to sloughing + necrosis of the medulla.

vignettes.q: First answer for Tx of all kidney stones on USMLE
vignettes.a: hydration / fluids.

vignettes.q: Tx for calcium oxalate stones?
vignettes.a: fluids, then alkalinize urine (citrate); prevent recurrence with thiazide (decrease urinary Ca).

vignettes.q: Tx for calcium phosphate stones?
vignettes.a: fluids; prevent recurrence with thiazide (decrease urinary Ca). Calcium phosphate stones form at higher pH, so do not alkalinize; CaOxalate stones form at lower pH, which is why citrate helps.

vignettes.q: Tx for struvite (ammonium magnesium phosphate) stones?
vignettes.a: fluids; acidify urine with ammonium chloride; surgery (because they’re often huge).

vignettes.q: Tx for uric acid stones?
vignettes.a: fluids + alkalinize urine with citrate; treat the underlying gout; avoid uricosurics such as probenecid indefinitely; avoid low-dose aspirin.

vignettes.q: Tx for cystine stones?
vignettes.a: fluids; alkalinize urine with citrate.

vignettes.q: Who gets calcium oxalate stones?
vignettes.a: classically those with intestinal malabsorptive disorders such as Crohn, Celiac, CF → malabsorption of fats means increased intraintestinal binding of fat to calcium → less calcium available to bind oxalate intraluminally → more o

vignettes.q: Who gets struvite stones?
vignettes.a: UTIs caused by urease (+) organisms. Proteus spp. is classic. Stones are coffin lid-shaped.

vignettes.q: Who gets uric acid stones?
vignettes.a: generally uric acid over-producers such as in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome or tumor lysis syndrome; alcoholics (USMLE wants under-excretion as mechanism via which EtOH causes gout, but EtOH also can increase production); stones are radiol

vignettes.q: Who get cystine stones?
vignettes.a: patients with cystinuria caused by inability to absorb COLA (cysteine, ornithine, lysine, arginine) → two cysteines (-SH) joined via disulfide bond make one cystine (-S—S-).

vignettes.q: Any factoid to know about cystine stones?
vignettes.a: AR disorder; generally young adults in USMLE vignette; nitroprusside urine test yields a magenta color; hexagon-shaped stones.

vignettes.q: What do I need to know about renal tubular acidosis type I (RTA I)?
vignettes.a: decreased ability of the DCT to secrete protons (urine pH is >5.5) → leads to metabolic acidosis; patient does not have hyperkalemia. Can be associated with bilateral renal parenchymal stones (i.e., not within the lumina but inste

vignettes.q: What do I need to know about renal tubular acidosis type II (RTA II)?
vignettes.a: decreased ability of the PCT to reabsorb bicarb (urine pH is >5.5) → associated with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and Fanconi syndrome (expired tetracyclines). Patient does not have hyperkalemia.

vignettes.q: What do I need to know about renal tubular acidosis type IV (RTA IV)?
vignettes.a: either hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism or aldosterone insensitivity at the kidney (urine pH <5.5) → patient will present with lab values resembling Addison disease, but the etiology will be chronic renal failure, not adrenal. For

vignettes.q: USMLE Q asks “decreased absorption” vs “no change” for Fanconi syndrome with respect to glucose, amino acids, phosphate, bicarb
vignettes.a: decreased absorption for all four.

vignettes.q: Explain RAAS system.
vignettes.a: reduced renal perfusion (low blood volume, renal artery stenosis, fibromuscular dysplasia) → juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin → renin cleaves angiotensinogen (produced by liver) in the plasma into angiotensin I → AT I goes to l

vignettes.q: Where does aldosterone act in the kidney?
vignettes.a: cortical collecting duct; binds to intracytosolic receptor, causing upregulation of basolateral Na/K-ATPase pumps (1, 2, 3 → for every 1 ATP utilized, 2 K secreted into tubular cell from blood; 3 Na reabsorbed from tubular cell in

vignettes.q: Another important point about renin secretion?
vignettes.a: USMLE wants you to know that beta-1 activity causes renin release. Sometimes you’ll get a Q where a patient has low blood volume and they’ll ask which is true, and the answer is “increased renal sympathetic activity.”

vignettes.q: Where does vasopressin (ADH) act in the kidney?
vignettes.a: medullary collecting duct → inserts aquaporins on apical membrane → increased free water reabsorption.

vignettes.q: Urine + serum findings in SIADH
vignettes.a: concentrated urine (high osmolality) + low serum sodium (<135 mEq/dL).

vignettes.q: Urine + serum findings in diabetes insipidus
vignettes.a: dilute urine (low osmolality) + high serum sodium (>145 mEq/dL).

vignettes.q: Four causes of nephrogenic DI or USMLE?
vignettes.a: lithium + demeclocycline are the two highest yield. NSAIDs and hypercalcemia can also cause it.

vignettes.q: Urine + serum findings in psychogenic polydipsia (patient drinks too much)
vignettes.a: dilute urine (low osmolality) + low serum sodium (<135 mEq/dL).

vignettes.q: In DI, comment on the urine osmolality relative to plasma (i.e., hypotonic, isotonic, or hypertonic) for PCT, JGA, medullary collecting duct
vignettes.a: PCT is always isotonic regardless of renal condition; JGA is always hypotonic regardless of renal condition (joins the early-DCT with the afferent arteriole); medullary collecting duct hypotonic. In SIADH, the latter would merely

vignettes.q: What is the JGA?
vignettes.a: juxtaglomerular apparatus contains JGC that secrete renin.

vignettes.q: What is the macula densa?
vignettes.a: modified smooth muscle cells of the DCT that sense changes in serum sodium, thereby triggering the JGC to secrete renin; if volume status is low, PCT is attempting to reabsorb more water to compensate; in order to do so, it reabso

vignettes.q: What do I need to know about mannitol?
vignettes.a: osmotic diuretic that acts by retaining water within the nephron lumina; USMLE likes proximal straight tubule (short segment after the PCT) as the answer if it shows you a drawing and is very specific; if proximal straight tubule

vignettes.q: What do I need to know about acetazolamide and the kidney?
vignettes.a: carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that acts to prevent bicarb reabsorption → causes a transient metabolic acidosis that can be used to counteract the respiratory alkalosis secondary to altitude sickness (kidney cannot physiologically c

vignettes.q: What do I need to know about Loops?
vignettes.a: Furosemide is standard first-line agent → does not decrease mortality in heart failure → used to fluid-unload in patients with generalized edema or symptomatic pulmonary edema → inhibits the Na/K/2Cl symporter on the apical membra

vignettes.q: How are calcium + magnesium reabsorbed in the thick ascending limb?
vignettes.a: paracellular (between the cells).

vignettes.q: What is Bartter syndrome?
vignettes.a: disease that presents as though the patient is indefinitely on loop diuretic (associated with JGC hyperplasia).

vignettes.q: What do I need to know about thiazides?
vignettes.a: hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) is standard drug → inhibits the Na/Cl symporter on the apical membrane of the early-DCT → associated with decreased urinary calcium and magnesium (in contrast to loops) → known to cause hyperGLUC (hyperg

vignettes.q: What is Gitelman syndrome?
vignettes.a: disease that presents as though the patient is indefinitely on thiazide diuretic.

vignettes.q: What do I need to know about amiloride and triamterene?
vignettes.a: simply that they’re ENaC inhibitors and are potassium-sparing (meaning they don’t cause kaliuresis).

vignettes.q: What do I need to know about spironolactone?
vignettes.a: aldosterone receptor antagonist used in heart failure after the patient is already on ACEi (or ARB) and a beta-blocker. Can also be used in patients with Conn syndrome / primary hyperaldosteronism. USMLE loves asking spironolacton

vignettes.q: What do I need to know about tolvaptan/conivaptan?
vignettes.a: vasopressin (ADH) receptor antagonists that can be used in SIADH (e.g., due to small cell lung cancer).

vignettes.q: What are the three main effects of parathyroid hormone (PTH) at the kidney?
vignettes.a: Upregulates apical Ca2+ reabsorption in the late-DCT (increases Ca reabsorption). Decreases phosphate reabsorption in the PCT. Upregulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase in the PCT → increases conversion of inactive 25-OH-D3 to active 1,25-(

vignettes.q: What kind of PTH-related pathology is seen in renal disease?
vignettes.a: secondary hyperparathyroidism is caused by chronic renal failure → kidney cannot reabsorb Ca in the DCT or synthesis 1,25-D3 in PCT (decreased intestinal absorption), leading to hypocalcemia. PCT goes up to compensate.

vignettes.q: Comment on vitamin D in relation to renal disease. → patient will have decreased 1,25-(OH)2-D3 and increased 24,25-(OH)2-D3 (the latter is an inactive storage form that is created by the shunting of 25- OH-D3;
vignettes.a: Vitamin D deficiency due to renal failure: low Ca + high PO4. Vitamin D deficiency not due to renal failure: low Ca + low PO4.

vignettes.q: What is renal osteodystrophy?
vignettes.a: any bone problem caused by renal disease, but is usually synonymous with “renal-induced osteomalacia” due to renal effects on reducing active Vit D3.

vignettes.q: Patient with chronic renal disease has a pseudofracture of the hip; Dx?
vignettes.a: osteomalacia → “pseudofracture” is pathognomonic for vitamin D deficiency; in this case, the pseudofracture is just a type of renal osteodystrophy that may be seen.

vignettes.q: Patient has renal failure + friction rub heard on auscultation of the chest; Dx + Tx?
vignettes.a: uremic pericarditis (a type of fibrinous pericarditis) → USMLE Tx is immediate hemodialysis.

vignettes.q: What is the biochemical / acid-base disturbance seen in renal disease?
vignettes.a: sodium is variable; potassium high; calcium low; phosphate high; bicarb low; pH low; CO2 low (compensation).

vignettes.q: What do I need to know about EPO and the kidney?
vignettes.a: Kidney secretes it in response to anemia / low oxygen states (e.g., COPD). EPO deficiency occurs in renal failure, leading to anemia of chronic disease. EPO excess secretion can occur in renal cell carcinoma.

vignettes.q: Smoker + hypercalcemia + polycythemia + hematuria; Dx?
vignettes.a: RCC (paraneoplastic EPO + PTHrp).

vignettes.q: Smoker + flank pain + red urine; Dx?
vignettes.a: RCC.

vignettes.q: Most common type of RCC?
vignettes.a: clear cell carcinoma (histo shows large clear cells on Step 1).

vignettes.q: Notable disease associated with RCC?
vignettes.a: Von-Hippel Lindau (VHL) → RCC can be bilateral. VHL is AD, chromosome 3, and also associated with retinal + cerebellar hemangioblastomas; caused by constitutive activation of hypoxia-inducible factor.

vignettes.q: Renal cancer in children?
vignettes.a: Wilms tumor.

vignettes.q: 3M + painless flank mass + no other info; Dx?
vignettes.a: Wilms tumor.

vignettes.q: 6M + painless flank mass + seizure + MRI of brain shows periventricular nodules; Dx?
vignettes.a: Tuberous sclerosis with renal angiomyolipoma.

vignettes.q: Anything else about Wilms tumor?
vignettes.a: increased incidence in horseshoe kidney in Turner syndrome.

vignettes.q: Horseshoe kidney key point?
vignettes.a: not only increased risk of Wilms tumor, but the kidney gets caught under the IMA.

vignettes.q: What is WAGR complex?
vignettes.a: Wilms tumor, Aniridia, Genitourinary malformation, Retardation; caused by WT1 gene mutation.

vignettes.q: What is Denys-Drash syndrome?
vignettes.a: Wilms tumor + male pseudohermaphroditism (secondary sex characteristics are female; primary sex characteristics are male); caused by WT1 gene mutation.

vignettes.q: What is Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome?
vignettes.a: Wilms tumor + neonatal hypoglycemia + macrosomia / macroglossia + hemihypertrophy +/- omphalocele; caused by WT2 gene mutation.

vignettes.q: Comment on AR vs AD polycystic kidney disease.
vignettes.a: ARPKD is chromosome 6 and a pediatric condition; it’s associated with hepatic fibrosis. ADPKD is chromosome 16 and presents in 30s or 40s; associated with HTN and circle of Willis saccular (berry) aneurysms.

vignettes.q: Most common extra-renal location for cysts in ADPKD?
vignettes.a: liver.

vignettes.q: What’s more important in management of ADPKD, serial BP checks or MRI angiogram circle of Willis?
vignettes.a: serial BP checks → renal cysts compress microvasculature, causing surges in RAAS.

vignettes.q: Comment on systemic sclerosis and the kidney?
vignettes.a: systemic sclerosis (diffuse type) can cause renal crises with malignant HTN.

vignettes.q: 68M + diabetic + Hx of intermittent claudication + CABG + gradually increasing BP past two years; Dx?
vignettes.a: renal artery stenosis.

vignettes.q: Cause of renal artery stenosis?
vignettes.a: atherosclerosis. They will always give RAS in a patient who has cardiovascular disease.

vignettes.q: 23F + high aldosterone + high renin + high BP; Dx?
vignettes.a: fibromuscular dysplasia → this is not renal artery stenosis; if you say RAS, that means atherosclerosis. FMD is a tunica media proliferative pathology resulting in RAS-like presentation; it’s seen classically in young women, where

vignettes.q: How to Dx FMD?
vignettes.a: MR angiography (HY on the USMLE) → NBME has actually said the buzz / colloquial phrase “string of beads” appearance seen on MR angiography.

vignettes.q: Patient with high BP is given an ACEi or ARB and gets a spike in either renin or creatinine; Dx?
vignettes.a: FMD if young patient; RAS if patient with CVD. USMLE loves this point and it shows up on USMLE Step 1. If you have FMD or RAS, renal blood flow is already reduced, so the kidney has a reduced capacity to remain within physiologic

vignettes.q: Hx of many pregnancies + downward movement of vesicourethral junction
vignettes.a: stress incontinence.

vignettes.q: Tx of stress incontinence
vignettes.a: pelvic floor exercises (Kegel); if insufficient → mid-urethral sling.

vignettes.q: Hyperactive detrusor or detrusor instability
vignettes.a: urge incontinence.

vignettes.q: Need to run to bathroom when sticking key in a door
vignettes.a: urge incontinence.

vignettes.q: Incontinence in multiple sclerosis patient or perimenopausal
vignettes.a: urge incontinence.

vignettes.q: Tx of urge incontinence
vignettes.a: oxybutynin (muscarinic cholinergic antagonist) or mirabegron (beta-3 agonist).

vignettes.q: Incontinence + high post-void volume (usually 3-400 in question; normal is <50 mL)
vignettes.a: overflow incontinence.

vignettes.q: Incontinence in diabetes
vignettes.a: overflow incontinence due to neurogenic bladder.

vignettes.q: Tx for overflow incontinence in diabetes
vignettes.a: bethanechol (muscarinic cholinergic agonist).

vignettes.q: Incontinence in BPH
vignettes.a: overflow incontinence due to outlet obstruction → eventual neurogenic bladder.

vignettes.q: Tx for overflow incontinence in BPH
vignettes.a: insert catheter first; then give alpha-1 blocker of 5-alpha- reductase inhibitor; then TURP if necessary.

vignettes.q: Innervation of external urethral sphincter
vignettes.a: pudendal nerve (somatic; voluntary).

vignettes.q: Innervation of internal urethral sphincter
vignettes.a: hypogastric nerves (sympathetic).

vignettes.q: Innervation of detrusor muscle
vignettes.a: pelvic splanchnic nerves (parasympathetic; S2-4).

vignettes.q: What is Brenner tumor?
vignettes.a: ovarian tumor with bladder (transitional cell) epithelium.

vignettes.q: Exquisitely tender prostate on digital rectal exam
vignettes.a: prostatitis.

vignettes.q: Prostatitis Tx
vignettes.a: ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolone → DNA gyrase / topoisomerase II inhibitor).

vignettes.q: Costovertebral angle tenderness + fever
vignettes.a: pyelonephritis.

vignettes.q: Costovertebral angle tenderness + granular casts
vignettes.a: pyelonephritis.

vignettes.q: Tx for pyelonephritis
vignettes.a: ciprofloxacin, OR ampicillin + gentamicin.

vignettes.q: Is chronic pyelonephritis ever an answer?
vignettes.a: usually young patient, i.e., 3-4-year-old, who has recurrent bouts of acute pyelo → need to know recurrent acute pyelo is what causes chronic pyelo. For Step 1 level, they will show an image of a small, scarred kidney and give you

vignettes.q: Tx for simple UTI
vignettes.a: nitrofurantoin is classic answer; TMP/SMX is also classic combo.

vignettes.q: 22F + Sx of dysuria for 6 months + anterior vaginal wall pain + U/A completely normal + afebrile; Dx?
vignettes.a: chronic interstitial cystitis → answer on one of the obgyn forms. Must have at least 6 weeks of UTI- like Sx without any identifiable pathology.

vignettes.q: Tx for asymptomatic bacteriuria
vignettes.a: if pregnant, must Tx. If not pregnant, do not Tx.

vignettes.q: Why must Tx asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy?
vignettes.a: progesterone slows ureteric peristalsis, increasing the risk of pyelo.

vignettes.q: 82F falls down stairs; urine dipstick shows 2+ blood and 3-4 RBCs/hpf on LM; Dx?
vignettes.a: rhabdomyolysis → need to know that false (+) blood on urine dipstick is rhabdomyolysis (dipstick cannot differentiate myoglobinuria from actual RBCs).

vignettes.q: 22F has Sx of UTI + U/A completely normal; next best step?
vignettes.a: test for chlamydia/gonorrhea.

vignettes.q: 25M + mucopurulent urethral discharge + culture grows nothing; Dx?
vignettes.a: chlamydia (obligate intracellular).

vignettes.q: Tx for chlamydia and gonorrhea on the Step
vignettes.a: If chlamydia, give azithromycin or doxycycline. If gonorrhea, give ceftriaxone PLUS either azithro or doxy (must co-treat for chlamydia). If you don’t see the gram (-) diplococci on light microscopy, you know gonorrhea likely isn’

vignettes.q: Most common type of bladder cancer?
vignettes.a: transitional cell carcinoma.

vignettes.q: Most specific cause of bladder cancer?
vignettes.a: industrial (aniline) dyes.

vignettes.q: Most common cause of bladder cancer?
vignettes.a: smoking.

vignettes.q: Type of bladder cancer seen with Schistosoma haematobium infection
vignettes.a: squamous cell carcinoma.

vignettes.q: What is Potter sequence?
vignettes.a: renal agenesis leading to oligohydramnios → causes pulmonary hypoplasia in fetus.

vignettes.q: Most common genitourinary (GU) abnormality in neonatal males?
vignettes.a: posterior urethral valves (PUV) → thin membrane(s) in the urethra preventing the outflow of urine.

vignettes.q: Male neonate + suprapubic mass + no passage of urine; Dx?
vignettes.a: PUV.

vignettes.q: Neonatal male with PUV; next best step in Dx?
vignettes.a: ultrasound then voiding cystourethrogram.

vignettes.q: 16M + skiing accident + bruising and/or pain over a flank + urinalysis is normal; next best step?
vignettes.a: no further investigations indicated.

vignettes.q: USMLE Q gives you creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL in 65M, then tells you 10 years later his Cr is 1.2 mg/dL; Dx?
vignettes.a: normal aging → creatinine clearance naturally decreases with age. There is no definitive cutoff for USMLE Qs, but the student should be aware that Cr of 1.5 or greater is always pathologic, and at Cr of 2.0, >90% of nephron functi

vignettes.q: USMLE Q says oophorectomy is being performed + ureter is damaged; during ligation of which vessel did the damage to the ureter occur?
vignettes.a: ovarian artery.

vignettes.q: What is water under the bridge?
vignettes.a: ureter travels under the uterine artery in women and vas deferens in men.

vignettes.q: Kid + bloody diarrhea + petechiae + red urine; Dx?
vignettes.a: hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) caused by EHEC O157:H7 or Shigella → HUS = triad of thrombocytopenia + schistocytosis (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia) + renal insufficiency.

vignettes.q: How does HUS contrast with TTP?
vignettes.a: TTP is caused by a mutation that results in defective ADAMTS13, or antibodies against ADAMTS13, resulting in the inability to cleave vWF multimers → platelet clumping → similar progression as HUS. One of the points of contrast is

vignettes.q: What is hepatorenal syndrome?
vignettes.a: liver failure causing renal failure; rare Dx but the correct answer USMLE wants is “normal renal biopsy.”

vignettes.q: Endocarditis following a genitourinary procedure (e.g., TURP) or catheterization; organism?
vignettes.a: USMLE wants enterococcus. HY RENAL

vignettes.q: Acid-base disturbance in aspirin toxicity after 20 mins
vignettes.a: mixed metabolic acidosis-respiratory alkalosis (low CO2, low pH, normal O2, low bicarb)

vignettes.q: High calcium + polyuria
vignettes.a: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (weird, but on NBME)

vignettes.q: Beta-lactam (e.g., nafcillin) or cephalosporin + rash + renal issue
vignettes.a: interstitial nephritis

vignettes.q: Interstitial nephritis
vignettes.a: WBCs in the urine (eosinophils)

vignettes.q: BUN/Cr > 20
vignettes.a: prerenal (hypovolemia) → heart failure

vignettes.q: BUN/Cr <20
vignettes.a: not prerenal

vignettes.q: Blood loss + oliguria
vignettes.a: acute tubular necrosis

vignettes.q: Sickle cell + nephrotic syndrome
vignettes.a: focal segmental glomerulosclerosus

vignettes.q: Cirrhosis or recent peritoneal dialysis or nephrotic syndrome + fever + abdo pain
vignettes.a: SBP

vignettes.q: Renal failure + friction rub over chest
vignettes.a: uremic pericarditis → do hemodialysis

vignettes.q: 40s male + hematuria + hemoptysis
vignettes.a: Goodpasture syndrome

vignettes.q: Antibodies in Goodpasture
vignettes.a: Anti-GBM (anti-collagen IV)

vignettes.q: Dx of Goodpasture
vignettes.a: antibodies first, but confirmatory is renal biopsy showing linear immunofluorescence

vignettes.q: Severe renal disease in Wegener or Goodpasture or MP
vignettes.a: rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (crescentic)

vignettes.q: SLE + red urine; Dx?
vignettes.a: lupus nephritis, more specifically, diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis (DPGN)

vignettes.q: Nephrotic syndrome in SS
vignettes.a: FSGS

vignettes.q: Chromosome for AR and AD polycystic kidney disease
vignettes.a: 6 for AR; 16 for AD

vignettes.q: Electrolyte abnormality in Cushing syndrome
vignettes.a: hypokalemia (chronically high glucocorticoid can cause potassium wasting distally in the kidney similar to aldosterone)

vignettes.q: “Wait, why is bicarb normal in acute asthma attack? Shouldn’t it go low to compensate if CO2 is low?”
vignettes.a: not enough time for bicarb to change; takes a minimum of 12-24 hours for renal elimination to have an effect on serum levels; this is why in altitude sickness, where CO2 is low (due to high RR bc of lower atmospheric O2), azetazol

vignettes.q: Electrolyte abnormality in rhabdo
vignettes.a: hyperkalemia (cell lysis + renal failure → myoglobin causes acute tubular necrosis)

vignettes.q: High-anion gap metabolic acidosis
vignettes.a: MUDPILES → methanol, uremia, DKA, phenformin, iron/INH, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates

vignettes.q: 12M + red urine 1-3 days after upper respiratory tract infection (URTI)
vignettes.a: IgA nephropathy, not PSGN; can also get IgA nephropathy from GI infections

vignettes.q: 12M + red urine 1-2 weeks after URTI or skin infection
vignettes.a: PSGN → can get it from Group A Strep skin infections

vignettes.q: 6F + red urine + abdo pain + arthralgias + violaceous lesions on buttocks + thighs; Dx?
vignettes.a: Henoch- Schonlein purpura; red urine = IgA nephropathy → HSP is tetrad of 1) IgA nephropathy, 2) palpable purpura, 3) arthralgias, 4) abdo pain

vignettes.q: 44M alcoholic + winter + they show a pic of his feet and they’re red; what electrolyte are we most worried about upon rewarming them
vignettes.a: hyperkalemia → alcoholics are notably susceptible to rhabo (ultra HY on the USMLE) → rhabdo causes myoglobin release, which is nephrotoxic and can cause acute tubular necrosis (potassium goes up); even if the patient doesn’t get f

vignettes.q: Patient with CVD is on various medications + has hyperkalemia; why?
vignettes.a: ACEi, ARB, and spironolactone all can cause hyperkalemia.

vignettes.q: Patient with CVD is on various medications + hypokalemia; why?
vignettes.a: furosemide (Loop diuretic)

vignettes.q: When do we start patients on furosemide?
vignettes.a: to fluid unload (dyspnea in heart failure or peripheral edema)

vignettes.q: Patient is started on furosemide + still has fluid overload; what’s the next diuretic to use
vignettes.a: spironolactone → essentially furosemide causes increased K wasting, so we must give a potassium-sparing diuretic to balance the effect (spironolactone).

vignettes.q: What’s the MOA of spironolactone
vignettes.a: aldosterone receptor antagonist.

vignettes.q: Side-effects of spironolactone
vignettes.a: hyperkalemia; gynecomastia.

vignettes.q: When do we give patients spironolactone apart from as a step-up from Loops?
vignettes.a: added onto heart failure management after a patient is already on ACEi (or ARB) + beta-blocker. In other words, for heart failure: give ACEi (or ARB) first, then add beta-blocker, then add spironolactone.

vignettes.q: BUN/Cr ratio in someone with NSAID-induced interstitial nephropathy
vignettes.a: >20 (pre-renal).

vignettes.q: What else is associated with linear immunofluorescence on the USMLE?
vignettes.a: Goodpasture syndrome (on biopsy of the kidney or alveoli).

vignettes.q: Mechanism for Goodpasture syndrome?
vignettes.a: antibodies against type IV collagen → “2, 3, 4… 2, 3, 4… 2, 3, 4. The Goodpasture is marching in the field, 2, 3, 4!”→ Type 2 hypersensitivity against the alpha-3 chains of type 4 collagen.

vignettes.q: 44M + hematuria + hemoptysis
vignettes.a: Goodpasture syndrome

vignettes.q: 32F + high BP + high aldosterone/renin
vignettes.a: fibromuscular dysplasia (tunica media proliferation in renal arteries) → this is not renal artery stenosis → if you say “renal artery stenosis,” that means atherosclerosis.

vignettes.q: Increased creatinine following medication administered to someone with renal artery stenosis; what was the drug?
vignettes.a: ACEi or ARB

vignettes.q: Pt has fatigue + normal Na, high K, low pH, low bicarb; Dx?
vignettes.a: Addison (sodium can sometimes be normal in aldosterone derangement).

vignettes.q: 22F + BP of 160/110 on multiple office visits + MR angiography of renal vessels confirms diagnosis of fibromuscular dysplasia + labs show normal Na, normal K, normal pH, normal bicarb (Q is: what are her AT-II
vignettes.a: high AT-II + high aldosterone → learning objective is: it’s rare, but biochemistry can be completely normal in aldosterone derangement (Google it if you don’t believe me) → this is on the USMLE; if you get a vignette where they 10

vignettes.q: Side-effects of thiazides
vignettes.a: hyperGLUC → hyperglycemia, -lipidemia, -uricemia, calcemia.

vignettes.q: Whom should you never give thiazides to?
vignettes.a: prediabetics or diabetics → will push people into type II DM and make current DMs worse. One of the worst/frequent pharmacologic mistreatments. Also don’t give to pts with Hx of gout (bc of hyperuricemia risk).

vignettes.q: Diabetic pt on HCTZ for HTN
vignettes.a: take them the off the thiazide and put them on an ACEi or ARB.

vignettes.q: Important use of thiazide apart from HTN management in select patients
vignettes.a: decreased risk of nephro- / ureterolithiasis (stones) because they cause hypocalciuria (and hence hypercalcemia).

vignettes.q: Delirium in patient on thiazide
vignettes.a: think hypercalcemia → high Ca is HY USMLE cause of CNS dysfunction → “hypercalcemic crisis.”

vignettes.q: Renal issue + hypercalcemia; Dx?
vignettes.a: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus → on the NBME.

vignettes.q: 6F + finds open bottle of aspirin; which of the following findings in the patient best suggests the dose consumed was toxic?
vignettes.a: increased respiratory rate; aspirin causes respiratory alkalosis acutely due to upregulation of respiratory centers (high pH, low CO2, no change bicarb [too acute to change]); after roughly 20 minutes, a mixed metabolic acidosis-r

vignettes.q: 40F + fibromuscular dysplasia + GFR is within normal range; what explains this latter finding?
vignettes.a: increased efferent arteriolar resistance; RAAS will upregulate in response to decreased renal blood flow → angiotensin II constricts efferent arterioles, causing increased filtration fraction, where GFR is held constant despite lo

vignettes.q: 19F + external compression of left renal artery but has normal renal perfusion pressure; what explains this latter finding?
vignettes.a: decreased afferent arteriolar resistance; just happens to be the answer they give in this hypothetical scenario; if the afferent perfusion is decreased due to compression of the renal artery, the only way perfusion pressure can st

vignettes.q: 28M + renal failure + hematuria + hearing loss; what’s the mechanism for this patient’s disease?
vignettes.a: mutation in type IV collagen (Alport syndrome, X-linked); wrong answer is antibodies against type IV collagen (Goodpasture); Alport → hematuria in a male + ear and/or eye problem; Goodpasture → male 20s-40s with hematuria and hemo

vignettes.q: 62F + flank mass + serum calcium of 11.5 mg/dL + hemoglobin of 18.5 g/dL; diagnosis?
vignettes.a: paraneoplastic syndrome; renal cell carcinoma can produce PTHrp (correct, similar to SCC of the lung) and EPO (causing high hemoglobin). USMLE might give you a vignette of a smoker who has hypercalcemia and polycythemia + show you

vignettes.q: 48M + BP 150/90 on multiple visits + normal BMI + non-diabetic; Q wants to know the best therapy for this patient
vignettes.a: hydrochlorothiazide; answer can also be a dCCB. Vignette doesn’t mention diabetes, pre-diabetes, atherosclerotic disease, or proteinuria (otherwise answer would be ACEi or ARB); if patient is non-diabetic with HTN and has mere ele

vignettes.q: 38M + diabetic + mild proteinuria + LDL 95 mg/dL + BP 120/80 + HbA1c of 7%; Q asks what is most likely to decrease morbidity in this patient?
vignettes.a: lisinopril; once again, start an ACEi or ARB in a diabetic if there is 1) any proteinuria; 2) any elevation in creatinine or renin; or 3) BP >130/80.

vignettes.q: 50M + on metformin + received IV contrast + now has creatinine of 1.5 mg/dL; Q wants to know what would have prevented this condition
vignettes.a: intravenous hydration; Dx is contrast nephropathy; metformin does not cause high creatinine; it is merely the case that if a patient has high creatinine, then we discontinue metformin due to lactic acidosis risk.

vignettes.q: 70M + high creatinine + taking amitriptyline; Q wants to know best way to prevent this patient’s condition → answer = avoidance of anticholinergic medications; patient has high creatinine due to post-renal obst
vignettes.a: In elderly, be very cautious administering TCAs, anti-psychotics, or 1st -generation H1-blockers (i.e., diphenhydramine). They can cause delirium, worsening of dementia, and in old men in particular, exacerbation of BPH.

vignettes.q: 16F + consumed pills + now has tinnitus + low bicarb, low CO2, and high anion-gap; risk factor?
vignettes.a: aspirin (salicylate) causing high anion-gap mixed metabolic acidosis / respiratory alkalosis.

vignettes.q: 27M + sickle cell + nephrotic syndrome; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: focal segmental glomerulosclerosis caused by sickle cell; in short, FSGS is the answer if patient has nephrotic syndrome in sickle cell. Can also rarely be caused by HIV / heroin use.

vignettes.q: 38F + rheumatoid arthritis + took gold salts for treatment + develops proteinuria; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: gold salts causing membranous glomerulonephritis; dapsone can also cause this.

vignettes.q: 40F + history of hepatitis B + proteinuria; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: membranous glomerulonephritis due to hepatitis B; this is renal Dx if patient has nephrotic syndrome in setting of hepatitis B or C.

vignettes.q: 40F + history of hepatitis C + blood in urine; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis; this is answer on USMLE if patient has nephritic syndrome in hepatitis B or C.

vignettes.q: 40F + SLE + blood in urine; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis due to SLE; answer on USMLE if patient has nephritic syndrome in SLE; if nephrotic syndrome in SLE, patient just has regular membranous glomerulonephritis. But DPGN is >>> higher yield for

vignettes.q: 12F + blood in urine 1-3 days after sore throat; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: IgA nephropathy; answer on USMLE when patient has blood in urine 1-3 days following sore throat (viral infection).

vignettes.q: 12F + blood in urine 1-3 weeks after sore throat; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: PSGN is answer on USMLE when patient has blood in urine 1-3 weeks following sore throat (group A strep infection).

vignettes.q: 50M + flank pain + blood in urine + high serum calcium + high hemoglobin; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: renal cell carcinoma; major risk factor is smoking; can produce ectopic PTHrp (similar to squamous cell of lung) and EPO.

vignettes.q: 50M + blood in urine + Hx of smoking; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: bladder cancer (transitional cell carcinoma); major risk factor is smoking. Aniline dyes (industrial dyes) and naphthylamine (moth balls) are also assessed for causing transitional cell carcinoma of bladder.

vignettes.q: 23M + swam in lake in Africa + now has blood in urine; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder due to Schistosoma hematobium; risk factor is swimming in fresh water in Africa.

vignettes.q: 64F + back pain + nephrotic syndrome + S4 heart sound; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: renal amyloidosis and cardiac amyloidosis; major risk factor for amyloidosis on USMLE is multiple myeloma.

vignettes.a: ↓ Estrogen, ↓ inhibin, ↑ LH, ↑ FSH. — Diagnosis is Turner syndrome (45XO). • Patient will have “streak ovaries” and “menopause before menarche.” • Turner syndrome presents with short height, webbed neck (cystic hygroma), shield ch

vignettes.q: 18F + runs cross country + BMI 16 + no menstrual period last 4 months. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for this patient’s estrogen, inhibin B, GnRH, LH, and FSH levels? (5 arrows)

vignettes.q: 45F + 17 weeks’ gestation + concerned about risk for Down syndrome. If the fetus does in fact have Down syndrome, what are the most likely arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for serum levels of alpha-fetoprotein (AFP),
vignettes.a: ↓ AFP, ↑ b-hCG, ↓ estriol, ↑ inhibin A. — Second trimester quad-screen (16-18 weeks) for Down syndrome will show low AFP (Down in Down syndrome). AFP will be high in neural tube defects, anencephaly, multiple gestation pregnancies

vignettes.q: 33F + G1P0 + 30 weeks’ gestation + BP 150/95 + protein in urine + schistocytes seen on blood smear. What are the arrows (i.e., ↑, ↓, or ↔) for platelet count, hematocrit, and liver enzymes?
vignettes.a: ↓ platelet count, ↓ hematocrit, ↑ liver enzymes. — Diagnosis is preeclampsia that has progressed to HELLP syndrome. • On USMLE, preeclampsia = proteinuria and hypertension after 20 weeks of pregnancy. I say “on USMLE,” because in

vignettes.q: Tx of stress incontinence
vignettes.a: pelvic floor exercises (Kegel); if insufficient → mid-urethral sling

vignettes.q: Incontinence in BPH
vignettes.a: overflow incontinence due to outlet obstruction → eventual neurogenic bladder

vignettes.q: Tx for overflow incontinence in BPH
vignettes.a: insert catheter first; then give alpha-1 blocker of 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor; then TURP if necessary

vignettes.q: Exquisitely tender prostate on digital rectal exam
vignettes.a: prostatitis

vignettes.q: Metastases to long bones in prostate cancer
vignettes.a: osteoblastic (Dx with bone scan); spine do MRI

vignettes.q: Breast imaging (if performed)
vignettes.a: ultrasound only under age 30; over age 30 do mammogram +/- ultrasound

vignettes.q: Premature ovarian failure + Turner syndrome + menopause
vignettes.a: high FSH (low inhibin) + low estrogen

vignettes.q: Anovulation + hirsutism
vignettes.a: PCOS

vignettes.q: Why high LH/FSH ratio important in anovulation/PCOS
vignettes.a: ovulation stimulated when follicle not ready → no

vignettes.q: What’s LH do?
vignettes.a: Stimulates theca interna cells (females) and Leydig cells (males) to make androgens

vignettes.q: What’s FSH do?
vignettes.a: Stimulates granulosa cells (females) and Sertoli cells (males) to make aromatase; also primes follicles

vignettes.q: Tx for PCOS
vignettes.a: if high BMI, weight loss first always on USMLE

vignettes.q: Tx for PCOS if they ask for meds and/or weight loss already tried
vignettes.a: OCPs (if not wanting pregnancy); clomiphene (if wanting pregnancy)

vignettes.q: PCOS increases risk of what
vignettes.a: endometrial cancer (unopposed estrogen)

vignettes.q: Tx of prostate cancer
vignettes.a: flutamide + leuprolide together (if they force a sequence, choose F then L).

vignettes.q: USMLE might ask you which muscle is not strengthened by Kegel exercises
vignettes.a: student then proceeds to have two thoughts: 1) “, I’m supposed to know Kegel exercises at that high level of detail?” and 2) couldn’t any muscle not be strengthened by Kegel exercises; I mean, the deltoid wouldn’t be for instance.

vignettes.q: 23F + really pad period pain + P/E shows nodularity of uterosacral ligaments
vignettes.a: endometriosis → do diagnostic laparoscopy.

vignettes.q: 16F is Tanner stage II + wide neck + bone age is equal to chronologic age; Dx?
vignettes.a: Turner syndrome → presents with genuine short stature (vignette will often say girl who’s 4’11”) + Tanner stage I or II + cystic hygroma (lymphatic insufficiency of neck; wide/webbed neck).

vignettes.q: Diffusely enlarged uterus + per vaginum bleeding
vignettes.a: adenomyosis

vignettes.q: Globular uterus + per vaginum bleeding
vignettes.a: leiyomyomata uteri (uterine fibroids)

vignettes.q: 84F + unilateral hydronephrosis caused by ureteral compression by a vascular structure; what’s the structure

vignettes.a: chance of rejecting a true null hypothesis. In other words, a true null hypothesis means there really is no increased risk of prostate cancer caused by sugar. But because the study said there’s a difference, they rejected the null

vignettes.q: Simple Q asking the function of Sertoli cells; answer = produces aromatase.

vignettes.q: 50F + being treated for breast cancer + develops cardiomegaly; Q asks biggest risk factor
vignettes.a: trastuzumab causing cardiotoxicity.

vignettes.q: 55F + perimenopausal + severe hot flashes + started on HRT a few months ago + stopped taking the progesterone component because of effects on her moods; Q asks what is most likely to be seen in this patient?
vignettes.a: endometrial hyperplasia; unopposed estrogen is risk factor for endometrial hyperplasia, which in turn can lead to endometrial cancer (↑ cell proliferation = ↑ risk of mutation).

vignettes.q: 50F + BMI of 30 + irregular menses for many years + new-onset heavier vaginal bleeding; Q asks what is most likely risk factor for this patient’s condition
vignettes.a: anovulation; diagnosis is endometrial cancer due to history of anovulation/PCOS. Mechanism: high BMI → insulin resistance → abnormal GnRH pulsation → high LH/FSH ratio → high LH over-stimulates theca interna cells (hirsutism); low

vignettes.q: 65F + started on tamoxifen as part of her breast cancer chemotherapy regimen; Q asks what aspect of her history makes her best candidate for this treatment
vignettes.a: history of hysterectomy; tamoxifen is risk factor for endometrial cancer due to its partial agonist effects at endometrium. Raloxifene is the classic SERM used in most patients who still have a uterus, as it is not a partial agoni

vignettes.q: 28F + pregnant at 35 weeks’ gestation + cocaine use + painful contractions of abdomen + vaginal bleeding; Dx + risk factors?
vignettes.a: abruptio placentae; risk factors are cocaine use and deceleration injury (i.e., fall or car accident). Presents as painful third-trimester bleeding.

vignettes.q: 28F + pregnant at 35 weeks’ gestation + painless vaginal bleeding; Dx + risk factors?
vignettes.a: placenta previa; notable risk factor is previous C-section; implication is, if lining of uterus has been disturbed, it makes sense that there would be future risk of abnormal implantation. Presents as painless third-trimester blee

vignettes.q: 28F + post-partum hemorrhage + placenta is seen attached to myometrial layer; Dx + risk factor?
vignettes.a: placenta accreta (placental attachment to surface of myometrium); risk factor is previous C-section, as well as concurrent placenta previa – i.e., placental attachment over the internal os increases risk of deeper attachment. Same
